scored.name: Captive Scent (natural odorant discovery from public GC-MS spectra)
scored.one_line: Mine public GC-MS and NMR spectra of plant, fungal and insect volatiles for unassigned peaks whose predicted structure is a high-impact odorant (musk, ambergris, sandalwood). Make a few mg and run an odour panel. File composition-of-use IP and sell the captive molecule to a fragrance house, which pays $5-50M for a patented captive.
scored.unproven_right: The right to the unassigned molecule is not bought but filed. Weak point: there is no cheap purchase from an owner. The only purchasable variant is buying lapsed odorant patent families from defunct fine-chemical firms.
scored.proving_step: Synthesis of 10-100 mg (~$10-30k CRO) plus a trained odour panel and threshold measurement; this takes weeks. Nature hides whether a molecule smells, and the odour-threshold outcome is in no database.
scored.proven_buyer: Givaudan, dsm-firmenich, IFF and Symrise, which pay heavily for captives (e.g., Ambrox-class and musk captives worth hundreds of millions a year in compound sales)
scored.public_data: MassBank, NIST/Wiley GC-MS literature spectra, the Pherobase, decades of scanned Flavour & Fragrance Journal and Perfumer & Flavorist chromatograms with unassigned peaks, and GNPS
scored.rough_step_up: ~$30k proof to $5-50M (~10^3x). The C4 'bought right' criterion fails, because the IP is filed rather than bought. Ladder: the molecule, then biocatalytic manufacture, then ingredient supply, then a fragrance-house-scale ingredients company.
scored.frame: The rung is "a novel odorant with a filed patent and panel data, licensed exclusively to a fragrance house". Inside that rung, discovery (which structure smells, and how strongly) is roughly 70-85% of the work; synthesising a few mg and running a panel is cheap (my estimate: $10-30k). The buyer is real and capitalised: Osmo launched an auction in June 2026 of exclusive perpetual licences to 10 captives, open to houses and chemical makers. But buyers know a lot of work remains after the rung. Scale-up process development is the first part (Givaudan tried 19 routes before Pomarose worked), followed by REACH/IFRA toxicology and stability/performance in base, before the molecule earns money. That discounts what the rung is worth, and discovery is not cleanly 80%+ of what the buyer pays for.
scored.step_up: Unproven: about $0 as an asset, plus about $20-50k for filing and synthesis (my estimate). Proven: no public price exists. I found no Osmo auction results or licence fees, and no disclosed royalty or sales numbers for Ambrox, Helvetolide or Javanol. The candidate's $5-50M per captive is unsourced. My estimate for an unscaled, untox'd odorant licence is $0.5-5M upfront plus royalties. That is about 10-100x on the cost of proving, or ~10^2-10^3 only if you assume the top of the range. The lift is also not "immediate on a hit": a binding bid needs a 12-week diligence and sampling period.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: 0.25% of molecules made and tested become commercially interesting. This is Osmo's own figure (Jan 2026 press release) and is not independently verified. Osmo claims its AI gives about 10x the hit rate and 5-10x better discovery cost efficiency. Cost per attempt: about $10-30k for CRO synthesis of 10-100 mg plus a panel (my estimate, matching the candidate). Traditional time to a captive is 7-10 years (Osmo blog). The lever is large; 1/base rate allows up to ~400x. But an AI incumbent with $130M raised has already taken the ~10x gain.
scored.data: Public and illegible, partly: MassBank, GNPS, Pherobase and scanned Flavour & Fragrance Journal / Perfumer & Flavorist chromatograms. Odour threshold and quality are in no structured field, so the outcome is not written down legibly, which is a point in its favour. But the signal is not uniquely unextracted. Fragrance houses have run headspace and natural-product odorant programmes for decades (Givaudan ScentTrek; GC-olfactometry is standard). Osmo trains odour-prediction models on structure and generates candidates de novo, so it does not need natural-product spectra at all. Also, an unassigned peak usually gives too little information to fix the structure (stereochemistry, which drives odour, is especially ambiguous), so the "predicted structure" step is weak.
scored.right_bought: This fails. Nothing is bought. The IP is filed first-come, and for this candidate's own category it is weak. Naturally occurring compounds cannot be patented as compositions in the US, and a molecule found in nature fails novelty (Chemistry in Australia, Patenting opportunities in the fragrance industry, 2020). So a natural odorant found from published spectra gets only use or process claims. Competitors could make the nature-identical molecule by another route, and the published spectrum itself may be prior art. The only purchasable version, lapsed odorant patent families, has no step-up: once lapsed, the molecule is in the public domain.
scored.buyer: Givaudan, dsm-firmenich, IFF and Symrise, plus chemical makers. Osmo's 2026 auction is the first open market for captive licences, so the buyer class exists. No clearing prices are public.
scored.ladder: The rungs are: molecule licence, then biocatalytic or chemical manufacture, then supply of the ingredient, then a full ingredients house, then finished fragrance. This is plausible, and Osmo is trying it now (a manufacturing site in Elizabeth, NJ). The whole flavour and fragrance market is about $30B a year: big, but not a trillion-dollar chain. A new entrant is also climbing behind a better-funded AI incumbent.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no defensible owned asset. Natural odorants found in public spectra are generally unpatentable as compositions (natural products in the US) and may be anticipated by the publication itself. So the "captive" is a weak use patent, not a cheaply bought right. And Osmo ($130M raised) already owns ML odorant discovery using synthetic novel scaffolds, which avoids that patent problem.
scored.one_line_reason: The hit rate is low (0.25%) and there is a real buyer class, but the right is filed rather than bought and naturally occurring molecules are barely patentable. The proven price is unverified, and Osmo already occupies the ML-discovery rung with patentable synthetic molecules.

scored.name: Enzyme Claims from Metagenomes (owned biocatalysts for one hard API step)
scored.one_line: Mine public metagenomes for an enzyme that performs one costly, metal-catalysed or chiral step in a top-selling API's route (the sitagliptin-transaminase pattern). Express the top ~50 candidates and prove activity in a plate assay. Patent the enzyme-in-process and sell or license it to the API maker.
scored.unproven_right: None bought; the right is the filed enzyme-use IP. To score on C4 it needs a purchase variant, such as buying environmental sample banks or lapsed enzyme patent families from defunct industrial-biotech firms (Codexis-era spinouts).
scored.proving_step: Gene synthesis plus expression plus activity assay on the real substrate (~$20-50k). Nature hides which of 10^9 sequences does the reaction.
scored.proven_buyer: Pharma process groups and CDMOs (Merck, Pfizer, Lonza), which save $10M+ a year on large-volume APIs
scored.public_data: MGnify, JGI IMG/M, UniProt, the AlphaFold DB, BRENDA, and scanned process-chemistry papers in OPRD (Organic Process Research & Development) describing pain-point steps
scored.rough_step_up: $50k proof to $5-30M licence (~10^2-10^3x). This is the closest to the 'discovery is 95%' frame, but it is weak on the bought-cheap-right criterion. Ladder: enzyme, then engineered variants, then biocatalytic API manufacture.
scored.frame: The proposed rung is "a wild-type enzyme sequence that catalyses one named API step, proven in a plate assay." Inside that rung, finding the sequence genuinely is most of the intellectual work. But the rung is not discrete or sellable, and the physical step is NOT trivial — it is the hard part. A plate-assay hit on the real substrate is typically 10^2-10^4 fold short of industrial requirements (space-time yield, substrate loading, co-solvent and temperature tolerance, cofactor recycle, >99.5% ee, metal-free ICH-compliant product). The sitagliptin transaminase that this pitch invokes is the counter-example to its own thesis: the starting ATA-117 wild type had essentially no activity on the bulky prositagliptin ketone, and the asset was created by ~11 rounds of directed evolution with ~27 mutations and a multi-year Codexis/Merck joint campaign (my characterisation of the published OPRD/Science account). So discovery is more like 15-30% of the work to a sellable asset, and the "physical step" (engineering campaign, kg-scale process development, re-filing the API route with regulators, requalifying a commercial process) is 70%+. Buyers are real and capitalised (Merck, Pfizer, Lonza, Dr Reddy's, WuXi), but they buy a validated process at scale, not a hit; a wild-type hit plus a use claim is a conversation starter, not a purchase order. Estimate, not a sourced number.
scored.step_up: Unproven side: the sequence itself costs $0 (open MGnify/IMG-M/UniProt download); the proving spend is the candidate's own $20-50k panel (my check: 1 kb gene synthesis at roughly $0.07-0.15/bp is ~$100-300/gene, so 50 genes plus expression, purification and substrate assay is ~$15-40k — the candidate's figure is about right). Proven side: the candidate claims $5-30M per licence. That is the price of a *developed, scaled, engineered* biocatalytic process, not of a wild-type hit. For a hit-stage enzyme-use patent family with no engineering and no scale data, realistic consideration is an option/research licence in the $50k-$500k range plus back-loaded milestones — i.e. ~3-10x over the $50k proving cost, realised years later and contingent on someone else doing the 70% of work that remains. Also, unlike a drill hit, the step-up is not immediate: it does not exist until the evolution campaign and the regulatory route change land. All figures here are my estimates; WebSearch was blocked by a classifier on the licensing-terms query, so I have no sourced comparables and am scoring the step-up conservatively (2) rather than taking the pitch's own 10^2-10^3 claim at face value.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate is genuinely low and the lever is genuinely large: in metagenomic/homology panel screening for activity on a specific non-natural industrial substrate, roughly 1-10% of expressed candidates show any detectable activity and well under 1% show activity worth developing (my estimate from published enzyme-discovery campaigns; I could not verify with a search). Cost per proving attempt ~$20-50k per ~50-member panel, i.e. ~$400-1,000 per sequence tested. So 1/base-hit-rate is in the 10-100x range and a sequence-to-function model that reorders the panel could plausibly cut discovery capex ~5-10x. That earns a 3, not a 5, for two reasons: (a) the assay is cheap and parallel enough that brute force at 10^4-10^5 variants is already affordable to incumbents, so the lever is not gated on ML; (b) this exact lever is the business of a crowded, well-capitalised field — protein language models (ESM-family), function predictors (CLEAN/DeepEC-style), and companies including Codexis, Ginkgo, Arzeda, Cradle, Basecamp Research, Enzymit and the big-pharma internal biocatalysis groups. Raising the hit rate is not a proprietary edge here; it is the industry's current default workflow.
scored.data: Wrong kind of public data for this rubric. MGnify, JGI IMG/M, UniProt and AlphaFold DB are public and enormous but they are maximally LEGIBLE — FASTA and PDB, already clustered, already embedded, already mirrored into every competitor's pipeline, with standing public benchmarks. There is no scanning, no OCR, no 1970s typewritten assessment report that nobody has parsed. The one genuine plus is that the OUTCOME is not summarised in a legible field: EC numbers and GO annotations in these databases are mostly transferred by homology and are known to be wrong or absent for the specific non-natural substrate that matters, so "does this enzyme do the prositagliptin ketone" is not written down anywhere. That is real and is why C4 is 1 rather than 0. The OPRD pain-point literature is likewise only semi-illegible and is read closely by exactly the process chemists who would be the buyer. Net: illegibility of the data is near zero; illegibility of the outcome is high.
scored.right_bought: This is where the candidate collapses, and the candidate admits it. Nothing is bought. The sequence is free to everyone simultaneously, so the "right" is only a first-to-file patent position in a race against better-funded players reading the same databases — the opposite of the Terranox structure, where the right is bought cheaply from an owner who cannot read the data and who hands over exclusivity before the proving spend. The two offered purchase variants do not fix it: (i) environmental sample banks — buying soil or marine sample collections gives physical DNA, but the public metagenome is what the ML reads, so the purchase buys no exclusivity over the signal you are actually acting on, and sequencing a bank just adds capex; (ii) lapsed enzyme patent families from defunct industrial-biotech firms — a lapsed family is in the public domain, so you can buy the file but not the exclusion right; and anything still in force claims the *old* enzyme, not the new metagenomic one you would find. There is also freedom-to-operate risk running the other way: broad enzyme-class and process claims held by Codexis and others can block your use claim rather than your claim capturing value.
scored.buyer: Real and capitalised: pharma process chemistry/API groups (Merck, Pfizer, Novartis) and CDMOs (Lonza, WuXi, Siegfried, Dr Reddy's CPS). Savings on a large-volume API route are genuinely $5-50M/yr, so willingness to pay exists. But the buyer's purchase trigger is a demonstrated kg-scale process with the enzyme at commercial loading and a regulatory path for the route change — not a plate-assay hit. And they buy late: the API route is frozen at filing, so for an approved product a route change means a post-approval change filing, which pushes adoption to generics, new NCEs pre-filing, or process-improvement programmes with multi-year cycles. The buyer is capitalised but does not buy the output of the rung you are selling.
scored.ladder: Genuinely good, the strongest criterion here. Enzyme hit, then engineered variant families, then enzyme supply, then biocatalytic step-as-a-service, then owning the API manufacture itself. Codexis and Lonza are the existence proof that each rung is real and that the top rung is a multi-billion-dollar business; a vertically integrated biocatalytic API manufacturer is a plausible very large company. 4 not 5 because the rungs are not cleanly sellable to each other the way a mineral claim is — each step up requires a new capability (evolution platform, cGMP fermentation, GMP API plant, DMF filings) rather than just capital, so climbing is a series of company rebuilds, not a ladder you buy your way up.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no unproven right to buy cheaply — the sequence is free and simultaneously available to every well-funded competitor, so there is no exclusivity to acquire before the proving spend and no owner who cannot read the data. Compounding it, the "physical step" is the hard part: a plate-assay hit is 10^2-10^4 fold short of an industrial biocatalyst, and the directed-evolution plus process-development plus regulatory-route-change work that creates the actual value is far harder than the discovery. That is precisely the geothermal-in-abandoned-coal-mines failure mode — finding the right candidate is easy relative to building the bespoke thing that makes it worth money.
scored.one_line_reason: Scores 12/25: real ladder and a real capitalised buyer, but the data is fully legible and free rather than illegible and purchasable, there is no unproven right to buy, and the engineering step after the hit is harder than the discovery — the counter-example pattern, not the Terranox pattern.
sources: NO SOURCES RETRIEVED: my first WebSearch call (Codexis/Merck biocatalyst licensing terms) was stopped by a safety classifier and no further searches ran, so every number in this scoring is explicitly my own estimate from prior knowledge, not a sourced figure. Treat the step-up and hit-rate numbers as unverified.

Background relied on from memory, not fetched in this session: Savile et al., Science 2010, 'Biocatalytic asymmetric synthesis of chiral amines' (the sitagliptin transaminase campaign, ~27 mutations over ~11 evolution rounds) — this is the basis for my claim that the engineering, not the discovery, was the bulk of the work.

Public databases named in the candidate and treated here as legible-not-illegible: EBI MGnify (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/metagenomics), JGI IMG/M (https://img.jgi.doe.gov), UniProt (https://www.uniprot.org), AlphaFold DB (https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk) — cited as the data's existence and format, not as a numeric source.
Competitive set asserted from memory, unverified: Codexis, Ginkgo Bioworks, Arzeda, Cradle Bio, Basecamp Research, Enzymit, plus in-house biocatalysis groups at Merck/Pfizer/Lonza.

scored.name: Die Hunter: finding rare die varieties and errors in bulk coin and stamp lots
scored.one_line: Buys bulk unsearched coins (at melt or face value) and estate stamp lots by the pound. ML on high-resolution imaging detects rare die varieties, doubled dies, overdates and printing errors described in scanned variety catalogues. PCGS, NGC or PSE certification ($20-60) proves the find, and Heritage-type auctions buy at once.
scored.unproven_right: Outright ownership of physical lots bought by weight from banks, estates, dealers and roll hunters who cannot inspect millions of items.
scored.proving_step: Automated imaging (trivial cost per item) followed by third-party grading and attribution. The physical step is close to zero, and the minting or printing process is what hides the outcome.
scored.proven_buyer: Heritage Auctions, Stack's Bowers and the collector market. Certified varieties trade instantly at published price-guide levels.
scored.public_data: Heritage's auction archive (millions of photographed lots), VAM, Wexler and CONECA variety catalogues (scanned and illustrated), Scott catalogues, and PCGS population reports.
scored.rough_step_up: About 10^3-10^5x per hit item ($0.01-1 to $1k-100k+). The hit rate is very low, which is exactly what ML imaging fixes. Weak ladder and modest total market.
scored.frame: The rung is: buy bulk lots, then image, attribute, certify and auction. Discovery (finding the one coin in roughly 10^4-10^5) makes up perhaps 60-70% of the work. The remainder is physical and not trivial: singulating and imaging both sides of millions of coins (coin counters, sorters, cameras), handling and re-banking the duds, waiting weeks for grading turnaround, and lotting for auction. Certified varieties do have capitalised buyers (Heritage, Stack's Bowers, collectors). For stamps, the physical step is soaking, sorting and flattening, which is labour-heavy. It is not a pure discovery frame.
scored.step_up: Per coin the cost basis is face value ($0.01-$1). My estimates, not searched: the typical attributable minor variety (minor Lincoln DDO/RPM, ordinary Morgan VAM) brings about $5-$50, which is 10-100x on a 25c-$1 base after a $20-60 grading fee. Trophy hits (1955 DDO cent ~$1,500-$2,500+, 1969-S DDO ~$25k+, 1972 DDO ~$300-$500) reach 10^4-10^5x, but they are vanishingly rare in circulation today. The price is set per item, but the weighted median hit is 10-100x, not 10^4x. Grading fees ($20-60) wipe out most minor finds, so only hits above roughly $100 are worth certifying.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimates only; the web-search budget was exhausted so nothing here was verified. Roll-hunter folklore suggests valuable (>$100) varieties turn up in about 1 in 10^4-10^6 circulating coins, while minor varieties are about 1 in 10^2-10^3. The proving step (PCGS/NGC/PSE, $20-60 plus an attribution fee) is NOT the costly, mostly-failing step. It is only paid on suspected hits, and those are already mostly right after a human loupe check. The expensive part is screening labour per coin, which ML or automation lowers. That is a throughput lever, not a 10x cut in costly proving shots like a drill hole. Grading fees per attempt stay fixed. So the Terranox-style lever (many more $100k shots) does not apply.
scored.data: The catalogues (VAM, Wexler, CONECA, Scott) and the Heritage archive are public, and they are illustrated but not structured, so building a diagnostic training set is a real but small moat. Against that, the varieties are already catalogued and diagnosed (VarietyVista, PCGS CoinFacts, NGC VarietyPlus). The answer key is legible; only which physical coin carries it is unknown. That makes this an image-recognition problem anyone can attack. Mint quality control has improved since the 1990s, so modern circulating coin yields few major varieties. Incumbents and competitors: thousands of hobby roll hunters, dealers who cherry-pick estates, coin-ID apps (CoinSnap, Coinoscope and others), and automated Morgan VAM attribution efforts. None of these was verified this run.
scored.right_bought: This part is strong. Circulating coin is bought at face value from banks, which is risk-free because the duds go back to the bank, and junk silver is bought at melt. Bulk stamp mixtures sell for about $10-50/lb (estimate). Supply is the constraint: banks ration boxes, and serious roll hunters already compete for them. Estate stamp lots usually pass through dealers who have already cherry-picked them, so 'owners cannot read the data' is only partly true. The best material has been searched before it reaches a bulk lot.
scored.buyer: Heritage Auctions (about $1.5B+ a year across all categories, estimate), Stack's Bowers, GreatCollections, eBay, and variety collectors via CONECA/VAM communities. The buyers are real and liquid, but demand for any one variety is thin: dumping hundreds of examples of the same minor DDO would push its price down.
scored.ladder: Weak. The rungs above are grading (PCGS/NGC, which are entrenched incumbents), auction houses and dealer networks, and maybe minting or collectibles more broadly. None of these becomes a trillion-dollar chain. The whole US rare coin market is perhaps $5-10B a year (estimate) and the variety/error niche is a small slice of it. There is no path to a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: Low expected value per item at a tiny total market size. Most hits are $5-50 varieties that grading fees ($20-60) wipe out. The 10^4x trophy hits are about one in a million or rarer in modern circulation. ML speeds up screening, but it does not cut the cost of an expensive proving shot, and the answer key (the catalogued diagnostics) is already public and legible to every roll hunter and app. The result is a profitable hobby business, not a 10^4 step-up engine with a ladder.
scored.one_line_reason: Buying at face value works and the per-item step-up can reach 10^4x, but the typical hit is 10-100x, grading fees eat the minor finds, the variety diagnostics are already public, and the ladder and market are too small (all figures are estimates; no search results were available).
sources: No web sources: the shared WebSearch budget (200 calls per turn) was used up before this candidate was searched. Every number is the agent's own estimate from prior knowledge and needs verifying.

Prior knowledge (estimates, not verified): PCGS/NGC grading fee schedules ($20-60+ per coin plus attribution), PCGS CoinFacts and Heritage price records for the 1955/1969-S/1972 DDO cents, VarietyVista/CONECA/VAM catalogues, bulk stamp mixture prices on eBay and dealer lists

scored.name: Suppressa: buying the microbiomes of fields that nature protects
scored.one_line: Use ML on public crop-loss and satellite data to find fields that stay healthy under severe regional disease pressure (natural disease-suppressive soils). Buy exclusive sampling and microbe-commercialisation rights from those farmers for a few hundred dollars, isolate the causal strain, and sell or license the proven biocontrol strain to ag-biologicals majors.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive contractual right to isolate and commercialise microbes from a specific field. The farmer cannot see that his soil is suppressive: the outcome is hidden in a yield anomaly, not in any record. Cost about $200-2,000 per field.
scored.proving_step: Paired 16S/shotgun metagenomics of suppressive vs conducive neighbour fields, then culturomics, then a greenhouse pathogen-challenge assay (Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, take-all, SCN). Cheap ($10-30k per field). Drilling-equivalent physical work is a soil core.
scored.proven_buyer: Syngenta Biologicals (paid $50M upfront for Rizobacter tie-up), Bayer (Ginkgo/AgBiome lineage), Corteva (Stoller/Symborg acquisitions), Novonesis, Indigo-type buyers. They actively scout biocontrol strains with greenhouse data.
scored.public_data: USDA RMA cause-of-loss by county/crop (decades), Sentinel-2/Landsat NDVI time series at field scale, USDA plant disease survey reports, state extension disease bulletins (PDF), NRCS SSURGO soils, SRA soil metagenomes from published suppressive-soil studies.
scored.rough_step_up: $1k field right to a greenhouse-validated strain licensable at $1-5M (10^3-10^4x). Base rate of a suppressive anomaly yielding a single transferable strain is maybe 2-5%, so the lever is about 20-50x. Caveat: majors increasingly want one field season before paying full value.
scored.frame: The candidate rung runs from a field sampling right to a greenhouse-validated strain. Inside that rung, discovery is plausibly 60-80% of the work, and the physical step (soil core, sequencing, greenhouse assay at $10-30k) is cheap. The problem is that this rung's output is not what capitalised buyers pay for. Buyers pay for consistent field efficacy plus formulation, shelf life and registrability. Greenhouse-to-field translation is the documented bottleneck: reviews describe a "translation gap" and "poor reliability of efficacy in the field". Development and launch cost $3-6M (Marrone exec) to $10-15M per product. Once you redraw the rung to end where a buyer pays real money (a field-proven strain), discovery falls to maybe 10-25% of the work (my estimate), and multi-season field trials dominate.
scored.step_up: Unproven right: $200-2,000 per field (candidate's figure; plausible, since US farmers have no Nagoya-type leverage). Proven value: no public price exists for a greenhouse-validated strain on its own. The closest reference points both sit well below the $1-5M claim. (1) In April 2024 Ginkgo bought AgBiome's platform assets: 115,000+ sequenced strains plus a dozen product candidates with greenhouse or field validation. Terms were undisclosed and widely read as a distressed sale, so per-validated-candidate value was probably far below $1M (estimate). (2) MustGrow-Bayer, a registered-stage, field-proven technology, was worth about $35-40M over 5-7 years, mostly milestones and not upfront. My estimate: a greenhouse-only strain licenses for $0-250k upfront, with value backloaded into field milestones. Against the true cost basis (about $1k right + $10-30k proving), the multiple on a hit is roughly 3-20x, not 10^3-10^4x. The 10^3x figure only appears if you ignore proving cost and take an optimistic license value.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt: $10-30k per field (candidate's estimate, reasonable for paired metagenomics + culturomics + greenhouse challenge). Base hit rate (suppressive anomaly yields a transferable strain): 2-5% (candidate's estimate; I found no source quantifying it). The expensive, mostly-failing step is the greenhouse-to-field transition, where costs run $1-10M of R&D per biological (Xite Bio CEO). ML on NDVI and RMA data does nothing to raise that hit rate. So the lever applies to a step that is already cheap. Spending $25k x 30 attempts (about $750k) to get one greenhouse hit is not a capex problem worth a 10x reduction.
scored.data: The data is public but weak, and legible where it matters. USDA RMA cause-of-loss is reported at county x crop level, not field level, so it can only flag regional disease pressure. Field-level 'healthy under pressure' from Sentinel-2/Landsat NDVI is heavily confounded by variety, planting date, fungicide use, drainage, rotation and tillage. A yield anomaly is not evidence of microbial suppression. Classic suppressive soils (take-all decline, Fusarium-wilt-suppressive soils, SCN-suppressive soils) are already well characterised and published, with SRA metagenomes, so the best-known cases are not hidden. Incumbents do not need hidden soils: Ginkgo/AgBiome alone holds 115k strains from 8,000+ environmental samples, and Bayer, Novonesis and Corteva have comparable libraries. Microbial diversity is not the scarce input.
scored.right_bought: Yes, an exclusive sampling and commercialisation contract can be bought cheaply ($200-2k) from farmers who cannot see suppressiveness. But the right is weakly excludable. The causal taxa (Pseudomonas with DAPG, Streptomyces, Bacillus and others) usually also live in neighbouring fields and other regions, so a competitor can isolate a near-identical strain elsewhere. Commercial protection comes from the patent and strain deposit on the isolate, not from the field contract. So the bought right does little to capture the step-up.
scored.buyer: Syngenta Biologicals, Bayer (Ginkgo partnership), Corteva (Stoller, Symborg), Novonesis, UPL NPP, FMC are capitalised and do in-license. They pay meaningful money mostly for field-validated, formulated or registered assets. MustGrow-Bayer was about $35-40M total, but over 5-7 years and milestone-heavy. Greenhouse-only strains are abundant, and in the AgBiome-Ginkgo deal a dozen validated candidates were folded into a platform asset sale. Competitors and incumbents in suppressive-soil discovery: Ginkgo Ag Bio (AgBiome library), Pivot Bio, Indigo, Loam, Biome Makers (soil metagenomics data across many fields), and academic labs (Raaijmakers/NIOO, Weller/USDA-ARS take-all decline).
scored.ladder: The ladder is: strain, then field-validated candidate, then registered biocontrol product (US EPA biopesticide about $300-400k in fees, about 13 months), then formulation, manufacturing and distribution, then a full biologicals company. The ladder exists, but its track record is poor for independents: AgBiome sold its platform, Marrone was sold to Bioceres, and Indigo restructured. The total biologicals market is real (about $15B) but fragmented. A path to a large company exists in principle, not a trillion-dollar one.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the scarce step. Majors already hold 100k+ strain libraries (Ginkgo/AgBiome: 115k strains, a dozen greenhouse-validated candidates sold as part of a platform deal). What buyers pay for is consistent field efficacy and formulation, which costs $1-15M and multiple seasons. ML on yield and NDVI anomalies does not de-risk that step. So the 'proven' output of the cheap rung (a greenhouse-validated strain) has no 10^3x step-up, and the field right does not exclude rivals from the same microbes.
scored.one_line_reason: The step that is actually expensive and mostly failing is greenhouse-to-field translation, not finding microbes. Greenhouse-validated strains are abundant and cheap (AgBiome's 115k-strain library went to Ginkgo in an undisclosed, distressed-looking sale). The field right is not exclusive to the causal taxa. Result: no 10^3x step-up and only a weak ML lever.

scored.name: Survivor Budwood Co. (citrus greening survivors)
scored.one_line: Buy budwood rights to rare citrus trees that kept a healthy canopy for years in Florida groves wrecked by HLB, many of them abandoned or bankrupt. ML separates truly tolerant trees from 'last to get infected' escapes. A graft-inoculation and qPCR proof turns a $50 tree into a licensable HLB-tolerant scion. Florida growers and nurseries (Alico, Southern Gardens/US Sugar, Parent Tree Program nurseries) pay for it.
scored.unproven_right: An exclusive budwood-collection and propagation option on individual trees in declining or abandoned Florida groves, bought from distressed grove owners for ~$100-1,000 per tree. Owners see a lucky tree, not a cultivar.
scored.proving_step: Pull budwood, graft-inoculate with CLas in a greenhouse, then run qPCR titer and canopy scoring over 9-15 months (~$2-5k per candidate). Do whole-genome resequencing to confirm somatic variants (Parson Brown and Hamlin clone sports). The physical step is a few grafts. Discovery, meaning knowing which 1 in 100,000 trees to graft, is the real work.
scored.proven_buyer: Florida citrus majors and certified nurseries (Alico, Southern Gardens Citrus, Peace River Packing, DPI Parent Tree Program nurseries) and processors needing juice supply (Tropicana, Florida's Natural). They would license per-tree royalties or buy the clone outright.
scored.public_data: USDA NAIP 0.6-1m aerial imagery (2005-2024), Sentinel-2 and Landsat NDVI time series per tree crown, Florida DOACS/FDACS grove and citrus tree inventory surveys, UF/IFAS HLB survivor reports (Buckhill grove), NCBI SRA sweet-orange resequencing. A per-tree, 15-year canopy trajectory exists only in the pixels. No registry records which trees survived.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10^4: tree or budwood right ~$100-1,000 to a validated tolerant scion worth $5-50M (royalty ~$1-3/tree over millions of replant trees). Base hit rate is near zero today (Gmitter: dozens of grower-found survivors all failed inoculation), so the ML lever is large. The weak point is buyers wanting replicated field trials before paying full value.
scored.frame: The rung is "own a budwood option on one tree and prove it is a tolerant scion." Within the greenhouse step, discovery (picking which tree to graft) is perhaps 60-70% of the work. That is my estimate. The frame does not hold up as a sellable rung, for three reasons. (1) Florida rule 5B-62.011/.013 says propagative material must come from registered source trees kept in DPI-approved screenhouses. A field tree infected with CLas cannot be propagated commercially until it has been shoot-tip grafted, retested and registered. That adds roughly 2-3 years of regulated physical work, which is my estimate since the rule sets no fixed timeline. (2) Buyers want replicated multi-site field trials over several years before paying full value. UF's OLL-8 was judged on "health at multiple sites over multiple years." So the step that actually converts the asset into value is a 5-10 year field program, which is neither trivial nor abstracted. (3) A 9-15 month greenhouse inoculation plus qPCR result is an intermediate signal that no one buys at scale. A capitalised buyer exists in principle (nurseries via FFSP-style licensing, Alico), but it buys at the end of the field trials, not at the end of this rung.
scored.step_up: Unproven: an option on a field tree at about $100-1,000 (candidate's figure; I estimate nearer $100). Proven after greenhouse work only: I found no market price. My estimate is $10k-100k as a licensing option, so roughly 10-100x, and it is not immediate. Proven after field trials and registration: the value depends on royalties. Florida orange propagations fell from 3.65M to about 800k trees per year over four seasons (Citrus Industry, Oct 2024), against about 4M trees per year of all citrus historically (FreshPlaza). I found no published per-tree royalty for UF cultivars, which are licensed non-exclusively through FFSP with nursery-remitted royalties; I estimate $0.5-2 per tree. If a new tolerant scion took 30% of about 1M orange plantings a year at about $1, that is about $300k per year, so an NPV of about $2-5M (my estimate, not the candidate's $5-50M). The headline 10^4 holds only at the fully proven end, years away. The near-term jump is about 10-100x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: Gmitter's UF team propagated and inoculated "several dozen" grower-reported survivor trees, and all of them became infected. Their stated conclusion was that no resistant trees had yet been found (Citrus Industry 2018; SWFREC seminar 2017). The base rate of true tolerance among visual survivors is therefore near 0/dozens, possibly truly zero, because Florida sweet orange is a near-clonal population with very little somatic variation. Cost per attempt: the candidate gives $2-5k for graft-inoculation, qPCR and 9-15 months, plus resequencing at about $500-1k (my estimate). At about $3-5k per shot, ML that is 10x better saves maybe $30-50k per hit. Discovery capex is small to begin with, so cutting it 10x is worth little. The real cost and failure point is the multi-year field trial and certification, which ML does not shorten. The lever is capped at 1/base rate, and if the base rate is essentially 0 there is nothing to multiply.
scored.data: The data is public: NAIP at 0.6-1m (1m before about 2016), Sentinel-2 at 10m, Landsat at 30m, FDACS citrus inventory, and NCBI SRA. Two weaknesses. First, Sentinel-2 and Landsat pixels cover several 4-6m crowns, and NAIP is captured only every 2-3 years, so a clean per-tree 15-year trajectory comes mostly from NAIP and is noisy. Second, the imagery is not especially illegible: drone, aircraft and satellite HLB detection is an active academic and commercial area (UF 2013 UAV/aircraft comparison; Sentinel-2 HLB lime study; Agrowing/VetorGEO). The outcome is not summarised in any legible public field. No registry of survivors exists, which is a genuine plus. The decisive test, however, is a wet-lab inoculation, not anything readable in the data.
scored.right_bought: Mostly yes. Distressed or abandoned grove owners would plausibly sell a budwood and propagation option for $100-1,000. A sport discovered in a cultivated area can receive a plant patent. The caveats are that the field tree itself can never be a legal budwood source (5B-62.011/.013), and that UF/IFAS already solicits grower survivor reports and tests them for free. Owners therefore have a no-cost alternative, and the best candidates may already have been screened.
scored.buyer: Licensing nurseries (FFSP licensees such as Agromillora Florida and Ben Hill Griffin), plus Alico, Southern Gardens/US Sugar and the Florida's Natural cooperative. The buyer pool is shrinking, because Florida orange plantings are down to about 800k trees a year. These buyers pay royalties on trees sold, not lump sums for greenhouse results. UF/FFSP is an incumbent supplier of tolerant scions (OLL-8, N13-32 Hamlin, Parson Brown selections, Sugar Belle) on cheap non-exclusive licences.
scored.ladder: Budwood → certified registered parent trees → nursery → grove ownership → juice processing. A ladder exists, but it sits on top of a collapsing industry: Florida orange output has fallen by more than 90% from its peak. No path leads to a very large company unless the trait proves genuinely resistant and transfers to Brazil and other markets, where Fundecitrus and the breeders are also the incumbents.
scored.fatal_flaw: The hits probably do not exist, and a hit would not count as proven when this rung ends. Florida sweet orange is a near-clonal population. UF already grafted and inoculated dozens of grower-found survivors, and every one became infected. So "survivors" are overwhelmingly escapes, and ML cannot raise a hit rate whose true value is about 0. When a hit does occur, value only arrives after shoot-tip grafting, DPI registration and multi-year field trials, which turns a "trivial physical step" into a 5-10 year breeding program. The end market is about 800k orange trees a year at roughly $1 per tree in royalties.
scored.one_line_reason: The base hit rate is effectively zero (dozens of survivors all failed inoculation), the asset only counts as proven after years of regulated field trials, and the royalty market is small and shrinking, so neither the 10^4 jump nor the ML lever is real.

scored.name: DropIn: electrolyte additives for existing Li-ion lines
scored.one_line: Searches computed molecular and electrolyte databases for electrolyte additives (SEI formers, HF scavengers, overcharge shuttles) that drop into existing cell production at under 2 wt%, so there is no bespoke build. It files on the hits, proves them with cheap cell cycling, and licenses to electrolyte makers, who pay at proof because adoption is a recipe change.
scored.unproven_right: Self-filed composition and use provisionals on additive molecules, about $3k each. New-use claims are also possible on old molecules found in scanned 1970s-90s non-English electrochemistry literature.
scored.proving_step: Coin and pouch cells cycled 300-500 cycles at elevated temperature, about $5-20k per candidate, in parallel. Base hit rate for a beneficial additive is roughly 2-5%. ML on redox windows, reduction potentials and SEI chemistry can plausibly lift it 5-10x.
scored.proven_buyer: Electrolyte formulators and cell makers: Capchem, Tinci, Soulbrain, Mitsubishi Chemical, Enchem, CATL. A proven additive that adds 20% cycle life is worth $5-50M as a licence or acquisition.
scored.public_data: Materials Project MPcules/electrolyte genome; PubChem/QM9-type quantum sets; NIST electrolyte data; full text of electrolyte patents; scanned historical journals (Elektrokhimiya, Denki Kagaku) via OCR.
scored.rough_step_up: $3-20k to $5-50M: about 10^3. The physical step really is trivial (blend into an existing line). The ladder: additive IP to own formulation supply to electrolyte manufacturing to cell components.
scored.frame: The candidate's rung is 'additive molecule with a provisional patent and 300-500-cycle coin/pouch data'. Buyers do not purchase that rung. Cell makers and OEMs requalify every additive in their own chemistry and format. Market reports put automotive qualification at 2-4 years and $200k-800k per candidate, covering extended cycling, gas evolution, abuse testing and OEM integration, and say the results do not transfer between cell makers (Mordor Intelligence, repeated by GII). A novel molecule also has to be synthesised at battery-grade purity at scale and supplied reliably. That is a real physical and supply-chain step, not a 'recipe change'. My estimate is that discovery is about 30-40% of the work needed to reach a rung someone actually pays for. The physical step is cheap for a known commodity additive such as VC or FEC. It is not cheap for a new molecule.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a provisional costs about $3k (the candidate's figure). The proving spend brings the cost basis to about $10-25k. Proven at coin-cell level: I found no published price for licensing or acquiring an electrolyte-additive patent. The ORNL-to-Safire licence (5 patents, 2022) and the Ascend-Samsung SDI cross-licence (2022) had confidential terms. My estimate is that an additive proven only in coin or pouch cells licenses for about $50k-500k upfront plus contingent royalties. The candidate's $5-50M figure only applies after customer qualification, 2-4 years later, and after the buyer has paid for that qualification. That makes the immediate step-up roughly 10x (score 2), not 10^3. 10^3 is reachable only after multi-year qualification, which belongs to a different rung.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate is about 2-5% (the candidate's estimate, consistent with how screening campaigns usually run, but unsourced). Cost per attempt is $5-20k at the coin/pouch stage (candidate figure). By reported market figures it is $200k-800k per candidate at qualification. So the theoretical lever is capped at 20-50x, and ML raising the hit rate 5-10x is plausible. However, the expensive, mostly failing step is customer qualification, not coin cells, and ML does little to cut that cost. At the coin-cell stage the absolute capex is already small (about $0.5-1M per hit at a 2-5% hit rate), so a 10x cut saves little.
scored.data: Most of the data is legible already. Materials Project, the electrolyte genome, QM9 and PubChem are structured, computed databases built specifically for ML screening. Patent full text is searchable. The only illegible slice is scanned Soviet and Japanese literature from the 1970s-90s, which is a niche source. Incumbents already extract this signal. SES AI (NYSE: SES) runs Molecular Universe, sells enterprise subscriptions and has a term sheet for a 90%-owned joint venture with Hisun to supply the materials it discovers. Aionics, a Stanford spinout, screens billions of formulations with ML plus quantum mechanics and now develops formulations itself. Microsoft/PNNL, Chemix and the in-house teams at Tinci, Capchem, LGES and CATL do similar work. No regulator status field records the outcome, so that part passes. Whether an additive works is not public until it is patented or published.
scored.right_bought: The right is not bought from owners who cannot read the data. It is a patent filed first-come, in an extremely crowded field: thousands of additive patents, many from Chinese formulators. New-use claims on old molecules face obviousness and prior-art problems precisely because the molecule is already published. The plan has no arbitrage between an owner who cannot read the data and a buyer who can, which is the core of the Terranox structure.
scored.buyer: The capitalised buyers exist: Tinci, Capchem, Soulbrain, Enchem, Mitsubishi Chemical, CATL and LGES. They buy qualified supply, not coin-cell IP. They usually run additive R&D in-house and take licences cheaply or work around patents with analogue molecules. The economics are not shown to work for both sides at the proof stage.
scored.ladder: The rungs are additive IP, then synthesis and supply of additives, then electrolyte formulation (Tinci and Capchem are multi-billion-dollar companies), then electrolyte manufacturing, then cell components and cells. It is a real ladder, but the rungs are low-margin, commoditised chemicals dominated by Chinese incumbents at scale. Moving up requires chemical plants, so it is not discovery-led. SES AI is already trying to climb this exact ladder.
scored.fatal_flaw: No capitalised buyer pays a step-up at the point of proof. Coin-cell cycling is not the proving step that matters. The value appears only after 2-4 years of customer-specific qualification that costs $200k-800k per candidate, and the buyer controls that step. On top of that, the right is a first-come patent in a crowded field, the data is already legible and mined by SES AI and Aionics, and there is no discounted-right arbitrage.
scored.one_line_reason: The physical step looks trivial, but the real proving step is a multi-year qualification run by the buyer. The right is a contested first-come patent rather than an undervalued asset bought cheaply, and the computed molecular data is already legible and being mined by SES AI, Aionics and the incumbents.

scored.name: SorbentRights: computed sorbents for capture and separation
scored.one_line: Screens hypothetical zeolite and MOF databases (millions of computed frameworks) for sorbents with breakthrough selectivity in a specific capitalised separation (DAC, natural-gas upgrading for CO2/N2 rejection, xenon/krypton recovery, lithium-free gas drying). It files on the hits, makes milligram batches and measures isotherms, then licenses to process licensors who pay at proof.
scored.unproven_right: Self-filed provisional on framework composition and use, about $3k. Also university MOF patents can be optioned for $10-25k from tech-transfer offices that cannot rank them.
scored.proving_step: Solvothermal synthesis plus PXRD plus single-component and mixed-gas isotherms and cycling stability, about $5-15k per candidate. Over 99% of hypothetical frameworks are never made and most made ones fail stability (base hit rate about 1-5%), so ML synthesisability and stability models are the lever.
scored.proven_buyer: Process licensors and capitalised capture players: Honeywell UOP, BASF, Air Products, Linde, Occidental/1PointFive, Climeworks, Svante. A proven sorbent licence is $5-30M.
scored.public_data: CoRE MOF 2019/2024, hMOF, ToBaCCo, Deem/Treacy hypothetical zeolite database, IZA structures, NIST/ARPA-E isotherm database, Materials Project; scanned zeolite synthesis patents from the 1970s-90s.
scored.rough_step_up: $3-25k to $5-30M: about 10^3. The outcome is hidden by nature (synthesisability and water stability). Weakness: scale-up and pelletisation is real work, and buyers often wait for pilot data.
scored.frame: The proposed rung is "computed hit plus milligram isotherms, then licence." Inside that rung, discovery is maybe 60-70% of the work (my estimate). The trouble is that the rung is not what buyers pay for. Process licensors and capture companies pay after kg-scale synthesis, shaping or pelletisation, humid cycling over thousands of cycles and pilot data. CALF-20 went from a University of Calgary discovery to a BASF scale-up agreement only after Svante spent about 2 years working with BASF (supply agreement, Oct 2023). Mosaic Materials (Berkeley mmen-MOF) was bought by Baker Hughes only after years of grant-funded scale-up, at an undisclosed price. In the rung a buyer actually pays for, scale-up and process engineering dominate and discovery is maybe 20-30% (my estimate). That is the geothermal pattern: the physical step is the hard part.
scored.step_up: The unproven right costs about $3k for a provisional or $10-15k upfront for an option on a university patent. A 2008-era tech-transfer guide gives $10-15k upfront for a single-bidder, non-groundbreaking licence, and Michigan and Nebraska startup templates charge $0 upfront with a 2% royalty. The candidate's claimed proven price of a $5-30M sorbent licence is not supported by any public deal I found. Svante-BASF was a supply agreement with no terms disclosed, and Baker Hughes-Mosaic terms were not disclosed. My estimate is that a milligram-validated, unpiloted sorbent can be sold or optioned for roughly $50-500k, a 10-100x step-up. The ~10^3x figure only shows up after pilot proof, which costs $1-10M+ and takes years.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Using the candidate's own figures, the base hit rate for synthesisability plus stability is about 1-5% at $5-15k per attempt. That puts discovery cost per hit at about $100k-1.5M. ML could at best lift this toward 10-20x (capped at 1/base rate, so 20-100x in theory). But the dollars saved are small next to the $1-10M+ scale-up and pilot step, which is the costly, mostly-failing step that buyers gate on, and ML does not touch it. I found no published field-wide experimental hit rate for ML-screened hypothetical MOFs. Searches turned up only individual shortlists, for example 239 candidates out of 12,415 hypothetical MOFs with one top performer validated. The hit-rate figures are therefore estimates.
scored.data: The data is public, but it is legible and heavily mined. CoRE MOF, hMOF, ToBaCCo and the Deem zeolite database are clean CIF and structured files, not scanned or illegible records. Meta FAIR and Georgia Tech's OpenDAC has 100M+ datapoints and was built with CuspAI. Synthesisability and water stability are not written into a status field, which is a point in favour. The illegible part, scanned 1970s-90s zeolite synthesis patents, is minor. Worse, publishing a hypothetical structure in a public database is arguably prior art against a composition claim, which leaves only narrower use or process claims.
scored.right_bought: The right is mostly not bought from owners who cannot read the data. A provisional patent is a free, first-come filing, and the hypothetical databases are public, so anyone can file on the same structures. University options are cheap ($0-15k upfront), but tech-transfer offices are not the information-blind party. The scarce asset is scale-up competence, and no undervalued holder sells that cheaply.
scored.buyer: Process licensors and capture players such as Honeywell UOP, BASF, Air Products, Linde, Climeworks, Svante, Occidental/1PointFive and Baker Hughes. They are capitalised, but they buy after pilot proof and often prefer to acquire a company (Baker Hughes-Mosaic) or co-develop (Svante-BASF) rather than license milligram-scale results. Well-funded competitors already run this exact screening: CuspAI ($130M raised by Sept 2025, with DAC sorbents as its first target), Orbital Materials ($16M Series A, 2024), Meta FAIR, NuMat, Promethean Particles, and academic groups such as Smit and Snurr.
scored.ladder: Sorbent IP leads to sorbent manufacturing (NuMat and Promethean model), then contactor or module supply, then owned capture plants, then sales of CO2 removal credits or processed gas. The ladder exists, but every rung above the first is bespoke hardware and process engineering, which is harder than discovery. DAC demand also depends on subsidies (45Q, voluntary carbon removal markets).
scored.fatal_flaw: The value step-up does not happen at the proving step. Milligram isotherms do not move a sorbent from near-zero to millions, because buyers pay only after kg-scale shaping, humid cycling and pilot data costing $1-10M+ over years, and ML does not make that cheaper. On top of that, the source databases are clean public files already mined by better-funded AI players (CuspAI $130M, Meta OpenDAC), and they act as prior art against composition claims. There is no information-blind seller to buy from.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is cheap and public, and the real gate is scale-up and pilot validation, so this fails like the geothermal counter-example: the hard part is physical, not finding the right material.

scored.name: FreeMag: rare-earth-free magnet compositions
scored.one_line: Uses DFT-trained ML on OQMD and Materials Project to find metastable Fe-, Mn- and Co-based phases with high magnetocrystalline anisotropy, then proves each with arc-melting and VSM measurement in a week. It licenses proven compositions to motor and magnet makers desperate for supply chains outside China.
scored.unproven_right: Self-filed provisional on the alloy composition and processing route, about $3k. Also optioning abandoned 1980s-2000s magnet patents and DOE lab inventions (Ames, ORNL) for $10-50k.
scored.proving_step: Arc-melt or melt-spin plus anneal plus XRD plus VSM for coercivity and remanence, about $2-5k and a week per composition. Historical base hit rate for a new hard-magnet phase is well under 1%, so the ML lever is high in principle (capped at 1/hit rate).
scored.proven_buyer: Automotive OEMs and magnet makers: GM, Toyota, Tesla, Niron, Proterial, VAC, MP Materials. Proven composition licences or acquisitions are $10-100M, given the strategic premium.
scored.public_data: OQMD, Materials Project magnetic orderings, AFLOW, the Novamag database, NIST/Ames scanned historical alloy reports, expired magnet patents.
scored.rough_step_up: $3k to $10M+: 10^3-10^4 if a hit is real. The risk is that a lab-scale coercivity hit is not yet bulk-processable, so the buyer may pay an option first and the full price later.
scored.frame: The candidate's rung is "lab-proven composition (arc-melt + VSM) sold as a licence". Inside that rung discovery is maybe 80% of the work. But buyers do not pay for that rung. They pay for a bulk-processable magnet with real (BH)max, coercivity and temperature stability. For the known candidates (MnBi, MnAl, L10 FeNi, Fe16N2), getting from a phase with high anisotropy to a bulk magnet with real coercivity has taken decades. The work is microstructure engineering and processing, at least 80% of the effort. My estimate is that discovery is about 10-20% of the rung that has a buyer. This is the geothermal counter-example: the physical step is the hard part. Ames was still at 1.2 kOe coercivity in Ni-rich L10 FeNi, well short of a usable magnet, with next steps of scaling to 1-10 g and filing IP (Ames CMI highlight).
scored.step_up: Unproven: a $3k self-filed provisional, or a $10-50k option on a DOE/old patent (the candidate's figures; I could not verify the Ames/ORNL licence fee terms). Lab-proven: I found no public deal paying $10-100M for a lab-scale composition. Niron, the closest proven case (iron nitride), had to become a manufacturer to capture value. It raised $21.3M (2021), $33M (2023) and $25M (2024, Samsung/Magna/Allison), received a $17.5M DOE grant, and got a conditional $150M Office of Strategic Capital loan (2026) for a plant. I found no disclosed licensing deal values. My estimate is that a lab-scale hit commands a $50k-$1M option or sponsored-research deal, roughly 10-300x on $3k. A 10^3-10^4 jump comes only after bulk processing and plant-scale work, which costs $10-100M+.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate is plausibly well under 1% for a new phase that is stable, has high anisotropy and is hard. The literature reports no measured experimental success rate. In a 2026 APS abstract (Fe-Co-S), ML screening narrowed >300,000 structures to 1,418, and DFT then left 3 (about 0.001%), none yet synthesized. Single ML-guided syntheses such as Fe3CoB2 (Xia et al. 2024) are anecdotes. Each proving attempt costs about $2-5k and a week (the candidate's figure, which is reasonable for arc-melt + XRD + VSM). Because attempts are cheap, a 10x hit-rate gain saves little capex in dollars: 100 attempts cost only about $300-500k. The lever is real as a ratio but small in dollars, and lab hits mostly fail later at bulk coercivity, which ML on intrinsic properties does not predict.
scored.data: The signal is in LEGIBLE, structured databases: OQMD, Materials Project, AFLOW and Novamag are clean, API-accessible and already carry computed magnetic moments and anisotropy fields. Everyone screens them: Ames/CMI, the Novamag consortium, Fraunhofer's MagnetPredictor, NIST, and big-lab generative models (GNoME, MatterGen). The intrinsic outcome is effectively already in a legible field, which is the failure mode named in the rubric. The only illegible part is scanned historical NIST/Ames alloy reports, a thin layer. The right is not bought cheaply from owners who cannot read the data: a provisional is free first-to-file, and published DFT entries and old literature create prior art that weakens composition claims. Optioning DOE patents is possible, but the labs know exactly what they hold.
scored.right_bought: A self-filed provisional (about $3k, first-to-file, not bought from an uninformed owner) or an option on an Ames/ORNL/expired-era patent ($10-50k, the candidate's estimate). The licensors are sophisticated and actively licensing (ORNL has licensed two high-performance magnet technologies per CMI). Composition claims are vulnerable to prior art from public DFT databases.
scored.buyer: The buyers are capitalised and strategically motivated: GM, Stellantis, Samsung, Magna, Volvo and Allison all invested in Niron, and DoD/OSC lends for plants. They want supply chains outside China. But they buy proven bulk magnets or manufacturers, not arc-melted buttons, so no buyer exists for the rung that FreeMag actually wins.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are real: bulk processing, magnet manufacturing (Niron's Sartell plant), motor supply and an EV/defense magnet market worth tens of billions. But the next rung up, bulk processing, is the expensive part that took decades, so winning the bottom rung gives little advantage in climbing.
scored.fatal_flaw: The rung with a buyer is not a discovery rung. A lab-scale phase with high anisotropy is worth little until someone solves bulk coercivity and processing, which is capital- and time-heavy and has taken decades for MnBi, MnAl, L10 FeNi and Fe16N2. That is the geothermal counter-example. On top of that, the input data is already legible, structured and screened by many well-funded groups, so FreeMag has no informational edge.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails like geothermal. Buyers pay for bulk-processable magnets, and processing, not discovery, is the decades-long bottleneck. The DFT databases are already clean and widely screened, so the ML edge and the cheap-right edge are both weak.

scored.name: Orphan Process IP (buy unlicensed university chemistry patents and prove them on high-value molecules)
scored.one_line: Buy or exclusively license, for $5-25k each, the long tail of unlicensed university catalyst, route and flow-chemistry patent families before lapse. Run ML over the scanned SI, theses and lab data to predict which method would cut cost of goods on a specific high-value API or intermediate. A gram-scale lab run proves yield and selectivity on that target, and the proven route IP is sold to the API owner or generics.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive licences or assignments of unlicensed TTO patents, which TTOs sell cheaply because most never earn back maintenance fees
scored.proving_step: Gram-scale route demonstration on the target molecule at a CRO (~$20-60k, 4-8 weeks). Nature hides whether the method transfers to the target's functional groups; the patent shows only the inventor's model substrates.
scored.proven_buyer: Innovator pharma near LOE seeking COGS cuts, generic houses (Teva, Sandoz, Dr. Reddy's) needing non-infringing routes, and CDMOs
scored.public_data: USPTO and EPO full text with scanned supporting-info PDFs, ProQuest and open-access theses, the Open Reaction Database, Pistachio/USPTO reaction extracts, and AUTM licensing surveys
scored.rough_step_up: $10-25k right to $1-20M licence or sale (~10^2-10^3x). The proof is a cheap lab run and the buyer is capitalised. Ladder: route IP, then CDMO manufacture, then owning generic API supply.
scored.frame: The rung would be "route IP proven at gram scale on one target API". Inside that rung, picking the method for the target is perhaps 50-60% of the work (my estimate). But the gram-scale CRO run is not the step the buyer pays for. Value only appears after kg scale-up, impurity and polymorph control, validation and regulatory filing. For a route change that means an FDA Prior Approval Supplement: route-of-synthesis changes are a listed drug-substance change type, review takes about 4 months, and the FY2017 fee was $35,240. So the physical and regulatory part that is still left dominates. Unlike a drill hit, the rung ends before the hard part.
scored.step_up: Unproven: TTO exclusive licences or assignments of unlicensed chemistry patents plausibly cost $5-25k. That is the candidate's figure and fits TTO practice, but I found no source. The 95%-of-patents-unlicensed figure (USDA OTT/les Nouvelles 2018) supports cheap supply. Proven: no market price was found for third-party route IP after a gram-scale proof. The closest comparables are royalties under litigation or settlement (Lilly/ScinoPharm gemcitabine API licence; Illinois/Prezista generic royalty settlement; omeprazole royalty of 50% of the generic's margin). These cover patents that blocked the drug. A cheap optional alternative route has no such leverage. Courts say royalty value falls when the buyer has non-infringing workarounds, and generic houses do. My realistic estimate is $0-500k per proven route, mostly $0, so about 10-30x on a rare hit. The claimed $1-20M (10^2-10^3x) is unsupported.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimate of the base hit rate is that an academic method works acceptably on a complex, drug-like target maybe 10-30% of the time. Merck's Chemistry Informer Library work (Chem Sci 2016, C5SC04751J) and the Glorius robustness-screen work (Nat Chem 2013) report that methods shown on simple model substrates often fail on drug-like ones, but give no single pooled rate. Cost per attempt: $20-60k at a CRO over 4-8 weeks (the candidate's figure; plausible). With a base rate of 10-30%, the lever is capped at about 3-10x. The total discovery spend is small anyway, so cutting it saves little. The binding constraint is buyer demand, not the cost of proving a route.
scored.data: The data is public. It is partly illegible: SI PDFs and theses. But reaction data is already heavily structured by incumbents: CAS/SciFinder, Reaxys, NextMove Pistachio and the Open Reaction Database. Retrosynthesis and condition-prediction ML already exists as products: Merck's Synthia, ASKCOS (MIT), IBM RXN, Iktos, PostEra, and in-house tools at big pharma. Whether a method transfers to a given API is not written in a legible field, which is a genuine plus. But incumbents with far more proprietary high-throughput experimentation data already do this prediction internally. On rights: TTO rights are bought, not first-come, and TTOs sell cheaply. That passes.
scored.right_bought: Exclusive licence or assignment of an unlicensed university catalyst, route or flow-chemistry patent family from the TTO, likely $5-25k plus assumed maintenance fees (estimate). Buying is feasible and cheap. The question is whether the right is needed at all: academic method patents are often narrow, near expiry or easy to design around.
scored.buyer: Claimed buyers: innovator pharma near loss of exclusivity, generic houses (Teva, Sandoz, Dr. Reddy's) and CDMOs. All are capitalised, but each has large in-house process R&D and route-scouting teams. Innovators rarely change a locked, validated commercial route near loss of exclusivity, because a PAS, bridging studies and supply risk cost more than the savings on a declining product. Generics design their own non-infringing routes as routine work. Demand to pay a large sum for an outside, gram-scale-proven route is weak.
scored.ladder: Route IP, then CDMO or contract API manufacture, then owning generic API supply. The ladder exists and is large: the API market is around $200B (my estimate). But the upper rungs are low-margin and dominated by Indian and Chinese API makers. They need plants, GMP and regulatory work, and owning route IP gives little edge on them.
scored.fatal_flaw: A gram-scale proof does not set a price. No capitalised buyer pays a step-up for it, because the real value is only realised after kg scale-up, validation and a regulatory filing (FDA PAS) that the buyer must do itself. The buyers (generic houses, CDMOs, innovator process groups) already scout routes in-house with better proprietary data and ML, and can design around narrow academic method patents. The proven asset is therefore still unproven to the buyer and worth close to nothing on its own.
scored.one_line_reason: Cheap TTO rights and illegible SI data are real, but a gram-scale route proof does not lift value 10^3x. Buyers do route scouting in-house, can design around academic patents, and only value a route after scale-up and regulatory filing, so there is no "drill-hit" moment with a capitalised buyer waiting.
sources: https://ars.usda.gov/ARSUserFiles/ott/New Website/Office of Technology Transfer (OTT)/Training/Can a Tech Transfer Office make a Difference   lesNouvelle Jun-2018.pdf

scored.name: JetLand (low-level-jet wind options at 160-200 m hub heights)
scored.one_line: Buy cheap wind-easement options on farmland that public resource maps (NREL WIND Toolkit at 80-100 m) call marginal, use ML on NEXRAD radar wind profiles to find hidden nocturnal low-level-jet shear, prove it with a 12-month vertical LiDAR, and sell the early-stage project (land control plus bankable wind data) to a utility-scale wind developer, who pays for the step-up.
scored.unproven_right: Wind lease or easement options on ~5,000-6,000 ha per 200 MW block, at about $2-5/acre/yr (roughly $50-100k in total). Landowners in 'poor wind' counties (e.g. the Mississippi delta, Arkansas, Louisiana, the forested Midwest) have no buyers and cannot read radar or aircraft wind data. Options are bought one by one, not filed first-come.
scored.proving_step: Rent a ground LiDAR or SoDAR (~$60-150k) and run an IEC-compliant 12-month campaign at 160-200 m to produce a bankable P50/P90 capacity factor. The physical step is cheap and abstracted; finding where the hidden jet sits is the work. Weakness: 12 months is not instant, and interconnection rather than wind is the main bottleneck for developers.
scored.proven_buyer: Utility-scale wind developers and IPPs (NextEra, Invenergy, Apex, RWE, EDF, Pattern) that buy early-stage pipelines with land control and met data. Benchmark: early-stage wind sells for about $20k/MW, rising to $100k+/MW near ready-to-build.
scored.public_data: NEXRAD Level II radial velocity and VAD wind profiles (NOAA open data on AWS, petabytes, almost never mined for resource); MADIS/AMDAR aircraft wind observations; IGRA radiosondes; NOAA ASOS; scanned 1970s-80s DOE/Battelle-PNL wind prospecting reports and the NREL tall-tower archive; FAA obstruction files. The outcome (true hub-height capacity factor at 200 m) is not in any legible field: WIND Toolkit is a model, and it is biased in the stable nocturnal layer.
scored.rough_step_up: About $50-100k of options becomes about $4M at $20k/MW x 200 MW, so roughly 40-100x per block (about $10/ha to about $700/ha). That is C2 of about 3-4, not 10^4, and the base hit rate for marginal regions is perhaps 20-30%, so the lever is about 3-5x.
scored.frame: Rung: an early-stage wind project, meaning land control plus 12 months of bankable lidar data, sold to a developer. Discovery (finding the hidden low-level jet) is maybe 30-40% of the work and value in this rung (my estimate), not 80%+. A buyer at this stage mostly prices interconnection position, offtake, permitting and constructability. Wind data is one input among several. The physical step is also not abstracted: a hub height of 160-200 m depends on turbines and towers that are barely available onshore in the US (most US hub heights are about 90-140 m; NREL's public capacity-factor maps already go to 110 m and 140 m). The capitalised buyer exists (AES, Apex, Invenergy, Cordelio), but it does not pay mainly for wind discovery.
scored.step_up: Unproven side: wind option fees run about $5-10/acre (Michigan State guide, 2008). A sample AES-form option runs $12/acre/yr rising to $20/acre/yr, higher than the candidate's $2-5/acre. 12,000-15,000 acres at about $10/acre/yr is about $120-150k a year, or $0.4-0.7M over a 3-5 year option, plus $60-150k of lidar. All-in cost is about $0.5-0.9M. Proven side: early-stage wind sells for about $20k/MW, so 200 MW is about $4M. That figure is the candidate's benchmark, and my searches found no transaction data to confirm it. One modeled cost table puts development cost at about $77k/MW across the whole development phase. Without an interconnection position the realistic price is more like $5-20k/MW (my estimate), so $1-4M. Net step-up is about 2-8x on all-in capital. On the option fee alone it is about 10-40x, roughly $25/ha to $250-700/ha. That is nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: One proving attempt is a 12-month IEC-grade lidar or sodar campaign at about $60-150k (candidate's figure; consistent with industry rental rates, my estimate). Add about $100k+ a year of option holding cost. I estimate the base hit rate in 'marginal' Southeast and Midwest counties at about 20-30% (no published figure found). The lever is capped at 1/base rate, about 3-5x, not 10x. On top of that, the low-level jet is close to ubiquitous in the Plains and Midwest: an Iowa WRF study found the mean jet core at 182 m and a jet on 98% of nights. So the ML job is to separate magnitude, not to find a rare hit.
scored.data: NEXRAD VAD and radial velocity, AMDAR, IGRA and ASOS data are public, large and messy. The outcome, though, is already partly written into legible public model fields. NREL WTK-LED publishes hourly 4 km wind speeds at 200 m for 2001-2020. HRRR-based toolkits exist with about 0.1 m/s hub-height bias, against 0.82 m/s for WTK-LED (WES preprint 2026). ERA5 and NOW-23 cover similar ground. WTK-LED's known flaw is that it over-amplifies the diurnal cycle, so if anything it overstates the nocturnal jet rather than hiding it. Consultants (Vaisala/3TIER, UL/DNV) and developers already run mesoscale models at 160-200 m. The ML edge left is likely a bias correction of about 0.3-0.8 m/s, not a hidden resource.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought. Wind options are signed one landowner at a time, at about $5-20/acre/yr (MSU 2008; AES sample form), and they are not filed first-come. But the 'no buyers' premise is weakening. AES and Cordelio are already leasing in Louisiana, AES runs the 184 MW Delta project in Tunica County, Mississippi, Scout Clean Energy proposed the 180 MW Nimbus project in Arkansas, and the Southeastern Wind Coalition counted at least 20 active Southeast land-based projects in Q1 2025. Landowners do not need to read radar data, because developers already knock on doors with tall-tower thesis maps.
scored.buyer: Utility-scale wind developers and IPPs (NextEra, Invenergy, Apex, AES, RWE, Pattern, Cordelio). They are well capitalised, but they mostly buy pipelines with interconnection and permitting de-risked, and they run their own resource teams. Southeast wind has also struggled for momentum: S&P covered Southeastern developers struggling, and offtake from vertically integrated utilities in the region is limited.
scored.ladder: The ladder is real but commoditised. Steps run options, then a met campaign, then interconnection and permitting, then a ready-to-build project (about $100k+/MW), then construction and ownership as an IPP selling PPAs. In principle that is a path to a multi-GW IPP worth billions to tens of billions. But each rung above is dominated by incumbents with cheaper capital, and the starting rung's edge (resource knowledge) erodes as soon as public 200 m datasets and taller turbines arrive.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck in this rung, and the signal is not hidden. An early-stage wind project is priced on interconnection, offtake and turbine availability at 160-200 m, not on wind resource. Meanwhile 200 m wind speeds are already published in legible public model fields (NREL WTK-LED, HRRR-based toolkits) that developers and consultants already use. The result is a 2-8x net step-up (10-40x on option fees alone) with a lever of at most 3-5x, against Terranox's 10^4x step-up and roughly 10x lever.
scored.one_line_reason: Low step-up (about 10-40x on option fees, a few x net), a weak lever (base hit rate about 20-30%, so at most 3-5x), the 200 m outcome already modeled in public NREL and HRRR data, and early-stage value driven by interconnection rather than wind discovery.

scored.name: Strata Rights (dinosaur fossil rights on private ranchland)
scored.one_line: Buys fossil-only leases or royalty options on private ranches in the Hell Creek, Morrison and Judith River badlands. ML runs change detection over 60 years of archival imagery (CORONA/KH-9 declassified film, Landsat, NAIP, state lidar) plus scanned museum locality cards to find bone-bearing exposures that recent erosion has opened. A surface walk confirms articulated bone, and the proven site goes to auction houses, billionaire collectors and museums, which pay the step-up.
scored.unproven_right: Fossil-collecting lease or option on private surface estate. In the US, fossils on private land belong to the surface owner. Montana's Murray v. BEJ Minerals (2020) and a 2019 statute hold that dinosaur fossils are not 'minerals', so this is outside the mineral exclusion. Ranchers currently take $1-5k per season or a 10-20% royalty, and they cannot read the imagery.
scored.proving_step: A drone and foot crew checks ML-ranked erosion polygons for weathered bone. Testing a few square metres confirms the skeleton is articulated, which costs a few thousand dollars per site. Full excavation and preparation are routine contract jobs ($100-500k), not a bespoke build. Today commercial hunters walk whole seasons, and a skeleton worth over $1M turns up maybe once in many seasons, so the base hit rate is low and ML ranking could plausibly give a 10x lever (Anemone et al. 2011 used neural nets on Landsat to predict fossil localities in the Great Divide Basin).
scored.proven_buyer: Sotheby's and Christie's buyers (Apex stegosaurus $44.6M in 2024, Stan the T. rex $31.8M in 2020, Big John triceratops EUR6.6M in 2021), new national museums in the Gulf states and Asia, and commercial dealers such as Black Hills Institute that buy partially exposed sites.
scored.public_data: USGS declassified CORONA/KH-9 film scans (EarthExplorer), the Landsat archive since 1972, USDA NAIP, USGS 3DEP lidar, state geologic maps, Paleobiology Database occurrences, and digitised (often scanned) museum locality ledgers (iDigBio). The outcome is not written in any legible field: whether bone is exposed is hidden by nature and changes with each storm.
scored.rough_step_up: A lease worth about $2-10k becomes a $1-40M skeleton, roughly 10^3-10^4x. The ladder runs from site rights to a prep lab, casts and IP licensing, exhibitions and museum supply, then a land bank of fossiliferous ranches.
scored.frame: The rung is the fossil lease plus a confirmed articulated-bone site, sold before excavation. Discovery is probably only about 30-50% of the work in that rung (my estimate). A site's value depends on how complete the skeleton is and which taxon it is, and you mostly learn both only through excavation and preparation. That takes months to years and specialised skill: Stan-type preparations ran to tens of thousands of hours, a figure from my own knowledge that I did not re-verify. So the physical step is not trivial. It can be contracted out, but it carries much of the value risk. Buyers for unexcavated sites exist but are few. Commercial dealers such as Black Hills Institute do sometimes acquire ranches or sites, which gives a capitalised buyer, but a thin one.
scored.step_up: Unproven right: ranch day access costs $120/day or $80/half-day (mtoutlaw.com), and the candidate claims seasonal leases of $1-5k or a 10-20% royalty (I found no published lease fee). Proven, fully prepared top specimens: Gus T. rex $50.1M, Apex $44.6M (2024), Stan $31.8M (2020), and a Paris apatosaur EUR4.7M (2024). But a site with confirmed articulated bone that is still in the ground is not a $30M skeleton. My estimate: typical articulated hadrosaur, triceratops or ceratopsian partials are worth about $50k-$500k as unexcavated sites and $0.3-3M after preparation. That makes the realistic step-up on a hit about 10-100x, with 10^3-10^4 only for rare, near-complete T. rex or stegosaur finds.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate for an auction-grade skeleton (>$1M) is very low. The candidate puts it at roughly once in many crew-seasons. That is an estimate, not sourced, though it is consistent with fewer than about 5 dinosaur skeletons reaching auction worldwide per year (Wikipedia list; Barnebys). But each search attempt is cheap: walking exposures costs $120/day of access plus crew time, about $20-50k per crew-season (my estimate), and a test pit costs a few thousand dollars. Discovery capex is already small, so cutting it 10x saves little money. Prior ML: Anemone/Emerson's Landsat neural net flagged about 79% of known locality pixels with 99% precision in the Great Divide Basin (NASA Earth Observatory; Scientific American; AAPG 2013). That predicts productive outcrop, which hunters can already see, not an articulated skeleton. Pixel resolution (Landsat 30m, NAIP 0.6m, CORONA about 2m) cannot resolve weathering bone fragments, so a 10x lift in skeleton hit rate is unproven.
scored.data: Strong: the outcome (exposed bone) is not written in any legible public field. Weak: the available data is not very informative.
