Fossiliferous formations such as Hell Creek and Morrison are already mapped on state geologic maps and are walked every season by commercial crews, academic field schools and ranchers. Change detection on erosion finds where new surface has opened, but every badland erodes every year. Locality cards (PBDB, iDigBio) mark places that have already been collected. The scanned archives are illegible, but they do not contain the signal for an articulated skeleton.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right can be bought. Fossils on private land belong to the surface owner (Murray v. BEJ Minerals: Montana Supreme Court 4-3, 2020, and the Ninth Circuit; 2019 Montana statute), and they can be leased cheaply ($120/day access; candidate claims $1-5k per season or a 10-20% royalty). But ranchers are not blind. After the Dueling Dinosaurs case, which ended in a $6M museum sale, and the Bloomberg coverage of the $32M T. rex, landowners demand royalties and walk their own land. Dealers also buy ranches outright. So the arbitrage against owners who cannot read the data is partial.
scored.buyer: Sotheby's and Christie's private buyers (fewer than 5 skeletons per year worldwide), Gulf and Asian museums, and dealers such as Black Hills Institute. These buyers are capitalised but sparse and idiosyncratic. Christie's withdrew the Shen T. rex over replica-bone questions, and paleontologists' opposition creates reputational and regulatory risk. There is no deep, repeatable buyer of unexcavated sites comparable to a mine developer.
scored.ladder: The ladder goes site rights, prep lab, casts and IP (Black Hills licenses Stan casts), exhibitions, then a land bank. The whole dinosaur specimen market is probably $50-300M per year (my estimate; there is no reliable total, and fewer than about 5 auction skeletons a year). No rung above leads into a large industrial chain, so the ceiling is a niche collectibles business, not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The market is tiny and thin: fewer than about 5 auction-grade skeletons sell per year worldwide, so the ladder caps at a few hundred million dollars. On top of that, the bottleneck is not finding exposures, which are already mapped and walked for $120/day. Remote sensing at 0.6-30m resolution cannot see the actual signal, an articulated skeleton. So the ML lever has little discovery capex to cut, and most of the value is decided during excavation and preparation, not at the proving step.
scored.one_line_reason: The legal right is clean and cheap to buy, but search is already cheap, the satellite signal cannot see bone, the value is decided after excavation, and fewer than 5 skeletons sell per year, so there is no 80% discovery rung with a deep buyer and no large ladder.

scored.name: Skyfall Classification: buying unclassified meteorites and identifying rare achondrites
scored.one_line: Buys unclassified North African and desert meteorite stones by the kilo at $0.2-2/g. ML on photos, magnetic susceptibility, density and handheld XRF flags lunar, martian, angrite and other rare achondrites. Formal classification (thin section plus microprobe, about $500-2k) proves the type, and the stone resells at $100-2000/g. This is borderline with the prospecting exclusion, but the company buys already-recovered stones rather than exploring land.
scored.unproven_right: Ownership of already-recovered stones bought from nomad hunters and wholesalers who sell by weight without classifying.
scored.proving_step: A non-destructive screen, then a Meteoritical Society classification from a university lab. The physical step is cheap and fast, and nature hides the type.
scored.proven_buyer: Christie's and Heritage meteorite sales, museums, research institutions (sample purchase programmes), and collectors.
scored.public_data: The Meteoritical Bulletin Database (about 70k entries with descriptions), published geochemistry tables, and dealer and auction photo archives.
scored.rough_step_up: About 100-1000x per gram on a hit (ordinary chondrite at about $1/g against lunar or martian at $500-1000/g). Small market and weak ladder.
scored.frame: The rung is buying an unclassified stone and getting it classified. Proving it takes cheap screening plus a classification, so discovery is roughly 90% of the work inside the rung (my estimate). The buyers are collectors, dealers and a handful of museums. They are not capitalised developers, and auction volumes are small. Not excluded: the company buys stones that have already been found and does not explore land. One caveat: buying NWA material that left Algeria can carry export-law risk.
scored.step_up: Unverified estimates from memory, not sourced; the web search limit was used up. An unclassified NWA ordinary chondrite sells for about $0.1-1/g in bulk. Classified lunar NWA material now sells for about $20-300/g wholesale and up to $1,000/g at retail or auction. Lunar prices have fallen over the last decade as supply grew. Martian shergottites sell for about $100-1,000/g. The per-gram step-up of 100-1000x is real, but a 50-500 g stone ends up worth only about $5k-100k.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimates. Lunar and martian meteorites are about 1% of approved MetBull names (roughly 600-700 lunar and 350-400 martian out of ~75k, counting pairings), and HED, angrite and other achondrites add a few percent. But the bulk lots sold by weight are adversely selected: Moroccan and Mauritanian middlemen already pull out achondrites by eye. My guess is that the base rate of rare achondrites in true kilo lots is below 0.1%. Each attempt is cheap. A handheld XRF or susceptibility screen costs dollars per stone. University labs often classify for free in exchange for a type specimen (20 g or 20% of the mass); commercial classification runs about $300-2,000. Because attempts are already cheap, ML does not cut a large discovery cost. It only speeds triage, and the lever is limited by how few rare stones are left in pre-screened lots.
scored.data: This fails the gold-rubric test. The signal sits in the physical stone, which you must hold to screen. It is not in public, illegible data. Once a stone is proven, MetBull records the type in a legible classification field. Its descriptions help train a model but do not point to underpriced assets. The sellers are not blind: Saharan hunters and NWA dealers have 25+ years of skill spotting lunar and martian material (feldspathic breccias, fusion crust, no chondrules, magnet tests). Their pricing already reflects that skill.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Stones are bought outright from nomad hunters and wholesalers, either by weight or per stone. The rights are bought cheaply, but the underpriced pool is the leftovers after experts have already screened the lots.
scored.buyer: Collectors, meteorite dealers, and auctions at Christie's, Heritage and Bonhams, where a big sale brings in a few $M a year. Museums and research institutions buy small amounts. My estimate is that the whole global meteorite market is in the tens of $M a year, and that lunar and martian prices fall when new supply arrives.
scored.ladder: The ladder is weak. Possible rungs are dealing, auctions, and supplying research samples. None of them leads to a large industrial chain, and the ceiling is a niche dealer with tens of $M in revenue.
scored.fatal_flaw: The edge is gone and the market is tiny. Expert Saharan middlemen already pull rare achondrites out of bulk lots by eye, so lots sold by weight hold almost no lunar or martian material. Selling more hits would also push down prices in a market of only tens of $M a year.
scored.one_line_reason: The per-gram step-up is real at 100-1000x, but the signal is physical rather than in illegible public data, the sellers already screen for rare types, attempts are already cheap, and the market and ladder are tiny.
sources: The web search limit was used up before any search ran (all three searches failed), so every figure is my own estimate from memory and none is sourced
Meteoritical Bulletin Database (lpi.usra.edu/meteor), category counts from memory, not checked this session
Meteoritical Society nomenclature guidelines: type specimen of 20 g or 20% deposited with the classifying institution, from memory

scored.name: SweetSource: sweet and flavour-modulating proteins from ethnobotanical leads
scored.one_line: Herbarium labels and colonial-era ethnobotanies hold thousands of notes like 'fruit intensely sweet' or 'leaf removes bitterness' that nobody has followed up. Buy exclusive ABS and collection rights for those taxa from source communities, express candidate proteins, and prove them on the human T1R2/T1R3 receptor. Food majors buy proven sweet proteins as sugar-reduction ingredients.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive commercial ABS/PIC agreement for a plant species or population with a community or national authority, about $5-25k, plus owned germplasm.
scored.proving_step: Transcriptome of the fruit or leaf, then ML ranking of small cysteine-rich and thaumatin-like candidates, then precision-fermentation expression, then a HEK293 T1R2/T1R3 cell assay and a sensory panel, about $20-50k per species.
scored.proven_buyer: Cargill, Tate & Lyle, ADM, Ingredion, Givaudan, and precision-fermentation sweetener companies (Oobli, Amai) that license or acquire novel sweet-protein IP.
scored.public_data: Scanned herbarium specimen labels (iDigBio/GBIF, 100M+ images, OCR-poor), colonial ethnobotany volumes on Biodiversity Heritage Library, 1KP transcriptomes, NCBI TSA plant transcriptomes.
scored.rough_step_up: $10k species right to a receptor-validated novel sweet protein licensable at $2-10M (10^2.5-10^3x). Base hit rate of ethnobotanical 'sweet' notes yielding a high-potency protein is about 2%. Ladder: fermentation production, then ingredient brand, then a sugar-reduction platform.
scored.frame: The rung would be "ABS right plus a receptor-validated sweet protein". Inside that rung, discovery is maybe 20-30% of the work needed before anyone pays real money (my estimate). A receptor hit does not make a sellable asset. The value comes after several further steps: getting fermentation titre and cost of goods to work (g/L scale), fixing taste problems (slow onset, lingering aftertaste) and heat/pH stability, and getting regulatory clearance (FDA GRAS letter, EFSA novel food), which takes years and millions. Brazzein was characterised in 1994 and monellin in the 1970s. Oobli only got FDA GRAS "no questions" letters for them around 2024-25, about 30 years later. Discovery was never the bottleneck. Buyers like Ingredion and Ajinomoto partner with companies at the GRAS/production stage, not at the assay-hit stage.
scored.step_up: Unproven: an ABS/PIC agreement at about $5-25k (candidate's figure; not verified). Proven: there is no public market price for a receptor-validated but unregulated novel sweet protein. The Oobli-Ingredion partnership (Feb 2025) disclosed no financial terms; Ingredion Ventures invested in Oobli's $18M Series B1, which was equity in a GRAS-cleared company. My estimate is that a raw assay-validated sequence licenses for $0.1-1M upfront, mostly milestones contingent on GRAS and scale-up, so roughly 10-50x realised immediately. The $2-10M figure only applies after regulatory and production de-risking that the rung does not include.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The 2% base rate is the candidate's figure and unverified. About 8-10 sweet or taste-modifying proteins are known (thaumatin, monellin, brazzein, mabinlin, pentadin, curculin/neoculin, miraculin, lysozyme). Almost all came from exactly these ethnobotanical leads, West African and Asian fruits noted as "intensely sweet", so the best leads are already used up. Cost per attempt is about $20-50k (candidate's figure; plausible for a transcriptome, expression and HEK293 assay). The proving step is cheap, so a 10x capex cut saves little in absolute terms: about $0.5M per hit at 2%, against $5M+ of downstream regulatory and scale-up cost.
scored.data: The data is public and genuinely illegible: herbarium label OCR in GBIF/iDigBio, Biodiversity Heritage Library ethnobotanies, and 1KP/NCBI TSA transcriptomes. No status field records whether a plant contains a sweet protein, so the outcome is not already summarised. The weaknesses: (1) Shiru (Flourish/ProteinDiscovery.ai platform, partnered with Ajinomoto Health & Nutrition in 2024) and Naturannova already mine plant protein space with AI. The transcriptome and sequence data is legible to them; only the label and ethnobotany text layer is not. (2) The right is weak. ABS/PIC agreements under the Nagoya Protocol rarely give real exclusivity, since the same species often grows in several countries and many communities. Natural protein sequences are hard to patent in the US after Myriad. The brazzein/University of Wisconsin biopiracy controversy shows the political risk. Competitors can find homologues or engineer variants (Amai designs proteins de novo), which bypasses any species right.
scored.right_bought: Exclusive commercial ABS/PIC agreement with a community or national authority, plus germplasm. The exclusivity is weak and non-geographic: other source countries and engineered variants get around it.
scored.buyer: Ingredion, Ajinomoto, Cargill, Tate & Lyle, Givaudan, plus sweet-protein startups Oobli, Amai and Shiru. They buy at the GRAS-cleared, scalable stage, not at the receptor-assay stage.
scored.ladder: The ladder exists: fermentation production, then ingredient brand, then sugar-reduction platform. That is a real multi-billion-dollar sweetener market. But every rung above discovery is capital-heavy biomanufacturing and regulatory work, and it is already crowded (Oobli, Amai, Shiru/Ajinomoto, Sweegen).
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck, so no rung exists where discovery is 80% of the work. Known sweet proteins (brazzein since 1994, monellin and thaumatin since the 1970s) sat for decades because of expression cost, taste profile and regulatory clearance, not for lack of finding them. A receptor hit therefore does not trigger the immediate 10^3x step-up: buyers pay at the GRAS/scale stage, which is the expensive physical part. This is closer to the geothermal-plant counter-example than to Terranox.
scored.one_line_reason: The illegible data source is genuinely interesting, but sweet-protein value is unlocked by regulatory clearance and fermentation scale-up, not discovery. The right is weakly exclusive, and AI discovery competitors (Shiru, Amai) already exist.

scored.name: Salento Survivors (Xylella-resistant olive clones)
scored.one_line: Satellite-scan the ~20M olive trees of Puglia that Xylella killed for isolated green survivors among dead neighbours. Buy propagation rights from ruined farmers for almost nothing and prove resistance by greenhouse inoculation and PCR. Sell or license the clones to Spanish and Italian super-intensive olive nurseries and growers facing Xylella's spread.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive cutting and propagation rights to specific centuries-old survivor trees, bought from Salento smallholders whose groves are worthless now. Monumental dead trees are often sold for firewood. Deal price ~EUR 200-2,000 per tree.
scored.proving_step: Root cuttings, then needle-inoculate with X. fastidiosa subsp. pauca ST53 in an approved containment greenhouse and measure bacterial load by qPCR at 12-18 months. Also genotype to exclude known tolerant cultivars (Leccino, FS-17) and keep truly novel genotypes. Cost ~EUR 3-5k per candidate.
scored.proven_buyer: Olive nurseries and super-intensive growers: Agromillora (Spain, the world's largest olive nursery), Deoleo-linked growers, Italian Coldiretti cooperatives, and EU/Puglia regional replanting programs. Today only Leccino and FS-17 may legally be replanted in the infected zone, so a third or fourth resistant cultivar, especially one suited to super-intensive hedgerow systems, is badly needed.
scored.public_data: Sentinel-2 10m and AGEA orthophotos (2013-2024) of Salento, Copernicus HR-VPP vegetation phenology, Puglia region Xylella monitoring and positive-sample maps (emergenzaxylella.it), EFSA Xylella reports, published olive genome panels. The survivor signal is spatial: one healthy crown among dead neighbours over 8+ years of infection pressure.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10^3-10^4: EUR 500 tree right to a resistant cultivar license worth EUR 2-20M (royalties on millions of replant trees across Puglia and at-risk Spain). Cheap greenhouse proof exists, but nurseries will likely want a field-season confirmation before paying the top price.
scored.frame: The rung would be "own propagation rights to a survivor tree and prove it resistant". Spotting candidates is cheap and could be ~50% of the work. Proving is not: it needs a containment greenhouse inoculation (12-18 months), then several years of field trials in the infected zone, then approval by the Puglia Phytosanitary Service. Lecciana was bred in 1998 and only approved for the infected zone in May 2024 (Resolution No. 48). So proving and regulatory approval are most of the time and cost, not a trivial physical step. A greenhouse-only result is not a sellable output at the top price. My estimate is that discovery is about 20-30% of the work inside this rung.
scored.step_up: Unproven: EUR 200-2,000 per tree right (candidate's figure; I found no market data). Proven: a licence the candidate puts at EUR 2-20M. I found no published royalty rate for Lecciana or Sikitita. My estimate is EUR 0.3-1 per plant, so a cultivar planted on tens of thousands of replanted hectares at 1,600-2,000 trees/ha could earn low tens of millions over 20 years. In theory that is about 10^3-10^4. In practice the jump does not happen on a hit: a greenhouse-positive clone is maybe worth EUR 20-100k as an option (my estimate, about 50x). The full value comes only after years of field data and regional approval, so the step is delayed and split into stages. Most monumental Salento trees are vigorous Ogliarola or Cellina types that do not suit super-intensive hedgerows, which cuts the licence value further.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate is very low. Pavan et al. 2021 (Frontiers in Plant Science, PMC8415753) collected 30 nearly or fully symptom-free survivor plants from badly hit Salento groves. 23 grouped genetically with Leccino or FS17. None showed resistance comparable to Leccino or FS17; only partial resistance turned up (for example in Frantoio and Nocellara Messinese). That puts the observed rate of truly new, highly resistant survivors at about 0 in 30. Cost per greenhouse attempt is ~EUR 3-5k (candidate's figure, plausible), plus field trials of perhaps EUR 50-200k per finalist over 3-5 years (my estimate). ML could filter out escapes, Leccino plantings and low-inoculum pockets, but the lever is capped by how rare true resistance is. Breeding programmes (Genforagris crosses with 9+ years in the field; the UniBa and Agromillora crosses) are a more reliable source of resistance than hunting survivors.
scored.data: The data is public: Sentinel-2 imagery, AGEA orthophotos, the emergenzaxylella.it positive-sample maps and EFSA reports. Resistance itself is not written into any legible field, which is good. But the survivor signal (one green crown among dead trees) is not illegible. It is visible to the eye and in plain NDVI, and the UniBa, CNR, CREA and JRC groups already run airborne hyperspectral and thermal campaigns (the POnTE project covered ~200,000 trees) and field-prospect survivors (Pavan 2021; the EIP-AGRI project "Olive biodiversity saving Salento"). Incumbents already extract this signal, so there is little ML edge.
scored.right_bought: Rights can be bought cheaply from ruined smallholders. There are three catches. First, monumental olive trees are protected under Puglia regional law (LR 14/2007), which limits what can be done with them. Second, EU Regulation 2020/1201 restricts moving plant material out of the demarcated infected zone, and cutting a survivor tree gives the landowner nothing to stop anyone else taking cuttings of the same genotype. Third, the genotype is not protected until plant variety rights (CPVO) are granted, which needs DUS testing. Ancient landrace genotypes may also have relatives elsewhere, which weakens distinctness and exclusivity.
scored.buyer: Agromillora is capitalised but is a direct competitor. It co-owns (50/50 with the University of Bari, exclusive licence) Lecciana, which was approved for the Xylella zone in May 2024 as the third resistant cultivar and is already suited to super-intensive hedgerows. That removes the candidate's claim that only Leccino and FS-17 exist and weakens its "badly needed" premise. Regional replanting programmes and cooperatives buy plants, not genetics licences, and pay little for IP.
scored.ladder: The rungs above would be owning a nursery for propagation, a royalty club (the Lecciana club model), then replanted groves and an olive-oil brand. The olive nursery and oil markets are worth billions, not trillions, and Agromillora already holds the nursery and club rungs. The ladder is moderate at best.
scored.fatal_flaw: This has already been tried and come up empty, and proving is slow. UniBa and CNR screened Salento survivor trees (Pavan 2021): 23 of 30 were Leccino or FS17 relatives and none beat them. Value only appears after years of field trials and regional approval, and the main buyer (Agromillora) already owns an approved, hedgerow-ready resistant cultivar (Lecciana, 2024).
scored.one_line_reason: The survivor signal is visible to the eye and academics already prospect it, the base rate of truly new resistance is about 0 in 30, proving takes 3-6+ years of field and regulatory work rather than an immediate jump, and the buyer already owns Lecciana.
sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8415753/ (Pavan et al. 2021, screening of 30 Salento survivor plants)
https://www.agromillora.com/lecciana/ (Lecciana approved for the Xylella zone, Puglia Resolution No. 48, 3 May 2024)

scored.name: TR4 Survivor Banana Clones
scored.one_line: Find Cavendish plants that keep standing in Fusarium TR4-infested plantations (Philippines, Mozambique, Colombia, Peru) using high-cadence imagery around mapped outbreaks. Buy the rights to suckers from smallholders and prove TR4 resistance in 3-4 month greenhouse inoculation trials. The proven clone goes to the banana majors, who face an existential disease and already paid for GCTCV somaclonal variants.
scored.unproven_right: Sucker and tissue-culture propagation rights to individual surviving Cavendish mats in infested farms, bought for ~$50-500 per mat with a benefit-sharing contract that satisfies Nagoya/ABS.
scored.proving_step: Tissue-culture the sucker and run a TR4 (VCG 01213) pot inoculation for 12-16 weeks to score internal vascular discoloration. Check genetic stability with SSR/resequencing. Cost ~$1-3k per candidate. Banana sterility makes every proven clone a fixed, sellable genotype.
scored.proven_buyer: Dole, Chiquita, Fresh Del Monte, Fyffes, and Rijk Zwaan/KeyGene-style breeders. Precedent: Taiwan Banana Research Institute's GCTCV-218/219 somaclonal selections are licensed globally, and Del Monte holds rights to QCAV-4. Cavendish is ~$10B+/yr of exports with no proven resistant drop-in replacement.
scored.public_data: Sentinel-2 and PlanetScope NICFI tropical basemaps (free monthly mosaics), Landsat archive, ProMusa/FAO TR4 outbreak distribution reports, MusaBase and NCBI Musa resequencing data. Infection fronts and per-mat survival exist only in imagery and patchy outbreak PDFs, with no outcome field anywhere.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10^4-10^5: $100 sucker right to a resistant Cavendish-type clone worth $10-100M+ to an exporter. The base hit rate is very low, since most 'survivors' are escapes from uneven inoculum, so ML on infection-front geometry is the lever. Risk: majors may demand field trials in hotspot plots, but those are cheap and fast (one crop cycle, ~12 months).
scored.frame: The rung is "own a candidate clone and prove it is TR4-resistant", sold to banana majors or breeders. Inside the pot-screen version of that rung, discovery (picking the survivor) is maybe 60-70% of the work. But the buyer does not pay for a pot screen. Majors adopt only after multi-cycle field trials in hotspot plots plus checks on yield, bunch weight, ripening, shelf life and taste. GCTCV-218 (Formosana) was held back for years by poor agronomics, not by its resistance. That puts the real proving step at 2-4 years and $100k-1M+ per clone (my estimate, unsourced), so the physical step is neither trivial nor abstracted. Once that is counted, discovery is under 30% of the work.
scored.step_up: My estimate (searches were blocked, so nothing here is sourced): the unproven right is about $50-500 per mat, as the candidate claims. A proven partial-resistance somaclone (GCTCV-218/219 class) is licensed as tissue-culture plantlets at roughly $0.3-1 per plantlet, with small royalties. TBRI's licensing income looks like low millions over decades, not $10-100M. A true drop-in resistant Cavendish might be worth $10-100M+, but any value realised immediately on a pot-trial hit is closer to $10k-$1M. That is about 100-10,000x on paper, discounted heavily for slow adoption and leakage.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimate (unsourced): among field survivors, the share that are truly heritable resistant variants rather than escapes is probably under 1%. TBRI screened tens of thousands of somaclonal plantlets to get a handful of tolerant lines. The cost per attempt is low: $1-3k for a pot screen (the candidate's own figure, which seems plausible). The lever is real but has a ceiling. At ~1% base rate, ML could improve it by up to ~100x in theory. In practice, imagery cannot tell an escape from a resistant mat (escapes are caused by patchy soil inoculum), so a realistic gain is maybe 2-3x. Worse, the cheap attempt cost means ML saves little absolute capex: 1,000 screens is about $2M, which incumbents already spend.
scored.data: There are two problems. First, imagery resolution: Sentinel-2 is 10 m and PlanetScope NICFI basemaps are about 4.7 m and monthly. Banana mats stand about 2-2.5 m apart, so individual-mat survival cannot really be read from these sources. You would need drones or field scouting, which is exactly what plantation staff already do. Second, the survivors are not illegible to their owners. Most export Cavendish in Mindanao, Colombia, Peru and Mozambique is grown on corporate farms or contract-grower farms tied to the majors. Their agronomists walk these blocks weekly and already collect survivors. Precedents: Chinese Guangdong selections (Nantianhuang, Baodao) came from TR4 field survivors and somaclonal screening, and growers in Mozambique (Matanuska) and the Philippines have run survivor programs. So the outcome lives in the owners' own scouting records, not in public data. Under Nagoya/ABS and Philippine bioprospecting rules, buying a mat right needs national permits, and smallholders have little export Cavendish.
scored.right_bought: In principle, a contract right to propagate one mat for $50-500 plus benefit-sharing. The right does not exclude anyone. Cavendish spreads by suckers, so the seller, their neighbours and anyone holding one sucker can multiply the clone. Plant variety protection is weak or slow in Mozambique, the Philippines and Peru, and a somaclone is hard to tell apart from its parent Cavendish by DUS (distinctness, uniformity, stability) tests or SSR markers. Somaclonal variants are near-identical genetically, so proving ownership requires resequencing.
scored.buyer:
Dole, Chiquita, Fresh Del Monte, Fyffes and large Philippine growers (Unifrutti, Lapanday, Sumifru) are the capitalised buyers. They are also the incumbents and competitors:
- Del Monte holds QCAV-4, the QUT GM Grand Naine line approved in Australia in 2024.
- Chiquita and KeyGene announced Yelloway One, a TR4-resistant non-GM line, in 2024.
- Gene-editing players include Tropic (UK) and Rahan Meristem.
- TBRI keeps putting out GCTCV lines.
- Bioversity and Stellenbosch screen field survivors as public programs.
Majors favour their own pipelines and are slow to adopt new lines because of retail spec risk.
scored.ladder: Possible rungs: own a clone, then a tissue-culture plantlet business, then contracting growers or owning plantations, then branded resistant-banana export. Bananas are a thin-margin commodity worth about $10-15B a year in exports, dominated by entrenched majors. The ladder exists but tops out at a mid-cap produce company, not a trillion-dollar chain, and each rung is low-margin agriculture.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no information asymmetry, and the asset leaks. The survivors stand on farms owned by, or contracted to, the same majors who would buy the result. Their agronomists already scout and collect survivors weekly; China's Baodao and Nantianhuang came from exactly this. Public 5-10 m imagery cannot resolve individual mats. Even if you hold a proven clone, vegetative sucker propagation and weak plant variety protection mean you cannot capture the step-up. And real proof needs years of multi-cycle field and agronomic trials, not a 12-week pot screen.
scored.one_line_reason: The farm owners and the buyers are the same majors, and they already scout survivors. Satellite imagery cannot resolve individual mats, the real proof takes years of field trials, and sucker propagation means a proven clone cannot be held exclusively.
sources: WebSearch was blocked by the auto-mode safety check in this session, so I could check none of these figures. Everything below is from background knowledge and must be verified.
Background knowledge, not checked: TBRI GCTCV-218 (Formosana) / GCTCV-219 somaclonal selection and their agronomic limits (Hwang & Ko 2004, Plant Disease).
Background knowledge, not checked: QUT QCAV-4 GM Cavendish, approved by FSANZ/OGTR in 2024, licensed to Del Monte via QUT.
Background knowledge, not checked: Chiquita-KeyGene Yelloway One TR4-resistant banana announcement (2024).
Background knowledge, not checked: Guangdong Academy of Agricultural Sciences somaclonal selections Nantianhuang/Baodao from TR4 fields.
Background knowledge, not checked: imagery resolution, Sentinel-2 10 m and Planet NICFI basemaps ~4.77 m monthly.
My own estimates: base hit rate under 1%, field-trial cost $100k-1M+ per clone, plantlet price $0.3-1.

scored.name: HoardSense (UK farmland detecting rights plus Treasure Act)
scored.one_line: Buys exclusive multi-year metal-detecting and fieldwalking agreements from English and Welsh farmers. ML on Environment Agency LiDAR, historic maps and cropmark imagery finds ploughed-out Iron Age, Roman and Viking hoard sites. Hoards go through the Treasure Act, where the Treasure Valuation Committee sets a market-value reward that a museum must pay, split between finder and landowner.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive detecting and finder agreements, structured so the company is finder and co-beneficiary of the Treasure reward and owns non-Treasure finds by contract. Farmers grant these for little or nothing today.
scored.proving_step: An ML model fuses LiDAR micro-topography, cropmarks in aerial and Sentinel imagery, scanned tithe and enclosure maps, Roman road and settlement priors, and PAS find-spot density to pick fields. Detecting plus a targeted GPR pass proves a hoard. It costs a few thousand pounds per field, against a near-zero base hit rate for random detecting.
scored.proven_buyer: Acquiring museums such as the British Museum and regional museums. They pay the TVC-set market value, funded by the Art Fund, the National Heritage Memorial Fund and the National Lottery Heritage Fund (the Staffordshire Hoard reward was £3.285M). Collectors buy non-Treasure coins through Noonans and Spink.
scored.public_data: EA National LiDAR Programme (1m, open, all of England). Historic England aerial archive and National Mapping Programme. Scanned tithe and enclosure maps (National Archives and county record offices). Portable Antiquities Scheme records, which are partly obfuscated and hold only finds already made. Old OS county series maps.
scored.rough_step_up: An agreement worth about £0-£500 becomes a hoard reward of £50k-£3M+, or 10^3-10^4x on a hit. The Treasure process takes 1-3 years, so 'immediately' only means a contracted valuation.
scored.frame: The rung is "hold a detecting right on a field and recover Treasure-eligible finds", and it is a real rung. Discovery (choosing the field) is about 85-90% of the work, and detecting is cheap. But the output has no capitalised buyer. Museums do not buy because of profit economics. They acquire with charitable and grant money (Art Fund, NHMF, NLHF), within limited acquisition budgets, and they can disclaim a find. When they do, the find goes back to the finder and landowner to sell on the open coin and antiquities market at auction prices. The buyer is therefore grant-capped and has no margin of its own, unlike a mine developer who is in at $40k/ha and collects $100k/ha.
scored.step_up: Unproven right: £0-£500 per field (my estimate; farmers grant permission for free or for a negotiated split). Under English law the landowner keeps non-Treasure finds by default and takes about 50% of any Treasure reward (NCMD template agreement). Proven value is heavily skewed. In 2016 there were 241 Treasure items with agreed valuations, totalling £643,683, an average of £2,671 per case (Treasure annual report via press, 2018). The median is likely a few hundred pounds. Hoards above £1M, like the Staffordshire Hoard at £3.285M, occur maybe once every few years across all of England and Wales. So a typical hit is about 10x (£250 to £2.7k, half of which goes to the landowner), and 10^3-10^4x only on rare outliers. It is also not immediate: the TVC process takes 1-3 years, and the reward can be abated for breaches of the Code.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cases rose from 1,116 in 2016 to 1,377 in 2023 and 1,540 in 2024 (British Museum, 2024 press release). These come from roughly 40k UK detectorists (my estimate), so the base rate per detector-day is very low. But each proving attempt is cheap: a detecting day costs about £100-£300 in labour, and a GPR pass about £1-3k per field (my estimates). Lowering capex 10x only helps if attempts are expensive, and here they are not. The lever is real for rare big hoards, but it is capped by how few there are. Expected value per field is lower than the candidate's own "few thousand pounds per field" proving cost.
scored.data: EA 1m LiDAR is open, and UK detectorists and amateur archaeologists already use it heavily (for example LiDAR Roman-road projects, and detecting forums that share hillshades). Historic England's National Mapping Programme already digitises cropmarks into a legible GIS layer. PAS find-spots are legible and searchable, although obfuscated to about 1km. Scanned tithe and enclosure maps are the only part that is genuinely illegible. The outcome is partly summarised already: known sites are mapped in the HER/NMP, and many of the best sites are scheduled monuments, where detecting is a criminal offence. So ML finds mostly what is either already mapped or off-limits.
scored.right_bought: Rights can be bought cheaply from farmers, and the right exists as a contract (NCMD/NFU permission agreements). But the farmer's share is protected by default: the landowner keeps about 50% of the Treasure reward and all non-Treasure finds unless the contract says otherwise. Exclusivity is also hard to enforce against nighthawks. And publicity around hoards has made farmers aware of value, so splits are negotiated rather than near-free.
scored.buyer: Acquiring museums, such as the British Museum and regional museums, pay the TVC market value. The money comes from Art Fund, NHMF and NLHF grants. Disclaimed finds go to collectors through Noonans, Spink and TimeLine. The whole Treasure reward pool is only about £0.6M-£3M a year across England and Wales (my estimate, scaled from 2016's £644k). The buyer is grant-funded and budget-capped, not a capitalised developer with a margin.
scored.ladder: The ladder is weak. Possible rungs above are buying farmland with high archaeological potential, which gives no uplift and is constrained by scheduling and planning; antiquities dealing, which is small, reputationally toxic and export-licensed; and heritage tourism or experiences. None of these leads to a large vertical chain. The total market is the UK antiquities and coin trade, worth hundreds of millions at most.
scored.fatal_flaw: The prize pool is tiny and the buyer is not capitalised. In 2016 Treasure valuations across England, Wales and Northern Ireland totalled about £644k over 241 cases, an average of £2.7k. About half of that goes to the landowner by default, and grant-limited museums pay it after 1-3 years. Expected value per field is below the cost of proving it, and the best ML-identifiable sites are often scheduled monuments that cannot legally be detected.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a lottery for heritage grants, not a 10^4 asset re-rating. Average Treasure value is about £2.7k, the total annual pool is around £1M, museums are budget-capped, the open LiDAR and mapped cropmark data is already used by about 40k detectorists, and there is no ladder above.

scored.name: ThermalBelt (frost-free microclimate land for premium perennial crops)
scored.one_line: Cold-air drainage creates narrow hillside thermal belts that stay frost-free and are worth vineyard, avocado or citrus prices, yet they sell as grazing or dry-farm land. ML on scanned historical frost-service records and nighttime satellite thermal imagery finds them. Buy or option the land, prove it with one season of logger grids, and sell to institutional farmland investors and premium wineries, who pay the step-up.
scored.unproven_right: Purchase options or fee title on grazing and dryland parcels on the climate-shifting viticulture frontier (Oregon and Washington benches, BC Okanagan edges, Sierra foothills, Tasmania, southern England). Owners price at ag-land comparables and cannot read the frost data.
scored.proving_step: One winter-spring season of a grid of ~$50 temperature loggers plus a soil pit, giving a certified frost-free-days, growing-degree-day and minimum-temperature map. Physically trivial (~$10-20k).
scored.proven_buyer: Institutional farmland investors (Nuveen Natural Capital, PSP, Manulife Investment Management), premium wine groups (Constellation, Jackson Family, Treasury), and avocado and citrus growers.
scored.public_data: Scanned Federal-State Fruit Frost Service records (California and Oregon, 1920s-1970s); NOAA COOP paper observer forms (scanned); Landsat and ECOSTRESS nighttime land surface temperature; USDA SSURGO soils; old county soil-survey PDFs. Microclimate is set by nature and summarised in no title or registry field.
scored.rough_step_up: About 5-30x ($3-8k/acre grazing to $40-150k/acre plantable premium vineyard bench). Much of the AVA premium only appears after planting, so the step-up at the proof stage is honestly about 3-10x. C2 about 2-3, but the ladder (plant, wine, brand) is real.
scored.frame: The rung is 'bare land with a certified frost-free microclimate'. Discovery (choosing the parcel) is maybe 40-60% of the work in that rung, by my estimate. The rest is land acquisition, water rights, zoning, soils and the sale itself, and water rights can decide the deal. The proving step is physically trivial, but it is also not where any uncertainty or cost sits. Buyers exist (Nuveen Natural Capital, Manulife, wine groups), but they pay for planted, producing assets more than for certified bare benches. They also do their own site work, and they are buying less: California removed about 38,000 vineyard acres (~7%) between Oct 2024 and Aug 2025, Washington was told to cut 10,000 of 61,200 acres, and Oregon's planted acreage fell 5.5% in 2025.
scored.step_up: Oregon pastureland statewide averages $1,080/acre (USDA June Area Survey 2025, OSU EM 9569). Willamette plantable unplanted land sells for $15-50k/acre; planted land reaches about $100k/acre, and Ribbon Ridge and Dundee Hills sales ran $90-100k (Oregon Wine Press, via a broker). The pasture-to-plantable gap looks like 15-40x, but that compares different land. Hillside parcels next to an AVA are already priced for location and lifestyle use, at roughly $5-15k/acre by my estimate. On the same parcel, a frost-certified bench is probably worth 2-5x more at the proof stage, my estimate. The jump to about $100k/acre only comes after 3-5 years of planting at roughly $30-60k/acre establishment cost (OSU cost-of-establishment studies). That is far from 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: One proving attempt costs about $10-20k for a logger grid plus a soil pit (the candidate's own figure, which I think is plausible). Against land at $1-5M per parcel, that is under 2% of the deal, so ML cannot cut discovery capex 10x when discovery capex is already close to zero. For DEM-screened mid-slope, south-facing sites, my estimate is that frost-free certification succeeds about 30-60% of the time. Cold-air drainage follows directly from topography (extension guidance: cold air pools in low ground, so pick moderate slopes under 15% and mid-slope positions), so the lever is capped at about 2-3x. The real costs are the land and the planting, and ML does not reduce either.
scored.data: Some of the data is illegible. Fruit Frost Service records are scattered, and I found none digitised in bulk (Calisphere holds one 1967 UC frost report; WSU's frost program has run since 1922). NOAA COOP forms are scanned images. The signal itself, though, mostly comes from legible sources: LiDAR and DEM terrain (cold-air drainage is a terrain calculation), PRISM gridded climate, Landsat and ECOSTRESS thermal imagery, SSURGO soils, and existing site models such as WSU's Vineyard Site Selection Model and Gregory Jones's GIS terroir work in Oregon. Microclimate is not written into any title field, but AVA boundaries and GDD maps already summarise most of it. Incumbent wine-region brokers, viticulture consultants and extension agents already read plantability.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Fee title or purchase options can be bought from ranchers and dryland farmers, and options are a real lever for capital efficiency. The problem is that sellers near known wine regions already price in viticulture potential, since brokers advertise 'plantable acres'. Any discount would only exist at the frontier (Tasmania, southern England, BC edges). Demand is thinnest there, and buyers are slow.
scored.buyer: Institutional farmland investors (Nuveen Natural Capital, PSP, Manulife IM) and premium wine groups (Jackson Family, Constellation, Treasury), plus avocado and citrus growers. They are capitalised, but in 2025-26 they are net sellers and removers of vineyard acreage, they buy proven producing assets, and they do their own siting diligence.
scored.ladder: There is a real ladder: certified land, then a planted vineyard (3-5 years, roughly $30-60k/acre), then grape contracts, a winery and a brand, or orchards for avocado and citrus. But each rung above the bottom one is capital-heavy, agronomic and slow, and the wine market is in structural oversupply. The upper rungs are worth billions, not a trillion.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is already cheap ($10-20k against a $1M+ parcel) and is mostly predictable from public terrain data. That leaves no expensive, mostly-failing discovery for ML to make 10x cheaper. Most of the value step-up only appears after years of capital-heavy planting, into a wine-grape glut.
scored.one_line_reason: Not excluded, but weak (10/25): discovery is cheap and predictable from terrain data, the step-up at proof is about 2-5x, and the value is captured by planting, not proving.

scored.name: Settled Ground: landslide- and subsidence-red-tagged lots that InSAR shows have stopped moving
scored.one_line: Buys lots red-tagged or held back because of landslide, sinkhole or mine-subsidence designations. Such lots sell for close to nothing. Multi-year Sentinel-1 InSAR displacement and LiDAR change detection show which ones have actually been stable for years. A geotechnical report and the jurisdiction lifting the hazard designation prove buildability, and the lot is sold to builders at market.
scored.unproven_right: Fee title to hazard-designated vacant lots, for example in active-slide areas of California, former coal-subsidence zones in PA, OH and IL, or Florida sinkhole areas. Owners have given up on them.
scored.proving_step: A geotechnical investigation with borings and inclinometer readings ($15-50k) plus a building permit or hazard-zone exemption. InSAR picks the lots whose motion has fallen to near zero.
scored.proven_buyer: Infill homebuilders and developers in high-cost coastal markets, where a buildable lot is worth $300k-$1M.
scored.public_data: ESA Sentinel-1 SLC archive and the NASA OPERA DISP-S1 displacement product; USGS landslide inventory; state geologic hazard maps; USGS 3DEP LiDAR epochs; Pennsylvania/OSMRE mine-subsidence maps; scanned municipal geotechnical reports.
scored.rough_step_up: About 30-300x in coastal California ($5-20k red-tagged lot to $500k+ buildable). About 5-20x elsewhere. Hazard status is a legible regulator field, but it is rarely revisited, so InSAR's evidence of present stability is the hidden variable. The lifting decision is discretionary and political, which is a risk.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a hazard-tagged lot, getting it entitled and selling it to a builder. Discovery (InSAR picking the stable lots) is roughly 20-30% of the work, by my estimate. Most of the work is non-technical: getting the jurisdiction to lift or exempt the hazard designation. That means the geotechnical work (borings plus inclinometer monitoring over months), permits, hearings, possible CEQA/EIR review and litigation. In Rancho Palos Verdes, Monks' 16 lots needed decades of litigation and a special ordinance (Ord. 498, 2009) before they could build. The city's own estimate for a geologic study proving a 1.5 factor of safety in Zone 2 was $500k-1M+. The physical/political step is the hard part, the same failure shape as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example. The capitalised buyer (infill builders) is real, but only for lots that are already entitled.
scored.step_up: No sale prices for the unproven or proven lots were found, so the multiples here are my estimates. The candidate claims a $5-20k red-tagged lot becomes worth $500k+ in coastal California (30-300x). The best real anchors come from Rancho Palos Verdes. A 2009 resident email says an ocean-view lot with approved plans sold for under $600k (an advocacy source). In the Monks case, plaintiffs valued their lots at about $2M each against the city's ~$1M. The city estimated $16-32M to buy the 16 plaintiffs' lots, about $1-2M per lot. Those valuations came from litigants hoping to build, which suggests tagged lots do not trade at ~$0. Hope value and takings-claim value hold the unproven price up, so the realistic multiple is roughly 10-50x in coastal California. In PA, OH, IL mine-subsidence areas and Florida sinkhole areas, building is generally not banned. Owners carry subsidence/sinkhole insurance, so the discount, and the step-up, is about 1.2-3x (estimate; not verified because the search budget ran out).
scored.hit_rate_capex: I found no published base rate for hazard designations being lifted. My estimate is that it is very low, and it is set by politics, not geology. Rancho Palos Verdes turned its 2023 two-year moratorium into permanent restrictions in 2025 (Ordinance 692), barring new construction on vacant lots and adding 8 more parcels. Its 31 unentitled Zone 2 lots stay frozen. Cost per proving attempt: the candidate cites $15-50k for geotech. The city's own figure for a Zone 2 factor-of-safety study is $500k-1M+, plus entitlement and legal costs and 2-10+ years. InSAR stability barely moves this hit rate, because the regulator's denial is driven by risk aversion and liability, not by a lack of evidence of stability. Slides are also episodic. Portuguese Bend crept slowly for decades and then sped up sharply after the 2023 rains. A few years of near-zero InSAR displacement does not show the 1.5 factor of safety that permitting needs. So the lever is far below 10x.
scored.data: Sentinel-1 and the NASA OPERA DISP-S1 product are public, but they are already processed and increasingly legible, and the EU's EGMS is a ready-made InSAR dataset. Commercial and ESA-funded parcel-level InSAR scorers already exist: Hi_Ground (formerly GIRP, UK), geo shield (France, with MAIF) and BODIS (Netherlands). So the signal is not illegible to incumbents. The outcome, buildable or not, is written into a legible regulator field: the hazard zone or moratorium designation. That field is exactly what has to change, and only a discretionary body can change it. Partial edge: owners and the market may not know a lot has gone quiet. Right: fee title to tagged lots can be bought from discouraged owners, which fits the bought-not-free test. But owners anchor on hope value and takings-claim value, so the price is not ~$0.
scored.right_bought: Fee title to hazard-designated vacant lots, bought from owners. It is a real purchased right. In the high-value markets, though, the lots are few: Rancho Palos Verdes has 132 privately owned lots across its whole landslide area, and about 31 unentitled lots in Zone 2.
scored.buyer: Infill homebuilders and individual custom-home buyers in coastal California. They pay market prices only for lots that are already entitled and insurable. Insurability and lender appetite for former slide areas is a second gate after the permit.
scored.ladder: From lot flipping to building homes on de-risked lots, then to geologic hazard abatement districts and slope stabilisation, then to a hazard-land developer or REIT. This is a niche real-estate roll-up, capped by the small number of high-value tagged lots. It is not a path to a trillion-dollar chain, and the higher rungs (construction, stabilisation) are capital-heavy commodity work.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is a discretionary political act, not a measurement. A hazard designation comes off through legislation, litigation or a regulator's exception, and regulators trend toward permanent bans: Rancho Palos Verdes made its moratorium permanent in 2025. InSAR evidence of a few quiet years does not change that decision, and it cannot prove the factor of safety that permits require for episodic slides. Where regulators do not ban building (PA, OH, IL mine subsidence; Florida sinkholes), there is no big discount to capture.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails the same way geothermal in coal mines fails: entitlement, not discovery, is the hard part. The outcome lives in a legible regulator field that only politics can flip. And the big step-up exists only in a handful of coastal California slide zones, where regulators are moving toward permanent bans.
sources: Note: web search budget was exhausted before PA/FL subsidence-lot pricing could be verified; those multiples are estimates

scored.name: Plumebug: PFAS-defluorinating cultures from aged AFFF plumes
scored.one_line: Buys exclusive sampling and strain-ownership rights at old firefighting-foam sites. ML over consultant groundwater reports finds plumes where PFOS/PFHxS mass falls along the flowpath faster than sorption and dilution explain. A cheap microcosm that shows fluoride release turns that site into the first proven PFAS-eating culture, which the PFAS liability holders (3M, Chemours, DuPont, DoD) and remediation majors pay for.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive bioprospecting and culture-ownership agreement (sampling plus all derived strains) from the private owner of an aged AFFF-impacted site (small airport, refinery tank farm, fire-training ground, rural landowner next to a base). About $2-10k, because to the owner the site is a liability and the microbes are invisible.
scored.proving_step: Anaerobic and aerobic microcosms or flask enrichments on site soil and groundwater, spiked with PFOS/PFOA. A hit is measured fluoride-ion release with fluorine mass balance (ISE plus 19F-NMR or LC-MS/MS) above abiotic controls. About $5-15k and 6-12 weeks a site. The base rate of real biotic defluorination is very low (<1%), so ML ranking is the lever.
scored.proven_buyer: PFAS liability holders: 3M ($10.3B water settlement), Chemours, DuPont, Corteva. Also the DoD (ESTCP/SERDP, about 700 AFFF sites), remediation majors (Jacobs, AECOM, Montrose, Geosyntec/SiREM) and Allonnia (Ginkgo-backed). Precedent: SiREM's KB-1 TCE-dechlorinating consortium came out of one Ontario contaminated site and became the industry-standard bioaugmentation product.
scored.public_data: California GeoTracker PFAS/ESI uploads (huge, partly scanned consultant PDFs); Michigan EGLE PFAS site files; Minnesota MPCA and New York DEC PFAS site reports; DoD AFFF Preliminary Assessment/Site Inspection reports; EPA UCMR5 PFAS results; USGS NWIS groundwater chemistry. The signal is hidden in the ratios of precursors to terminal acids and the attenuation along the plume. No regulator writes 'biodegrading here' into a field.
scored.rough_step_up: $5-10k right to a $10-50M license or acquisition for the first verified PFOS-defluorinating culture: about 10^3-10^4. Each hit gives the buyer avoided treatment cost on sites that cost $10-100M each.
scored.frame: The proposed rung is "a verified PFAS-defluorinating culture isolated from one AFFF plume." Discovery share is genuinely high (ranking plumes + enrichment is ~90% of the work; the microcosm is a $5-15k bench step), so the discovery/physical ratio looks Terranox-like. But the rung is not discrete or sellable: a culture is unregistered IP, not a titled right, and no arms-length market clears on "a culture." The real object a capitalised buyer (3M, Chemours, DoD) will pay for is a permitted, field-demonstrated remedy with verified fluorine mass balance at site concentrations — which means scaling an acidic, iron-reducing, 100-day-half-life process into an in-situ or ex-situ treatment train. That scale-up is harder than the finding, which is the geothermal-plant-in-a-coal-mine failure mode exactly. C1 = 1.
scored.step_up: Claimed $5-10k access agreement to $10-50M license (10^3-10^4). No observed transaction supports it. The closest real comparable, Acidimicrobium sp. A6 (Huang & Jaffe 2019, PubMed 31529965), is the single best-known PFOA/PFOS-defluorinating organism in existence; it has been published for ~7 years out of Princeton with SERDP and NIEHS funding and has produced no disclosed license, acquisition or product at any price. Allonnia (Ginkgo-backed) is the best-capitalised buyer in this exact space and has raised ~$30M Series A plus a $30M extension (businesswire 2023); its disclosed PFAS activity is a distribution deal for OPEC Systems' SAFF foam fractionation (a physical separation technology, not biology) and a 2-year ESTCP SAFF demonstration — i.e. the capitalised buyer is buying separation hardware, not cultures, and no strain-license value is disclosed anywhere I could find. The SiREM KB-1 precedent is a consumables/service product line inside Geosyntec, not an asset revaluation event. Step-up observable on the purchased right: ~1x. My estimate of realistic value accruing to the site right specifically: near zero, because value attaches to the strain/enzyme patent, which the site agreement does not secure. C2 = 1.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base rate is genuinely very low and the attempt is genuinely cheap, which is the candidate's strongest leg. SERDP's 2018 biodegradation call awarded $2.75M across five projects (Jinxia Liu/McGill, Peter Jaffe/Princeton, Yujie Men/UC Riverside, Bruce Rittmann/ASU, Pedro Alvarez/Rice; SERDP FY2020 SON and news items). After ~8 years of that work the field's state of the art is 11.5-56.9% removal of perfluoroalkyl acids over 120 days under engineered Fe(III)/NH4+ feammox conditions (J. Hazard. Mater. 2024), and a Rice-hosted Nov 2025 review still states the defluorination mechanism remains unresolved. So "<1% of sites yield a real biotic defluorinator" is plausible; cost per attempt $5-15k and 6-12 weeks is realistic (consistent with commercial microcosm treatability study pricing, my estimate). The problem: the Terranox lever requires the failures to be *search* failures. Here they look like *thermodynamic/biochemical* failures — the C-F bond is the strongest in organic chemistry and the organism may simply not exist in most geochemistry at any abundance. If the true base rate is ~0 rather than 0.5%, 1/base-rate is not a lever, it is division by zero. Also, 19F-NMR/ISE fluorine mass balance on real site matrices is notoriously false-positive-prone (background fluoride, mineral dissolution), so some fraction of "hits" will not survive replication. C3 = 2.
scored.data: Strong on the illegibility test, weak on the inference test. California GeoTracker ESI/PFAS uploads, Michigan EGLE PFAS site files, MPCA, NY DEC and DoD PA/SI reports are genuinely huge, partly scanned, consultant-authored PDFs, and no regulator writes a "biodegradation occurring" status field — this is the opposite of the prior failures where the outcome was already in a legible column. That is a real 4 on data illegibility. But the target variable is not recoverable from it. The claimed signal (PFOS/PFHxS mass falling faster than sorption and dilution explain) is confounded by the dominant process at every AFFF site: biotransformation of polyfluorinated precursors (fluorotelomers, AFFF betaines) *into* terminal PFOS/PFOA, which makes terminal-acid mass rise and fall for reasons unrelated to defluorination. Add chain-length-dependent sorption and matrix diffusion, unknown source strength and release history, non-standard analyte lists across decades of reports, and inconsistent detection limits, and the label is unmeasurable even in principle from these files. Expected ML edge: small, and unvalidatable before spending the microcosm money. On the right-purchase half: a $2-10k exclusive sampling agreement is cheap and owners will sign, but it buys no exclusivity over anything that matters.
scored.right_bought: A private landowner's signature on an access-and-derived-strain agreement. This is the structural break with Terranox. A mineral claim is a registered, excludable, transferable title over a unique volume of rock; a microbe is not. The agreement cannot exclude: regulators and the site's own consultants who sample the same monitoring wells, the owners of every adjacent parcel the plume crosses, the ~700 DoD AFFF sites that SERDP/ESTCP investigators already sample freely, or any lab that isolates a functionally equivalent organism from similar iron-rich acidic geochemistry anywhere on earth. Enforceable exclusivity would have to come from a patent on the strain, the consortium or the rdhA-type dehalogenase — which is won in a lab and at the USPTO, not bought from a landowner for $5k, and which five well-funded academic groups are already racing for. The purchased "right" is therefore decorative: it protects nothing about the asset that holds the value.
scored.buyer: Nominally capitalised and real: 3M ($10.3B public water settlement), Chemours, DuPont, Corteva, DoD (ESTCP/SERDP, ~700 AFFF sites), Jacobs, AECOM, Montrose, Geosyntec/SiREM, Allonnia. But none of them buys the output of this rung. They buy permitted remedies with demonstrated field performance and regulatory sign-off on destruction. Allonnia, the one buyer explicitly built to buy biology, is in practice distributing SAFF separation hardware for its DoD/ESTCP work. So the buyer is capitalised for the top of the ladder, not for this rung's deliverable — the raw-dollars arithmetic that makes Terranox work (developer in for $40k/ha, collects $100k/ha) has no analogue here, because a lab culture has no per-site dollar value until the treatment train exists.
scored.ladder: Real and the best part of the thesis: proven culture to patented bioaugmentation consortium to consumable product (the KB-1 path) to in-situ treatment contracts to owning PFAS liability transfer on sites that cost $10-100M each. That is four or five genuine rungs with increasing capital intensity, and the SiREM-into-Geosyntec history shows the climb happens. Capped at 3 because the ladder is a products-and-services ladder with remediation-sector margins, not a resource-ownership ladder, and the top rung (buying PFAS liability) is a balance-sheet business that a strain does not privilege you to win.
scored.fatal_flaw: The unproven right is not excludable. A $2-10k landowner sampling agreement confers no ownership of a microorganism, its genes or its enzymes — exclusivity in biology comes from a strain/enzyme patent won in a lab against five already-funded academic groups, not from a site title — so even a confirmed hit does not give the company an asset it alone can sell, and the 10^3-10^4 step-up cannot be captured. Compounding it: the label ML would predict (biotic defluorination along a flowpath) is unrecoverable from consultant PFAS reports because precursor-to-terminal-acid transformation and chain-length sorption dominate the mass signal, so the ranking edge is likely near zero on top of a base rate that may be zero for scientific rather than search reasons.
scored.one_line_reason: Genuinely illegible public data and a cheap, low-base-rate proving step, but the thing being bought cannot be owned exclusively and the thing buyers pay for is a field-permitted remedy, so the step-up leaks entirely to patents and scale-up the company has no edge in.
sources: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31529965/ - Huang & Jaffe, defluorination of PFOA/PFOS by Acidimicrobium sp. strain A6: up to 60% removal over 100-day incubations; the canonical and still essentially only organism of its kind

https://pfascentral.org/science/us-department-of-defense-funded-research-on-treatment-of-per-and-polyfluoroalkyl-substance-laden-materials - DoD-funded PFAS treatment research; $2.75M awarded across five biodegradation projects from the 2018 call

https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/blogs.rice.edu/dist/3/1390/files/2025/11/441.pdf - Rice-hosted Nov 2025 review: microbial defluorination mechanisms remain unresolved

https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20230712559399/en/With-New-30M-Series-A-Extension-Allonnia-Takes-Aim-At-Scaling-Solutions-to-the-World%E2%80%99s-Toughest-Environmental-Challenges - Allonnia $30M Series A extension; the best-capitalised potential buyer of a PFAS culture

scored.name: Anomaly Fields: nitrogen-fixing and stress endophytes from overperforming farms
scored.one_line: Uses satellite time series to find fields that keep high canopy nitrogen and yield under low fertiliser or drought, against soil- and weather-adjusted expectations. Buys strain rights from those farmers, proves nitrogen fixation or stress tolerance in a cheap assay, and sells the strains to ag-biologicals majors.
scored.unproven_right: Sampling plus exclusive ownership of isolated microbes from a farmer's field (rhizosphere and endophytes), at $1-5k a field. The farmer has no way to know his yield anomaly is microbial.
scored.proving_step: Isolate the strains, then run an acetylene reduction assay, 15N incorporation, and N-free gnotobiotic pot trials (or drought-stress pots). About $2-5k a field. The base rate of commercially strong diazotrophs is low (<1%).
scored.proven_buyer: Pivot Bio, Corteva Biologicals, Bayer (Ginkgo JV legacy), Syngenta Biologicals, Novonesis and UPL. They acquire biological strains and companies at high multiples. Caveat: the biggest checks usually wait for field trials, so payment at the proof stage is smaller.
scored.public_data: Sentinel-2/Landsat archives (huge, illegible); USDA NASS Cropland Data Layer; USDA RMA crop-insurance yields by county and unit; SSURGO soils; PRISM weather; state nutrient-management plan filings. The outcome is hidden in plant physiology and is not summarised anywhere.
scored.rough_step_up: $3k right to $0.3-3M at greenhouse proof, rising to $10-30M after field validation: about 10^2-10^3 at proof. Weaker on C2 than PFAS.
scored.frame: The rung would be sampling, isolating and greenhouse-proving one field's microbes. Inside that rung, discovery is about 70-80% of the work and the physical step (sampling, ACC/ARA assays, 15N, gnotobiotic pots) is cheap. The problem is that no buyer pays much at the end of this rung. Majors pay real money only after multi-site, multi-season field trials (2-3 seasons, estimated $0.2-1M+). Inside that larger rung, discovery is well under 50% of the work and the field trial is the hard, bespoke part. That is the same pattern as the geothermal counter-example, where the physical step dominates.
scored.step_up: Unproven right: $1-5k per field (the candidate's own figure; no market exists). Proven-in-greenhouse wild isolate: I found no disclosed single-strain ag deal. The only disclosed figures are platform-level: the Novozymes-Monsanto BioAg Alliance paid $300M upfront for a whole pipeline and capabilities, and the MustGrow-Bayer licence is worth an estimated $35-40M over years for a field-validated biocontrol technology. Dyadic's strain licence was $0.5M upfront for a non-ag production platform. My estimate for a greenhouse-only, likely unpatentable wild diazotroph is $0-100k. That is about 1-30x, not 10^3. Majors already hold libraries of tens of thousands to 100k+ isolates, so one more wild strain with a greenhouse result is close to a commodity. The candidate's $0.3-3M at greenhouse proof has no support I could find.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate is genuinely low. A 2016 maize study (PMC4705218) took 92 isolates through screening and 8 significantly enhanced maize growth parameters, so about 9% of pre-screened isolates were hits in the greenhouse. A nifH colony-PCR workflow in a nitrogen-fixation patent (US 11993778) started from about 1,000 colonies. For commercially strong diazotrophs, a rate under 1% is plausible (my estimate). Cost per attempt is about $2-5k per field (candidate's figure; plausible as an estimate). Greenhouse-to-field translation is notoriously poor, but I found no published rate (Indigo publishes none). The ML lever is weak. Field yield anomalies against soil and weather are dominated by management (hybrid, planting date, drainage, manure history), not by microbes. The satellite signal is a noisy proxy, so I would expect much less than a 10x enrichment of the hit rate. The bigger cost, field trials, is untouched by the ML.
scored.data: Sentinel-2, Landsat, CDL, SSURGO and PRISM are public and huge, but they are legible and widely used. Agronomic analytics firms (Climate FieldView, Indigo, Farmers Edge, academic yield-gap groups) already compute field-level yield anomalies. RMA unit-level yields are not public at field resolution. It is true that the microbial cause is not summarised in any field. But the anomaly-to-microbe link is weak, so the hidden data does not hold the answer the way assessment files hold drill results.
scored.right_bought: Weak to nonexistent. A farmer has no enforceable exclusive property in the microbe species in his soil. The same species (Kosakonia sacchari, Klebsiella variicola, Azospirillum and others) recur across many fields and continents. Wild isolates face product-of-nature limits: Funk Bros. v. Kalo Inoculant (1948) held natural bacterial combinations unpatentable, and post-Myriad USPTO practice requires markedly different characteristics. Pivot Bio's value comes from gene-edited, nitrogen-sensing-removed derivatives, not from the wild isolate. A competitor can sample the neighbouring field or a public culture collection and get an equivalent strain. So the $1-5k buys a contract, not a moat.
scored.buyer: Pivot Bio, Corteva Biologicals (Symborg, Stoller), Bayer (Ginkgo JV legacy), Syngenta Biologicals (Valagro), Novonesis (Novozymes plus Chr. Hansen), UPL NPP, AgBiome/Ginkgo and ENAI (Indigo's biologicals spin-out). They are capitalised, but they mostly discover in-house from large proprietary libraries. They pay serious money only for field-validated, registered or patent-protected products or whole platforms (Novozymes-Monsanto $300M upfront), not for greenhouse-stage wild isolates.
scored.ladder: A real ladder exists: strain library, then gene-edited proprietary strain, then field validation, then EPA/state registration, then fermentation and formulation, then distribution and branded product. Pivot Bio climbed it and raised more than $600M at a reported valuation of about $2B. The biologicals market is about $15-20B (estimate). But each rung above the first is dominated by engineering, field trials, regulation and channel, not discovery. And the first rung is not defensible, so winning it does not confer a ladder advantage.
scored.fatal_flaw: The asset being bought cannot be owned and is not where the value is. Wild soil microbes are non-exclusive: the same strains sit in neighbouring fields and in culture collections. They are largely unpatentable as found (Funk Bros. 1948). Majors already hold libraries of tens of thousands to 100k+ isolates and create value through gene editing and multi-season field trials. So a greenhouse hit gives at best about a 10x step-up, not 10^3-10^4, and no capitalised buyer pays at the proof rung.
scored.one_line_reason: Cheap assays and a low hit rate fit the shape, but the farmer cannot sell an exclusive right to ubiquitous, unpatentable wild microbes. Majors' strain libraries make greenhouse hits near-commodities, and the real step-up comes only after expensive field trials and engineering, where discovery is a small share of the work.

scored.name: Effluent Hunters: biocatalysts from treatment plants that quietly destroy hard chemicals
scored.one_line: Mines discharge-monitoring and permit records for industrial wastewater plants that remove recalcitrant compounds (1,4-dioxane, nylon/PU oligomers, acrylonitrile, sulfolane, PET monomers) far better than their design predicts. Buys the sludge and culture rights from the plant, proves the degrader in flasks, and sells the strains or enzymes.
scored.unproven_right: Purchase of activated sludge or biofilm samples plus exclusive rights to derived strains from the plant operator, at $1-10k. The plant pays to landfill this sludge and sees it as waste.
scored.proving_step: Flask enrichment on the target compound as sole carbon source, with GC/LC disappearance and 13C mineralisation. About $3-8k. Most anomalies turn out to be dilution or volatilisation, so the true hit rate is low.
scored.proven_buyer: Chemical producers facing new effluent limits (1,4-dioxane rules in New York and California), remediation firms for 1,4-dioxane plumes, enzyme companies and plastic recyclers (Carbios, Samsara Eco).
scored.public_data: EPA ECHO DMR data (legible numbers, but the anomaly needs influent and design modelling); NPDES permit applications and fact sheets (scanned PDFs); TRI releases; state pretreatment reports. The removal mechanism is never recorded.
scored.rough_step_up: $5k to $1-10M: about 10^2-10^3. 1,4-dioxane and nylon-oligomer degraders are the high cases.
scored.frame: The proposed rung is "buy sludge + exclusive rights to derived strains, prove a degrader in flasks, sell the strain/enzyme." The physical step really is trivial and cheap (flask enrichment, GC/LC, $3-8k per attempt — plausible, matches academic enrichment costs), so that half of C1 holds. But discovery is nowhere near 80% of the work in the rung that a buyer actually pays for. A flask-positive enrichment is not a sellable asset: between it and revenue sit isolate purification, kinetics at field-relevant concentrations (the binding constraint — ENV487 needs ~0.6 mg/L 1,4-dioxane to sustain steady-state biomass, far above the 10-50 ug/L plume concentrations that matter, per the 2024 propanotroph study and the Parsons low-concentration trial), scale-up and fermentation, field pilots, and for subsurface use state injection approval (TSCA 5(h)(4)/biotech rule for intergeneric strains). Carbios raised ~EUR114M and partnered with Novozymes for enzyme production, and Samsara Eco raised US$65M Series A+ — their money goes into enzyme engineering and scale-up, not into finding the wild organism. So discovery is maybe 20-30% of this rung, and the capitalised buyer is buying the 70% Terranox-style framing assumes away. No buyer writes a cheque against a flask result.
scored.step_up: Unproven right: $1-10k for sludge/biofilm plus a contractual assignment (candidate's own figure; credible — plants pay to dispose of waste sludge). Proven right: the candidate claims $1-10M. I could not find a single disclosed strain-license value. The only real anchors found: Carbios's stated model of upfront licence fees plus catalyst sales at roughly one PET plant per year (Edison note, amounts not disclosed), and the fact that comparable commercial bioaugmentation cultures (SiREM/ENV487, CL-OUT, SL-D) are sold per-litre of inoculum, not as asset sales. My estimate: a flask-proven wild isolate with no IP moat licenses for $0-250k upfront, and most of the value accrues only after years of development. That is ~10-50x on a multi-year horizon, not 10^3 immediately on a hit. Scored 2.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt $3-8k (candidate's figure; consistent with academic enrichment work — this is the problem, not the strength). Base hit rate: no published figure exists; my estimate is 5-20% of DMR anomalies surviving enrichment, since most apparent over-removal is stripping, volatilisation, dilution or sampling error, as the candidate concedes. That caps the ML lever at ~5-20x in principle. In practice the lever is near-worthless because the proving step is too cheap: at $5k a shot, screening every plausible plant in the US (a few hundred) costs $1-3M, which any incumbent remediation or enzyme firm can brute-force without any model. Terranox's lever exists because a drill hole costs ~$0.5-2M; here the economics invert. Scored 2.
scored.data: Mixed, and the useful half is the half ML cannot read. EPA ECHO DMR is fully legible structured numbers (influent and effluent, monthly, machine-readable API) — so the "anomalous removal" screen is a spreadsheet query any grad student can run, not an illegible-data edge. The genuinely illegible part is NPDES permit applications and fact sheets as scanned PDFs, plus state pretreatment reports, which is where design basis and unit-process configuration live. The candidate is right that removal mechanism is never recorded in any field — that is the one real Terranox-style gap. But the outcome variable is partly pre-summarised: DMR already states percent removal, and permit fact sheets state design removal, so the "anomaly" label itself is computable from legible data; ML only helps on the weak secondary question of which anomaly is biological. For 1,4-dioxane specifically, the literature has already enumerated the plants and sites where degraders were found (CB1190 from a Michigan industrial sludge, ENV487, strain 21198), so the top of the list is public.
scored.right_bought: This is where it breaks. You cannot own a wild microbe. A naturally occurring isolate is not patentable subject matter in the US absent engineering (Funk Brothers / Myriad; Chakrabarty required a man-made construct), so the "exclusive rights to derived strains" clause with the plant operator binds only that operator — it does not stop anyone from enriching the same organism from any of the thousands of plants treating the same compound, or from simply ordering the known one: Pseudonocardia dioxanivorans CB1190 is deposited as ATCC 55486 / DSM 44775 / JCM 13855 and shippable to anyone for a few hundred dollars. There is no scarce, excludable, transferable right to buy, so the $1-10k purchase buys a sample, not a claim. Contrast the mineral right, which is a registered exclusive title on a defined parcel. Scored 1.
scored.buyer: Named buyers are real but buy the wrong thing. Chemical producers facing new 1,4-dioxane limits (NY 1 ppb drinking-water MCL, California notification level) buy treatment outcomes under performance guarantee, not strains. Remediation firms (Parsons, Geosyntec/SiREM) already run their own culture programs — SiREM commercialises aerobic dioxane cultures and tested one at 10 and 50 ug/L, so the buyer is the incumbent competitor. Enzyme companies (Novozymes) and recyclers (Carbios, Samsara Eco) buy engineered enzymes they develop in-house via directed evolution; a wild isolate is the cheap input they already have. Verdict: capitalised, yes; willing to pay a 10^3 step-up for a flask result, no.
scored.ladder: Genuinely the strongest criterion. The rungs above are real and large: wild strain -> engineered enzyme -> own the effluent treatment contract (take-or-pay on a 1 ppb limit) -> own the depolymerisation/recycling plant. Carbios walked exactly this ladder from enzyme to owning a PET plant, which proves the chain exists and is worth hundreds of millions to billions. But every rung above the first is capital- and engineering-heavy, which is the opposite of the Terranox shape where the small rung is sellable on its own and the climb is optional. Scored 3.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no excludable right to buy. A wild microbe is not an ownable asset: natural isolates are unpatentable without engineering, the same organism can be enriched from any of thousands of comparable plants, and the known 1,4-dioxane degrader is already on the shelf as ATCC 55486. The $1-10k sludge purchase therefore conveys a sample, not title — so even a true hit cannot be fenced, and the 10^3 step-up has nothing to attach to. Compounding it, the proving step is so cheap ($3-8k) that an incumbent can brute-force the entire candidate list for ~$1-3M, leaving no room for an ML capex lever.
scored.one_line_reason: Cheap, clever discovery with no asset to own: the found organism is unpatentable and independently re-isolable, the DMR anomaly screen is a legible spreadsheet query rather than an illegible-data edge, and the buyers (SiREM, Novozymes, Carbios) are incumbents who spend their money on the engineering and scale-up that come after discovery — total 9/25.
sources: https://open.clemson.edu/all_dissertations/2710 (ENV487 mixed propanotrophic culture; nutrient addition required)

https://public.magnet.fsu.edu/AToth/NSF%20publication%20access/2024/05%20Newly%20Entered%20Pubs%20May%202024/2024_Isolation%20and%20Characterization.pdf (minimum 1,4-dioxane to sustain steady-state biomass: ENV487 0.6 mg/L, ENV425 1.0, 21198 1.3)
https://www.parsons.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/LaurenTurner_Jun2_H3.pdf (commercial aerobic dioxane culture tested at ~10 and 50 ug/L over 90 days)
https://patents.google.com/patent/US8241500 (bioaugmentation to remediate dioxane in groundwater; CL-OUT consortium)
https://www.edisongroup.com/research/commercial-revenues-in-2020-2/24720/ (Carbios licence model: upfront licence fees plus catalyst sales, ~one PET plant per year)
https://www.biofuelsdigest.com/bdigest/?p=139780 (Carbios ~EUR114M raise to build PET recycling plant)
