scored.name: Taq Again: thermostable and extremophile enzymes from privately owned extreme habitats
scored.one_line: Uses ML over remote sensing and scattered limnology and field reports to find privately owned hypersaline, alkaline, hot-effluent or acidic habitats with unusual chemistry. Buys exclusive sampling rights, proves extreme-condition enzymes in cheap activity assays, and licenses them to enzyme and diagnostics majors. The precedent is Taq polymerase from a Yellowstone hot spring, whose PCR rights Roche bought for $300M.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive bioprospecting and benefit-sharing agreement with the private landowner of a soda lake, salt pan, industrial hot-water outfall or ranch spring, at $2-10k. Abroad, Nagoya ABS permits are cheap but formal. Avoid geothermal energy framing entirely: this is sampling only, with no drilling.
scored.proving_step: Metagenome the samples, then express ML-ranked candidate genes and run activity assays at extreme temperature, pH or salt (polymerases, cellulases, lipases, CRISPR nucleases). About $5-20k a site. Most sites yield nothing novel.
scored.proven_buyer: Roche, Thermo Fisher, NEB, Qiagen (molecular enzymes); Novonesis and IFF (industrial enzymes). They pay upfront licenses for novel polymerases and nucleases.
scored.public_data: Landsat/ASTER spectral anomalies of water bodies, USGS NWIS water chemistry, state well and spring water-quality records, scanned 20th-century limnology surveys, and NCBI SRA metagenomes with poor metadata.
scored.rough_step_up: $5k to $1-50M per enzyme license: 10^2-10^4 with fat-tailed outcomes. The hit rate is low and the buyer is real.
scored.frame: The rung is: sampling right, then a characterised novel enzyme, then a license to an enzyme or diagnostics major. Picking the site is maybe 20-30% of the work in that rung. Most of the work is metagenomics, expression, characterisation, engineering to commercial spec, and patenting. Commercial polymerases are mostly engineered: Phusion is a Pfu-Sso7d fusion, Q5 is engineered, and Taq itself came out of a public ATCC culture. So the physical step is not trivial. Buyers pay for performance plus IP, not for where a sample came from. I estimate site discovery is under 30% of the value-creating work, well below the 80% bar.
scored.step_up: Unproven: about $2-10k for a site agreement (candidate's figure). Yellowstone-Diversa (1997) was $100k paid over 5 years plus 0.5-10% royalties, for one of the most valuable extreme habitats on Earth (CBD case study). Proven: the much-cited $300M Roche paid Cetus in 1991 bought the PCR process plus Taq patents, not an enzyme found on a site. Cetus got Taq as a $35 culture. Typical novel-enzyme license upfronts are rarely disclosed. I estimate $0.1-2M, with most hits going unlicensed. The expected value of a proven site is maybe 10-100x over $5k, not 10^3-10^4. And the uplift sits in the sequence and patent, not in the land right.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate puts the cost at $5-20k per site for metagenome plus expression and assays. I estimate the full cost to a licensable, characterised enzyme at $0.5-3M. I estimate the base rate of a commercially novel enzyme per site at well under 5%. Diversa/Verenium is the industry-scale test: it sampled extreme habitats worldwide for about 20 years, its revenue was "largely contract research" (Xconomy 2011), and BASF bought it in 2013 for about $62M EV. ML can rank sites, but most of the cost is downstream of site choice, so a 10x capex cut on discovery does not hold up.
scored.data: The signal is partly illegible: scanned limnology, NWIS chemistry, spectral anomalies. But the outcome, the gene sequences, is increasingly public and legible. NCBI SRA, MGnify and JGI IMG hold billions of sequences that anyone can mine without a site right. Generative protein models (for example Profluent's OpenCRISPR) design novel enzymes with no sampling at all. Microbes and gene families are cosmopolitan, so the same thermophile clades turn up in hot springs and outfalls across many owners. A US private land right is cheap, but it is not exclusive over the biology: a competitor samples a similar spring next door or uses public metagenomes.
scored.right_bought: Yes, at $2-10k from a private landowner (my estimate). In the US, private land has no ABS regime, so the right is just a property-access contract. But exclusivity over a site does not create exclusivity over an enzyme: the value lives in the patent on the sequence or engineered variant. The right buys a sample, not the asset that steps up.
scored.buyer: Roche, Thermo Fisher, NEB, Qiagen and Novonesis are real and capitalised. But they mostly engineer polymerases and nucleases in-house and buy rarely. Basecamp Research already runs this exact model: consent and benefit-sharing agreements at extreme-habitat sites in 19+ countries, a proprietary metagenomic database, and ML protein design. It is VC-funded and the clear incumbent. Earlier players include Diversa/Verenium (BASF), Amylomics and Swissaustral.
scored.ladder: The ladder could run from an enzyme license to own enzyme manufacturing and kits, then a diagnostics or reagents company. But that path is a crowded, low-margin reagents market (Taq sales were about $100M/yr per a 2007 estimate). Diversa tried to climb from discovery into products and ended up a $62M acquisition. There is no trillion-dollar chain, and owning more sites does not compound.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up does not attach to the right that gets bought. Microbial genes are cosmopolitan and increasingly public (SRA/MGnify) or designable de novo by protein language models. So an exclusive sampling right on one spring gives no exclusivity over the enzyme. The value sits in the sequence patent and the engineering, which anyone can reach without the land. Diversa/Verenium spent about 20 years on this exact thesis and sold for about $62M.
scored.one_line_reason: The buyers are real, but the bought right does not capture the value: the genes are found in many places and public databases, the proving work is mostly downstream engineering, Basecamp Research already does this, and Diversa's 20-year run ended in a $62M exit.

scored.name: Polymorph Keys (non-infringing solid forms for generic entry)
scored.one_line: For blockbuster drugs whose compound patent expires but whose solid-form patents block generics, buy distressed or orphaned salt, cocrystal and polymorph patent families or applications. Run ML crystal-structure prediction over public CSD data and the scanned prosecution histories to find a stable, bioequivalent, non-infringing form. A lab crystallisation and stability screen proves it, and Paragraph IV generic filers buy the form.
scored.unproven_right: Assignments of obscure or abandoned-for-fee solid-form patents and applications from small CROs and universities; otherwise the new form itself is filed rather than bought
scored.proving_step: Solid-form screen plus XRPD plus accelerated stability plus dissolution (~$50-150k). Thermodynamics, not a registrar, hides whether a viable form exists.
scored.proven_buyer: Generic and 505(b)(2) companies, for which first-filer exclusivity on a blockbuster is worth hundreds of millions
scored.public_data: Cambridge Structural Database, the FDA Orange Book, USPTO PAIR/Patent Center file wrappers (scanned prosecution histories), and PTAB IPR records
scored.rough_step_up: $100k proof to $10-100M licence (~10^2-10^3x). The rights purchase is weak, and the edge is partly service-like, so the company must keep the form IP to qualify. Ladder: form IP, then 505(b)(2) product ownership, then a specialty generics company.
scored.frame: The rung would be a validated, non-infringing solid form plus a patent on it, sold or licensed to an ANDA or 505(b)(2) filer. Inside that rung, finding the form is maybe 30-40% of the work. My estimate is that most of the cost and risk is legal: freedom-to-operate opinions, the 30-month stay, and Hatch-Waxman litigation, which typically costs several million dollars per case. The Katten review of 13 polymorph cases calls the area fact-specific and full of pitfalls for both sides. The rest is manufacturing scale-up and bioequivalence. The physical step is not trivial. You need GMP-reproducible crystallisation and proof that the form does not convert to the patented form during manufacture or storage, and that conversion is exactly what generics get sued over. So the 80%+ discovery frame does not hold.
scored.step_up: I found no published price for an unproven solid-form patent family; my estimate is low thousands to tens of thousands of dollars, or just filing fees if you file the form yourself. The proven value is the candidate's claimed $10-100M licence, which I could not verify. Search found no per-blockbuster first-filer value. The closest figures were about $870k for 30 extra days of exclusivity on average across 37 generic markets (Springer 2025, IQVIA data) and an FDA estimate of $363M per year in societal cost per delayed drug (2019 House report). The bigger problem is who captures that value. The 180-day exclusivity goes to the first Paragraph IV filer, not to whoever owns the form. A form patent cannot keep other generics out once the original-form patents expire. And the buyer could run its own roughly $100k screen instead. Realistic licence value, my estimate, is a royalty of about $1-10M on the rare winners, so roughly 10-100x on the $100k proof. Scored 2 to reflect that buyers can replicate the work.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt: my estimate is about $50-150k for screen plus XRPD plus stability plus dissolution, which matches the candidate's number. CROs (Ardena, Eurofins) do not publish prices; Eurofins runs 384-experiment high-throughput plates, and Ardena's enabling screen uses under 1.5 g of drug substance. Base hit rate for finding some new form: high, my estimate 50%+. Most small-molecule drugs have multiple polymorphs, salts or cocrystals, and screens usually find something. The hit rate for a form that is stable, bioequivalent, scalable, non-infringing and survives litigation is much lower but unknown; my estimate is 10-20%. Losses come mostly from the law and from conversion to the patented form, not from thermodynamics. ML crystal-structure prediction can trim the screen, but the screen is already cheap compared with the litigation. So ML might cut the lab portion of the cost 2-3x, not cut total proving cost 10x.
scored.data: The Cambridge Structural Database is structured, curated and licensed, so it is not illegible. Orange Book patent listings, PTAB records and Patent Center file wrappers are public and read routinely by every generic firm's IP department and by litigators. Generic companies already read prosecution histories on every target as standard Paragraph IV diligence. The outcome is also largely legible: the Orange Book lists form patents, and PTAB, district court and Federal Circuit decisions publish validity rulings (for example Salix v. Norwich 2024 on rifaximin, Grunenthal v. Alkem 2019 on tapentadol). The one signal that is truly hidden, whether a viable form exists, sits in thermodynamics, not in illegible documents. A cheap screen reveals it, so neither ML reading of documents nor crystal-structure prediction gives a durable edge.
scored.right_bought: Mostly not bought. The candidate itself says the new form would be filed rather than bought. Abandoned form applications from universities and CROs are rare, and after abandonment they become prior art, not purchasable rights. Owners of blocking form patents are brands, which will not sell to a generic-enabler. There is no pool of mispriced rights held by owners who cannot read their value, so there is no purchase discount to capture.
scored.buyer: Generic and 505(b)(2) companies (Teva, Sandoz, Viatris, Dr. Reddy's, Sun, Aurobindo, Hetero, MSN, Apotex) are well capitalised. But all of them keep in-house solid-state and IP teams that do design-around form work as a core competency. CROs also sell this as a service: Crystal Pharmatech, Solid Form Solutions, SSCI/Albany, Eurofins, Ardena, and XtalPi with crystal-structure prediction via XtalGazer. A buyer exists, but it pays service-level prices, not asset-level prices.
scored.ladder: Plausible rungs: form IP, then owning a 505(b)(2) product, then a specialty generics or specialty pharma company. The ladder is real but crowded, and each rung adds regulatory, manufacturing and litigation work rather than discovery. Specialty generics is a low-margin, consolidated industry. It is a path to a large company, not a trillion-dollar one.
scored.fatal_flaw: The capitalised buyer already does this itself. Every major generic company runs its own solid-form screen and file-wrapper review for each Paragraph IV target for about $100k, and CROs and XtalPi sell crystal-structure prediction as a service. The risk that sets the value is litigation and conversion to the patented form, not discovery. The 180-day exclusivity belongs to the first filer, not to the form's owner. So there is no frame where discovery is 80%+ of the work, there is no purchasable mispriced right, and owning the asset collapses into a service business.
scored.one_line_reason: Finding a viable solid form is cheap, usually succeeds, and generic firms already do it in-house. The value sits in litigation and in first-filer exclusivity, neither of which comes from owning the form, so there is no 10^3x discovery step-up to capture.

scored.name: Subrogated Cargo Wreck Rights (insurer-owned metal cargoes)
scored.one_line: Buy the ownership or salvage rights to unlocated WWI/WWII merchant wrecks carrying silver, tin, copper or nickel ingots from the war-risk insurers or governments that paid the loss. Use ML to cross-read scanned manifests, convoy logs and loss reports against public multibeam and side-scan archives to pin each wreck. Prove the wreck with a cheap ROV identification dive, then sell or JV the arrested wreck to a deep-ocean salvor or metals trader.
scored.unproven_right: Title or salvage contracts held by UK DfT (war-risk), US MARAD and Lloyd's syndicates, plus admiralty salvor-in-possession status. The Gairsoppa precedent priced these at about 20% to the owner and 80% to the salvor. Owners hand out contracts cheaply because they cannot locate the wrecks.
scored.proving_step: An ROV or AUV dive on the ML-ranked target box. It confirms hull ID (bell, hull form, cargo-hold signature) and sights the cargo, then the wreck is arrested in admiralty court. That costs roughly $0.3-1M per verified target, against $5-10M for a blind search today.
scored.proven_buyer: Deep-ocean salvors and recovery contractors, or metals traders and family offices that finance recoveries. They pay for a located, legally arrested, cargo-confirmed wreck.
scored.public_data: UK National Archives ADM/BT scanned convoy and casualty files, Lloyd's War Losses volumes, UKHO wreck database ('position approximate' and 'unlocated' entries), NOAA AWOIS/ENC wrecks, EMODnet and GEBCO bathymetry, NOAA NCEI multibeam and side-scan archives, IHO crowdsourced bathymetry.
scored.rough_step_up: Contract cost: about $0. Located wreck with cargo: $5-50M of net salvage value (Gairsoppa recovered about $38M of silver). That is about 10^3x on the location right, cleared once the wreck is located.
scored.frame: The pitched rung is "located, ROV-identified, arrested wreck with cargo sighted". That frame barely exists as something you can sell. For the deep silver wrecks that carry the value (Gairsoppa at ~4,700 m, City of Cairo at 5,150 m), the hard and costly part is recovering the cargo: bespoke deep-ocean salvage is the deepest work ever done. Finding the wreck is not the hard part, so this is the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern. Even the pitched proving step is not trivial. Confirming a wreck at 4-5 km needs a deep-tow sonar or AUV survey plus a work-class ROV from a ship costing tens of thousands of dollars a day (my estimate). My estimate is that discovery is ~20-40% of the work inside this rung, not 80%+. Buyers who pay for a located wreck alone are thin. Odyssey Marine and Deep Ocean Search both did their own search and recovery as one job under a single DfT contract. No market for selling located wrecks on to someone else turned up.
scored.step_up: Unproven side: the DfT salvage contract costs ~$0 upfront, but it is won by competitive tender (Gairsoppa contract tendered in 2010). The salvor keeps 80% of net salved value, after expenses are paid back out of the gross. Proven side: Gairsoppa produced ~2,792 ingots (Odyssey) and City of Cairo ~$50M of silver (gCaptain/Maritime Executive, 2015). A located-but-unrecovered wreck is only worth the option on a recovery costing tens of millions (my estimate), so its value is far below gross cargo value. The nominal 10^3x "from $0" is an artefact of the right being free. Against the actual spend (search plus ID dive, ~$0.3-1M), a located wreck's realisable value is plausibly 10-50x (my estimate) and depends on recovery economics.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate on well-documented targets looks HIGH, not low. Deep Ocean Search found City of Cairo after "several weeks" of searching in 2011. Odyssey found both Gairsoppa and Mantola in its 2011 campaign, and called the Mantola search low incremental cost. The archival positions from convoy and loss reports are already good enough for professionals. I found no public per-search cost. My estimate is $1-5M for a deep sonar search campaign, against the candidate's $5-10M. With base hit rate on prioritised targets at maybe 50%+ (my estimate), the lever is capped at ~2x, nowhere near 10x.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible: TNA ADM/BT files, Lloyd's War Losses, UKHO entries marked unlocated. But the outcome that matters is already written down in legible form. Cargo type and insured value are recorded in War Risk claim payouts: Gairsoppa paid £325,000 in 1941, and Mantola's ~600,000 oz claim is also recorded. Ownership is known (the state took the cargo rights by paying the claim), and approximate sinking positions sit in those same records. Incumbents (Odyssey's research department, DOS/John Kingsford, independent wreck historians) already do exactly this archival cross-reading. Only a tiny number of WWI/WWII wrecks carry high-value metal cargo at depth, and the best ones are already found and recovered.
scored.right_bought: The right is not bought cheaply from owners who cannot read the data. UK DfT runs competitive tenders, and the counterparty is a single sophisticated government seller that already knows what cargo it owns and roughly where it lies. Salvor-in-possession status needs physical possession plus continuous recovery effort, so it cannot be warehoused cheaply. US MARAD and Lloyd's syndicate rights are similarly concentrated. Some foreign (sovereign or warship) and UNESCO-sensitive wrecks are not available at all.
scored.buyer: Thin and undercapitalised. Odyssey Marine (OMEX), the main deep-cargo salvor, has a ~$284M accumulated deficit (2023), a going-concern warning, and a $22.2M working capital deficit (June 2026). It has pivoted away from shipwrecks to seabed minerals. Deep Ocean Search and Ocean Infinity are small private operators that run their own searches. Metals traders or family offices would be funding the recovery risk, not paying ~$10k/ha-style markups for a location. Raw dollars do not clearly work for the buyer once deep recovery costs are counted.
scored.ladder: Weak. The chain above (deep recovery, then refining and sale of ingots) is small and lumpy, with a few $20-50M events per decade globally. The obvious adjacent ladder is seabed mining, which is effectively the excluded mineral category and is where Odyssey went. Odyssey has tried to build the whole chain for 30 years, and the ceiling looks like a sub-$1B company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value sits in deep-ocean recovery at 4-5 km, which is bespoke and dominates cost, not in location. The few high-value silver wrecks are documented in claim records, owned by a government that tenders them competitively, and largely already found by incumbents (Odyssey, Deep Ocean Search). That leaves no cheap rights, no low base hit rate for ML to raise, and only a buyer pool that, going by Odyssey, has lost money doing this.
scored.one_line_reason: The pattern matches the geothermal counter-example: recovery, not discovery, is the hard and costly step. Cargo and ownership are already recorded in War Risk claim records, rights are competitively tendered, the few good targets are mostly taken, and the leading operator, Odyssey, lost ~$284M and pivoted.

scored.name: FlagTree (ridge wind from tree deformation in aerial imagery)
scored.one_line: Use ML on decades of public aerial and NAIP imagery to read wind-flagged tree crowns (the Griggs-Putnam index, nature's own century-long anemometer) on ridges and mountain gaps that coarse models smooth out. Option those ridges cheaply, prove them with a short LiDAR or mast campaign, and sell the proven site to a wind developer, who pays for the step-up.
scored.unproven_right: Wind easement options on private ridge and gap land (Appalachia, the Northern Rockies foothills, prairie escarpments) bought from timber and ranch owners at a few $/acre/yr.
scored.proving_step: A 6-12 month LiDAR or 60 m tilt-up mast (~$40-100k) to confirm the speed-up the flagging predicts. Physically trivial.
scored.proven_buyer: Onshore wind developers (Invenergy, Avangrid, Apex, Clearway) buying early-stage sites with bankable data.
scored.public_data: USDA NAIP 60 cm imagery (the whole US, every 2-3 years); USGS EarthExplorer scanned historical aerial photos back to the 1930s; USGS 3DEP LiDAR canopy point clouds (crown asymmetry); PNL's 1970s-80s ecological wind-indicator field studies (scanned). Flagging is a natural integral of wind that no registrar summarises.
scored.rough_step_up: About 30-100x on option cost (early-stage $20k/MW). Ridge sites face permitting and visual opposition, and blocks are small (50-150 MW). C2 about 3; the lever is perhaps 3-5x.
scored.frame: The rung would be a wind site with option-held land and a confirmed resource, sold to developers as an "early-stage" project. Inside that rung, finding the wind is maybe 20-30% of the work (my estimate). Buyers set early-stage value by interconnection position, permitting outlook, transmission, offtake and land assembly across many owners, not by the wind resource. Developers do not pay for a resource-only site. So the place where discovery would be 80%+ of the work is not a rung anyone buys. On ridges the permitting step is far from trivial: visual and ridge-protection opposition is fierce, and North Carolina's 1983 Ridge Law effectively bars tall structures on protected ridges. My estimate is that the share of value created by discovery is 25% or less.
scored.step_up: Unproven: wind options are $1.25-$40/acre/yr (SD PUC filing: $1.25/acre; ND legislature: $2-10; Landgate: $5-40; AES form: $12-20). A 100 MW ridge block on about 3,000-5,000 acres costs roughly $15-50k/yr in options (my estimate). Proven: Enerdatics puts the early-stage onshore wind premium at about $20k/MW, rising to at least $100k/MW at ready-to-build. 100 MW x $20k = about $2M, but buyers pay that for a site that also has interconnection and land control, not for mast data alone. Counting the full cost to get there (options plus a $50-100k mast or LiDAR campaign plus legal work, about $150-250k), the gain is about 8-15x. Measured against the option fee alone it is 40-100x, which overstates it. Prices are mostly milestone or earn-out payments, not paid up front, so this is not an immediate step-up on a hit. There is no jump from $1/ha to $10,000/ha.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step (a 60 m tilt-up mast or LiDAR for 6-12 months) costs about $40-100k, per the candidate and consistent with industry norms. On sites already screened with public tools (Global Wind Atlas at 250 m, NREL WIND Toolkit, CFD or WAsP run on public 3DEP elevation data), my estimate is that 40-60% of masts confirm a commercially viable mean speed. A base hit rate that high caps the lever near 2x, not 10x. The proving step is also cheap compared with the downstream costs that actually decide the project: interconnection studies and deposits of $1-10M+, and permitting.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible: NAIP 60 cm imagery, scanned USGS historical aerial photos, 3DEP LiDAR, and the PNL wind-indicator studies. My search found no published work applying ML to Griggs-Putnam flagging in aerial imagery, so the method itself is novel. But the outcome, ridge speed-up, is already largely legible from a different public dataset. Terrain-driven acceleration on ridges is exactly what microscale CFD and WAsP compute from public elevation models, and Global Wind Atlas, AWS Truepower/UL and Vaisala/3TIER already serve it at 50-250 m resolution. The Griggs-Putnam index is also coarse: seven bins of 1-2 m/s each. Bankability needs about ±0.2 m/s, because about 1 m/s changes energy output by about 30%. So flagging adds little information beyond public terrain models, and the extra precision gained is likely small.
scored.right_bought: The right can be bought cheaply: options at $1-40/acre/yr from timber and ranch owners. But the owners are not the ones lacking information, because every developer sees the same wind maps. Developers with field agents compete for the same parcels, and landowners can see nearby projects. Ridge sites also need contiguous assembly across several owners, so there is holdout risk.
scored.buyer: Onshore wind developers (Invenergy, Apex, Avangrid, Clearway, NextEra) and IPPs. They are well capitalised, but they buy early-stage sites for interconnection position and permitting status, not for resource data. In the US the buyer pool is also shrinking: wind tax credits are being phased out after the 2025 budget law (OBBBA) and federal wind permitting has turned hostile. Ridge blocks of 50-150 MW are small for these buyers.
scored.ladder: The ladder exists: site origination, then development (interconnection, permits, PPA), then construction, ownership as an IPP and operations. Developer to IPP is a proven path (Apex, Invenergy). But the bottom rung, resource-proven land, is not where the differentiation lies, so winning it does not give an edge higher up. The higher rungs are crowded, commoditised and capital-heavy.
scored.fatal_flaw: Wind resource is not the binding constraint, and it is not illegible. Developers already map ridge speed-up from public terrain data with CFD and wind atlases. Early-stage value ($20k/MW, rising to $100k/MW at ready-to-build) comes from interconnection position and permitting, not from proving the wind, and ridge sites are the hardest to permit. So the proving step is neither the bulk of the work nor the source of the step-up.
scored.one_line_reason: The resource signal is already largely captured by public terrain CFD and wind atlases. Masts confirm resource on screened sites often enough (about 50%, my estimate) that the lever is about 2x. And developers pay for interconnection and permits, not proven wind, which gives about a 10x gain on all-in cost, mostly as delayed milestone payments, on ridges that are hard to permit.
sources: https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/10/6/1915 (deformation index needs about 2 m/s correction in urban settings; species not accounted for)

scored.name: FirmSite (24/7 wind-solar complementarity campuses for AI data centers)
scored.one_line: Find rare off-grid sites where the nocturnal low-level jet and desert sun combine into anomalously firm renewable output (70-85% of hours covered with modest storage), using ML on radar and satellite archives. Option ranch land, prove hourly firmness with a 12-month LiDAR and pyranometer station, and sell the 'firm-power-proven' campus site to an AI data-center or power-first developer, who pays the step-up.
scored.unproven_right: Purchase options on 10-50k acres of ranch or BLM-adjacent private land (West Texas, eastern New Mexico, Wyoming, the Nevada basins) at $300-1,500/acre, from owners who see only grazing value.
scored.proving_step: A 12-month co-located LiDAR plus pyranometer and ceilometer campaign (~$200k) that yields a bankable hourly joint wind-solar time series and a firmness certificate. Cheap, but the buyer's later build is a heavy bespoke behind-the-meter GW plant (the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure mode).
scored.proven_buyer: Behind-the-meter AI campus developers and hyperscalers (Crusoe, Intersect Power/Google, Lancium, Stargate partners), now paying $20-100k+/acre for sites with a credible power story.
scored.public_data: NEXRAD VAD profiles; GOES-16/18 cloud and irradiance archive (NSRDB is modelled and summarises mean GHI, not joint hourly firmness with wind at 200 m); MADIS aircraft winds; scanned BLM and state land records for parcel ownership.
scored.rough_step_up: Roughly 20-100x ($500/acre to $10-50k/acre for a power-proven campus). Buyer appetite is strong now, but value depends on the build and on interconnection-free economics. C2 about 3-4, C1 is weakened by the bespoke build, and C5 is very strong (land, power, compute).
scored.frame: The rung is "option the land, run a 12-month LiDAR plus pyranometer campaign, sell the site with a firmness certificate". Inside that rung, discovery is maybe 30-40% of the value the buyer actually pays for (my estimate). The buyer is paying for deliverable GW-scale power: the GW of wind, the GW of solar, 2-4 h of storage over 10,000+ acres (Bloomberg/Intersect benchmark), and in practice gas backup. Lancium and Crusoe at Abilene use on-site gas turbines for 24/7 reliability even at one of the windiest US sites. The physical step is not trivial or abstracted: it is the bespoke behind-the-meter plant. That is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure mode. A firmness certificate on its own is not a product anyone has been seen buying.
scored.step_up: Unproven: ranch land at the candidate's own $300-1,500/acre. Proven: I found no comparable sale of a "firmness-proven" site. Real data-center land comps in Texas are about $2,200/acre for bitcoin-to-data-center conversions (oilprice.com) and $8,000/acre for 1,040 acres of El Paso city land (Bisnow). Taylor TX sold at about $115k/acre, but that is a small 87-acre parcel near a utility, an outlier. For large ranch parcels that gives roughly 3-15x. That step-up is driven by announcements and interconnection, and the measurement campaign would not create it. The LandBridge/PowerBridge Reeves County deal was structured as a lease option, not a sale at a premium. The candidate's 20-100x is not supported by these comps. My estimate is about 5x on a hit.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I found no public dollar figure for a campaign. My estimate is ~$150-250k per 12-month LiDAR station plus irradiance sensors. RES/Vaisala report standalone LiDAR as 37% cheaper than a met mast. The base hit rate is high, not low. NREL's 2022 study of more than 1.7M CONUS locations found most non-mountainous locations show hourly wind-PV complementarity. Measurement campaigns mostly confirm modelled P50s within roughly 5-10% (my estimate from standard WRA practice). They are confirmatory, not discovery shots that mostly fail. With a base hit rate likely above 50%, the lever is capped below 2x, nowhere near 10x. The campaign is also already cheap relative to the land, so cutting its cost moves little.
scored.data: The signal is not illegible. NREL WIND Toolkit gives modelled hourly (5-min for wind) speeds at 10-200 m for all of CONUS, free under CC-BY. NSRDB gives hourly irradiance. ERA5 and HRRR are open too. NREL has already published hourly wind-PV complementarity for more than 1.7M locations, so the outcome is effectively summarised already in a legible public product. Developers (Intersect, NextEra, Lancium) run exactly this screening in-house. NEXRAD VAD and GOES add only marginal resolution on low-level-jet structure.
scored.right_bought: Options on private ranch land can be bought, but owners are no longer blind. The West Texas "AI land rush" is widely reported (oilprice.com, Bisnow). Taylor County median land prices are more than double the statewide rural average. Brokers list "data center sites" on Crexi. The purchase discount from owners who cannot read the data is mostly gone, and the price is set by power and interconnection stories, not by firmness.
scored.buyer: The buyers named are real and capitalised: Google/Intersect (acquired for ~$4.75B), Crusoe/Lancium, Stargate partners, LandBridge/PowerBridge. But they buy powered land: interconnection, gas access, water, fibre, and their own generation development. Each runs its own resource assessment, and none has been seen paying a premium for a third-party firmness certificate. Intersect and Lancium are themselves the vertically integrated competitors doing this rung.
scored.ladder: The ladder is strong in principle: land, then generation development (wind/solar/storage), then powered shell, then compute campus operations. Intersect's ~$4.75B exit to Google shows the top of the ladder is valuable. But incumbents already sit on the higher rungs, and the bottom rung offers no defensible discovery edge.
scored.fatal_flaw: The outcome is already public and legible. NREL's WIND Toolkit and NSRDB hourly data, plus NREL's published complementarity analysis of 1.7M sites, show complementarity is common, not rare. Value comes from the bespoke GW behind-the-meter build plus gas backup, not from discovery. So there is no hidden 10^3x hit to find and no low base hit rate for ML to lift.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is a small share of value here: the firmness signal is already mapped in free NREL hourly datasets, the measurement campaign almost always confirms the models, land comps show about 5x rather than 10^3x, and buyers pay for the GW plant and interconnection, not the certificate.

scored.name: Senior Water (surface-water rights proven by historic irrigation imagery)
scored.one_line: Buys undervalued senior surface-water rights on the Colorado Front Range and in the West from farm owners whose decrees carry abandonment risk or an unquantified historic consumptive use. ML over 60 years of archival imagery (CORONA, USGS aerial photos, Landsat NDVI/ET) quantifies historic irrigated acreage, the proof a water court needs to approve a change of use, and the proven rights go to municipalities. This is surface rights, not groundwater exploration.
scored.unproven_right: Agricultural ditch shares and decreed rights with an undocumented historic consumptive use, priced at an agricultural discount because the owner cannot prove what was actually used.
scored.proving_step: An ML reconstruction of historic irrigated area and evapotranspiration from imagery, then filing in water court with an engineer's report. Proving is mostly data work and the physical step is none.
scored.proven_buyer: Front Range municipalities and water districts (Aurora, Thornton, Northern Water) paying $30-70k per acre-foot for transferable consumptive use.
scored.public_data: The USGS aerial photo archive, declassified CORONA, Landsat/OpenET, and scanned ditch-company ledgers and water-court decrees at Colorado DWR/CDSS. Partly legible: the decree is in a registry, but actual historic use exists only in imagery.
scored.rough_step_up: About 3-10x (an agricultural right at $5-15k/AF becomes a municipal transferable right at $30-70k/AF). Large absolute dollars, but a weak multiple. This is the honest low end.
scored.frame: The rung is: buy agricultural ditch shares, get a water-court change-of-use decree, and sell the transferable consumptive use (CU) to a city. Imagery-based reconstruction of historic consumptive use (HCU) is only part of the work, maybe 20-30% (my estimate). Most of it is adversarial litigation with objectors, and that can take years (Colorado Judicial Branch guidance: at least 3 months uncontested, years when opposed). The physical steps are not trivial either: dry-up covenants, revegetation and return-flow obligations. The buyer does have capital (Aurora, Thornton, Northern Water and others), but those cities run the same change cases in-house all the time. Proving is not the 80%+ of the work it is in Terranox's rung.
scored.step_up: About 3-10x at best, so no 10^3 jump. Proven, municipal-grade water: Colorado-Big Thompson units cost about $57,487/AF in 2025 per Northern Water's historical price table, or about $85,000/AF per WestWater Research (peak $101k in 2022). The Feb 2024 Hall and Hall auction cleared at about $52-75k/AF. The unproven agricultural price (my estimate) is $5-20k/AF of consumptive use for native ditch shares, and less in remote basins. On the Front Range, many native shares already trade near municipal value because cities are the marginal buyers. The FRICO case also shows the proving step can cut the yield: the water court sharply reduced HCU, so the proven quantity can come out smaller than the decreed paper right.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Change cases rarely fail outright. Most end in a decree, but with an HCU haircut (FRICO, Busk-Ivanhoe) or a denial for poor proof (Boulder County v. Boulder & Weld County Ditch, Ready Mixed Concrete). Base hit rate on getting some decree is roughly 80-90% (my estimate). The uncertain part is the haircut size, not a yes/no hit, so the 1/base-hit-rate cap limits the lever to about 1.2x. Cost per attempt is roughly $100k-$1M+ in legal and engineering fees and 1-5+ years (my estimate; searches found no published dollar figures). That cost is mostly litigation, which ML does not shrink 10x.
scored.data: This is the weak point. Much of what the candidate calls the hidden signal is already in legible public form. Colorado Decision Support Systems (CDSS) publishes GIS irrigated-parcel layers for many years (e.g. 1956, 1976, 1987, 1993, 2001, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020) with crop type and ditch assignment. HydroBase holds structure-level diversion records going back decades. OpenET publishes field-scale ET for free. Consulting engineers already use aerial photos in HCU reports as standard evidence, and courts weigh old imagery skeptically (Kruse Partnership v. Cotten threw out a 1936 photo). The answer is largely in legible fields already, which is the same failure pattern earlier hunts found. Can the right be bought cheaply? Partly: rights are bought, not claimed first-come. But sellers are farmers with brokers (WestWater, Hall and Hall auctions) and cities bidding directly, so the price is not set by people who cannot read the data.
scored.right_bought: Agricultural ditch shares and decreed rights bought from irrigators. The transaction is real, but the market is fairly efficient: brokers, auctions and cities buy directly, and the published market prices (Northern Water C-BT data) reach the sellers.
scored.buyer: Front Range municipalities and water districts (Aurora, Thornton, Greeley, Northern Water members). They have capital, but they buy agricultural water directly and run their own change cases, so an intermediary takes only a thin margin.
scored.ladder: Moderate ladder: aggregation of water rights, storage and reservoirs, then wholesale water utility and leasing (alternative transfer methods, drought leases). Two Rivers Water Company tried a similar plan in Colorado. The total market is large, but it is limited by regulation and local politics ("buy and dry" backlash), so there is no clear path to a trillion-dollar company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is not a low-probability binary hit. It is a mostly-successful but drawn-out adversarial water-court case. Its key input, historic irrigated acreage and diversions, is already legible in the CDSS irrigated-parcel GIS layers, HydroBase diversion records and OpenET, and engineering firms already use it. That leaves only a 3-10x spread and an ML hit-rate lever of about 1.2x.
scored.one_line_reason: The absolute dollars are large ($50-85k/AF proven), but the step-up is only 3-10x, change cases mostly succeed (so there is little hit-rate lever), and historic use is already published in CDSS/HydroBase/OpenET, so ML extracts no hidden edge. Total about 9/25.

scored.name: Uplandia: wetland-mapped parcels that are dry land after Sackett
scored.one_line: Buys land that the National Wetlands Inventory marks as wetland, which owners price as unbuildable at about $300-1,500/acre. ML on LiDAR, Sentinel-1/2 hydroperiod and soils finds tracts with no continuous surface connection to a navigable water. A cheap delineation plus a USACE Approved Jurisdictional Determination (AJD) proves the land is not WOTUS. Homebuilders and industrial or data-center developers pay entitled-land prices for it.
scored.unproven_right: Fee title or an option on rural or peri-urban acreage mapped as NWI wetland, or held back by an old preliminary JD. Owners and their brokers treat it as unbuildable and sell it at a deep discount.
scored.proving_step: A field wetland delineation (about $3-10k per tract) plus a USACE AJD request, which costs nothing to file and takes about 60-120 days. Since Sackett v. EPA (2023), many mapped wetlands no longer meet the 'continuous surface connection' test. The ML ranks which tracts flip. An AJD is valid for 5 years, which makes the asset transferable.
scored.proven_buyer: Public homebuilders (Lennar, DR Horton, which hold land through option banks), industrial REITs and data-center developers. They already pay $20-150k/acre for entitled sites in Sunbelt growth corridors.
scored.public_data: USFWS National Wetlands Inventory polygons (mapped from 1980s air photos and badly outdated); USGS 3DEP LiDAR DEMs; Sentinel-1 SAR inundation time series; NRCS SSURGO hydric-soil ratings; USACE RIBITS and posted AJD memoranda (scanned PDFs on district sites, which serve as training labels); county parcel and sales data.
scored.rough_step_up: About 20-200x per acre, from $500-1,500/acre for 'wetland' to $30-100k/acre for developable land in growth counties. Below 10^3, but about 50x is typical and the proof costs under 1% of the uplift. Weakness: the NWI status field records an outcome, but it is stale, so the edge is the gap between the map and reality. Regulatory regime risk if WOTUS is redefined again.
scored.frame: The rung is "buy mapped wetland, get an AJD, resell it to a developer," and the rung exists. But in that rung discovery is not 80%+ of the work. Whether a parcel is federally jurisdictional is the cheap part: a delineation runs about $3-10k (the candidate's own figure), and Sackett plus the November 2025 proposed rule have made the answer obvious for most isolated wetlands. Three other things decide whether a homebuilder pays $30-100k/acre: zoning and entitlement, utilities, and location. Those are slow, bespoke and political, which is the same shape as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example (my estimate: discovery is about 10-25% of the work of turning rural NWI acreage into "developable land"). Also, the buyers (Lennar and DR Horton through option banks, industrial REITs) buy entitled or entitleable sites, not "non-WOTUS rural land."
scored.step_up: The quoted 20-200x mixes two things: the value of the jurisdiction flip and the value of being in a growth corridor with zoning. What the flip alone is worth is much smaller. A Louisiana hedonic study found a parcel that is 50% wetland sells for only about 1% less than one with no wetland (TRERC/TAMU). A New York appraiser cited $1,000-6,000/acre for wetland acreage, and another cited $3,500-7,500/acre in larger parcels (Main Street Mag), against nearby upland that is often in the low tens of thousands. Lawley (2014) found prairie pothole acres discounted but with no step function. My estimate for the uplift from the flip alone is 2-10x on the wetland acres, and about 1-3x on whole parcels where the market has already priced uncertainty rather than treating the land as unbuildable. The real cost a JD avoids is mitigation of up to about $1M per impacted acre (Taft Law), and that is avoided cost, not land you buy for $1 that becomes $10,000.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is cheap, and after Sackett it mostly succeeds, which is the reverse of what this lever needs. The EPA and Corps regulatory impact analysis for the November 2025 proposed rule projects an 81% decrease in wetland acreage under federal jurisdiction (EPA fact sheet; ASDWA). On that basis the base flip rate for NWI wetlands with no adjacency is plausibly 50-80% (my estimate). A delineation costs $3-10k and filing the AJD is free, though it takes 60-120 days or more, and the Corps paused AJDs entirely in 2023. With a base hit rate of 0.5 or higher, the lever is capped at about 2x, and capex per attempt is already trivial. ML adds little beyond a rules filter: NWI polygon, distance to an RPW, and an adjacency/abutment test on 3DEP.
scored.data: The inputs are public and mostly legible: NWI, 3DEP LiDAR, SSURGO hydric ratings and Sentinel-1. The AJD memos are scanned PDFs on district sites (for example Vicksburg's 2025 Pre-2015-regime AJDs), so they are somewhat illegible and usable as labels. But the outcome is effectively in a legible field already. NWI polygon plus adjacency to a relatively permanent water is the legal test itself, and anyone can run it in GIS, so a lookup table will roughly match the ML, as it did with interconnection queues. The bigger problem is the counterparty. Sophisticated buyers never relied on NWI; they routinely order delineations. Rural sellers in growth corridors sell through brokers to the same developers who run those delineations. And Sackett is the most widely publicised wetlands event in 50 years, so there is no information asymmetry to buy against. State wetland programs (NY, NJ, MI, MN, WI, CA, FL, VA and others) keep many of these acres regulated whatever the federal answer. Finally, the regime is in flux: the 2023 conforming rule, the 2025 proposal, and possible future reversal.
scored.right_bought: Yes, fee title or options bought from private owners, which fits the "bought, not free first-come" condition. But there is no proven deep discount. The hedonic evidence above suggests the market discounts wetland only partly, and the parcels with the largest uplift (peri-urban Sunbelt) are exactly where land brokers and homebuilder acquisition teams already compete.
scored.buyer: The buyers are capitalised: public homebuilders through land banks, industrial REITs and data-center developers. But they pay entitled-land prices for entitled land, not for a negative AJD on unzoned rural acreage. For unentitled raw land they pay raw-land prices plus an option, with the jurisdictional risk already handled by their own consultants (Kimley-Horn and others).
scored.ladder: The ladder is land banking, then entitlement, then horizontal development (lots), then vertical building or a powered industrial shell. The upper rungs are real and large, but this is the conventional, crowded land-development business with thin moats. It is not a path to owning a proprietary chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no discovery asymmetry to exploit. Sackett and the 2025 proposed rule, which projects an 81% drop in federal wetland acreage, are fully public and widely discussed. The test is close to a deterministic GIS rule. Buyers already run cheap delineations on every deal. And most of the "20-200x" uplift comes from entitlement, utilities and location, which are slow and bespoke like the geothermal counter-example, rather than from proving the land is not WOTUS.
scored.one_line_reason: Proving a parcel is non-WOTUS is cheap, mostly succeeds after Sackett, and is already public knowledge, so ML has little to add. The big price jump comes from entitlement, not discovery.

scored.name: PercRight: rural lots written off as septic failures
scored.one_line: Buys rural lots that failed a percolation test or carry poor SSURGO septic ratings. These trade at $1-5k as unbuildable. ML over soils, LiDAR micro-topography and scanned county perc and well logs predicts which lots will pass a new deep-hole perc test or qualify for an approved alternative system. The proven buildable lot is resold to builders at $40-150k.
scored.unproven_right: Fee title to lots marked 'failed perc' or 'not buildable'. These often show up at tax sales or sit with heirs who cannot see why they failed.
scored.proving_step: A new soil evaluation or perc test ($300-1,500) and a county septic permit for a conventional, mound or drip system. This is the cheap 'drill hit', and the permit is a transferable, legible proof.
scored.proven_buyer: Rural spec builders and manufactured-home lot developers, plus private buyers. This is the weakest buyer class: fragmented and only moderately capitalised.
scored.public_data: NRCS SSURGO septic and absorption-field ratings; USGS 3DEP LiDAR; county environmental-health perc and septic permit archives (scanned, unstructured); state well logs for water-table depth; tax-sale and parcel records.
scored.rough_step_up: About 10-50x per lot ($2k to $60k+). Tickets are small, and the county permit database is partly a legible outcome field for past tests. The ML edge rests on predicting re-test success, which is plausible but unproven.
scored.frame: The rung is "own a written-off rural lot and get a septic permit for it". Inside that rung, discovery (picking lots that will pass a retest or qualify for a mound/drip system) is maybe 50-60% of the work (my estimate). The rest is buying the title (tax sales, heirs, quiet title), the soil evaluation, engineered system design, county permitting and resale. That is many small one-off deals, not a trivial physical step. Alternative systems cost 2-3x a conventional one (BuildingAdvisor). That cost comes off the price a builder will pay, so the cleanup is not abstracted away. The buyers are fragmented spec builders, manufactured-home lot developers and private buyers, and they are only moderately capitalised. No buyer with Terranox-style economics ($40k in, $100k out per unit) exists. Partial frame, weak buyer.
scored.step_up: Sold-comp data from Kent Island, Maryland (2003-2012): 197 buildable lots averaged $137,382, and 117 non-buildable lots (failed perc or never tested) averaged $16,098 (QAC appraisal study). That is about 8.5x. Unbuildable lots are not near zero, because they still have recreational, hunting and camp-site value (Montana DNRC appraisal). The candidate's claimed 10-50x ($2k to $60k+) applies only to the cheapest tax-sale lots. Even there, if the lot needs a mound or drip system, the builder pays $15-40k more (my estimate from the 2-3x multiplier), which cuts the net uplift. That puts the realistic step-up at about 3-10x, 10^0.5 to 10^1, far below 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: A perc or soil evaluation costs $400-1,200 plus design and permit fees (BuildingAdvisor). No published retest pass rate exists. Sources call it "a roll of the dice". My estimate is a 20-40% retest or alternative-system approval rate among lots that previously failed, which caps the hit-rate lever at about 2.5-5x. The test is not the expensive part of an attempt. The dominant cost is buying the lot ($2-16k) plus about $1-3k in title and closing costs. ML only helps choose which lots to buy, so the capex cut is about 2-3x at best, not 10x. The proving step is cheap and is often not failing for lack of insight: many failures come from seasonal water tables or clay that a retest will not change.
scored.data: The signal is partly public and illegible. Scanned county environmental-health perc and septic records and state well logs are messy. But SSURGO septic absorption-field ratings are a legible, nationally mapped field, and incumbents already use it in web soil survey screening. County permit archives record past pass/fail outcomes, so the answer is partly written down already, which is the pattern that killed earlier hunts. Pass/fail also depends heavily on local code: the same soil can fail in one county and qualify for a mound in the next. That code layer is legible, but a soils model does not capture it. I found no evidence that ML over LiDAR micro-topography beats a soil scientist's site visit.
scored.right_bought: Yes, fee title is bought, not claimed first-come, through tax sales, heirs and absentee owners, at roughly $2-16k. But the owner can resolve the information asymmetry with a single $400-1,200 test. An informed seller (or the county, or a tax-sale bidder) can retest instead of selling cheap, so the discount mainly survives where the lot really fails. Land-flipping investors (the "Land Geek" style operators that mail cheap offers to delinquent rural owners) already buy these lots in bulk. Many make the sale contingent on a passing perc, which prices out much of the mispricing.
scored.buyer: Rural spec builders, manufactured-home lot developers and private buyers. They are fragmented and price-sensitive, and buy on contingency. They are not deep-pocketed, unlike a mine developer.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are permitted lots, then site work and septic installation, then manufactured or spec homes, then rural subdivision development. Each rung is real but low-margin and fragmented, and the land is local and heterogeneous. The path leads to a regional homebuilder or land developer, not a path to a trillion dollars.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step costs only $400-1,200, so anyone (the owner, a tax-sale bidder, a land flipper) can run it. That kills the information asymmetry. Where the test really fails, the uplift is only about 8x (Maryland comps: $16k to $137k), and the alternative system's cost ($15-40k, my estimate) eats much of it. That leaves a 3-10x, small-ticket arbitrage sold to weak buyers, not a 10^4 step-up.
scored.one_line_reason: The test is cheap enough that owners can prove their own lots, the real uplift is about 8x, not 10^4, and the outcome is partly legible already in SSURGO and county permit records.

scored.name: WildTrait (crop wild relatives on private US land)
scored.one_line: Buys exclusive collection and commercial germplasm rights from private landowners for wild crop relatives: wild sunflower, Humulus neomexicanus hops, wild Solanum, wild Cucurbita, pecan, grape and Vitis rootstocks, wild Capsicum in Texas and Arizona. Uses ML over scanned herbarium sheets to find populations with likely stress or disease-resistance traits, proves them with a leaf genotype and a fast phenotype assay, then sells exclusive licences to seed and trait majors.
scored.unproven_right: An exclusive access-and-collection agreement and a germplasm option on the wild population on a private parcel. US land is outside Nagoya ABS, and plants belong to the landowner. It costs hundreds to low thousands of dollars per parcel, and landowners have no idea a sought-after allele grows in their arroyo.
scored.proving_step: Collecting seed or tissue, then low-cost sequencing to confirm a target R-gene or haplotype is present, plus a detached-leaf or greenhouse disease or drought assay. About $1-5k per population. Introgression breeding is the buyer's later build.
scored.proven_buyer: Seed and trait majors and craft-trait breeders: Bayer, Corteva, Syngenta, BASF Vegetable Seeds, Hop Breeding Company/Yakima Chief, grape rootstock programmes. Precedent: wild H. neomexicanus from New Mexico became the licensed Medusa and Zappa hop varieties. Early trait and germplasm licences carry upfront payments of about $0.5-5M plus royalties.
scored.public_data: iDigBio and SERNEC scanned herbarium sheets (tens of millions of images, often un-georeferenced, with handwritten labels and lesions visible on the specimen); USDA GRIN-Global passport data and scanned evaluation reports; GBIF and iNaturalist occurrences; SSURGO soils; PRISM climate extremes as a selection-pressure proxy.
scored.rough_step_up: A right at about $1-2k becomes an exclusive validated-trait licence at about $0.5-5M: roughly 10^3. Base hit rate (a novel, useful allele in a sampled population) is about 1-5%, so the lever is 10x or more. Risks: the buyer pays for discovery data before field trials, so the size of upfront payments must be confirmed; trait value is realised slowly, over a 5-10 year breeding cycle.
scored.frame: The rung is a wild population genotyped and phenotyped for a trait, then optioned. Discovery (where to sample, plus genotyping) is maybe 60-70% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). But the buyer does not value the output until the trait has been introgressed and field-validated over 5-10 years. That breeding step is the bespoke hard part, as in the geothermal counter-example, and it is pushed onto a buyer who discounts for it.
scored.step_up: Claimed: a right at about $1-2k becomes a licence at $0.5-5M (10^3). I could not verify this because the shared search budget was already used up, so these figures are my estimates from prior knowledge. Licences for unadapted wild germplasm from universities and USDA usually run from free to the low tens of thousands of dollars, plus small royalties. Upfronts of $1M or more go to breeding-ready, field-validated traits. A realistic step-up is $1-2k to $10-100k, about 10-50x, and only on the rare cases a buyer takes up.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate is 1-5% per sampled population (the candidate's figure, not verified). A proving attempt costs about $1-5k (genotyping plus a detached-leaf assay), which is cheap, so discovery capex is not the bottleneck. A 10x lever saves only about $50-200k per hit. The real cost and risk sit in the buyer's introgression and field trials, which ML over herbarium sheets does not reduce.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible: SERNEC and iDigBio hold millions of scanned sheets with handwritten labels and visible lesions, which is a genuine illegibility edge. But USDA GRIN-Global already carries structured evaluation and descriptor fields (disease ratings, for example) for many Helianthus, Vitis, Cucurbita, Capsicum and Solanum accessions. Wild-relative research has also published resistance-gene sources for decades (for example, sunflower Pl downy-mildew genes from wild H. annuus). The outcome is therefore often already legible for the very species the candidate lists.
scored.right_bought: The right can be bought cheaply in a nominal sense, from my estimate of $100s-$1000s per parcel for access. But exclusivity is illusory. Wild relatives such as H. annuus, Cucurbita foetidissima, Vitis and H. neomexicanus range across many parcels, roadsides, BLM and Forest Service land, and Mexico. The same allele usually exists in other populations, and in GRIN accessions that USDA hands out free to breeders. Seed blows off the parcel. A buyer can therefore route around the option.
scored.buyer: The buyers named are Bayer, Corteva, Syngenta, BASF Vegetables, hop breeders and grape rootstock programmes. They are capitalised but rarely pay large upfronts for raw wild germplasm, and they have their own wild-relative collection and genebank access. The Medusa and Zappa hop precedent came from breeders' own wild collections that were then bred into varieties: the value was captured by the variety, not by a landowner's right (from memory, not verified).
scored.ladder: Above this rung: pre-breeding and introgression lines, owned varieties protected by PVP or utility patents, then seed production and sales. That is a real path to becoming a specialty seed company, for example in hops or rootstocks. But each rung takes 5-10 years, the markets are niche, and the majors are entrenched, so this is not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The asset is not scarce or excludable. The trait-bearing allele almost always exists in other populations on public land and in free USDA GRIN accessions, so an exclusive private-parcel option has no scarcity value. The real value is created only in the buyer's slow introgression breeding, so there is no immediate 10^3 step-up on a hit.
scored.one_line_reason: Cheap, illegible discovery, but the right is non-exclusive and buyers can route around it via public land and free GRIN germplasm. Value appears only after 5-10 years of buyer breeding, so the step-up is closer to 10x than 10^3x.
sources: No web searches ran: the shared search budget for this turn was already used up. Every figure is my estimate from prior knowledge and is marked as such.
Prior knowledge (unverified): USDA GRIN-Global distributes germplasm free to researchers and breeders, with structured evaluation descriptors
Prior knowledge (unverified): the Medusa hop was bred from wild H. neomexicanus collections and licensed as a variety

scored.name: TartufoGround (soil-eDNA proven white truffle grounds)
scored.one_line: Buys or leases cheap marginal riparian woodland in Piemonte, Marche, Molise and Istria, uses ML to predict Tuber magnatum habitat, proves mycelium is present with a soil qPCR/eDNA test, registers the land as an exclusive controlled truffle ground (tartufaia controllata), and sells or leases it to truffle houses.
scored.unproven_right: Freehold or long lease on marginal poplar, willow or oak riparian woodland valued at about €2-8k/ha. Under Italian law, truffles on unregistered land can be collected by any licensed hunter, so the owner captures nothing and does not realise the value.
scored.proving_step: A soil core grid with species-specific T. magnatum qPCR (about €50-100 per sample), confirmed by a hunter with a trained dog during the season. Registering a controlled ground is administrative.
scored.proven_buyer: Truffle houses and investors: Urbani Tartufi, Sabatino, Savini, plus high-end hospitality groups. White truffle sells for about €3-6k/kg wholesale.
scored.public_data: Regional truffle-hunting licence and harvest records; ISPRA and regional soil maps (scanned and unstructured); Corine land cover and riparian hydrology; scanned literature from historical truffle-ground surveys; GBIF Tuber occurrences; Copernicus soil moisture.
scored.rough_step_up: Land at about €5k/ha becomes a proven controlled ground yielding 1-5 kg/ha/yr (about €5-25k/ha/yr), capitalised at about €50-200k/ha: about 10-40x on land, closer to 10^2-10^3 on a lease or option. Base hit rate for magnatum mycelium in candidate stands is about 10-20%. Weaker on C2 than the fossil idea, but the outcome is truly hidden in the soil.
scored.frame: The rung is: own marginal riparian woodland, show it yields T. magnatum, and get it recognised as a controlled truffle ground ("tartufaia controllata"). Finding the right stand is maybe 50-60% of the work (my estimate), not 80%+. The rest is physical and slow. Under Law 752/1985 art. 3, a controlled ground needs real improvement work (thinning, managing the water regime, planting mycorrhized trees) plus regional recognition and boundary signs. Proof of yield takes multiple seasons of dog hunting, because magnatum fruiting swings hugely from year to year with drought. There is also no capitalised buyer for proven ground. Truffle houses (Urbani, Sabatino, Savini) buy truffles from hunters and do not pay for land, so the rung's output is a crop sold year by year, not an asset a developer pays for. Not hard-excluded: this is biological, not mineral or fluid. But it is structurally close to prospecting.
scored.step_up: Unproven: riparian poplar, willow or oak woodland at about €2-8k/ha (the candidate's figure; I could not verify it because search was unavailable). Proven: realistic natural magnatum yield is about 0.2-2 kg/ha/yr (my estimate from the literature I recall; the candidate's 1-5 kg/ha is optimistic). At a harvester price of about €1.5-4k/kg, that is about €0.5-6k/ha/yr gross, before paying for guarding, hunters and improvement work. Capitalised, that is about €10-50k/ha, a step-up of about 3-10x on freehold. That is far from 10^3-10^4. An option or lease raises the multiple on cash put in, but not the multiple on the asset's value.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: the candidate claims 10-20% of candidate stands hold magnatum mycelium (unverified). That caps the ML lever at 5-10x. The proving step is also cheap: a qPCR grid of 20-50 cores at €50-100 each comes to about €1-5k/ha (my estimate). So discovery capex is not what holds the business back. Multi-year confirmation of fruiting is. Known science, from memory and not checked this session: the species-specific qPCR assay for T. magnatum soil mycelium exists (Iotti et al., 2012). Follow-up studies found the mycelium spread widely in soil, including in spots that produce no truffles. A qPCR hit therefore does not reliably prove yield, which weakens the proving step itself.
scored.data: The data is public and messy: scanned regional soil maps, old surveys of truffle grounds, regional licence and harvest records, GBIF occurrence points. The outcome is not written into a legible field, which is good. But the real signal sits in the private, secret knowledge of local truffle hunters ("trifolao"), and that is not public data. Harvest records are summarised by region, not by parcel. Productive grounds in Langhe/Roero, Marche and Molise are already locally known, and hunters guard them.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the land can be bought or leased from owners, so rights are bought, not claimed first-come. But the information gap is weak. Owners in truffle districts usually know, or have heard from hunters, that their woods produce truffles. Exclusivity is not purely administrative: it needs improvement works, regional recognition and signs, and in some regions it faces political pushback from hunter associations (my recollection, unverified).
scored.buyer: Weak. Urbani Tartufi, Sabatino and Savini buy truffles by the kilo, not productive land. Hospitality groups might buy a showcase ground for marketing, which is a niche. There is no buyer equivalent to a mine developer who pays a large premium for a proven asset.
scored.ladder: Rungs above: harvesting, grading, cold chain and export, branded truffle products, and magnatum cultivation if it becomes reliable (INRAE/Mycorrhizal Applications reported the first cultivated white truffles in France around 2019). Even the whole chain is small. My order-of-magnitude estimate: global white truffle supply is tens of tonnes a year, worth about €100-300M at wholesale. There is no path to a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: Proving the ground does not create a large asset step-up that a capitalised buyer will pay for. Proven magnatum ground is worth only about 3-10x more than unproven land (yields of about 0.2-2 kg/ha/yr, very volatile). A qPCR hit for mycelium does not reliably predict fruiting. Truffle houses buy truffles, not land. The total market is about €100-300M, so neither the step-up nor the ladder works.
scored.one_line_reason: The outcome really is hidden in the soil, but proven ground is worth only about 3-10x unproven land, eDNA presence does not reliably mean yield, no capitalised buyer pays for proven land, and the market is tiny.
sources: Italian Law 16 Dec 1985 n. 752, art. 3 (tartufaie controllate/coltivate: exclusive owner rights need improvement works and boundary signs), from memory, not fetched
Iotti M. et al. 2012, Soil Biology and Biochemistry, species-specific qPCR for Tuber magnatum soil mycelium, from memory, not fetched
Later studies (Zampieri, Murat, Bonito et al.) finding T. magnatum mycelium spread widely in soil, including unproductive spots, from memory, not fetched
INRAE / Mycorrhizal Applications, first cultivated T. magnatum in France (~2019), from memory, not fetched
Candidate brief, for land price (€2-8k/ha), qPCR cost (€50-100/sample) and hit rate (10-20%), unverified

scored.name: Dendrofiddle: proving the attribution of unattributed old Italian string instruments
scored.one_line: Buys 'Italian school, c.1700' and unlabelled violins, violas and cellos for $5-50k. ML over dendrochronology chronologies, CT scans and Cozio and auction archives flags tops whose wood matches trees used by Stradivari, Guarneri or Amati. A $1-3k dendro test plus a CT scan proves it, and the instrument resells for $0.5-15M.
scored.unproven_right: Outright ownership of the instrument, bought from dealers, estates and orchestras who have no access to tree-ring matching across the full reference set.
scored.proving_step: Non-destructive dendrochronology of the top plate (a photo or scan of the rings, about $1-3k) cross-dated against master-maker reference chronologies, plus CT and varnish spectroscopy. If the wood comes from the same tree as a known Strad, the case is made.
scored.proven_buyer: Tarisio and Bonhams sales, instrument foundations (Stradivari Society, Nippon Music Foundation), and HNW collectors. The market is liquid at the attribution stage.
scored.public_data: The Tarisio Cozio archive (scanned provenance for about 40k instruments), published dendro reference chronologies (Ratcliff, Topham, Grissino-Mayer), CT-scan atlases from museum studies, and decades of scanned auction catalogues.
scored.rough_step_up: About 100-1000x on a hit ($10k to $1M+), though hits are rare. A strong ladder into restoration, a lending fund, and fractional ownership as an asset class.
scored.frame: The rung is buying an unattributed instrument, re-attributing it and reselling it, and a liquid capitalised buyer exists (Tarisio, Bonhams, foundations, collectors). By my estimate discovery is about 70-90% of the work and the physical step is cheap. But the step that creates the value is not the dendro test. It is an expert certificate (Beare, Tarisio, Machold, Bein and Fushi). Dendro only gives a date range and sometimes a match to the same tree. Workshops shared wood and forgers use old wood, so a same-tree match is evidence, not proof. The proving step is a social one controlled by incumbents.
scored.step_up: Unproven: 'Italian school c.1700' instruments sell for about $5-50k (candidate's figure, roughly consistent with auction ranges I remember; not verified). Proven: a realistic re-attribution to a named mid-tier maker (Gagliano, Testore, Grancino) takes about $20k to $150-500k, roughly 10-25x (my estimate). Stradivari or del Gesu ($2-20M) would be 100-1000x, but I estimate under one such rediscovery per decade. The expected step-up is about 10-30x, not 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt: a dendro report is about $500-1,500 (my estimate of typical Ratcliff/Topham/Caluori fees), plus $1-3k for CT and spectroscopy. That is already cheap, so ML has little proving capex to cut. Base rate that an unattributed $5-50k Italian instrument is a top-maker sleeper: well below 0.1% (my estimate). About 650 Strads and 150 del Gesus survive, and nearly all are catalogued. The real cost is buying each instrument at $5-50k, and ML cannot make the hidden population bigger. Search budget ran out, so these numbers are unverified.
scored.data: Mostly legible, and held by the incumbent. Cozio is run by Tarisio, which is itself a buyer and seller in this market. The best dendro reference chronologies are private files in the dendrochronologists' labs, not public data. The outcome is already written down in a legible form: the expert certificate and the Cozio attribution, which is the 'status field' problem again. Many trade dendro reports exist, and dealers already order dendro on anything promising.
scored.right_bought: You can buy outright ownership, but the sellers are mostly dealers and auction houses, the very experts who would read the signal. Estates and orchestras usually consult those same dealers before selling. Very little cheap, unread supply reaches the market.
scored.buyer: Tarisio and Bonhams auctions, the Stradivari Society, Nippon Music Foundation and HNW collectors. They are capitalised and liquid, but they buy only with a certificate from a recognised expert, and dendro alone does not provide one.
scored.ladder: Restoration, certification, dealing, a lending fund, fractional ownership. The whole fine-instrument market is small, on the order of low single-digit billions of dollars (my estimate). That is not a trillion-dollar chain, and the certification rung is reputation-gated, not something you climb with capital.
scored.fatal_flaw: Value comes from expert-consensus attribution, not a physical test. The incumbents who issue certificates (Tarisio, Beare and others) also own the archive and already run dendro routinely. After 150 years of combing by the trade, the pool of hidden top-maker instruments is close to zero.
scored.one_line_reason: A cheap proving step, a tiny hidden population and attribution gated by incumbent experts mean ML can neither cut much capex nor create a 10^3 step-up.
sources: No web sources: the shared WebSearch budget was used up before any search ran, so all figures are labelled estimates from prior knowledge
Tarisio Cozio archive (tarisio.com/cozio) - known incumbent, not fetched this session
Peter Ratcliff, John Topham, Andrew Caluori dendro practices - known from prior knowledge, not fetched

scored.name: Sirecraft (elite sires hidden in commercial herds)
scored.one_line: Buys bull calves or embryo rights cheaply from commercial dairy and beef herds whose genetics are unrecorded, uses ML over public pedigree, registry and phenotype data to predict which matings carry elite genomic merit, proves each calf with a $30-50 genotype test, and sells the rare elite bulls to AI studs.
scored.unproven_right: Bull calves bought at near-slaughter price ($50-500) from commercial herds, or first-refusal rights on calves from flagged cows, sold by owners who never genotype males.
scored.proving_step: A SNP genotype ($30-50) and genomic evaluation. The physical step is trivial, and finding the right calf is the work.
scored.proven_buyer: AI studs and genetics companies (Select Sires, ABS/Genus, STgenetics, Semex), which pay $50k-$500k+ for top genomic young sires.
scored.public_data: CDCB public genomic and traditional evaluations, breed-association pedigree and type records, DHI herd test summaries, and USDA cow-performance data.
scored.rough_step_up: A $200 calf becomes a $50k-$500k elite sire (10^2-10^3x). Base hit rate is about 0.1-1%. Weakness: the signal sits in fairly legible databases, and studs already genotype intensively, so the ML edge is mainly in finding untested herds.
scored.frame: The rung is: own a bull calf, genotype it, sell it to an AI stud. The physical step really is trivial (a hair or tissue sample plus a $30-50 SNP chip), so in that sense discovery is about 90% of the work. But the frame only exists as a discrete sellable rung on paper. AI studs mostly source young sires from their own IVF/ET nucleus programs and contracted elite herds (STgenetics, ABS/Genus, Select Sires, Semex all run their own). Independent bull calves from commercial herds are not a meaningful supply channel. The buyer is capitalised but already vertically integrated over the very rung you want to sell into.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a commercial Holstein bull calf sells for about $50-500 at auction (my estimate from 2024-25 calf-market knowledge, not verified this turn). Proven: studs typically pay about $5k-50k for a contracted genomic young sire, and only the rare top bulls fetch $100k-500k+ (my estimate; the candidate's $50k-500k figure covers only the top tail). Typical step-up is about 10-100x, and about 1000x only for outliers. Scored 3 on the typical case.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving cost is about $30-50 per genotype (Zoetis CLARIFIDE / Neogen GGP pricing, from memory, not verified this turn). The candidate's 0.1-1% base hit rate is an estimate for elite-dam matings. For calves from commercial (non-elite) dams, my estimate is well below 0.01%. Genomic merit is roughly the parent average plus Mendelian sampling of SD about 0.5x additive SD, so a calf from an average dam almost never reaches the top 1% of GTPI that the elite IVF calves from top-0.1% dams already occupy. The proving step is already cheap, so there is no expensive failed-proving capex for ML to cut 10x. The cost is buying and raising the calves, and ML can only re-rank parent averages that are already public.
scored.data: The data is legible and it already contains the answer. Sire PTAs are public in CDCB/breed evaluations, and commercial herds overwhelmingly use known AI sires. CDCB holds about 9-10M+ genotypes (my estimate from memory), mostly females, so many commercial dams are themselves already genotyped, with a genomic PTA sitting in a structured field. Where they are not genotyped, there is little signal at all: unrecorded dams with only DHI production records predict little beyond parent average. This is the 'regulator writes the answer in a field' failure mode: the outcome (a genomic PTA) comes straight out of a standardised evaluation, not a hidden signal in illegible files.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right can be bought cheaply and is not first-come-free: bull calves are bought at commodity price and owners rarely genotype males. However, owners and studs can genotype any calf themselves for $30-50, so the information asymmetry is tiny and closes as soon as a herd's calves start getting tested. The other path in, first-refusal contracts with elite herds, is exactly what stud sire analysts already do.
scored.buyer: AI studs and genetics companies: Select Sires, ABS/Genus, STgenetics, Semex, URUS/Alta. They are capitalised but have a strong internal supply of candidates from their own nucleus IVF herds. Genetic progress also obsoletes young sires within about 2-3 years, so a bull's value decays quickly.
scored.ladder: There are rungs above (an embryo/IVF program, a sire portfolio, sexed semen, a full genetics company), but the ceiling is modest. Genus plc is worth about $1.5-2B and global bovine genetics is about a $5-8B market (my estimates). That is a solid company, not a trillion-dollar chain, and the upper rungs are dominated by entrenched incumbents with their own nucleus herds.
scored.fatal_flaw: Elite genomic merit is inherited and already priced: top sires come from elite x elite IVF matings that studs already genotype by the thousands. Commercial-herd calves have parent averages that are public (known AI sire, often a genotyped dam) and far below elite. So there are almost no hidden elite calves to find, the $30-50 proving step is already cheap, and the outcome is already a legible public PTA field.
scored.one_line_reason: The physical step is trivial, but the signal is legible and already priced (CDCB PTAs). Elite bulls almost never come from commercial dams. Genotyping is already cheap, leaving no capex lever, and studs supply their own sires through vertical integration.

Prior knowledge: CDCB (uscdcb.com) genomic evaluation database size and public PTA/GTPI listings
Prior knowledge: Zoetis CLARIFIDE / Neogen GGP genotype pricing (~$30-50 per test)
Prior knowledge: Genus plc annual reports (ABS) for market cap and sire sourcing via IVF nucleus herds

scored.name: Heirloom Germplasm Mining
scored.one_line: Buy private breeder and heirloom seed collections cheaply, sequence them, use ML to find disease-resistance genes, prove each gene with a cheap leaf assay, then license the trait to seed majors.
scored.unproven_right: Ownership of seed collections from retiring breeders, plus exclusive trait rights
scored.proving_step: Transient expression assay or detached-leaf pathogen challenge, a few thousand dollars per gene, binary result
scored.proven_buyer: Bayer, Corteva, Syngenta, KWS trait-licensing groups
scored.public_data: USDA GRIN accession records, NCBI SRA plant resequencing, published R-gene catalogs
scored.rough_step_up: ~10^2-10^3x (about $10k collection cost to a $1-20M trait license)
