scored.frame: The proposed rung is "an R gene validated by a leaf assay". That rung is not discrete and nobody buys it as a finished product. To get from an assay hit to a licensable trait, the gene still needs stable transformation or introgression, multi-season field trials, durability and pathogen-race testing, and regulatory work. CropLife/Phillips McDougall put the full cost at about $136M and 13.1 years per trait (2008-2012 data); a 2022 update cited by the ABA gives about $115M and 16.5 years, with regulatory work alone about $35M and 4.8 years. Discovery and early proving are roughly 10-25% of that (estimate from the phase breakdown), not 80%+. The physical and regulatory steps after the assay are the hard part, which is the same shape as the geothermal-plant counter-example.
scored.step_up: The pitch claims about $10k for a collection becoming a $1-20M license. I found no public disclosed price for licensing a single disease-resistance gene; the public record leaves these deals undisclosed. Disclosed trait deals are large only for broad packages: Syngenta's corn-trait licenses to Vilmorin/KWS had about $200M in upfronts, and DuPont's Roundup Ready royalties to Monsanto were $802M plus $950M, but those are proven, approved, commercial traits. Fortiphyte, a Berkeley startup doing exactly this (supplying R-gene traits to seed companies), has raised only about $1-2M in total, mostly grants. That signals the market does not pay millions for assay-validated genes. My estimate is that an assay-validated R gene earns option or research-license fees of about $50k-$500k, with royalties contingent on years of further development. Against a $10k collection plus about $50-200k of sequencing and assay costs, that is about 3-30x realised, not 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is cheap. Transient or detached-leaf assays cost a few thousand dollars each (the candidate's own figure; I estimate $2-10k). Hit rates are already decent: AgRenSeq plus association genetics cloned 4 stem-rust genes from one diverse wild-wheat panel (Arora et al. 2018). Because the assay is neither expensive nor mostly failing, ML has little discovery capex to save, and the method stack (RenSeq, MutRenSeq, NLR annotation pipelines) is already standard in academia and at the majors. The real cost-and-failure gate is the $100M+ field and regulatory stage, and ML on sequence data does not change that.
scored.data: The data is public but already legible. NCBI SRA resequencing, published R-gene and NLR catalogues, and GRIN accession records with disease-screening descriptors are structured, machine-readable and already mined by JIC, 2Blades, KAUST, Corteva and others. Known R genes are already written into public catalogues, which is the equivalent of the outcome sitting in a legible field. Private breeder collections are not sequenced, but the ML edge there comes from paying to sequence them, not from reading illegible public records.
scored.right_bought: The right is weak and mostly not exclusive. USDA NPGS sends germplasm free of charge to professionals (about 120,000 samples a year; requesters pay only shipping), so diversity is a free public good, not something cheaply bought from owners who cannot read the data. Buying a retiring breeder's collection does not give exclusivity over a resistance allele that also exists in free GRIN or CGIAR accessions. ITPGRFA and Nagoya benefit-sharing rules, plus patent prior art from the public catalogues, can block patenting a gene found in public germplasm. The only defensible right is a patent on a novel isolated gene, which anyone with free accessions can race you for.
scored.buyer: Bayer, Corteva, Syngenta, KWS and GDM trait-licensing groups are capitalised, but they buy traits that are de-risked in the field and in regulation. They already run in-house RenSeq and germplasm-mining programmes and partner with academia (JIC/2Blades) cheaply. There is no evidence they pay seven figures for leaf-assay hits, and Fortiphyte's tiny funding suggests they do not.
scored.ladder: There is a real ladder above this rung: gene, then validated trait, then trait stacks, then a germplasm or seed company, then branded seed. Seed and traits is a market of about $50B+ a year. But each rung above the first costs about $100M and more than a decade, and incumbents own the distribution, so the climb is slow and capital-heavy.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step does not prove the asset. A leaf-assay hit is a long way from a sellable trait, and the value step-up only happens after about $115M and 16.5 years of field and regulatory work, where discovery is a minority of the cost. On top of that, the right is not exclusive, because the same genetic diversity is distributed free by USDA NPGS and catalogued publicly.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is cheap and already done well by incumbents, the leaf assay is not the real proving step (field and regulatory work costs about $115M and 16.5 years), the public data is already legible, and the germplasm is free and not exclusive, so there is no 10^3 jump that a buyer pays for at this rung.

scored.name: Heartwood: finding resinated agarwood trees before cutting
scored.one_line: Buy standing-tree harvest rights to wild and plantation Aquilaria and Gyrinops trees from smallholders, who sell them at timber/sapling value because only ~10% of trees naturally form resin. ML fuses satellite canopy stress, public forestry inventories, CITES trade data and cheap in-tree sensing to pick the resinated ones, then sells proven oud wood to perfume houses.
scored.unproven_right: Purchased, CITES-compliant harvest right to an individual living tree, at about $10-100/tree.
scored.proving_step: Non-destructive proof: acoustic or electrical-resistance tomography plus a micro-core GC-MS (resin chemotype). Minutes and a few dollars per tree. The physical step is trivial.
scored.proven_buyer: Gulf and Asian oud houses and fragrance majors (Givaudan, Firmenich-DSM, Ajmal, Arabian Oud). High-grade agarwood trades at $10k-100k+/kg.
scored.public_data: CITES trade database, Indonesian/Malaysian/Assam forest inventory PDFs, herbarium records (GBIF/iDigBio), Sentinel/Planet imagery of canopy dieback correlated with fungal infection, published agarwood GC-MS chemotype literature.
scored.rough_step_up: Tree right at about $50 to a resinated tree worth $5k-100k (10^2-10^3x). Base hit rate is about 10%, so the lever is capped near 10x. Caveat: the illegible-data edge is weaker here (it is mostly sensing, not public records). Strong on C1 and C2, weaker on C4 and C5 (ladder runs to inoculated plantations and fragrance brands).
scored.frame: The rung is a bought standing-tree harvest right that is proven to hold resin. In wild trees, finding the resinated ones is roughly 70-90% of the work (my estimate). But that rung is mostly gone or illegal. Wild Aquilaria is listed on CITES Appendix II, wild stocks are poached nearly to extinction, and most remaining wild trees sit in state or protected forest where a smallholder has nothing to sell. In plantations, discovery is not the work at all, because resin is manufactured by inoculating the tree. Inoculation reports about 95% success (Lampung bioserum) and 3-7 kg of resin per tree in 1-3 years. The buyer also does not fit the gold rubric. Oud houses buy graded, processed chips and oil. Nobody is a capitalised buyer of 'proven standing trees' paying a developer-style premium.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a candidate tree at about $10-100, the candidate's own figure, unverified. Proven: in Bangladesh one buyer offered about $160 per inoculated tree, and one naturally resinated tree once sold for about $2,450, described as a one-off (Mongabay 2026). A Malaysian MTIB trial got about 5 kg of core agarwood per tree at RM800/kg, roughly $850 per tree. Promotional claims reach about $1,000 per tree. The $10k-100k/kg figure is for rare top-grade wild kyara, and a typical tree yields a few hundred grams to a few kg of mostly low grade, so it does not apply per tree. Realistic step-up is about 3-50x (my estimate), not 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Wild base hit rate is about 10% (PMC review, UPSI paper, CIFOR model). Some sources say under 2% (secondary estimate). CIFOR models 40% for agroforest and plantation trees. The proving step itself (sonic or ECT tomography plus a micro-core) is cheap: a few dollars to tens of dollars per tree, my estimate. Field validation is weak. PiCUS sonic tomography showed only 1.1% difference between inoculated and control trees, and ECT has only been simulated. So proving is neither expensive nor the main cost. The main cost is buying trees and waiting. Inoculation at about 95% success makes the outcome manufacturable, so a better hit rate saves little money.
scored.data: There is almost no public-but-illegible signal at tree level. CITES trade data is aggregated by country and year. Forest inventories report stand-level counts, not which individual tree is infected. Satellite imagery cannot resolve fungal resin inside a sub-canopy trunk. The edge would be in-field sensing, which is a physical-ops edge, not a records edge. The other side of the trade is not blind either. Gaharu hunters and smallholders already pick dying or wounded trees (poachers' usual target per NST/FRIM). Planters inoculate and know their own trees.
scored.right_bought: Plantation trees can be bought from smallholders, but those are increasingly inoculated, so the seller already knows or controls the outcome. Wild trees are mostly on state land under CITES non-detriment-finding quotas, so a cheap, legal, individual-tree harvest right is largely unavailable. Buying from people who cannot read the signal is weak here.
scored.buyer: Agarwood traders and oud houses (Ajmal, Arabian Oud) and fragrance majors that use synthetic or plantation oud. They buy graded wood and oil by the kg, not proven standing trees. Givaudan and Firmenich mostly use synthetics or plantation material.
scored.ladder: The chain runs plantation, then inoculation, then distillation, then grading and trading, then an oud fragrance brand. It is real but modest. Incumbents (Asia Plantation Capital and many Indonesian and Vietnamese plantations) already integrate it, and the market size is single-digit billions, my estimate. The discovery rung does not anchor the ladder, because the bottom of this ladder is growing and inoculating trees, not finding them.
scored.fatal_flaw: Resin can be manufactured. Plantation inoculation reports about 95% success and 3-7 kg per tree in 1-3 years, so discovery is not the scarce step anywhere legal. The only frame where discovery is the work, wild trees, is CITES-restricted, poached out, and not available as cheap purchasable rights.
scored.one_line_reason: Resin is manufacturable by inoculation, wild rights are not legally buyable, the per-tree step-up is about 3-50x, and the edge is sensing rather than illegible public records, so it fails the Terranox shape.

scored.name: Greenkeeper Mutants (off-type turfgrass mining)
scored.one_line: Every elite ultradwarf bermudagrass (Champion, FloraDwarf, MiniVerde) began as a spontaneous off-type patch that someone noticed on an existing golf green. Scan decades of aerial imagery of ~15,000 US golf course greens for persistent patches that differ in colour or texture, or that survived winter kill and drought. Buy plug rights from superintendents, prove the patch in a one-season greenhouse/stress screen with genotyping, and license the cultivar to sod and turf licensors.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive rights to collect, propagate and patent off-type plugs from a specific green, bought from the club for ~$500-5,000 (free greens renovation sweetens it). Clubs see the patches as contamination to be removed.
scored.proving_step: Take plugs, run SSR/GBS genotyping to confirm a novel somatic mutant, and grow in the greenhouse with cold-tolerance, shade, mowing-height and drought assays plus small-plot evaluation. Cost ~$5-20k and 6-12 months. Plant-patent filing follows directly.
scored.proven_buyer: Turf licensors and sod producers with royalty programs: Sod Solutions, The Turfgrass Group, Pike Creek Turf, Tifton Physical Genetics/UGA licensees, Scotts and Pennington. They pay upfront plus per-acre or per-square-foot royalties. Southern golf, sports-field and lawn sod is a multi-billion-dollar market.
scored.public_data: USDA NAIP and USGS historical orthoimagery (1990s-2024), Sentinel-2, state 15cm leaf-off orthophotos (e.g., Florida, Texas, Georgia county programs), and USGA/GCSAA green renovation records. Off-types are visible as colour or texture anomalies that persist across years. No registry records them.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10^3-10^4: a $1-5k plug right to a patented cultivar worth $2-20M in licensing (TifEagle and Latitude 36 scale royalties). The hit rate is low, since most off-types are inferior contaminants, so ML on persistence and stress-survival filters candidates. Market is smaller than the crop ideas but the proof is cheap and fast.
scored.frame: Rung: exclusive plug rights to an off-type patch, proven with genotyping and a greenhouse screen, then sold as a cultivar license. Finding the patch is cheap, but proving it is not a single step. Genotyping plus one greenhouse season does not make a cultivar licensors pay serious money for. They want multi-year field and on-green performance data, and adoption is slow. Champion was found in 1987, released in 1995, and was on only 335 courses by 2007. So inside the rung, discovery is maybe 30-40% of the work (my estimate). The rest is years of field proving and market seeding. The output is also not bought outright at a step-up price. It is paid as royalties over time by small sod licensors.
scored.step_up: Unproven: about $500-5,000 for plug rights (the candidate's own estimate; no market price exists). Proven, a top-tier outcome: TifTuf, UGA's best release ever, earned more than $13M gross licensing over about 10 years (UGA research awards, 2026). UCR's El Toro earned $1.6M in royalties. A greens-only ultradwarf serves a niche of a few thousand courses. Champion reached 335 courses after 12 years. A realistic hit is therefore worth about $0.3-3M NPV in deferred royalties, plus perhaps a $25-100k upfront fee (my estimate). The immediate step-up on proving is about 10-100x. The ~1000x appears only in tail cases, after years of adoption.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: Reasor et al. 2017 (Hereditas) genotyped 47 off-type and desirable samples from southeastern greens. Only 11% (5 of 47) were genetically divergent from the standard cultivars. Fewer still would be agronomically superior; my estimate is under 1-2% of candidates end up commercially valuable. Cost per attempt: about $5-20k (the candidate's estimate; GBS costs about $50-100 per sample). Because each attempt is so cheap, ML only cuts tens of thousands of dollars of screening spend. The binding costs are the multi-year field trials and market adoption, and better hit rates do not shorten those.
scored.data: The data is public: NAIP (0.6-1 m), Sentinel-2 (10 m), and county orthos (about 15 cm). But an off-type patch on a green is often under 1 m² when it is noticed, and superintendents remove it or topdress over it. Daily mowing, painting, overseeding and pigment sprays dominate the colour signal. So the signal is mostly unresolvable or confounded in the imagery. It is not legible data that incumbents have simply failed to extract. Superintendents see these patches every day, and the existing winners were found by sod-industry insiders on the ground (Morris Brown of Coastal Turf found Champion). Universities have also been systematically collecting and genotyping off-types since 2013 (Reasor et al.). No legible field records the outcome, but the people who own the rights can see the asset themselves.
scored.right_bought: Yes, cheaply. Clubs treat these patches as contamination and would sell plug rights for a few thousand dollars or a free renovation. There is a legal risk, though. Many current greens are patented TifEagle, MiniVerde or Champion, and sod purchase and licence terms often restrict propagation. A sport of a patented plant invites infringement or ownership disputes with the original patent holder (UGA/USDA, HGT, Coastal Turf). The cheap acquisition is real; clean title is uncertain.
scored.buyer: Turf licensors and sod producers: Sod Solutions, The Turfgrass Group, Coastal Turf, Tifton Physical Genetics and UGA licensees, and the TifEagle Growers Association. They are small, thinly capitalised firms. They pay mostly through per-acre or per-square-foot royalties after adoption, not large upfront sums. Non-certified bermudagrass sod sells for about $0.29 per sq ft (UF 2024 survey), so royalty pools are thin. There is no buyer who can pay $40k/ha and collect $100k/ha on the spot.
scored.ladder: The ladder is short and small: own the cultivar, then a sod farm, then greens renovation contracting, then a broader turf breeding company. The southern turf sod market is a few billion dollars, but the greens-cultivar segment is tens of millions at most. There is no path to a very large company. A lawn or sports-field cultivar would need a different discovery source, since green off-types are ultradwarfs bred for greens.
scored.fatal_flaw: Aerial imagery cannot see the signal: off-type patches are sub-metre and masked by mowing, painting and overseeding. The people who can see them (superintendents, sod insiders, university off-type surveys) already scout them on the ground. And a hit is a small, slow royalty stream in a few-thousand-course niche, with patent-derivation risk, not an immediate 10^3-10^4 step-up.
scored.one_line_reason: The rights are cheap and the precedents are real (Champion, MiniVerde), but there is no ML edge: the patches are below imagery resolution and already visible to people on the ground. Proving takes years of field trials and adoption, and the payoff is thin deferred royalties from small sod licensors in a niche market.

scored.name: Lost Sire Bank (frozen semen archaeology)
scored.one_line: Buy forgotten frozen bull semen inventories (estate sales, retired AI studs, dispersed herds) for a few dollars a straw. Use public pedigree, genomic and phenotype records to predict which long-dead sires carry rare, valuable alleles or diversity lost from today's inbred Holstein and Angus populations. Prove the allele by genotyping one straw, then sell the proven straws and sons to AI companies.
scored.unproven_right: Title to physical straws of untested historical sires, bought at ~$2-20 per straw in bulk lots from tanks the sellers cannot value.
scored.proving_step: Extract DNA from one straw and run a low-pass sequence or SNP chip (~$50-200) to confirm haplotypes, e.g. heat-tolerant SLICK-like variants, polled, A2/A2, BB-free fertility haplotypes, or lost Y-chromosome and mitochondrial lineages that cut inbreeding. The physical step is trivial. Choosing which of millions of archived straws to test is the work.
scored.proven_buyer: Genus ABS, Select Sires, STgenetics, Semex, URUS. They pay for outcross genetics and rare-allele sires to produce IVF/IVP sons. Precedent: rare historical sires' straws resell at $100-2,000+ each.
scored.public_data: CDCB/USDA AIPL pedigree and evaluation archives, Holstein Association and American Angus Association herdbook pedigrees, 1000 Bull Genomes, NCBI SRA cattle resequencing, and scanned breed-journal sale catalogues. Haplotypes of untested dead sires are imputable from relatives but have never been computed for orphan straws.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10^2-10^3: $5 straw to $500-5,000 per straw, or a $50-500k sire-line deal for a proven rare-allele outcross. The ladder exists (own IVF sons, then herds), but the step-up is smaller and the hit rate is higher than in the plant ideas, so the ML lever is limited.
scored.frame: Rung: own straws of untested historical sires, confirm haplotypes, sell the proven straws or sire-line rights. Inside this rung, choosing which straws to test is maybe 70-80% of the work (my estimate), and the physical step (one $50-200 SNP chip) is trivial. The buyer side is weak, though. AI studs (Genus ABS, Select Sires, STgenetics, Semex, URUS) already own the largest historical archives, and USDA NAGP holds over 1M samples from 64k+ animals, including an ABS donation of 200,000+ units from about 6,000 bulls dating to the 1960s. Pre-1990s sires are far behind modern genomic merit (NM$), so demand for outcross genetics is a small diversity niche, not a capitalised buyer paying for a step-up.
scored.step_up: Unproven: about $2-20 per straw in bulk (the candidate's figure, not verified). A normal straw costs about $15-75 (creatures.com). A CSIRO auction of nearly 5,000 rare tropical-composite beef straws, genetics no longer readily available, topped at $60/straw (Red Angus lot) and $36/straw (Tuli), about $17k in total (Countryman). The exceptions are sires with a huge proven progeny record, not rare-allele finds: Greensons Gigolo (born 1991) sold at £787/straw because he has 1,500+ registered progeny, and the Arubial Wagyu record of $150k/straw was a famous living-line sire. Realistic step-up on a rare-allele hit is about 3-10x ($5 to $20-60). The candidate's 100-1000x needs a demand shock (for example SLICK-like heat tolerance in Holstein) that is not shown.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about $50-200 per straw on a SNP chip or low-pass sequencing (candidate's figure; it matches commercial genotyping prices, my estimate). For defined targets the base hit rate is high, because pedigree alone predicts carrier status for polled, A2, the HH haplotypes and Y/mtDNA lineages; CDCB already traces carrier status through ungenotyped ancestors. A high base rate plus a cheap test caps the ML lever at about 2-3x (my estimate). Testing every straw blindly costs only $50-200 each, so ML barely moves capex.
scored.data: Fails the legible-outcome test. CDCB/AGIL imputes haplotypes for all Holstein bulls and their ancestors first, then uses them as priors for 2M females (Hoard's/CDCB). It publishes haplotype status codes (carrier, probable carrier, probable homozygous) as legible fields, and tracing goes through ungenotyped ancestors (CDCB HCD note). The candidate's claim that haplotypes of dead sires have never been computed is largely false for any registered AI sire. ARS has already genotyped NAGP historic sires against daughter records, and a 2022 study analysed 36,179 Jersey bulls including 782 NAGP sires born 1953-2016. Truly orphan straws mostly come from those same registered AI sires, whose identity is printed on the straw.
scored.right_bought: Partly. Straws in estate and dispersal tanks can be bought cheaply from sellers who cannot value them. But many AI-stud straws come with use restrictions that bar producing bulls for AI or selling sons without stud permission (my understanding of industry sire contracts, not verified here), which can block the resale of sons and sire-line deals.
scored.buyer: Genus ABS, Select Sires, STgenetics, Semex and URUS buy small numbers of outcross genetics. They already hold their own historical archives and have access to the NAGP repository (NAGP germplasm is available for research and, in some cases, breeding). Breed societies and rare-breed conservancies pay little (CSIRO lots at $36-60/straw).
scored.ladder: Proven straws, then IVF/IVP sons, then your own AI stud (competing with Genus and URUS), then herds. The rungs exist, but each one above the first is a capital-heavy, commodity-margin breeding business where genomic merit, not rarity, wins. It is a decent niche company (my estimate tens of $M), not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The answer is already legible and already owned. CDCB imputes and publishes haplotype or carrier status for essentially every registered AI sire and its ancestors. AI studs and USDA NAGP already hold and genotype the historic archive. And old sires' low genomic merit keeps the value of a proven rare-allele straw at about 3-10x, not 10^3.
scored.one_line_reason: Cheap, high-hit-rate test plus haplotypes CDCB already imputes and publishes plus thin outcross demand ($36-60/straw for rare lots) leaves no hidden 10^3 step-up and almost no ML lever.

scored.name: Orphan Mutant Library Licensing (non-GMO knockouts)
scored.one_line: Thousands of university EMS/TILLING and exome-captured mutant populations (wheat, barley, rice, sorghum, tomato, soybean) were sequenced into NCBI SRA and then abandoned when grants ended. Exclusively license the dormant seed stocks from tech-transfer offices for a few thousand dollars. ML-mine the raw reads for loss-of-function alleles in high-value target genes. A one-generation greenhouse phenotype proves the trait, and seed majors buy the edit-equivalent, non-GMO allele.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive commercial licenses to whole mutant populations (seed in a freezer) from university TTOs that cannot tell which of 5,000 lines are valuable, at ~$5-25k per library. A priced license, not a free first-come right.
scored.proving_step: Call variants from SRA reads with ML-based LoF and impact prediction to pick lines with knockouts in genes like MLO (mildew), SBEIIa (high-amylose wheat), gliadin genes (celiac-safe wheat), LCYE or PPO (non-browning), or shatter and dormancy genes. Grow out and run a greenhouse/biochem assay (~$2-10k per line). The output is a non-regulated (conventional) mutant allele usable in the EU.
scored.proven_buyer: Corteva, Bayer, BASF, KWS, Limagrain, Syngenta, and specialty-trait firms (e.g., Arcadia's high-fiber wheat precedent). EU-market traits are valued because a conventional mutant avoids GMO/NGT rules and gene-editing IP stacks (CRISPR royalties).
scored.public_data: NCBI SRA and EBI ENA exome-capture and whole-genome reads of TILLING populations (UC Davis wheat TILLING, John Innes, Rice TILLING, sorghum Purdue/USDA EMS lines), and GrainGenes. Deposited reads are huge and uncalled for most genes. Published papers summarise only the genes the original authors cared about.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10^2-10^3 per library license: a $10k license to a $1-10M trait out-license. The hit rate per target gene is moderate (many TILLING libraries saturate), so the lever is about ~10x, and some TTOs already offer the lines non-exclusively. The edge is limited unless exclusivity is secured.
scored.frame: The rung is: find a loss-of-function mutant line, prove the trait in the greenhouse, and out-license the allele to a seed company. Finding the line is not 80% of the work, because the flagship populations already have their variants called. The real work is crossing out the background EMS mutations (each line carries thousands), stacking homoeologues (wheat needs the A, B and D copies knocked out together, which takes 2-3 crossing generations), backcrossing into elite germplasm and field trials. The "one-generation greenhouse proof" is not realistic for polyploid crops. My estimate is that discovery is about 10-20% of the work in this rung. Buyers (Corteva, KWS and others) exist, but they buy elite-adapted traits, not raw EMS lines.
scored.step_up: Unproven: SeedStor sells individual Cadenza/Kronos TILLING lines for a £15 maintenance fee, or £200 per line with commercial freedom to operate included (SeedStor cart page). That is non-exclusive, at list price, from a public catalogue. Proven: no public price exists for a raw mutant-allele license. The Arcadia high-amylose (SBEIIa TILLING) wheat deal with Bay State Milling and Arista was royalty-based, with undisclosed terms, and only followed years of litigation. My estimate: an allele license for a knockout that is not already patented is worth $50k-1M. It is capped by what it costs to make the same knockout with CRISPR, which by my estimate is $20-100k and 6-12 months. So one line goes from about $250 to $50k-1M, roughly 10^2-10^3 on paper. In practice there is no buyer for most single knockouts, and the step-up only arrives after years of introgression, not right away.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate for finding a line is already high. Krasileva et al. 2017 called more than 10 million EMS mutations across 2,735 exome-captured lines (1,535 Kronos, 1,200 Cadenza). Their paper reports truncation or deleterious alleles for roughly 90% of genes, so a breeder searching for any gene usually finds several knockout lines straight away from the public database. The step that fails is phenotype proving: polyploid redundancy and background mutations make many single-line knockouts show no phenotype. ML variant calling does not fix that. My estimate for one proving attempt: $2-10k for a greenhouse assay, rising to $50-200k with homoeologue stacking and backcrossing. Upside from ML is at most about 1.5-2x. The 10x lever is not available because 1/base hit rate is small.
scored.data: Fails. The data is public, and for the most valuable populations it is already legible. The Kronos/Cadenza exome-capture mutations are called and annotated with predicted effects (SIFT, stop-gained, splice) and can be searched gene by gene through wheat-tilling.com, Ensembl Plants and the Dubcovsky lab database. The outcome sits in a legible field, which is exactly the regulator-status-field failure seen in earlier hunts. The same is true for the rice, tomato and sorghum TILLING databases. Orphaned SRA populations whose variants were never called may exist, but they are the minor, small populations.
scored.right_bought: Fails. These rights are not bought cheaply from owners who cannot read the data. The owners publish the variant calls themselves and sell lines non-exclusively to everyone at a posted price (£200 per line with commercial FTO, from SeedStor). Several groups may already hold the same line. EMS alleles also arise independently, and a competitor can recreate the same knockout with CRISPR. Under EU NGT Regulation 2026/1388 (in force 16 July 2026, applying from 17 July 2028), a Category 1 edited knockout is treated like a conventional plant, which removes the "non-GMO EU premium". Existing trait patents also cover the phenotype whatever the allele's origin (the CSIRO/Arista SBEIIa patents led to the Arcadia litigation). An exclusive license to a population therefore protects almost nothing.
scored.buyer: Seed majors (Corteva, Bayer, BASF, Syngenta, KWS, Limagrain) and specialty-trait or milling firms (Bay State Milling, Arista Cereal Technologies). They are well capitalised, but they buy traits that are already in elite germplasm and backed by patents. They source raw knockouts in-house or through CRISPR, and they already screen these same public TILLING databases themselves.
scored.ladder: The ladder is plausible on paper: allele, then a trait introgressed into elite germplasm, then owned varieties, then a branded seed or specialty-grain company (the Arcadia GoodWheat model), then a seed major. But Arcadia climbed exactly this ladder with TILLING wheat and stayed a sub-scale company. I would give it 3, not 5.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no information asymmetry and nothing exclusive to own. The flagship TILLING populations already have their mutations called and annotated in public, searchable databases, and single lines sell non-exclusively for £200 with commercial rights. Under the EU NGT regulation, any knockout can now be recreated with CRISPR and treated as conventional, so a mined EMS allele is capped at the cost of editing that gene.
scored.one_line_reason: The outcome is already written into public variant-effect databases (wheat-tilling.com, Ensembl Plants), lines sell non-exclusively at £15-200 each, the base hit rate for finding a knockout is already ~90% per gene, and the EU NGT regulation lets CRISPR replicate any knockout as "conventional", so there is no 10x lever, no cheap exclusive right and no durable step-up.

scored.name: Pozzo: proving waste piles as cement supplements
scored.one_line: Leases or buys the rights to legacy industrial byproduct stockpiles (slag heaps, ponded and landfilled coal ash, kiln dust, mine-free calcined clays, glass cullet) that owners hold as liabilities near zero or negative value. It predicts pozzolanic or latent-hydraulic reactivity from public chemistry and disposal records, proves it with a $500 R3 reactivity test, and sells the material as a cement supplement (SCM) to cement majors at market price.
scored.unproven_right: Offtake or ownership rights to stockpiles, often at $0 or paid to remove, from utilities, steel successors and municipalities who do not know which piles are reactive. These are not mineral exploration claims.
scored.proving_step: Core sampling plus the ASTM C1897 R3 reactivity test and mortar-cube strength-activity index, about $1-5k a pile in days. Base hit rate for spec-grade reactivity in random legacy piles might be 10-20%. ML over chemistry, disposal history and combustion records raises it.
scored.proven_buyer: Cement and concrete majors facing an SCM shortage and carbon rules (Holcim, Heidelberg Materials, CEMEX, CRH, Eco Material/Eco-Mat), who pay about $40-80/t for qualifying SCM.
scored.public_data: EPA CCR rule compliance websites (per-impoundment reports, scanned PDFs); state solid-waste permits; EIA-923 coal quality by plant; historical steel mill and smelter records; USGS slag surveys; Materials Project glass/phase data for reactivity modelling.
scored.rough_step_up: Roughly -$5 to $0.1/t to $40-80/t: about 100-500x per tonne, on million-tonne piles. Caveats: adjacent to the killed landfill-mining idea and borderline on the mineral exclusion; utilities already market some ash. The ladder runs to SCM supply and then to low-carbon blended cement.
scored.frame: The candidate's rung is "a proven reactive pile under contract". No one buys that rung on its own. Cement majors buy spec-grade, dry, low-LOI, consistent material delivered by rail or truck. Pond or landfill ash has to be excavated, dried, classified, ground and carbon-treated before it meets ASTM C618. SEFA lists those steps for its harvested-ash process, and the Alabama Power Plant Barry permit for 630k dry t/yr names two rotary dryers, two air classifiers and two carbon-removal systems. In the sellable frame, discovery and proving (a $1-5k R3 test) is my estimate of under 5% of the work. The beneficiation plant, which I estimate at tens of millions of dollars per 250-600k t/yr site with no public figure found, plus 10-20 years of operations, is the other 95%. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example almost exactly: the bespoke physical plant is much harder than finding the right pile.
scored.step_up: Unproven: about $0/t, or negative, since utilities treat harvesting as a way to offset closure costs (Georgia Power VP, 2022). Proven and processed: IMARC puts US fly ash at $121.9/t (Dec 2025), and the candidate assumes $40-80/t for qualifying SCM. That gross figure is not available on proving. It only arrives after beneficiation, which I estimate at $20-50/t opex plus plant capex. The jump from proving alone, meaning a pile known to be reactive but unprocessed, is small. Indian pond ash sells for Rs 40/t against Rs 400/t for dry fly ash, so the unprocessed form is worth about 10x less. Net margin per tonne after processing is perhaps $20-60/t. On a nominal $0.1/t right that is a large ratio, but it is not realised immediately, so I score this as roughly 3-10x real value creation per tonne at the proving step.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt is about $1-5k (the candidate's estimate; an R3 test plus a strength-activity index is cheap, and I agree). Base hit rate: class F pond and landfill fly ash is mostly beneficiable to C618. SEFA has processed more than 5M t of recovered CCR and Winyah STAR 2.4M t since 2015, which suggests the hit rate is high for ash once it is processed. Legacy air-cooled slag heaps are known to be crystalline and largely non-reactive. A University of Kentucky WOCA 2026 abstract says harvested ash "often fails ASTM specs" before processing, but the fix is processing, not discovery. Even if the base hit rate were 10-20%, a 5-10x lift on a $5k test saves about $20-45k per success. That is negligible against plant capex in the tens of millions. There is no discovery-capex lever.
scored.data: The CCR rule websites (scanned PDFs) are illegible, and they give pile volumes. But the utility owners already hold their own combustion records, LOI and chemistry, and EIA-923 is a legible coal-quality field. Ash type (class F or C) is effectively known from the coal rank. Who controls the rights is the bigger problem. Utilities run competitive RFPs or have long-term contracts with Eco Material Technologies (Georgia Power Plant Bowen, about 600k t/yr and more than 9M t in total), Heidelberg/SEFA (three Duke STAR plants at Buck, Cape Fear and H.F. Lee, 250-400k t/yr each, under North Carolina's CAMA mandate), Charah, STET (Talen Brunner Island, 600k t/yr), and Ash Grove/Boral successors. The owners are sophisticated and can read their own data. In NC, state law mandates beneficiation. The cheap right sold by an owner who cannot read the data mostly does not exist for the large piles.
scored.right_bought: In practice, offtake and harvest rights to large utility ash ponds and landfills are awarded through RFPs and multi-decade contracts with incumbent marketers, often with the utility sharing closure-cost savings. They are not bought cheaply from naive owners. Smaller, orphaned municipal or industrial piles might be cheap, but they are small, contaminated and far from cement markets.
scored.buyer: Capitalised buyers exist and are short of SCM. L.E.K. says the US needs 6-7M t of additional SCM just to hold a 14% inclusion rate, after fly ash production fell 63% from 2013 to 2021. Named buyers are Holcim, Heidelberg, CEMEX, CRH and Eco Material. But they buy finished, spec-grade, logistics-reliable supply, not proven piles. Heidelberg (SEFA) and Eco Material are vertically integrated into harvesting themselves.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are plausible: harvest and beneficiation, SCM marketing, then blended or low-carbon cement. But each rung up is capex- and operations-heavy and occupied by incumbents (Eco Material, SEFA/Heidelberg, Charah). The total market is a few $B/yr of US SCM, not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. The value is created by a tens-of-millions-of-dollars beneficiation plant, which is the geothermal counter-example. The piles' character is already known to their sophisticated utility owners. Those owners award harvest rights through RFPs and multi-decade contracts to incumbents (Eco Material, Heidelberg/SEFA, Charah, STET). So there is no cheap illegible right to buy, and a $5k R3 test leaves no discovery capex for ML to cut.
scored.one_line_reason: The hard part is processing, not finding: harvested ash must be dried, classified, ground and carbon-treated in large plants run by incumbents who already hold the utility contracts. That leaves the ML discovery edge with nothing material to cut.

scored.name: Private Tideland Geoduck Beds (Washington State)
scored.one_line: Washington sold its tidelands into private hands, and many waterfront owners don't know there are commercial wild geoduck beds below the low-tide line. Buy or lease harvest rights to individual parcels cheaply, after ML ranks them on LiDAR, sediment and eelgrass maps plus adjacent DNR survey tracts. Prove the bed with a diver density survey, then sell the harvest rights to a large shellfish company.
scored.unproven_right: Harvest leases or easements on privately owned tidelands, bought from homeowners for a few thousand dollars per parcel. The owners cannot read sub-tidal survey data and value the parcel as beach frontage.
scored.proving_step: A two-day dive transect survey counting geoduck 'shows', at about $5-15k per parcel. The base rate of commercial-density beds on random parcels is low (well under 10%).
scored.proven_buyer: Large shellfish growers and licensed geoduck harvesters, who sell into the Asian export market at $20-40/lb landed. They buy proven tracts and harvest rights at once.
scored.public_data: WA DNR geoduck tract survey reports (scanned PDFs going back decades), Puget Sound LiDAR Consortium topo-bathy, WA Ecology ShoreZone imagery, DNR eelgrass monitoring, Washington Sea Grant sediment maps, county parcel records.
scored.rough_step_up: Lease: about $1-5k per parcel. Proven bed: about $100k-1M of standing stock per acre. That is 10^2-10^3x on the right.
scored.frame: The rung would be: lease or easement on a private tideland, then a dive survey, then sale of the right to a grower or harvester. Discovery and proving (siting plus the survey) is maybe 50-60% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). The rest is not trivial. Before a buyer can monetise a bed, it needs a WDFW/DOH harvest certification, county shoreline permits (geoduck farms on private tidelands routinely draw neighbour lawsuits, e.g. Henderson Inlet and Dungeness Bay), boundary buoying below extreme low tide, and a negotiated tribal share. A capitalised buyer exists (Taylor Shellfish and other growers), but that buyer already leases private tidelands directly.
scored.step_up: Claimed: $1-5k lease rising to $100k-1M of standing stock per acre (100-1000x). Realistic, my estimate: the 1000x figure would need commercial-density wild beds. Those sit at -18 to -70 ft MLLW (2003 WA Senate bill report), which is state-owned bedland, not private tideland. Private ownership ends around extreme low tide. Natural intertidal geoduck on private parcels is sparse, and tribes are entitled to up to 50% of naturally occurring shellfish on private tidelands (Rafeedie, U.S. v. Washington 873 F.Supp.1422, upheld 9th Cir 1998). Wild product is also cheap: DNR's 2026 auctions bill $4.00/lb plus bonus bids, against $15-30/lb for farmed. So the realistic step-up on the owned right is about 3-30x, mostly as farm-site value rather than standing wild stock.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: under 10% per random parcel is the candidate's own guess. It is not sourced, and the true rate for commercial-density natural beds on private tideland is probably much lower, close to zero (my estimate, given the depth band). Cost per proving attempt: $5-15k per dive survey (candidate estimate, plausible). That is roughly equal to or above the price of the right itself, so ML at best saves a few hundred thousand dollars over a whole campaign. The lever is capped at 1/base rate, but each shot only buys a small prize.
scored.data: The DNR geoduck tract survey PDFs cover state subtidal tracts, not private intertidal parcels, so they do not describe the asset. LiDAR, ShoreZone, eelgrass and parcel data are public and moderately legible. The outcome is legible to the owner too: geoduck 'shows' (siphons) are visible on the owner's own beach at low tide. Growers have systematically canvassed tideland owners for decades; Taylor alone had 65 private homeowner leases by 2010, up from about 40 five years earlier. Incumbents already extract this signal through local knowledge, so the illegibility edge is weak.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought, not free first-come. Owners lease or sell harvest rights privately. But it is not a blind purchase: owners can see their beach, growers bid for the same parcels, and neighbour opposition plus tribal claims reduce what the right is worth. Expect real competition for good parcels, not a 10^3 discount.
scored.buyer: Taylor Shellfish and smaller geoduck growers and licensed harvesters, who export to China and Hong Kong. They are capitalised but small, and they already source private tidelands themselves. The total WA geoduck market is roughly $100M/yr (my estimate).
scored.ladder: Above this rung: farming (planting and tubing), harvest, processing, then export marketing. This is the Taylor Shellfish model. The whole chain is a niche worth around $100M/yr, capped by the supply of suitable Puget Sound tideland and by Chinese tariff and demand swings. There is no path to a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The asset mostly isn't on private land. Commercial wild geoduck beds are harvested at -18 to -70 ft MLLW, which is state-owned bedland managed by DNR auction and co-managed with the tribes. Washington's privately sold tidelands end around extreme low tide. Whatever natural geoduck exists on private parcels is sparse, carries a 50% treaty-tribe entitlement (Rafeedie), and is visible to the owner and to growers who have been leasing these parcels for decades.
scored.one_line_reason: Commercial wild geoduck lives on state subtidal land, not on private tidelands. What is left is a niche, competitive tideland-leasing business that growers like Taylor already run, with a small step-up and no big ladder.
sources: https://lawfilesext.leg.wa.gov/Biennium/2003-04/Htm/Bill%20Reports/Senate/5266.SBR.htm (commercial harvest -18 to -70 ft; state tracts DNR-auctioned; tribes 50%)
https://nwifc.org/about-us/shellfish/rafeedie-decision/ (tribal 50% share incl. natural beds on private tidelands)

scored.name: Clearfield (prove-absence archaeology and paleontology for land options)
scored.one_line: Buys options on sites that developers avoid because of archaeological risk, such as English HER and allocation sites and Japan's buried-cultural-property zones. ML over thousands of grey-literature excavation reports predicts which sites are actually clean, cheap evaluation trenches confirm it, and housebuilders buy the de-risked sites.
scored.unproven_right: Purchase options on land discounted for archaeological risk.
scored.proving_step: An ML model reads the OASIS and ADS grey literature (tens of thousands of PDFs) plus LiDAR and geophysics, and predicts deposit absence. A geophysics pass plus trial trenching (about £20-50k) proves the site so planning can discharge the condition.
scored.proven_buyer: Volume housebuilders and land promoters (Barratt, Persimmon, Japanese developers), who pay a full residential land price once risk is retired.
scored.public_data: OASIS and ADS grey-literature archive, Historic Environment Records, EA LiDAR, and Japan's prefectural maizo bunkazai maps and excavation reports (scanned and only in Japanese).
scored.rough_step_up: Only about 1.3-3x, because the discount is modest and the step-up comes from planning, not proof. This is the honest low scorer of the set and is included for its strong capitalised buyer and long ladder into land promotion.
scored.frame: The rung would be buying an option on land discounted for archaeological risk, proving it clean, and selling it. That is not a real discrete rung, because housebuilders buy land with consent, not land with archaeology cleared. Archaeology is one planning condition among many (highways, ecology/BNG, drainage, viability, S106). My estimate is that clearing archaeology is under 10% of the work and cost of getting a site to a sellable state, and planning promotion is the other 90%+. The physical step is not abstracted either. The LPA archaeologist requires geophysics plus 2-5% trial trenching (Brighton thesis), sometimes up to 7-10% (Highland HER), whatever an ML model says.
scored.step_up: There is a large step-up on English land, but it comes from planning, not archaeology. Farmland is about GBP 20k/ha, and land with residential permission is about GBP 2m/ha outside London (IEA, 2014 data; about 93x) or "about 275x" (CPP/NHF, contested by CLA). The archaeology-only share of that step-up is small. Only about 0.01% of planning applications are refused on grounds that include archaeology (ALGAO via CIfA). So the archaeology risk discount on allocated land is my estimate of about 5-30% (1.05-1.3x), not 10^3. The candidate's own 1.3-3x is generous.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate is high, not low. Most evaluations find nothing significant or only minor remains; Upper Achintore (about 10.9 ha, 6% trenched) found nothing significant. My estimate is that 60-80% of evaluated development sites need no major excavation, so the lever is capped at 1/0.7, about 1.4x. Cost per proving attempt is my estimate of about GBP 20-50k per site for geophysics plus trenching (the candidate's figure; I found no published per-hectare benchmark). Proving is cheap and mostly succeeds, so ML has very little capex to save. It cannot skip the trenching either, because the planning condition demands it.
scored.data: The data side is partly real. OASIS/ADS grey literature (tens of thousands of PDFs) and Japan's scanned prefectural maizo bunkazai reports are illegible and largely unextracted. But HER event records already summarise outcomes in legible text (for example "no significant archaeological finds, features or deposits" in Highland HER entries). Japan's buried-property zone maps are a legible flag, and the outcome needs a mandatory survey anyway. Prediction is also hard: the Brighton thesis shows trenching itself has systematic false negatives, so labels are noisy.
scored.right_bought: The right is bought, which is good: options and promotion agreements are standard in England. But owners do not price on archaeology; they price on planning hope value, and land agents already know it. There is no evidence of a measurable archaeology-specific discount for an ML reader to capture. Owners of allocated sites already expect full residential value minus planning costs.
scored.buyer: The buyers are strong and well capitalised: volume housebuilders (Barratt Redrow, Persimmon, Taylor Wimpey), land promoters (Gladman, Catesby, Richborough) and Japanese developers. But they buy consented land, so the buyer is real for the planning rung, not for the archaeology-cleared rung.
scored.ladder: The ladder is long and real: options, then strategic land promotion (outline consent), then serviced plots, then housebuilding, then build-to-rent/SFR ownership. Land promotion is a multi-billion-pound GBP industry. But the candidate enters at a non-rung (archaeology), and the next rung up (planning promotion) is already crowded by incumbents with no data edge on this signal.
scored.fatal_flaw: Archaeology is almost never what stops or discounts development land in England: only about 0.01% of applications are refused on grounds that include it. So there is no discount to buy and no 10^3 step-up to capture. The value jump comes from planning permission, which ML over excavation reports does not deliver. The LPA requires trial trenching regardless of any prediction, and most sites pass anyway (high base hit rate), so the lever is about 1.4x at best.
scored.one_line_reason: The data is illegible and the buyers are strong, but archaeology risk is a small, rarely binding planning condition with a high pass rate and mandatory trenching. The step-up comes from planning, not proof, which leaves maybe 1.1-1.3x and almost no ML lever.
sources: https://iea.org.uk/?p=43538 (agricultural about GBP 21k/ha vs residential about GBP 1.96m/ha, 2014 data)
https://archaeologists.net/node/3492 (CIfA citing ALGAO: about 0.01% of applications refused for reasons including archaeology)
https://her.highland.gov.uk/Event/EHG5894 and https://her.highland.gov.uk/Event/EHG6175 (HER entries summarising evaluation outcomes; 7-10% trenching required)
https://hbsmrweb-highland.esdm.co.uk/Event/EHG5837 (Upper Achintore 10.87 ha, 6% trenched, no significant finds)
Estimates (mine): archaeology discount 5-30%; clean-site base rate 60-80%; GBP 20-50k per evaluation (the candidate's figure, not verified)

scored.name: Accreta: claiming accreted and relicted land beside riparian parcels
scored.one_line: Nature moves shorelines. Under the doctrine of accretion, land that slowly builds up beside a riparian parcel belongs to that parcel's owner, but the tax maps still show the old line. Landsat and NAIP shoreline histories plus LiDAR find parcels that have quietly gained acres. The company buys the narrow riparian parcel cheaply, a quiet-title action proves the accreted acreage, and the larger holding is sold to adjacent developers or conservation buyers.
scored.unproven_right: A riparian or littoral parcel bought at its assessed (old-boundary) price from an owner who does not know their boundary has moved.
scored.proving_step: A boundary survey plus a quiet-title or declaratory judgment ($10-40k). ML separates gradual accretion, which goes to the owner, from avulsion, which does not, using the Landsat time series since 1984.
scored.proven_buyer: Waterfront developers, ports and industrial users, and conservation or mitigation buyers.
scored.public_data: Landsat archive since 1972; NAIP imagery; USGS 3DEP and NOAA coastal topobathy LiDAR; historical USGS topo sheets and GLO plats (scanned); county parcel maps.
scored.rough_step_up: Per dollar spent, about 10-1000x when a $20k sliver gains 50+ acres. The opportunity is sparse and lumpy, state claims to sovereign submerged lands bring litigation risk, and the ladder is weak.
scored.frame: The rung is "buy a riparian parcel, then get a court to confirm its accreted acreage." Discovery (finding gained acres in Landsat, NAIP and LiDAR) is maybe 30-40% of the work in this rung (my estimate). Most of the work and risk is legal: the boundary survey, the quiet-title or declaratory action, the accretion-versus-avulsion fight, the state's sovereign-lands claim, how accretion is split among neighbouring riparian owners, and closing a purchase from an owner. The physical step is not trivial. It is contested litigation that can drag on for years. Search results show these cases often get past summary judgment, and the state or the United States sometimes wins (Omaha Tribe in the 8th Circuit; the 10th Circuit "omitted land" ruling for the US). A buyer exists (waterfront developers, conservation buyers), but the output is a lawsuit-backed title that title insurers routinely except, not a clean asset that sells straight away.
scored.step_up: No real per-acre sales numbers were found; the search budget ran out after 2 of 5 searches. My estimate: the unproven parcel already sells at waterfront or bottomland market value, not at about $0. River accretion is mostly floodplain bottomland, roughly $2-8k/acre for agricultural use (estimate), and often wetland or flood-restricted for development. Coastal accretion in states like Florida is limited by erosion control lines; Stop the Beach Renourishment (2010) upheld the state's claim to new land seaward of the ECL. A $20k sliver that gains 50 acres of floodplain worth $2-5k/acre gives about 5-12x on the purchase price before legal costs. After $10-40k of survey and litigation it is about 2-5x. That is nowhere near 10^3-10^4. The added acres are the same kind of land, often worse than the original parcel, so the value per hectare does not jump at all. Only the acreage changes.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate for the proving step (quiet title) is not low, because you only sue when the imagery already shows accretion. My estimate is that well-chosen cases win 50-70% of the time, so the cap on the lever (1/base hit rate) is about 1.5-2x, not 10x. The cost per attempt is $10-40k (the candidate's own figure; plausible for a survey plus an uncontested action). Contested cases against a state attorney general or neighbouring owners probably cost $100k+ (my estimate). ML mainly sorts accretion from avulsion, and that is decided by expert testimony and historical evidence in court, not by a classifier score.
scored.data: The imagery (Landsat since 1972, NAIP, 3DEP and NOAA LiDAR) is public and already fully machine-readable. Shoreline-change products such as USGS DSAS and NOAA shoreline datasets already pull out exactly this signal, so the data is not illegible. The outcome is not written into a legible field, since parcel maps keep the old lines, which is the only plus here. The bigger problem is the information gap with the owner. Accreted land sits physically next to the owner's parcel and is visible to them. They usually farm it, mow it or use it as their beach, and many assessors revalue riparian parcels. So it is hard to buy at the old-boundary price from an owner who "cannot read the data." They can see it from their porch.
scored.right_bought: Yes, it is bought, not claimed first-come. But the price is full riparian market value, and sellers and their brokers market waterfront by its visible frontage. The discount is thin and depends on the owner not knowing, and the owner usually does know.
scored.buyer: Waterfront developers, ports and industrial users, conservation buyers and mitigation buyers. These are real but sparse and local. Accreted floodplain or beach land is often not developable, which limits what developers will pay. Conservation buyers pay modest per-acre prices.
scored.ladder: Weak. The next rungs above (riverfront development, ports, conservation land management) are ordinary real estate with no compounding data edge. Accretion events are rare and scattered, so the ladder does not lead to a single large integrated chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The 'hidden' asset is neither hidden nor much more valuable. The owner can physically see the accreted land and usually uses it, and the land itself is low-value floodplain or beach that states contest. So you pay market price for the parcel, then spend on litigation to get roughly a 2-5x gain in acreage of the same kind of land. There is no jump from about $1/ha to $10,000/ha.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a legal-risk arbitrage, not a discovery business. The unproven parcel already sells at market value, proving it means contested litigation against states and neighbours, and the step-up is about 2-10x of an acreage gain with no change in value per hectare. Note: only 2 of 5 searches ran before the budget ran out, so the dollar figures are my estimates.
sources: Estimate/knowledge: Stop the Beach Renourishment v. Florida DEP, 560 U.S. 702 (2010); USGS Digital Shoreline Analysis System (DSAS)

scored.name: Leveeworks: re-accrediting levees to re-rate the land behind them
scored.one_line: FEMA de-accredits many levees for lack of certification paperwork rather than physical failure, which maps whole districts into the floodplain. The company buys options on the cheap land behind those levees. InSAR crest-settlement analysis and LiDAR profiles find levees that are physically sound. One 44 CFR 65.10 certification, funded through the levee district, re-rates every parcel behind the levee at once, and the land is sold to industrial developers.
scored.unproven_right: Options on large agricultural or industrial tracts behind de-accredited levees (shown on FIRMs as Zone A/AE with a 'levee not accredited' note), held by owners who assume the levee is failing.
scored.proving_step: Engineering certification of crest height, embankment stability and seepage, plus a FEMA LOMR. This costs more than a drill hole ($0.5-3M per levee system), but one proof lifts thousands of acres.
scored.proven_buyer: Industrial and logistics developers, data-center developers and ag-to-industrial land funds.
scored.public_data: FEMA NFHL levee layers; USACE National Levee Database (NLD) inspection ratings; Sentinel-1 InSAR crest settlement; 3DEP LiDAR; scanned levee-district O&M reports.
scored.rough_step_up: About 2-10x on the optioned acreage (flood-zone ag land at $3-8k/acre to developable industrial land at $30-80k/acre). This fails the 10^3 bar, and the certification work starts to look like the bespoke-build trap.
scored.frame: The rung would be "optioned land behind a levee, then a FEMA re-accreditation, then sale to developers." Discovery (finding which levees are physically sound) is only about 20-40% of the work inside this rung (my estimate). Most of the effort is the 44 CFR 65.10 certification package: geotechnical borings, seepage and stability analysis, an interior-drainage study, an O&M plan, and the community and levee-owner sign-off and LOMR/PMR, which takes 1-3 years. Often there is also remedial construction, such as raising freeboard or adding seepage berms, because under updated hydrology many levees fail freeboard or seepage criteria. Few fail on paperwork alone. The company does not own the levee. The levee district and the community must sponsor the submission, so the physical and political step is not abstracted away. A buyer exists (industrial, logistics and data-center developers), but they buy the land, not the output of the proving rung.
scored.step_up: The candidate's own figures put flood-zone ag land at $3-8k/acre and developable industrial land at $30-80k/acre, about 4-10x at best. Much of that uplift comes from entitlements, utilities and rezoning, not from the flood zone. Zone AE land is already developable with fill and elevated construction, and the change in flood-insurance cost alone is worth far less. My estimate is that the share of uplift actually caused by re-accreditation is 1.5-3x. That is not live-verified, because the search budget was exhausted.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I estimate the cost per proving attempt at about $0.5-3M per levee system for certification. That figure is not live-verified. Certification estimates commonly run $100k-$1M+ per levee mile, and this excludes remediation, which can reach tens of millions (Sacramento/Natomas-type upgrades were roughly $500M+ from memory). The proving step does not "mostly fail" for random reasons. Engineers and districts already know roughly which levees are deficient from USACE periodic inspections. Remote screening (InSAR and LiDAR crest height) can rule levees out, but it cannot certify seepage or underseepage, which is the common failure mode. My estimate of the base hit rate among de-accredited levees being certifiable with no or minor work is 20-40%, so the lever is capped at roughly 2.5-5x, not 10x. The search budget for this turn was exhausted, so none of these numbers were live-verified.
scored.data: The outcome is largely summarised in legible fields. The USACE National Levee Database carries inspection ratings (Acceptable, Minimally Acceptable, Unacceptable), the FEMA accreditation status and the Levee Safety Action Classification risk rating. FEMA's NFHL marks accredited and non-accredited levees. FEMA's LAMP procedures (since 2013) already analyse "sound reaches" of non-accredited levees and give partial credit, which pre-empts much of the ML edge. InSAR and LiDAR are public but only weakly predictive of certifiability, because seepage is subsurface. The right is also poorly matched. Options on land can be bought, but the asset that has to be proven (the levee) is owned by a public district. Every neighbouring parcel free-rides on a certification the company pays for, and the levee district and its landowners are already motivated, since they pay the NFIP premiums. The owners are not unable to read the data.
scored.right_bought: Yes, in part. Options on ag tracts behind de-accredited levees can be bought, probably at little or no discount to ag value. Owners see the same FIRM, and the levee's condition is publicly rated. The company cannot buy or control the levee itself, and the certification needs the levee owner's and the community's sponsorship.
scored.buyer: Industrial, logistics and data-center developers, and ag-to-industrial land funds, are capitalised. Their willingness to pay depends on utilities, entitlements, transport access and zoning far more than on Zone X versus Zone AE.
scored.ladder: The ladder is modest. It runs from land options and re-accreditation, to entitled industrial parks, to developer or REIT, and possibly to levee O&M or infrastructure ownership. This is a real-estate development ladder with ordinary margins, not a path to the whole chain at trillion-dollar scale. The levee-engineering side is a service that districts already hire firms to provide.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is a bespoke engineering, construction and permitting project that the company does not control, rather than a cheap discovery step. Seepage and freeboard deficiencies usually need remediation, and the levee district plus the community must sponsor it. The outcome is already legible in the NLD inspection ratings, the accreditation status and FEMA's LAMP analysis. And the uplift attributable to re-accreditation is about 2-5x, not 10^3-10^4. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines trap in levee form.
scored.one_line_reason: Fails the rubric on every axis. The step-up is about 2-10x (mostly from entitlements), certification and remediation is bespoke public-sponsored construction rather than trivial proving, NLD and NFHL already publish levee status legibly, and neighbours free-ride on the levee the company would pay to certify.
sources: Web searches attempted, but the turn's search budget was exhausted, so no live sources were retrieved; all figures are estimates from prior knowledge
44 CFR 65.10 (FEMA mapping of areas protected by levee systems), from prior knowledge
USACE National Levee Database (levees.sec.usace.army.mil) inspection ratings and LSAC fields, from prior knowledge
FEMA Levee Analysis and Mapping Procedures (LAMP), 2013, from prior knowledge
Candidate's own land-value figures ($3-8k/acre ag vs $30-80k/acre industrial)

scored.name: LostCrop (rediscovering lost coffee and cacao wild populations)
scored.one_line: Mines colonial-era botanical archives and herbarium sheets at Kew, Paris and Leiden to relocate lost or forgotten wild populations of climate-resilient Coffea (such as C. stenophylla, rediscovered in Sierra Leone through herbarium records in 2018) and disease-resistant wild cacao. Signs exclusive ABS and benefit-sharing contracts with landholding communities and governments before relocating them, proves presence and genotype, and sells exclusive germplasm and breeding licences.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive Nagoya-compliant ABS and Mutually Agreed Terms contracts covering a forest block or community land, negotiated before the population is confirmed, while the holders and the state value it near zero.
scored.proving_step: A field relocation expedition, leaf genotyping and a cupping or heat-tolerance assay on a small cherry harvest. About $20-100k per target.
scored.proven_buyer: Coffee and cocoa majors with climate-adaptation budgets: Nestle/Nespresso, JDE Peet's, Starbucks, Mars, Barry Callebaut, Olam/ofi, plus World Coffee Research consortia. A heat-tolerant arabica-quality species threatens a market of more than $400B.
scored.public_data: Kew, MNHN Paris and Naturalis Leiden scanned herbarium sheets with handwritten 1890-1960 locality labels; Biodiversity Heritage Library scanned expedition reports; GBIF Coffea and Theobroma occurrences; Global Forest Watch loss layers to drop populations that are likely gone.
scored.rough_step_up: An ABS contract at about $10-50k becomes an exclusive licence for a validated resilient population at about $5-50M: roughly 10^3. The base hit rate for relocating a lost population is low (about 5-10% per expedition), so the lever is about 10x. Risks: sovereign ABS politics; a genetic resource cannot be fully owned, so exclusivity rests on contract.
scored.frame: The rung is: find a wild Coffea or Theobroma population again, confirm it is there and get its genotype. Inside that rung discovery really is most of the work, perhaps 70-80% (my estimate). The physical step is cheap: a trip into the forest plus leaf sequencing, roughly $20-100k as the candidate says. The problem is that nobody buys what comes out of this rung. A wild population is not a variety. Value only appears after 15-25 years of coffee breeding: crossing, trials over several harvests, and UPOV variety registration. Majors and World Coffee Research pay for finished varieties, or fund research grants. They do not pay millions for a location plus a genotype. So in practice the sellable rung is the whole breeding programme, and discovery is a small share of that.
scored.step_up: Estimates only; I found no market evidence. The unproven ABS/MAT contract might cost about $10-50k (the candidate's figure, plausible). The claimed $5-50M exclusive licence for a validated population has no observed comparable. I know of no transaction where a coffee or cocoa major paid millions for exclusive rights to an unbred wild accession. The real benchmark points the other way. C. stenophylla was rediscovered in Sierra Leone in 2018 and published in Nature Plants in 2021 (Davis et al.: arabica-like flavour, mean annual temperature tolerance about 6C above arabica). The result was public trials and no licensing windfall. The realistic step-up is research-grant money, maybe 1-3x the cost. It is not 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I did not verify the base hit rate. The candidate's 5-10% per expedition is unsourced. For well-labelled herbarium localities, the Kew stenophylla trips succeeded after a few attempts, so my estimate is 10-30% per targeted expedition. That caps the lever at about 3-10x on cheap trips of $20-100k each. Total discovery capex is small to begin with, so cutting it 10x saves little. The binding cost is the decades of breeding that come after.
scored.data: The data is public, but it is not illegible and it is not unexploited. Aaron Davis's team at Kew built a curated Coffea monograph from these same herbarium sheets. They georeferenced specimens and in 2019 assessed the IUCN Red List status of all 124 Coffea species (Science Advances: 60% threatened, including "possibly extinct" flags). GBIF already holds the Coffea and Theobroma occurrences in digitised form. So the outcome (where a species was, and whether it is thought lost) is already summarised in legible fields, the IUCN status and GBIF records. The likely targets are the ones Kew, CIRAD, CATIE and Bioversity are already chasing. Cacao wild germplasm (Amazonian Theobroma) is likewise heavily collected and held in the ICGT Trinidad and CATIE genebanks.
scored.right_bought: The right is weak and not cleanly buyable. Under the Nagoya Protocol the state owns sovereign rights over the genetic resource and issues the permit (PIC). Communities can be parties to the Mutually Agreed Terms, but a state can refuse exclusivity, and many do not have working ABS systems. Exclusivity over a species that grows in several countries, or already sits in other collections (stenophylla is now held at Kew, in Sierra Leone and in trials), cannot be enforced. Once seed or budwood leaves the country, contract terms leak. Wild species themselves cannot be protected by UPOV or by patents in most of these jurisdictions. Unlike a mineral claim, the owner cannot sell you a clean, exclusive and transferable title.
scored.buyer: The buyers would be World Coffee Research (budget in the low tens of millions a year, member-funded, and it releases varieties open-access), Nestle/Nespresso, JDE Peet's, Starbucks (its Hacienda Alsacia farm breeds in-house), Mars, Barry Callebaut and ofi. They are capitalised, but they buy finished, de-risked varieties or fund pre-competitive public research. They do not buy raw wild accessions at millions each. Reputationally they also avoid anything that looks like biopiracy of community resources.
scored.ladder: There is a ladder: wild germplasm, then breeding and varieties, then nurseries and seedlings, then farms, then green coffee trading, then roasting and brands. But each rung above discovery is slow (a coffee breeding cycle takes decades), commoditised, or held by entrenched majors. Winning discovery gives no structural edge on those rungs. The path is real but long and low-margin, and it does not lead to a trillion-dollar company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up does not happen when a population is found. A relocated wild population has no market price. It earns value only after 15-25 years of breeding, and by then the exclusivity (a Nagoya contract over a sovereign, leak-prone genetic resource) has worn away. So no capitalised buyer pays roughly $10^3x for the output of the discovery rung. Kew has also already curated the same herbarium data and published it openly (Coffea monograph, IUCN statuses for all 124 species).
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is cheap and doable, but the output of the discovery rung has no buyer at a 10^3 step-up. Value comes only after decades of breeding. The rights are sovereign contracts, not ownable title. The herbarium signal has already been extracted and published by Kew.
sources: Web search was unavailable (the shared per-turn search budget was used up), so this scoring rests on prior knowledge, not new searches. Claims that need checking are marked as estimates.
Davis AP et al. 2021, 'Arabica-like flavour in a heat-tolerant wild coffee species', Nature Plants 7:413-418 (stenophylla rediscovery in Sierra Leone, about 6C higher temperature tolerance)

Davis AP et al. 2019, 'High extinction risk for wild coffee species and implications for coffee sector sustainability', Science Advances 5:eaav3473 (IUCN assessment of 124 Coffea species, 60% threatened)
Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit-sharing (CBD, 2010): sovereign rights, PIC/MAT
World Coffee Research: open-access variety releases and member-funded breeding programme (worldcoffeeresearch.org)
International Cocoa Genebank Trinidad (ICGT) and CATIE cacao collections

scored.name: HiveRight (high-DHA Leptospermum apiary rights in Australia)
scored.one_line: Buys cheap apiary-site licences and private-land hive-access leases across eastern Australia, uses ML to predict where stands of high-DHA Leptospermum species exist (bioactive Australian manuka at UMF/MGO grades that sell for 10-50x commodity honey), proves them with a one-week nectar DHA test or a single test hive, and sells or leases the proven sites to manuka marketers.
scored.unproven_right: State forest apiary-site permits and private-land hive-placement leases, typically tens to hundreds of dollars per site per year. Landowners and the state set prices by generic floral value.
scored.proving_step: Sampling nectar for DHA (a lab assay, around $100) or a single test hive harvest with MGO lab testing. The physical step is trivial: put a box down.
scored.proven_buyer: Manuka marketers and integrated apiarists: Comvita, Capilano/Hive+Wellness, the Medibee JV (Comvita bought into it, valuing manuka apiary assets at $A9.2M), Manuka Health. Australian and NZ manuka land leases have been bid up sharply where grade is proven.
scored.public_data: Scanned AVH (Australasian Virtual Herbarium) Leptospermum specimens; University of the Sunshine Coast species-level DHA potential study covering 55 species, with figures above 16,000 mg/kg in L. whitei; state regional ecosystem and vegetation mapping, which is coarse and unstructured; state apiary-site registers; Sentinel-2 imagery of flowering phenology.
scored.rough_step_up: A site lease at about $50-200/yr becomes a site producing about $20-80k/yr of high-MGO honey, capitalised at about $100-300k: roughly 10^3 on the right, but only about 10-30x on the honey itself. The base hit rate is uncertain, maybe 10-20% of candidate sites. Risks: weak C2 if the buyer only pays a site premium rather than a capitalised value; label and regulatory fights over the 'manuka' name.
scored.frame: The rung is "hold a hive-access right and prove it produces high-MGO manuka". Finding the right stand is maybe 30-40% of the work in this rung (my estimate). The rest is operations: placing and keeping hives every flowering season (Leptospermum blooms for 2-6 weeks), handling heat and drought years, extracting the honey, holding it in storage while MGO rises from DHA conversion, and getting it graded. Proving the site is also not a one-off event like a drill hit. Yields and MGO swing from season to season, so a site needs several seasons of results before a buyer pays for it. Buyers do exist (Comvita, Hive+Wellness/Capilano, Manuka Health/Medibee). But what they buy is honey, or access to hives at a premium. They do not buy a capitalised asset, so the rung is only sellable in a weak sense.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a state forest apiary site or private hive-placement deal costs roughly A$100-500 per site per year (my estimate, from memory of NSW Forestry Corp and Queensland apiary-site fees; not checked because the search budget ran out). Proven: in NZ, landowner fees on proven manuka blocks are about NZ$100-300 per hive per year, or a 10-30% share of honey revenue (from memory). Applied to a ~50-100-hive site, that is about A$5k-30k/yr. So the rent step-up on a proven site is about 10-100x, and it accrues to the landowner, who reprices when the lease renews. Honey value: MGO 263+ wholesales at roughly A$30-80/kg, against A$3-6/kg for commodity honey, about 10-20x (from memory). The NZ manuka glut in 2018-2024 and Comvita's write-downs pushed prices down further. The pitch's 10^3 multiple compares one year's rent with a capitalised value, but a short, renewable licence is not an asset that holds a capitalised value.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt: a nectar DHA assay is about A$50-150 plus a field visit. A test-hive season with an MGO test (about A$60-100 per test) costs about A$1-3k per site (my estimates). Base hit rate: unknown. Plausibly 10-30% of candidate Leptospermum sites reach MGO 263+ (my estimate). The pitch's own guess is 10-20%. Even raising that 3-5x saves only a few thousand dollars per proven site. Discovery capex is already tiny, so a ~10x cut in it does not change the economics. The real bottleneck is beekeeping operations and season-to-season variance, not the cost of looking.
scored.data: Herbarium records from the Australasian Virtual Herbarium (AVH) are already digitised, georeferenced and downloadable through the Atlas of Living Australia. They are not illegible. The species-level DHA potential figures are published (the University of the Sunshine Coast study cited in the pitch, about 55 species). State regional ecosystem mapping is public, structured GIS data. Incumbent beekeepers already know where jellybush and other Leptospermum flower, from decades of migratory beekeeping and from their own MGO test results. Those private test results are the real outcome data, and incumbents hold them. A model on Sentinel-2 flowering imagery is a modest gain over that local knowledge. The outcome is not written into a public status field, which is a point in favour, but the edge is small because the knowledge is spread through the industry rather than missing.
scored.right_bought: The rights can be bought cheaply: state apiary-site permits are allocated by application or tender, and private hive placement is negotiated with landowners. But they are short licences, typically 1-10 years. Landowners and state forestry agencies now know about manuka premiums and reprice on renewal or demand a share of the honey. So the step-up mostly goes to the land owner, not the holder of the licence. Buying the land outright gets the step-up, but rural land is not priced near $1/ha. Leptospermum is only one floral input, and land prices do not jump 10^3x on proof of it.
scored.buyer: Comvita (which paid about A$9.2M for a stake in the Medibee apiary JV, as the pitch notes), Hive+Wellness (Capilano), Manuka Health, Berringa, Australian Manuka Honey Association members. They buy honey on MGO grade, or vertically integrate their own hives. They do not pay capitalised value for a lease from a third party. The buyer side is also financially stressed: Comvita has had losses and write-downs (from memory). There is also an unresolved fight with NZ over who may use the "manuka" name in export markets.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are: owning hives and doing the beekeeping, extraction and storage, MGO grading, an own brand, export and medical-grade products (wound dressings).
