That is a real chain, but the whole Australian plus NZ manuka market is only about US$1-2B/yr in retail value (my estimate), and part of it is oversupplied. A large company is possible, but nowhere near the trillion-dollar path. Each rung up is operations-heavy, which is the same failure pattern as the geothermal counter-example.
scored.fatal_flaw: The unproven right is a short-term licence that can be repriced, not an asset that can be owned. When a site is proven to be high-MGO, the landowner or state captures the value at renewal. Buyers pay a premium in rent or per kilo of honey, not a 10^3x capitalised price. Proving costs only about $100-3k, so the ML hit-rate lever saves almost nothing.
scored.one_line_reason: Fails the Terranox test. The step-up flows to the landowner and is about 10-100x in rent, not a 10^3x capitalised gain. Proving is already cheap, so ML adds little. The data is mostly legible and incumbent beekeepers already know where the stands are. Beekeeping operations, not discovery, are most of the work.
sources: Web search budget for this turn was exhausted before any query ran; all figures are from prior knowledge and are labelled as estimates
Candidate brief: University of the Sunshine Coast Leptospermum DHA study (55 species, L. whitei >16,000 mg/kg), Comvita/Medibee A$9.2M figure
Atlas of Living Australia / AVH (digitised, georeferenced Leptospermum records) - general knowledge
NZ manuka hive-site fee and royalty-share practice, and the 2018-2024 manuka oversupply and Comvita write-downs - general knowledge, unverified this session

scored.name: PreListing Habitat Options (species about to be listed)
scored.one_line: Buys cheap options or easements over rangeland and forest where ML predicts a species proposed for listing (lesser prairie-chicken, northern long-eared and tricolored bat, monarch, gopher tortoise, dunes sagebrush lizard) actually occurs. Proves occupancy with acoustic or eDNA surveys, then sells the proven sites to mitigation bankers and to wind, solar and pipeline developers who must offset once listing or critical habitat hits.
scored.unproven_right: Options or term conservation easements over private rangeland and forest at about $5-50/acre. Owners price by grazing value.
scored.proving_step: Passive acoustic monitoring (bats), lek counts or drone thermal (prairie-chicken), and eDNA for aquatic and herp species. About $2-10k per site.
scored.proven_buyer: Mitigation bank sponsors (Ecosystem Investment Partners, Restoration Systems, RES), the WAFWA range-wide plan, and utility-scale wind, solar and transmission developers facing ESA Section 7/10 incidental-take requirements.
scored.public_data: USFWS Federal Register proposed listings; scanned state natural heritage programme reports; GBIF, eBird and iNaturalist; NABat acoustic archives; scanned EIS biological appendices on agency sites, huge and unstructured.
scored.rough_step_up: An option at $5-50/acre becomes proven occupied habitat that sells as credits at about $1-10k/acre-equivalent: about 10^2. The bespoke step (bank approval and a long-term management endowment) undercuts C1, and this is close to the previously weak wetland mitigation bank idea. Included for honesty as a likely 2-3 per criterion.
scored.frame: The rung would be 'option over private land, then occupancy proven'. That rung is not sellable on its own. Mitigation bankers and developers buy USFWS-approved credits, not occupancy data, and occupancy is not what makes a site eligible. Credit value comes from habitat-quality and service-area metrics plus a perpetual easement, an endowment and a USFWS-approved bank instrument (banking agreement, management plan, financial assurances). That approval typically takes 1-3 years (estimate, from the general USFWS conservation-banking process). Within the rung that actually sells (an approved bank), discovery or proving is perhaps 10-20% of the work (estimate). The rest is legal, entitlement and perpetual-management work. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern: the bespoke step dominates.
scored.step_up: Unproven: option or term easement at about $5-50/acre, as the candidate states (consistent with grazing-lease values of roughly $5-25/acre/yr; estimate). Proven: credits at roughly $1-10k per acre-equivalent. I think published LPC and Indiana-bat bank credits fall in the low thousands per acre, but I could not verify this; it is an estimate from memory. The credit cannot be sold until a perpetual easement is bought, typically 40-70% of fee value on land worth about $500-3,000/acre (estimate), plus an endowment of perhaps $500-2,000/acre (estimate). So the option premium shows about 100x on paper. The realised step-up on capital actually at risk is about 2-5x, and only after years. Occupancy alone moves land value about 1x, because nobody pays for unapproved occupied habitat.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving cost is about $2-10k per site (candidate's figure). That is plausible for 2-4 weeks of passive acoustic monitoring at roughly $1-3k/detector-season, or for eDNA at roughly $100-500 per sample (estimates). Base hit rate inside known range is moderate, not low. Rare targets like the white-nose-crashed NLEB (I recall roughly 90%+ declines, but did not verify) might hit about 10-30% per site (estimate). Gopher tortoise, monarch and range-core LPC habitat would hit 30-60%+ (estimate). The lever is capped at 1/base rate, about 2-5x, and proving is a small share of total bank cost, so ML cuts total capex well under 2x.
scored.data: The data is partly public and illegible: scanned state natural heritage reports, EIS biological appendices and NABat archives. But much of the outcome is already legible. USFWS IPaC and critical-habitat shapefiles define the action areas. The WAFWA LPC plan publishes focal and connectivity areas and a habitat-evaluation tool. GBIF, eBird and iNaturalist are structured. Heritage element-occurrence data is gated, but consultants license it routinely. So regulators largely write the answer into legible maps and range polygons. Rights are bought from landowners who price by grazing value, which is good. But the credit market is concentrated in incumbents: WAFWA's own program, EIP, RES and Common Ground Capital (estimate). Those incumbents already run site selection with heritage data.
scored.right_bought: An option or term easement over private rangeland or forest at about $5-50/acre. The right is bought cheaply from owners who price by grazing value. To monetise it, the company must still convert it to a perpetual easement and an approved bank.
scored.buyer: Wind, solar, transmission and pipeline developers who need Section 7 or 10 incidental-take offsets, buying through mitigation bank sponsors (EIP, RES, Restoration Systems) or through the WAFWA range-wide plan. They are capitalised, but they buy approved credits, not occupancy. Demand depends on politics. I recall the LPC listing was challenged and vacated in 2025, the tricolored bat and monarch listings remain proposed or stalled, and the eastern gopher tortoise was not listed in 2022, but I could not verify any of these by search.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are bank operator, then credit broker, then perhaps developer-side permitting. The whole chain is the US species conservation-banking market, which I estimate at hundreds of millions of dollars a year (estimate). That is small, fragmented and regulator-capped. There is no trillion-dollar chain; the top of the ladder is a mid-size environmental-markets firm like RES.
scored.fatal_flaw: Proven occupancy is not a sellable product. Value comes only after the bespoke, years-long USFWS bank approval, the perpetual easement and the endowment. Discovery is therefore a minor share of the rung's work, and the 100x step-up on option premium collapses to about 2-5x on capital at risk. Demand also depends on listings that are being reversed or delayed. This is essentially the previously weak wetland-mitigation-bank idea again.
scored.one_line_reason: Like wetland mitigation banks, value appears only after the bespoke step (bank approval, perpetual easement, endowment), not at the occupancy hit. The base hit rate inside known range is moderate. Range maps already make the outcome legible, and demand is hostage to listing politics.
sources: WebSearch budget was exhausted before any search ran (shared 200-call limit). All figures are my estimates from prior knowledge and are unverified.
USFWS Conservation Banking program guidance (fws.gov/service/conservation-banking): approval requires a banking agreement, perpetual easement and endowment (from memory)
WAFWA Lesser Prairie-Chicken Range-Wide Conservation Plan: focal areas and habitat evaluation tool are public (from memory)

Federal Register: LPC listing Nov 2022; NLEB reclassified endangered Nov 2022; tricolored bat proposed Sept 2022; monarch proposed Dec 2024; eastern gopher tortoise not listed Oct 2022; dunes sagebrush lizard listed May 2024 (from memory)

scored.name: Figure (hidden figured tonewood and veneer in standing timber)
scored.one_line: Buys per-tree or per-stand cutting rights cheaply from small woodlot owners at pulp or sawlog stumpage, uses ML to predict which bigleaf maple, red and sugar maple, Sitka and Engelmann spruce, and claro walnut carry quilted, curly or birdseye figure, proves it with a bark window or core, and sells figured logs to tonewood and veneer buyers.
scored.unproven_right: Standing timber cutting rights on private woodlots priced at ordinary stumpage, about $50-500 per tree.
scored.proving_step: Pulling a small bark window or taking an increment core to read the figure (the poaching trade shows it takes minutes). Felling is routine.
scored.proven_buyer: Guitar and instrument tonewood suppliers and veneer mills (Taylor/Pacific Rim Tonewoods-type buyers, figured-veneer exporters). A quilted bigleaf maple or master-grade spruce can fetch $10-50k per tree.
scored.public_data: USFS FIA plot data; USGS 3DEP LiDAR crown metrics; scanned state forest inventory cruise reports; timber-theft court records as a label source; Sentinel-2 imagery.
scored.rough_step_up: Stumpage at about $100-300 per tree becomes a figured tree at $5-50k: about 10^2 to 10^2.5 per tree. Figure occurs in about 1-3% of trees, so the lever is large. The weakness is C4: figure is barely visible in public data, so the ML edge is unproven and the market is small, which caps C5.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a figured tree's cutting right, confirming the figure and selling the log. Discovery is perhaps 40-60% of the work inside it (my estimate). Felling, yarding, permits, bucking and quartering a 1-3 m diameter maple without wrecking the figure are real logging jobs, not trivial ones, and buyers mostly want blanks or billets rather than standing trees. A capitalised buyer exists (tonewood mills, veneer exporters), but it is a small, fragmented niche and not a developer-scale buyer.
scored.step_up: These numbers are estimates from memory, not search results; the search budget ran out before any search went through. Pulp or sawlog stumpage for a large bigleaf maple is roughly $100-500 per tree. A strongly quilted tree sells for roughly $5k-20k as a log or billets, and rare exceptional trees for more. Washington poaching cases (the 2018 Maple Fire / Wilke case) valued stolen figured maple in the tens to low hundreds of thousands of dollars across several trees. That gives about 10-100x per tree, short of 10^3. Part of the uplift also depends on the milling work done afterwards.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These are estimates; no search result supports them. Strong commercial figure probably shows up in 1-5% of mature bigleaf maples, and in far fewer spruce trees at master grade. A bark window costs minutes of a cruiser's time, maybe $20-100 per tree including access. The proving step is therefore already cheap. The real cost is walking woodlots and negotiating with owners, not failed proving attempts. ML could cut cruising effort a little, but there is no expensive failing step for it to replace, so the 10x capex lever does not hold.
scored.data: Figure is an internal grain trait. FIA plots record species, DBH and grade, not figure. 3DEP LiDAR and Sentinel-2 show crowns, not wood grain. Cruise reports rarely note figure. Theft court records are a sparse, biased label set, likely in the tens to hundreds of trees. Nothing summarises the outcome legibly, which is good, but the bigger problem is that the signal is probably not in the public data at all. The best you could get is a weak prior from species, size and site. Rights can be bought from small woodlot owners. However, figured-maple buyers and 'maple hunters' in the Pacific Northwest already cruise for figure and pay premium stumpage, and owners increasingly know figured maple is valuable, so the discount shrinks once a buyer shows interest.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Per-tree or per-stand timber rights are bought from private owners, not claimed first-come. Washington and Oregon specialised-forest-products and timber-theft rules require documented permits and sale records for maple, which adds friction but keeps it legal.
scored.buyer: Tonewood suppliers and luthier wood dealers (Pacific Rim Tonewoods, Taylor's sourcing arm, small figured-wood dealers) and figured-veneer mills and exporters. The total market is small. My estimate is under $100-300M a year for figured tonewood plus figured veneer, and it saturates easily. Incumbents already include Pacific Northwest maple buyers who cruise woodlots and read bark.
scored.ladder: Above this rung: milling into billets or sets, drying, then instrument components and possibly instruments or architectural veneer. Each rung is a small craft market, and instruments are a crowded consumer-goods business. There is no path to a very large company. The ceiling is a niche specialty-wood business, not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is already cheap (a bark window takes minutes) and the figure signal is probably absent from public remote-sensing and inventory data. That means there is no expensive failing step for ML to make cheaper and no illegible public signal to extract. The market is also too small for the ladder to matter.
scored.one_line_reason: Real 10-100x uplift per tree, but proving costs minutes, the figure is likely invisible in public data, and the market is niche, so Terranox's capex lever and trillion-dollar ladder are both missing.
sources: No web searches ran: the turn-wide search budget was used up, so every number here is my own estimate from memory and is flagged as such.
From memory (not verified this turn): USFS FIA database documentation, which records species, DBH and tree grade but no wood-figure field.
From memory (not verified this turn): news coverage of the US v. Justin Wilke Olympic National Forest maple theft and 2018 Maple Fire, which valued figured bigleaf maple sold to tonewood mills.
From memory (not verified this turn): Washington DNR specialized forest products permit rules (RCW 76.48) covering maple sales.

scored.name: CT Fossil: finding rare species inside cheap fossil and amber lots
scored.one_line: Buys commercially legal fossil lots, unprepared nodules and Burmese-alternative and Baltic amber in bulk at $/kg. ML on micro-CT and on scanned museum and auction descriptions flags rare or new taxa (vertebrates in amber, complete specimens hidden in matrix). A $200-1000 CT scan plus a specialist description proves the find, and it sells to collectors or institutions.
scored.unproven_right: Ownership of legally sourced specimens from private-land quarries and dealers (US, Baltic) selling unprepared material by weight.
scored.proving_step: Micro-CT segmentation is cheap and fast and reveals the hidden specimen without preparation. Nature hides what is inside.
scored.proven_buyer: High-end natural history auctions (Sotheby's 'Stan'-style sales), museums, and private collectors.
scored.public_data: The Paleobiology Database, iDigBio and GBIF specimen records, MorphoSource CT archives, and scanned auction catalogues.
scored.rough_step_up: About 100-10^4x on a hit ($50-500 lot to $50k-5M specimen). Ethical and legal sourcing constraints apply, and the ladder is weak.
scored.frame: Rung: buy a bulk lot (amber by the kg, unsplit nodules), CT it, describe what's inside, sell it. Within that rung, finding the specimen is maybe 60-80% of the work (my estimate). But preparation, getting it described or published, provenance paperwork and selling to a thin collector market are real work, not trivial steps. The buyers are not a capitalised industrial buyer with a fixed economic yield the way a mine developer is. They are individual collectors and museums with small, irregular budgets, and museums mostly want donations, not purchases. Holotype rules also push new taxa into public collections at below-market prices.
scored.step_up: Estimates from prior knowledge, because the shared web search budget was used up before any query ran. Unproven: rough Baltic amber is about $20-300/kg depending on piece size. A bulk lot is $50-500. Proven: a typical piece with an insect inclusion sells for about $20-500, a 2-10x step-up on its own weight of amber. Rare vertebrate inclusions (lizards, frogs, feathers) have sold for about $5k-100k+, which is 10^2-10^3x on a lot. The $1M-$45M numbers (Stan, Christie's 2020, $31.8M; Apex stegosaurus, Sotheby's 2024, $44.6M) are field-excavated dinosaurs. They never come from bulk lots bought by weight, so they do not belong in this step-up. Realistic expected step-up on a hit is about 10-1000x, and the market for each hit is very thin.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimates, not sourced. Baltic amber: commonly cited figures are about 1-2% of pieces carrying any animal inclusion, with vertebrates far rarer than one in a million pieces. Cost per proving attempt: visual inspection under a lamp costs almost nothing for clear amber. Micro-CT is about $200-1000 per scan, and is only needed for opaque amber or matrix nodules. Mazon Creek-type nodules cost about $5-20 each and can be opened free by freeze-thaw. The proving step is already cheap, so ML has little capex to cut. The only lever is choosing which lots to buy, and public data cannot see inside a lot before you buy it.
scored.data: PBDB, iDigBio, GBIF and MorphoSource describe specimens already found and accessioned. They contain no information about unbought dealer lots, so they cannot rank purchases. Clear amber is transparent and dealers grade it by inclusion, so the outcome is effectively a visible field. Valuable pieces are pulled and priced before material is sold by weight, and the bulk kg remainder is adversely selected. ML on micro-CT only works after the scan, and the scan is the proving step. That makes ML a segmentation convenience, not a discovery edge. Competition: amber dealers in Gdansk, Kaliningrad and Lithuania, academic CT groups, and the established Burmese amber trade.
scored.right_bought: Yes, mechanically. Material is bought by weight from dealers and private-land quarries (Baltic amber, US private-land fossils). But sellers can read the 'data' themselves by looking at the material, so there is little information asymmetry. Burmese amber is ethically and legally toxic: Kachin conflict sourcing, a 2020 SVP call for a moratorium, and many journals refuse papers on it. That removes the richest vertebrate source.
scored.buyer: High-end natural history auctions (Christie's, Sotheby's, Bonhams), private collectors and a few museums. They are thin, taste-driven and illiquid. Museums rarely pay market prices, and the scientific community pushes against commercial sale of holotypes.
scored.ladder: Weak. The natural rungs above are a dealer or auction house, field excavation of dinosaurs (fossil prospecting, close to the excluded exploration category), and replicas or media. The total market is perhaps hundreds of millions of dollars a year (my estimate). There is no path to a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no information edge before purchase. Clear amber is transparent and dealers already grade and pull every visible inclusion, and nothing in the public data says what is inside a lot that has not been bought. The only way to prove a find is to scan or split the material, which is already cheap. So ML cannot raise the hit rate on what gets bought, and the 10^3+ outcomes (rare vertebrates, dinosaurs) are close to non-existent in bulk lots sold by weight and go to a thin collector market.
scored.one_line_reason: Proving is cheap and visual, sellers already screen out the value, public databases cover only specimens already found, and the buyer market is a thin, ethically constrained collector niche with no ladder.

scored.name: BoneField: fossil-rights land banking from airborne radiometrics
scored.one_line: Buy fossil rights or fee land on private Hell Creek, Morrison and Judith River ground, where US fossils belong to the surface owner. Rank parcels with ML over gamma-ray maps, because fossil bone concentrates uranium. Prove each parcel by walking it with a shielded scintillator and digging test pits. Sell the specimens to auction-house buyers (Stan the T. rex sold for $31.8M, the Apex stegosaurus for $44.6M) or sell excavation rights to commercial dig firms. The collector market pays the step-up.
scored.unproven_right: Fee-simple badlands ranch parcels or severed fossil/excavation leases from ranchers, at about $500-1,500/acre or a few thousand dollars a season. Owners cannot read radiometric or outcrop data.
scored.proving_step: An ML prior (radiometric U/Th ratio anomalies, mapped outcrops of the right formations, erosion rate from repeat imagery), then a ground gamma survey and hand excavation of 1-3 test pits. This is cheap labour, not a bespoke build.
scored.proven_buyer: Auction houses (Sotheby's, Christie's), private collectors and Gulf-state or Asian museums that buy skeletons for $1-45M. Commercial excavators (Black Hills Institute types) buy proven quarry leases.
scored.public_data: USGS NURE aerial radiometric (gamma-ray) surveys; USGS state geologic map compilations (SGMC); Montana/Wyoming/SD state survey outcrop maps; NAIP and Sentinel-2 imagery for erosion change; published bone gamma-signature literature (Jones & Chure; US patent 5773821).
scored.rough_step_up: A $1,000/acre parcel holding one articulated large dinosaur is worth $1-30M, about 10^3-10^4x per acre on a hit. Base hit rate per parcel is low, but NURE resolution is coarse, so the ML lift is uncertain. Note for scoring: the gamma signal is uranium-based, so it sits next to Terranox's science, but the asset is fossils, not minerals.
scored.frame: The rung would be "own a fossil-bearing parcel or excavation right and prove a quarry on it." Discovery is not 80%+ of the work inside that rung. Finding bone in Hell Creek and Morrison outcrops is already cheap: people walk the eroding badlands and look. Most of the value comes after discovery, from excavation, jacketing, transport and multi-year preparation and mounting. My estimate is that this physical work is 50-70% of the effort and cost. Stan took Black Hills Institute tens of thousands of person-hours (from memory, not re-checked). So the physical step is bespoke and expensive, not trivial. A capitalised buyer exists (auction houses and collectors), but it buys a prepared specimen, not a proven parcel. The candidate's other buyer, commercial excavators, mostly just lease from ranchers directly.
scored.step_up: Unproven right: badlands grazing land at about $400-1,500/acre (my estimate; the candidate says $500-1,500). Proven right, rare case: one articulated, mostly complete marquee dinosaur. Sale prices, from memory: Sue $8.36M (Sotheby's 1997), Stan $31.8M (Christie's 2020), Dueling Dinosaurs about $6M (NC Museum 2020), Big John triceratops about EUR 6.6M (2021), Apex stegosaurus $44.6M (Sotheby's 2024). On one parcel that is 10^3-10^4x. Typical case: a hadrosaur or partial skeleton worth roughly $10k-$500k gross (estimate), before prep costs and the landowner's share. So the realistic step-up is about 10-100x, the ~10^4x hits are very rare, and the value only appears after excavation and prep, not immediately on a hit. Scored 3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate (all my estimates): turning up fragmentary bone on Hell Creek outcrop is common, perhaps most well-exposed sections in a season. An auction-grade articulated large dinosaur is extremely rare. Only about 50 reasonably complete T. rex specimens are known after more than 100 years of searching, roughly 0.5-1 per year across the whole formation (from memory). Cost per proving attempt: walking a parcel and digging test pits is a few thousand dollars of field labour per parcel-season (estimate). The proving step is cheap, so there is no large discovery capex for ML to cut 10x. The real cost is excavation and prep after a hit. The ML signal is also weak. NURE aerial gamma-ray lines were flown roughly 1-6 miles apart at about 400 ft above ground (from memory, not re-checked this session). That gives km-scale pixels, while bone gamma anomalies are metre-scale and only show where bone is exposed at the surface, where an eye or a handheld scintillator finds it anyway. Lever is close to zero.
scored.data: NURE radiometrics, the state geologic map compilation (SGMC) and NAIP/Sentinel imagery are public and already legible and gridded. They are not scanned or illegible. Their resolution is far too coarse to resolve individual bones. Formation outcrop maps are legible too, and every collector already knows where Hell Creek, Morrison and Judith River crop out. The outcome is not written into a status field, which is a plus. But the only illegible signal, exposed bone on eroding slopes, is read directly by people walking the ground. Bone gamma detection with a handheld scintillator (Jones & Chure; the patent the candidate cites) is a ground method, not a remote-sensing edge.
scored.right_bought: The right can be bought. Under US law fossils on private land go with the surface estate. The Montana Supreme Court decided this in Murray v. BEJ Minerals (2020), the Dueling Dinosaurs case, and Montana wrote it into statute (from memory). But owners are not ignorant. After the publicity around Sue, Stan and the Dueling Dinosaurs, Hell Creek and Morrison ranchers know fossils can be worth millions. Commercial hunters already lease land or split proceeds with them (my estimate: a landowner share of roughly 10-50% or a per-season fee). So there is no information gap to buy into at grazing-land prices. Owners price in the lottery ticket or insist on a share of the proceeds.
scored.buyer: For prepared specimens: Sotheby's and Christie's, private collectors (hedge-fund buyers, for example Ken Griffin bought Apex) and new Gulf-state or Asian museums. My estimate is about 3-10 sales over $1M per year worldwide, roughly $50-150M a year in total. That market is thin, swings on publicity, and faces pushback from academic palaeontologists. For quarry access: commercial excavators such as Black Hills Institute, but they lease directly from ranchers and do their own prospecting. The incumbents doing this today are commercial fossil firms and freelance prospectors who have walked these formations for decades.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are limited: a prep lab, casting and replica sales, licensing exhibitions, perhaps a private museum. The whole chain is a niche collectibles business worth perhaps a few hundred million dollars a year (my estimate). There is no trillion-dollar path. Total supply is capped by geology and the number of buyers is capped by demand for trophy objects.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no expensive, mostly failing discovery step for ML to lever. Fossils are found cheaply by walking eroding outcrops, while NURE gamma data is km-scale and cannot resolve metre-scale bone. Meanwhile the real cost and value sit in bespoke excavation and preparation, sold into a thin market of a handful of trophy buyers per year, using rights held by ranchers who already know what fossils are worth. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern: the hard part is not finding the asset.
scored.one_line_reason: The rare 10^4x jackpot exists, but discovery is already cheap eye-prospecting, the remote-sensing signal is far too coarse, ranchers already price in fossil value, the value only appears after costly excavation and prep, and the collector market is too thin for a ladder: total 8/25.

scored.name: Bud Sport (discovering natural fruit mutations)
scored.one_line: Licenses or buys mutation rights across large commercial orchards and vineyards, uses ML over repeat high-resolution aerial and multispectral imagery to flag limbs whose phenology, colour or vigour differs (candidate sports, like the bud-sport origins of Gala, Fuji and Pink Lady clones), proves each with a cheap DNA and phenotype check, then patents it and sells or licenses the variety to nursery and club-variety consortia.
scored.unproven_right: Contractual rights to any sport found on a grower's trees, bought for a small fee from growers who do not systematically scout for sports.
scored.proving_step: Targeted limb inspection and fruit sampling plus a genotype or methylation assay, about $500 per candidate. Bud-wood propagation for confirmation is cheap. Patent filing follows.
scored.proven_buyer: Nursery and variety-management firms (Stark Bro's, Van Well, Proprietary Variety Management, International Fruit Obtentions), which buy or license promising sports.
scored.public_data: NAIP and Planet imagery, state orchard-block registries, USPTO plant patents (hard-to-read text), and UPOV/PVP filings that show which traits earn premiums.
scored.rough_step_up: A rights fee of about $1k per orchard becomes a sport license worth $100k-$5M+, so up to 10^3x. But proof of commercial value takes 1-3 fruiting seasons, so the step-up is slower than immediate and is weaker on C2 timing.
scored.frame: The rung is "own a confirmed, patentable sport and license it to a nursery or variety manager." Finding the limb is maybe 20-30% of the work (my estimate). Most of the work is physical and slow: propagating bud-wood, checking that the mutation is stable and not a reverting chimera across 2-4 fruiting seasons, running multi-site trials, filing the patent, and only then signing a nursery deal. The buyers (Stark Bro's, Van Well, PVM, IFO) are real but small. They pay modest per-tree royalties, not large sums up front. So discovery is not 80%+ of the rung, and the physical step is neither trivial nor abstracted.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a limb on a grower's tree has roughly zero standalone value. The candidate's own figure is about $1k per orchard for the rights. Proven: US apple plant-patent royalties are typically about $1-3 per tree (my estimate from industry knowledge, not verified this run, because the search budget was exhausted). A sport that reaches 0.5-2M trees earns about $0.5-5M over a 20-year patent term, and most color sports of Gala, Fuji or Red Delicious earn far less because the market already holds dozens of them. The value comes as a slow royalty stream over 5-15 years. Nothing is paid immediately on a hit, and a freshly flagged limb would sell for maybe $0-20k. So the immediate step-up is about 3-10x and the eventual one about 100-1000x, discounted heavily for time and risk.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is cheap, about $500 per candidate (the candidate's figure), plus low-cost propagation. Because each attempt costs so little, discovery capex is not a meaningful cost to cut 10x. The real cost and risk sit in the multi-year stability and commercial-value trials. Base hit rate (my estimate, unverified): spontaneous visible sports appear about 1 per 10^5-10^6 buds. Of the sports found, well under 5% become commercially licensed varieties, because most are redundant color strains. ML can only raise how often visible limbs get flagged. It cannot raise the commercial-value hit rate, which is set by the market and by trials.
scored.data: The data is not public-but-illegible in the useful sense. NAIP is about 60 cm GSD and Planet about 3 m, which cannot resolve a single limb's fruit color or phenology. Doing this needs proprietary drone or ground imaging at about 1-5 cm, flown each season by the company itself, so the public-data edge is gone. The outcome also shows up in plain sight: a red-sport limb is obvious at harvest, and pickers and growers already watch for them (many Gala and Fuji sports were found exactly this way by growers). USPTO plant patents and PVP filings show which traits earn a premium, but that is market intelligence, not a hidden signal.
scored.right_bought: You can contract with growers for sport rights, but the most valuable trees are contractually blocked. Under UPOV 1991, a sport of a protected variety is an Essentially Derived Variety and needs the original breeder's authorisation to commercialise. Club and managed-variety contracts (Cosmic Crisp, SweeTango, Pink Lady/Cripps Pink via IFO and APAL, Envy, Jazz) typically assign any mutation rights to the variety owner. The only sports that are free to own come from old public-domain varieties (Gala, Fuji, Red Delicious, Honeycrisp after its patent expired), where the sport market is saturated. Growers of high-value blocks also know sports have value, so the "owners can't read the data" asymmetry is weak.
scored.buyer: The buyers are nurseries and variety managers: Stark Bro's, Van Well, Willow Drive, PVM, IFO, Rubens/Inored-type consortia. Their capital is modest, they pay per-tree royalties of about $1-3 per tree (estimate) rather than lump sums, and several own or control the parent varieties whose sports they would be buying. Incumbents also already do this: nurseries routinely evaluate grower-found sports, sometimes paying finder's fees, and companies like Van Well and Columbia Basin Nursery run sport-evaluation pipelines.
scored.ladder: The ladder runs: sport rights, then nursery propagation, then club-variety management (marketing levies per carton), then orchards and packing. The climb is real, but the value pool is small. Global apple nursery and variety royalties are probably a low-billions-of-dollars market (estimate), and growing and packing fruit is low-margin farming. There is no path toward a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: Ownership is blocked exactly where the value is. Sports of protected and club varieties belong to the parent variety's owner (UPOV 1991 Essentially Derived Variety rules plus club contract clauses), and sports of free varieties are already saturated, low-royalty color strains. The signal is also visible to the naked eye at harvest and cannot be resolved in public imagery (NAIP 60 cm, Planet 3 m). That leaves no illegible-data edge and no cheap right worth buying.
scored.one_line_reason: The rungs are slow and trial-heavy, the sport rights are captured by Essentially Derived Variety rules and club contracts, the public imagery can't resolve a limb, the outcome is visible to growers at harvest, and per-tree royalties are small. It fails C1, C4 and C5, and C2's timing is weak.
