scored.name: Landrace Clone Scouting (hops, cacao, grape)
scored.one_line: Use public genomic and climate data to find smallholder landrace clones likely to carry valuable aroma or disease-resistance alleles, buy propagation rights cheaply, prove each clone with a marker test, and sell to breeders.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive propagation rights to specific clones, bought from farmers
scored.proving_step: Marker genotyping at about $30-100 per plant, binary
scored.proven_buyer: Hop merchants and breeders, cacao processors, nurseries
scored.public_data: Crop genome and diversity panels in NCBI and CacaoGenDB, WorldClim
scored.frame: Rung: 'owning a clone with a confirmed allele.' Discovery here is maybe 30% of the work (my estimate), not 80%. A marker hit is not the proven asset. Breeders pay for multi-year field, agronomic, processing and sensory proof (brewing trials for hops, flavor and yield trials for cacao and grape). Citra went about 17 years from cross to release (cross in 1990, release in 2007). That long physical trial is the real proving step, and it is neither trivial nor abstracted. Breeders mostly buy proven varieties or free genebank germplasm, not single-marker hits.
scored.step_up: Unproven: an informal purchase of cuttings or rights from a smallholder, probably $10-$1,000 per clone (estimate, no market price exists). Marker-confirmed: there is no observed market price for a clone that only carries a marker hit. Breeders get comparable alleles from genebanks (USDA GRIN, ICGT Trinidad, Vavilov) at roughly zero cost under SMTA. Proven: a released proprietary variety can be worth a lot. HBC's royalties were estimated at more than $22M in 2022 across Citra, Mosaic and others (MacKinnon Report Substack, an outside estimate). But that value comes after about a decade of trials and branding, not at the marker step. Immediate step-up at the marker step: under 3x (my estimate).
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving attempt: genotyping at about $30-100 per plant (the candidate's figure, consistent with SNP-panel pricing). That is too cheap for ML to matter. Genotyping a whole village costs a few thousand dollars, so raising the hit rate saves almost nothing. The costly, mostly-failing step is the multi-year field and sensory trial (est. $50k-$500k+ per variety; most selections fail, likely 1 in 100 or worse, my estimate). Public genomic and climate data can't predict sensory or agronomic success well enough to skip those trials.
scored.data: The public data (NCBI SRA diversity panels, CacaoGenDB, WorldClim) is already structured and machine-readable, and breeders and academics already mine it (GWAS, environmental association, landscape genomics). It is legible, not illegible. Sequenced accessions are mostly genebank-held and already characterised, so the outcome is effectively summarised in published passport and characterisation data. The un-sequenced smallholder clones that would be the actual target are by definition not in the data, so the ML has nothing to read on them.
scored.right_bought: Weak to illegal. A landrace already grown by farmers fails PVP and UPOV novelty and distinctness tests (it was commercialised or distributed before), so no enforceable exclusive right can be bought. One cutting propagates the clone, so exclusivity can't be policed. Cacao and grape are not in ITPGRFA Annex 1, so Nagoya bilateral prior informed consent and mutually agreed terms with the source country apply. Buying cheaply from smallholders who can't read the data is the textbook biopiracy pattern, and it carries legal and reputational kill risk (Nagoya Protocol Art. 5; Arche Noah summary). Where material falls under the Annex 1 multilateral system, restricting it triggers a benefit-sharing payment of about 1.1% of sales (Seed World).
scored.buyer: Hop Breeding Company (Haas/Select Botanicals JV), Yakima Chief Ranches, Barth-Haas, cacao processors (Barry Callebaut, Mars and its cacao genome work), grape nurseries and INRAE and Davis breeding programs. They are capitalised, but they run their own breeding and genebank access and pay for proven varieties, not for marker-hit clones.
scored.ladder: Clone scouting, then trialing, variety release and licensing, then proprietary-variety farming and branded ingredient sales. That's a real ladder (HBC shows proprietary hops can be a roughly $20M+/yr royalty business), but it's a niche ceiling, nowhere near a trillion-dollar chain. Each rung up is long-cycle agronomy, not discovery.
scored.fatal_flaw: The cheap marker test isn't the real proving step and creates no ownable, sellable value. Value comes only after about 10+ years of field and sensory trials. An already-cultivated landrace can't be made exclusive (it fails PVP novelty, propagates from one cutting, and buying it falls under Nagoya ABS and biopiracy constraints). So the step-up neither happens immediately nor accrues to the scout.
scored.one_line_reason: Genotyping at $30-100 is too cheap for ML to matter. The real proof is a decade of field and sensory trials. The data is already legible and the outcome largely summarised. And no enforceable exclusive right to a farmer landrace can be bought cheaply without novelty and Nagoya problems.

scored.name: Sinker Log Salvage Leases (Great Lakes and Pacific NW log ponds)
scored.one_line: Old-growth logs sank during 1850-1930 log drives and survive on lakebeds and in estuaries; they fetch $5-20k each as reclaimed tonewood and specialty lumber. Use ML to read historic log-drive, boom and mill records together with public side-scan sonar to find dense log fields. Lease the submerged-land salvage rights, prove a field with one sonar and dive pass, then sell it to specialty mills.
scored.unproven_right: State submerged-log recovery permits or bottomland leases (Wisconsin, Michigan, Minnesota, BC and Oregon have permit regimes) and private millpond bottoms, bought cheaply from owners who see a muddy pond.
scored.proving_step: A towed side-scan survey plus a diver core sample on a few logs to confirm species and condition, at about $10-30k per field. Most leases surveyed blind today hold little.
scored.proven_buyer: Tonewood makers (guitar and piano soundboard suppliers) and specialty reclaimed-lumber mills, who pay for proven log inventory.
scored.public_data: State historical society scanned log-drive and boom-company ledgers, USACE and NOAA Great Lakes side-scan and multibeam archives, GLERL bathymetry, historic Sanborn mill maps, USGS scanned river surveys.
scored.rough_step_up: Permit: about $1k. Proven field of 500-5,000 logs: about $1-10M wholesale. That is 10^3x, though permit throughput caps scale.
scored.frame: The rung would be "permit area with a sonar-proven log field." Finding the logs is not 80%+ of the work inside that rung. The logs lie near known boom sites, mills and drive routes, and side-scan finds them cheaply. Most of the effort and cost is in permits (state plus USACE), state 30% stumpage, a bond, recovery dives and rigging, slow drying of 6 months air or weeks in a kiln, and milling and grading. My estimate is that discovery is about 10-20% of the work. Selling a proven-but-unraised field is not an established transaction, and no capitalised buyer exists for one.
scored.step_up: Unproven: the Wisconsin BCPL permit costs a $500 application fee plus a bond of at least $10,000, covering up to 160 acres for 5 years (BCPL program explanation). Proven: there is no market price for a proven field. Michigan legislative analyses say individual logs are "as high as $30-40k" (2011 testimony) and "$10k or more, but the exception rather than the norm" (1999). Sinker lumber sells wholesale for about $7-10 per board foot (forum, 2012). My estimate is that a typical log yields a few hundred to about $2k in lumber, before the state's 30% and recovery cost. The net value of a proven field to a buyer is maybe 10-100x the permit cost, not the 10^3x the pitch claims.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimate is that the base hit rate for a sonar pass over a permit area chosen from boom-site and mill records is moderate to high, because logs sank at known booms, sorting grounds and mill sites. The pitch quotes $10-30k per proving attempt, which is already cheap compared with recovery costs. ML might lift hit rates from about 30-50% to 70% or so, which is under 3x. It cannot cut capex 10x because discovery is not where the capex is.
scored.data: The log-drive ledgers and boom records are scanned and illegible, which fits the thesis. But the locations of boom sites and mills are already well known to local historians and salvors. NOAA, USACE and GLERL bathymetry and side-scan archives are mostly legible, though coverage is coarse. No status field records log density, so the outcome is not pre-summarised. That part helps the candidate.
scored.right_bought: No, the right is not bought. On Great Lakes and state bottomlands the logs are state property (Michigan NREPA Part 326; Wisconsin s.170.12). Access is a state permit, applied for first-come, with the state taking 30% of stumpage, and it is likely non-transferable. Michigan reported in 2011 that few permits had been issued and no logs had been recovered, and USACE approvals had stalled. Private millpond bottoms could be bought or leased cheaply, but they are small, scattered, and carry riparian and environmental (sediment disturbance) restrictions.
scored.buyer: The buyers are tonewood suppliers and reclaimed-lumber mills. They are small, thinly capitalised cottage firms that buy logs or lumber, not unraised log fields. Superior Water-Logged Lumber, the Ashland, WI pioneer, had "yet to make a profit" in 1997, and later coverage said there was "never enough cash." There is no capitalised developer equivalent to a mine developer paying about $40k/ha.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are recovery, then drying and milling, then branded reclaimed lumber and tonewood. The total market is my estimate of tens of millions of dollars a year in North America, and the resource is finite and non-renewable. The ladder tops out as a niche specialty-lumber business, not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The physical step is the business, the way the plant was in the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example. Recovery, permits, the state's 30% royalty, drying and milling dominate the cost, and finding the logs is cheap and largely already known from boom-site history. The proven output also has no capitalised buyer, because it is sold to a tiny, cash-poor specialty lumber market.
scored.one_line_reason: Locating logs is cheap and mostly known already, while raising, drying and milling them is the hard part. The rights are state permits with a 30% royalty, not bought assets, and the only buyers are small cottage lumber firms in a niche market.

scored.name: Shellfish/Seaweed Aquaculture Lease Proofing (Maine/Massachusetts/BC)
scored.one_line: Use ML to read water-quality buoys, satellite chlorophyll and temperature, bathymetry and current models to find sheltered parcels with top growth rates. File cheap experimental lease applications there, prove growth with a one-season test cage, then sell the de-risked standard lease to scaling oyster and kelp growers.
scored.unproven_right: Limited-purpose or experimental aquaculture leases (Maine LPA and experimental leases cost a few hundred dollars), plus purchase of underused existing leases.
scored.proving_step: A one-season gear trial measuring growth and survival (about $10-30k).
scored.proven_buyer: Scaling oyster farms and seaweed companies that need proven sites, plus consolidators buying farms.
scored.public_data: NERACOOS and IOOS buoy archives, NASA MODIS/Sentinel-3 chlorophyll and SST, Maine DMR lease records, NOAA ENC bathymetry, state shellfish water-classification files.
scored.rough_step_up: $500 lease to a $50-500k proven farm site, about 10^2-10^3x. However, the regulator's lease process sets the pace and buyers are small.
scored.frame: The rung would be: get a lease, prove growth on it, sell the proven site. Discovery (picking a site with good growth) is maybe 20-30% of the work in that rung (my estimate). The rest is permitting and social licence. A Maine standard lease takes 10-14 months, always needs a public hearing, and often draws opposition from waterfront owners and lobstermen (e.g. the Mere Point/Maquoit Bay dispute ended up in court). It also requires a real season of gear deployment, stocking and husbandry. The physical step and the regulatory step are the hard parts. Discovery is not.
scored.step_up: Unproven costs, from the DMR fee table: LPA $100/yr resident or $400/yr non-resident; experimental lease $750 application plus $100/acre/yr rent; standard lease $1,500-2,000 application plus $100/acre/yr. Proven price: I found no public price for a bare proven lease. DMR transfer filings record approvals, not sale prices. The only farm sale listing found was a Willapa Bay, WA operation of ~260-300 acres at a $3.8M asking price. That is about $13-15k per acre, and it bundles fee-simple tideland, stock, gear and business, so the bare-right premium is well below that. My estimate for the lease-site component is about 3-30x the fees paid. The candidate's $50-500k figure is mostly gear, stock and brand, not the right.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I have no published base rate for one-season growth trials. My estimate is that 60-80% of sheltered, approved-water sites in Maine grow oysters acceptably, because the growth gradient is mostly temperature and chlorophyll and those are already mapped. That caps the hit-rate lever at about 1.3-1.7x (1/base rate), not 10x. The candidate's own figure for a proving attempt is $10-30k, against a few hundred to $2k in fees. The real failure modes are lease denial and user conflict, not poor growth.
scored.data: The data (buoy archives, MODIS/Sentinel/Landsat SST and chlorophyll, bathymetry, shellfish water classifications) is public but mostly legible. It is gridded and structured, not scanned. The University of Maine Darling Marine Center has already coupled Landsat 8 SST and Sentinel-2 chlorophyll to an eastern oyster DEB model, validated it on 4 farms, and is building a free online siting tool for farmers. Connecticut runs the FARM growth model inside its Aquaculture Mapping Atlas. Water classification, an outcome-like field, is already published by the state. So the edge is largely open-source already.
scored.right_bought: The right is not bought cheaply from owners who cannot read the data. New leases are granted by DMR through a public, first-come application and hearing process. Existing leases change hands only with DMR transfer approval, a 30-day public comment period and acreage caps of 1,000 acres. Sellers are working farmers who know their own site's growth better than any model. The state can also act against unused leases, so holding speculative leases to flip carries non-use risk.
scored.buyer: The buyers are small family oyster farms and seaweed startups (e.g. Mere Point Oyster, Tapley Cove, Restorative Aquaculture). They are thinly capitalised and can usually get their own lease for about $2k in fees plus a year's wait. A few consolidators exist, but there is no buyer whose economics are like a mine developer paying 10^4x.
scored.ladder: The ladder is modest: lease, then farm, then hatchery and seed, then processing and brand, then distribution. US oyster aquaculture is roughly a few hundred million dollars a year in total (my estimate). It is fragmented and caps well below a very large company outcome.
scored.fatal_flaw: The lease right has almost no scarcity value that discovery creates. Most sheltered approved waters grow oysters fine, so the hit rate is high and the ML lever is under 2x. Buyers can get their own lease from the state for about $2k. The real bottleneck, permitting and social licence (a public hearing and 10-14 months), is not a data problem. The siting model already exists free from UMaine.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is not the hard part, the lease is a cheap state grant that can't be flipped at a 10^3x premium, the base hit rate is high, and the siting data is legible and already modelled by UMaine, so this fails the rubric despite clearing the hard exclusions.

scored.name: Blue Carbon Restoration Site Rights (seagrass/salt marsh)
scored.one_line: Use ML over historic aerial photos, sediment cores and hydrology to find degraded coastal parcels where seagrass or marsh restoration will reliably take hold. Option the land or seabed carbon rights cheaply, prove restorability with a pilot planting survival test, then sell the validated project to carbon developers.
scored.unproven_right: Carbon and restoration easements on private degraded marsh, diked farmland or leased seabed, bought from owners who see waterlogged land.
scored.proving_step: Pilot planting plus one season of survival monitoring. Restoration success rates are low (often under 40%), which is the hit-rate lever.
scored.proven_buyer: Blue-carbon project developers and corporate carbon buyers, who pay a premium for verified high-integrity removals.
scored.public_data: NOAA C-CAP land cover, USGS historical aerial imagery, Smithsonian CCRCN coastal carbon core atlas, Seagrass-Watch and SeagrassSpotter records, Sentinel-2 time series.
scored.rough_step_up: About 10-50x. The bespoke build (restoration) and verification are heavy, so the rubric's frame criterion is weak. Included as a comparison point.
scored.frame: The rung is "restorable-site right plus a pilot survival test", which is real but thin. Discovery (picking the site) is maybe 20-30% of the work, my estimate. The physical step is the bespoke restoration itself: breaching dikes, regrading, planting, then decades of MRV. It costs about $15k/acre (UK dike breach, about $37k/ha), around $40k/acre (about $99k/ha, Chesapeake), and NZD 20k to 350k+/ha (NZ). This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: building the thing is far harder than finding the site. A pilot plot cannot be split off as a sellable rung, because the buyer still has to pay for full-scale restoration, and that is where the risk sits.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a wetland easement is about $160/acre (North Dakota prairie-wetland easement study; tidal is a weak proxy). Diked coastal farmland is probably $1k-10k/acre (my estimate, no source found). Proven: blue-carbon credits sell for about $13-35/tCO2e (Chesapeake report, mangrove prices). Seagrass and marsh sequester roughly 1-7 tCO2e/ha/yr (my estimate from the literature). That gives about $30-250/ha/yr gross, or about $1k-5k/ha undiscounted over 30 years. Against that, restoration costs $37k-350k/ha. Break-even carbon price is $300 to $10,000+/t (NZ TNC study) and about $690/t at Deal Island (Chesapeake). A proven site is therefore worth at most about 1-3x the land, and often less than zero net of build cost. This is nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base trial survival is about 37% (global meta-analysis of 1,786 seagrass trials, Global analysis of seagrass restoration, J Appl Ecol). On the US West Coast, 32-60% of eelgrass plots failed by project end. Success depends heavily on method (bundles about 78%, outplanting about 18%) and on scale. Those are partly engineering variables, not only site variables. The lever is capped at 1/0.37, about 2.7x, not 10x. A pilot planting plus one season of monitoring costs perhaps $10k-100k per site (my estimate). One-season survival is also a poor predictor of long-term persistence.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible: USGS historic aerials, CCRCN sediment cores, Sentinel-2 time series. But current extent is already legible in NOAA C-CAP land cover and in seagrass mapping, and past restoration outcomes are compiled in databases (e.g. the WA/OR/CA eelgrass restoration database on Dryad). Incumbents (TNC, Restore America's Estuaries, Silvestrum, state agencies, Verra project developers) already do site-suitability modelling with exactly these layers. A lot of the predictive variance comes from method and scale, not from hidden site signal.
scored.right_bought: The right is weak. Most seagrass grows on state-owned submerged lands under public-trust doctrine, so leases come from regulators, not from owners who cannot read the data. Diked farmland can be bought or put under easement, but owners and land trusts already know it is marsh-restoration candidate land, and NRCS Wetland Reserve Easements pay standard rates for it. Changing tidal flow needs permits (Army Corps Section 404/10, state coastal zone). There is no information asymmetry to buy cheaply.
scored.buyer: The buyers are blue-carbon developers and corporate removal buyers paying about $13-35/t. Premium high-integrity blue-carbon credits fetch more, but nowhere near the $300-10,000/t break-even. The buyer pool is small, and most US tidal restoration is grant-funded (NOAA, state, mitigation), so there is no capitalised buyer paying a large premium for a de-risked site.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are full restoration and build, then MRV and credit issuance, then credit trading or mitigation banking, then coastal resilience services. The whole chain is small: the voluntary blue-carbon market is in the hundreds of millions of dollars a year at most (my estimate). The path to a very large company is weak, and the adjacent mitigation-bank route was already killed.
scored.fatal_flaw: The physical step dominates and loses money. Restoration costs $37k-350k/ha, while the proven asset earns about $1k-5k/ha in carbon credits (break-even needs $300-10,000/t vs $13-35/t market). Proving a site therefore creates almost no value, and may destroy it, regardless of how good the site selection is.
scored.one_line_reason: This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern: the bespoke build is the hard and expensive part. The proven step-up is about 1-3x or negative, not 10^3-10^4. The hit-rate lever is capped near 2.7x. The rights are mostly state-owned or already known to owners, not cheap from people who cannot read the data.
sources: https://www.marine.gov.scot/sma/node/17628 (Global analysis of seagrass restoration, ~37% trial survival, 1,786 trials)
https://escholarship.org/uc/item/1x80s86s (LA marsh carbon project not financially feasible at ~$13.50/t)
https://le.uwpress.org/content/80/4/501 (wetland easement implicit price ~$160/acre, prairie proxy)

scored.name: FallLine (radar-located meteorite strewn fields on private land)
scored.one_line: Mines the 30-year NEXRAD archive for radar returns of falling meteorites (Marc Fries-style detections, now automated), then buys recovery rights from farmers and ranchers under the strewn fields. Drone and ML imaging plus walkers recover the stones, which sell to dealers, collectors and institutions.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive meteorite search and recovery leases on private land. In the US, meteorites belong to the surface owner, and owners have no idea a fall landed on them years ago.
scored.proving_step: The company finds a radar dark-flight signature, models the wind-drift ellipse, and buys leases over the ~1-5 km² high-probability core. A drone with a dark-stone classifier (and magnetometer for irons) surveys it, and recovering the first stones proves the field. Each field costs about $10-30k, and today most reported fireballs never yield recovered stones.
scored.proven_buyer: Established meteorite dealers and auction channels (Christie's and Heritage meteorite sales), university and Smithsonian collections, and private collectors. A rare type (achondrite, lunar, carbonaceous) draws institutional bidders. Buyers pay for verified classified mass, so the whole step-up arrives at recovery.
scored.public_data: The NOAA NEXRAD Level II archive (petabytes on AWS, completely unindexed for meteorites). American Meteor Society and IMO fireball reports. NASA all-sky camera and GLM lightning-mapper bolide detections. USDA NAIP imagery and county parcel data for owners.
scored.rough_step_up: Rights cost close to $0 (a few hundred dollars per lease). A recovered field is worth about $20k-$500k for ordinary chondrites and $1M+ for a rare type, so the step-up on the right is 10^3x or more. The absolute dollars per field are small, though, and the buyer base is thin.
scored.frame: The rung is "lease a strewn field and recover the first classified stones." Finding where the field is makes up about 50-60% of the work (my estimate). The rest is physical: walkers, drones and magnetometers grid-searching 1-5 km² of farmland, forest and pasture, which is not trivial. The terrain notes on NASA ARES event pages (heavily wooded, not recovered) show that recovery often fails on the physical step, not on discovery. The buyers are collectors, dealers and a few institutions, not a capitalised developer who earns a multiple on what it buys. Borderline on exclusion: meteorite hunting is surface prospecting for rock. I left it unexcluded because there is no mining, no subsurface work and no mineral title.
scored.step_up: An unproven lease costs about $0-$500 (the candidate's estimate; I found no standard lease rate). Landowner deals are often a share of the finds instead. Buzzard Coulee: the hunters kept half the finds by mass. Proven value depends on freshness. A fresh fall sells for $50-$200+/g (2025 Georgia fall offered at >$200/g; Chelyabinsk about $50/g two weeks after its fall, per the Galactic Stone 2025 market report). Older and weathered ordinary chondrites sell for $0.5-$20/g (Meteorite Market listings: Bassikounou $2/g, Juancheng fall about $20/g). The candidate's whole pitch is falls that landed years ago and were never recovered, which means weathered stones at the cheap end. A 5-20 kg field at $2-10/g is worth $10k-$200k. Against a $300 lease that is nominally 10^2-10^3x. After a 50% landowner split and $10-30k of search cost, the step-up on the capital actually deployed is about 1-10x. Rare types (lunar, carbonaceous) would be far higher but are a tiny fraction of falls.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: by Fries's 2024 NASA abstract, NEXRAD has detected 34 recovered falls and 33 unrecovered probable falls since the late 1990s. So about 50% of radar-detected falls are already recovered (my arithmetic), and the ML lever is capped at about 2x, not 10x. That is about 1-2 new US radar falls per year (the 2014 Fries paper: about 1 per year, 18 since 1998). Cost per attempt is about $10-30k per field (the candidate's estimate; my estimate is consistent, at a 2-5 person team for 1-3 weeks plus drones). Automation could lift the detection count somewhat, but the total universe is around 30 unrecovered US probable falls plus about 1-2 a year. Adding foreign radar networks (about 3.6x NEXRAD's coverage, per the 2014 paper) runs into weaker ownership law outside the US.
scored.data: The signal is not illegible. NASA ARES (Fries) publishes an event page for each radar-detected fall, with an "probable" or "possible" status, a composite radar image and a color-coded landing-site map. That is exactly the "outcome written into a legible status field" pattern that kills the ML edge. Hankey et al. (AMS) have already presented automatic NEXRAD fall detection at ESA. American Meteor Society reports, GLM bolide detections and the NASA strewn-field maps (e.g. the Houston 2024 map) are released publicly, and hunter communities swarm any announced field within days. What remains for ML is low-confidence detections that Fries has not flagged. Those are the very events with low recovery odds.
scored.right_bought: Yes, legally. In most US states, meteorites belong to the surface owner, and finds on state land often belong to the state. Federal land law is unsettled. Owners can be approached before others do, and they usually don't know about falls years old. But once NASA ARES publishes a map, the owners get approached by many hunters and often negotiate a share of the finds (50% at Buzzard Coulee). So the right is cheap only for unpublished falls. A field also typically spans many parcels, so 1-5 km² means 5-30 landowners to sign (my estimate), and any one holdout cuts out part of the field.
scored.buyer: Meteorite dealers, Heritage/Christie's meteorite sales, private collectors, and university and Smithsonian collections. Institutions mostly receive type specimens through the classification process (Meteoritical Bulletin deposit requirements), not purchases. None of these buyers are capitalised in the sense of earning a multiple on the purchase. They are end consumers in a thin collectibles market: the global meteorite trade is about tens of millions of dollars a year (my estimate). Fresh-fall prices collapse as supply hits the market.
scored.ladder: There is essentially no ladder. Above recovery come only classification (done by university labs), cutting and preparation, and retail and auction sales, which together form a small collectibles niche. There is no path from strewn fields to a larger industrial chain. Asteroid mining is unrelated and not reached from here. The ceiling is a boutique meteorite dealer making about $1-5M a year (my estimate).
scored.fatal_flaw: The discovery output is already public and legible: NASA ARES publishes radar-detected falls with "probable" status and strewn-field maps, AMS already automates NEXRAD detection, and about half of radar-detected US falls are already recovered. That caps the hit-rate lever at about 2x. The rest sits in a supply of 1-2 falls a year, each worth about $10k-$200k as weathered stones, sold into a thin collectibles market with no rung above it.
scored.one_line_reason: Fails. The signal is already published by NASA ARES with "probable" status and maps, the base hit rate is about 50% (lever ≤2x), there are only 1-2 falls a year at about $10k-$200k each, collectors are not capitalised buyers, and there is no ladder.
sources: https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20140016924 (Fries 2014: ~1 radar fall/yr, 18 since 1998; foreign radar 3.6x coverage)
https://ares.jsc.nasa.gov/meteorite-falls/events/prescott-az (NASA ARES public probable-fall pages with strewn field maps)

scored.name: DeepKauri (buried subfossil swamp kauri under NZ farmland)
scored.one_line: Buys timber-extraction options on Northland dairy and drystock farms. ML on LiDAR, peat and soil maps and old drainage records locates buried 30,000-50,000-year-old kauri log rafts. A GPR survey and core prove each raft, and high-end furniture, instrument and architectural buyers purchase the logs.
scored.unproven_right: An option or profit-a-prendre on buried subfossil timber under private farmland, which farmers who do not know about the logs value at near zero.
scored.proving_step: ML on peat extents, LiDAR swamp paleochannels and scanned 1900s gum-digger and drainage-board records picks paddocks. A towed GPR array plus one auger core proves log volume and quality for about $5-15k per paddock.
scored.proven_buyer: Licensed swamp kauri processors and luxury millwork and table makers. Exports are tightly restricted by MPI (Forests Act), so the realistic buyer is the domestic processing chain, which is a weak point.
scored.public_data: LINZ national LiDAR, the Landcare Research S-map and peat layers, scanned Northland drainage-board plans and gum-field survey maps, and historic aerial photos.
scored.rough_step_up: An option at about NZ$100/ha becomes NZ$50k-$500k of proven timber per hectare, roughly 10^3x. Regulation and a thin buyer pool make the 'capitalised buyer' part shaky.
scored.frame: Proposed rung: an option or royalty agreement over a proven buried log raft, sold to an extractor. Discovery is well under 80% of the work in this rung; my estimate is 10-25%. Wikipedia describes extraction as slow, costly and technically difficult, done by skilled heavy-machinery operators in wet ground, and each log must be carefully brought to the surface. Operators must also pre-notify the Northland Regional Council, report volumes, restore the site, then dry and mill the timber. The physical step is the bulk of the work, not a trivial one. The model also looks like subsurface prospecting with an auger core. Timber is not on the literal exclusion list, so I did not mark it excluded, but it sits right next to the excluded mineral-exploration category.
scored.step_up: Unproven: the candidate assumes an option at about NZ$100/ha (unsourced). Northland farmers have known about swamp kauri since the gum-digging era, and they negotiate royalties with operators. One farmer refused entry over soil damage, and a neighbour was not paid his royalty (dealsonwheels article, via search summary). So the land is not valued at near zero. Proven: no reliable in-ground price per hectare exists. Finished timber is quoted at up to NZ$5,000-5,700/m3 retail (Green Party; Alibaba listing about 2014). Raw logs in the ground are worth a fraction of that once excavation, drying, milling and losses are paid; my estimate is NZ$300-1,000/m3 net. A rich raft of perhaps 50-200 m3/ha (my estimate) gives the landowner or rights holder a realistic uplift of about 10-100x over a fair option price, not 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I found no published hit rate for GPR plus core surveys. Logs are traditionally found with steel probes (the gum-spear method, Te Ara) and are exposed by farm drains and ploughing, so the base hit rate on known swamp paddocks is probably moderate to high (my estimate 30-60%). Cost per proving attempt is the candidate's own figure of NZ$5-15k per paddock (unsourced), small next to the cost of excavation. With a base hit rate that high, ML lifts it by 2-3x at most, so the claimed ~10x cut in discovery capex is not available.
scored.data: Public data: LINZ LiDAR, S-map and the peat layers are legible and already used. NIWA has already mapped likely swamp kauri sites and found that most are on farmland, with 50-70% of Northland's swamp kauri still in the ground (Wikipedia/NIWA, via search summary). Drainage-board scans are the only truly illegible source. Outcome field: since about 2015 the Northland Regional Council requires pre-notification of extraction and volume reporting, and MPI tracks milling and export, so the regulator already records where extraction happens. Rights: they are bought through royalty deals with farmers, which fits the rubric, but the owners are not uninformed about the resource. Incumbents: established Northland extractors and millers such as Ancient Kauri Kingdom already know the swamps.
scored.right_bought: A profit-a-prendre or royalty agreement with the farmer. Extraction on farmland is a permitted activity under the Northland Regional Plan, but it requires pre-notification. Farmers already charge royalties and some refuse because of soil and drainage damage, so the right is neither near-free nor easy to buy at a discount.
scored.buyer: The buyer pool is weak and thin. It is a handful of domestic Northland extractors and millers plus luxury furniture makers. MPI rules restrict export to finished products, or to stumps and roots not from indigenous forest land with MPI approval, and fines reach NZ$200,000. That caps prices and shuts out a capitalised global buyer. No one is like a mine developer who will pay 10^4x for a proven deposit.
scored.ladder: The ladder is short and capped: rights, then extraction, then milling, then finished products. The resource is finite and non-renewable, and the luxury niche market is small; my estimate is tens of NZ$ millions a year. The industry is politically contested, with calls for an inquiry and Green Party opposition, and the government has steadily tightened the rules. There is no path to a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. Wet-peat excavation, restoration and regulated milling make up most of the cost and risk. The proven output has no capitalised buyer willing to pay a 10^3x step-up, because exports are restricted to finished goods and the domestic market is a niche one. Farmers already know the logs exist and charge royalties.
scored.one_line_reason: A geothermal-in-coal-mines analogue: finding buried kauri is cheap and already known (probes, drains, NIWA maps), while extraction and an export-restricted niche market dominate, so the frame, the step-up and the ML lever all fail.

scored.name: HighGround: buying floodplain land that LiDAR shows sits above base flood elevation
scored.one_line: Buys parcels that FEMA FIRMs put in Special Flood Hazard Areas or floodways. These sell at a discount or as unbuildable. Where 3DEP LiDAR shows natural ground above the base flood elevation, a surveyor's elevation certificate plus a FEMA LOMA or LOMR-F legally removes the parcel from the floodplain. The parcel is then resold to builders as ordinary developable land.
scored.unproven_right: Fee title or options on land mapped Zone A or AE (often 'approximate Zone A' with no detailed study) and on floodway-fringe tracts. Owners, appraisers and lenders take the map at face value.
scored.proving_step: A licensed survey and elevation certificate ($500-3k), then a LOMA application, for which FEMA charges no fee for single lots and natural ground. Determinations take about 60 days. ML compares LiDAR terrain against the mapped flood surfaces and predicts which lots FEMA will grant.
scored.proven_buyer: Homebuilders, land developers and lenders. Removal also cuts NFIP-mandated insurance and opens agency mortgage financing, so production builders buy at full market price.
scored.public_data: FEMA NFHL / FIRM panels and approximate-A zones; USGS 3DEP 1m LiDAR; FEMA LOMA/LOMR records (outcome labels); HEC-RAS models where published; county parcel and sales records.
scored.rough_step_up: About 2-5x for buildable-but-penalised lots. About 10-50x for tracts held back as unbuildable floodway or approximate-A land that turn out to be upland. FEMA's map is the legible field, but its approximate zones are known to be wrong, and LOMAs already exist as a cottage service, so the edge is narrower than for wetlands.
scored.frame: The rung is: buy a mapped-SFHA parcel, get a LOMA or LOMR-F, and resell it as X-zone land. Inside that rung the physical step is close to free. A survey and elevation certificate costs $500-3k (candidate's figure; I did not verify it), FEMA charges no LOMA fee for single lots on natural ground, and FEMA accepts government LiDAR in place of a survey (FEMA Region V LiDAR LOMA fact sheet, 2018). So discovery would be about 80-90% of the work. But the discovery is mostly a deterministic comparison: lowest lot elevation from 3DEP against the published BFE. FEMA's own guidance tells homeowners how to do it. Approximate Zone A has no BFE, and FEMA's Base Level Engineering estimates increasingly fill that gap (my belief, not verified this session). Builders do buy the output, so the frame exists, but it is thin and resembles a free self-service. My estimate is that discovery is about 85% of the rung, but there is little hidden information to discover.
scored.step_up: Unproven: the meta-analysis of 37 studies puts the inland 100-year-floodplain discount at about 4.6% (range -75% to +61%). Local studies found 6.3% (Boulder) and 9.4% (Benton County). One Snohomish study found a discount for undeveloped floodplain land but none for developed land. Proven: full X-zone price. So the typical step-up is about 1.05-1.10x. My estimate for the best case, a vacant tract truly treated as unbuildable, is perhaps 3-10x. The candidate's 10-50x floodway case is mostly unavailable: FEMA guidance says LiDAR cannot be used for lots in the regulatory floodway. My understanding is that floodway land cannot be removed by any LOMA and needs a full LOMR with hydraulic modelling. Nothing here is near 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I found no published FEMA LOMA approval or denial rate after two searches; that would take a FOIA request or Online LOMC data. A proving attempt costs $0-3k (FEMA fee is $0; LiDAR overlay can replace the survey). Because the attempt is so cheap and the LiDAR-vs-BFE screen already happens before applying, my estimate is that the hit rate on submitted LOMAs is already high, probably over 50%. ML's lever is capped at about 1/base rate, so it is likely under 2x, and it applies to a capex that is already trivial. This is the reverse of Terranox, where each drill hole costs $100k+ and most fail.
scored.data: The data is public and legible. NFHL is vector GIS, 3DEP is gridded DEM, and BFEs are published attributes in detailed-study zones. The outcome is summarised in a legible field: the BFE versus the DEM elevation gives the answer directly, and issued LOMAs are attached to FIRM panels as determination records. Only approximate Zone A lacks a BFE, which needs hydraulic estimation, and BLE datasets are shrinking that gap. Incumbents and cottage firms already do this: surveyors, LOMA-mill firms, and floodplain administrators running state tools such as the WV Flood Tool LiDAR-for-LOMA guide. Forerunner explains LOMAs to communities. The opposite of Saskatchewan's scanned assessment files.
scored.right_bought: Rights are bought, not free first-come, which is a plus. The discount is small, though (about 5-10% typical). Sellers or their brokers can file the free LOMA themselves before selling. Lenders and flood-zone determination vendors flag SFHA status, and LOMA removal is widely marketed to homeowners. So the seller's information gap is small, except perhaps for rural approximate-A acreage held by unsophisticated owners.
scored.buyer: Production homebuilders and land developers are capitalised and pay full price for X-zone entitled land. The catch is that they can run the same LiDAR/BFE screen during due diligence, and often do. So the premium you capture is only the seller's mispricing, not a value jump the buyer has to pay for.
scored.ladder: Land banking leads to entitlement, then horizontal development (lots), then homebuilding. These rungs are real, but they are a crowded, commoditised, low-margin, capital-heavy industry. Flood-map arbitrage is not a durable wedge into it. A large company is possible in theory (a land developer or homebuilder), but the edge does not carry up the chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up is about 1.05-1.10x, not 10^4x. The market discounts floodplain land only about 4.6-9%. Removal is a free, deterministic, self-service FEMA process: LiDAR elevation against the published BFE, which FEMA itself accepts. The large-uplift floodway case is legally excluded from LOMA. So there is neither an illegible signal nor a big jump to capture.
scored.one_line_reason: The proving step is nearly free and already high-yield, the signal is a legible GIS subtraction FEMA invites homeowners to do, and removal from the floodplain lifts value only about 5-10%, so ML has nothing to multiply.

scored.name: OSTI Lazarus: re-proving declassified and abandoned DOE/NASA/DTIC results under a licensable patent position
scored.one_line: Mines millions of scanned DOE OSTI, NASA NTRS and DTIC reports for anomalous engineering results that were dropped when programmes were cancelled (high-temperature alloys, thermal coatings, radiation-hard electronics, sorbents). The company buys or licenses the government-owned or contractor-owned patents still in force for a nominal sum, cheaply reproduces the result plus an improvement patent, and sells to a defence or aerospace prime.
scored.unproven_right: A licence on a government patent (via the federal patent licensing programmes, often $1-10k) or a contractor patent bought from a defunct firm. Owners treat it as dead because the report sits in a scanned PDF no one reads.
scored.proving_step: Coupon-scale reproduction ($30-100k): furnace, creep, irradiation-proxy or wind-tunnel coupon tests. The original data shows a result exists. Only a reproduction proves it still holds with modern feedstock.
scored.proven_buyer: Defence and aerospace primes and their venture arms (Lockheed Ventures, RTX, GE Aerospace) and the DoD (AFWERX/DIU), which pay for validated TRL-4 IP.
scored.public_data: OSTI.gov (about 3M scanned technical reports), NASA NTRS, DTIC public reports, NIST data, and the federal tech-transfer licensing databases.
scored.rough_step_up: About 100-1000x on licence value ($5k licence to a $1-10M assignment, or a prime's acquisition). Weaker on the 'immediate' requirement because some buyers want more validation.
scored.frame: The proposed rung is a TRL-4 IP package: a licence plus a coupon-scale reproduction plus an improvement patent. Finding the anomalous result is maybe 40-60% of the work inside that rung (my estimate), not 80%+. The reproduction is not the trivial physical step that drilling is for Terranox. It means bespoke metallurgy or coatings work with modern feedstock, plus creep tests that run 1,000-10,000 hours. And the rung is not really sellable on its own. Aerospace primes adopt a new alloy or coating only after qualification (MMPDS-style design allowables, engine or flight testing), which typically takes 5-15 years and $10M+ (my estimate from general industry knowledge). So the output of this rung is not a finished product that a capitalised buyer takes as-is the way a developer takes a drilled discovery. DIU and AFWERX fund work through SBIR/OTA contracts; they do not buy IP assignments.
scored.step_up: Claimed: a ~$1-10k licence becomes a $1-10M assignment (100-1000x). Realistic (my estimate, not sourced, because the search budget ran out): there is no liquid market for orphan TRL-4 materials patents. Typical sales of individual patents or licences outside litigation-driven portfolios go for low tens to low hundreds of thousands of dollars. Federal lab licence income is concentrated in a few NIH biomedical hits, and the median federal licence earns very little (my estimate, recalled from the NIST federal tech-transfer annual reports: a few hundred million dollars a year across thousands of active licences). Primes acquire teams and companies with qualification data, not bare patents. A realistic step-up on the right itself is about 3-30x, illiquid, and not immediate. The candidate itself concedes it is weak on 'immediate'.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving cost of $30-100k per coupon reproduction is the candidate's own figure. That is plausible for furnace or oxidation tests, but low for creep (long-duration rigs) and for irradiation (real irradiation costs far more than $100k; proxies are not accepted by buyers). The base technical hit rate is probably HIGH, not low: government-funded reports from programmes like NASA HITEMP and DOE fossil and fusion materials work generally record real measurements, so a reproduction will usually confirm them (my estimate, maybe 30-60% after allowing for feedstock and processing drift). The failures are commercial: no buyer, no qualification path, and the result was superseded by commercial alloys like single-crystal superalloys or EBCs. ML cannot raise the commercial hit rate. And because the technical hit rate is already high, the cap of 1/base hit rate limits ML to about 2-3x, not 10x.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible. OSTI has ~3M+ records, NTRS ~500k+ and DTIC hundreds of thousands, with many pre-1995 scans of uneven OCR quality. But the OUTCOME is usually already summarised in a legible field: each report has an indexed abstract stating the headline result, and OSTI and NTRS are full-text searchable. Competitors already mine these collections: national-lab and NASA tech-transfer offices actively market their portfolios (NASA's Technology Transfer portal lists patents and software), firms like IP brokers and the materials-informatics companies (Citrine Informatics, which has DOE and DoD ties), and Lens.org and similar patent-literature tools that link patents to reports. The anomalous result is legible in the abstract; what is illegible is whether anyone still cares commercially.
scored.right_bought: The right mostly does not exist. US utility patents last 20 years from filing (35 USC 154). So the scanned, cancelled-programme results the thesis depends on (roughly the 1960s-1990s, and the cancellations of the 1990s and early 2000s) have patents that have expired, or were never filed. Worse, the published reports are themselves prior art (35 USC 102). They put the core result in the public domain, which bars any new composition-of-matter patent and limits the 'improvement patent' to narrow, obviousness-vulnerable claims that competitors can design around. Patents still in force (filed after about 2006) come from the born-digital era, where the reports are legible and the tech-transfer offices are actively advertising them. Exclusive federal licences also are not a nominal $1-10k purchase. Under 37 CFR 404 the agency must publish a notice in the Federal Register and evaluate a commercialisation plan. There are royalties and milestone payments. And the government keeps a royalty-free licence and march-in rights, so an exclusive government licence cannot be sold to a defence buyer as an exclusive asset. Startup licences through programmes like NASA's startup initiative are cheap precisely because the IP is low-value. Contractor patents from defunct firms are scattered and also mostly expired.
scored.buyer: The named buyers are defence and aerospace primes (Lockheed, RTX, GE Aerospace), their venture arms, and DIU/AFWERX. They are capitalised, but they buy qualified technology, companies with teams, or programme-funded R&D. They do not buy bare TRL-4 patents. The government already holds a licence to government-funded inventions, so DoD has little reason to pay for an IP assignment on government-originated work. No clear buyer pays out immediately for the output of this rung.
scored.ladder: There are rungs above: becoming a specialty materials or coatings producer, then a qualified supplier, then a component maker (in the mould of PCC, ATI, Howmet, Oerlikon). That chain is real and large. But each rung needs heavy capex and multi-year qualification, and the IP moat at the bottom rung is weak because the core result is prior art. So winning the smallest rung does not lock in the chain. It looks more like a materials R&D shop than a land-grab.
scored.fatal_flaw: Patent term and prior art do not line up with the illegible data. The results that are buried in illegible scans are old enough that their patents have expired and the reports themselves are public-domain prior art. Anyone can practise them, so there is no cheap, ownable unproven right to buy. The results that still have patents in force are born-digital and already marketed by tech-transfer offices. On top of that, the proving step does not create a sellable asset, because aerospace buyers pay for qualification, which costs 100x more than discovery.
scored.one_line_reason: Fails the right test. The illegible scanned results are 20+ years old, so their patents have expired and the reports are public-domain prior art, while in-force government patents are legible and actively marketed. Separately, primes do not pay millions for unqualified TRL-4 coupon data, and the technical hit rate is already high, so ML has little room to cut capex.
sources: Web searches were attempted but not performed: the shared per-turn search budget was exhausted, so all figures not marked as statute are estimates from prior knowledge
35 U.S.C. 154 (patent term of 20 years from filing) - https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/35/154

37 CFR Part 404 (licensing of government-owned inventions: Federal Register notice and commercialisation plan required for exclusive licences, government retains rights) - https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-37/chapter-IV/part-404
35 U.S.C. 203 / Bayh-Dole march-in and government licence - https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/35/203
NIST Federal Laboratory Technology Transfer annual reports (licence counts and income, recalled not re-verified) - https://www.nist.gov/tpo/reports-and-publications
NASA Technology Transfer Portal (agency actively markets in-force patents) - https://technology.nasa.gov
