scored.name: Data-Poor Quota Arbitrage (ITQ systems)
scored.one_line: Buy individual transferable quota in data-limited stocks, whose catch limits are set on precautionary proxies and so trade cheap. Use ML over decades of scanned survey and acoustic echogram archives to show the true biomass, and fund an independent survey that forces the catch limit upward. The quota then reprices for the fishing majors.
scored.unproven_right: Quota shares in NZ QMS, Iceland, or US catch-share programmes for minor stocks that trade at depressed prices because the catch limit is held low by missing data.
scored.proving_step: A chartered acoustic and trawl survey plus an accepted stock assessment. That is expensive and slow, and the regulator decides the outcome.
scored.proven_buyer: Vertically integrated fishing companies such as Sanford, Talley's and the Iceland majors, which buy quota when catch limits rise.
scored.public_data: NOAA AFSC/NEFSC acoustic echogram archives (EK60 raw data on NCEI/AWS), NIWA scanned trawl survey reports, ICES DATRAS, Global Fishing Watch effort data.
scored.rough_step_up: About 3-10x on quota value. The step-up is weak and set by a regulator, which fails the rubric's 'nature hides it' criterion. Included as a comparison point.
scored.frame: The rung is "own quota in a data-limited stock, then prove the biomass so the catch limit rises." Discovery is not 80%+ of the work inside this rung. My estimate: ML reading of echograms and survey archives is about 20-30%. The rest is a chartered survey (a vessel at roughly NZ$30-60k/day for 2-4 weeks, my estimate; NIWA publishes no day rate, and Tangaroa is mostly government-allocated at about 135 days/yr), getting the stock assessment accepted through MPI/NOAA/ICES working groups, and a ministerial decision made 1-3 years later. The physical and political step is the hard part, not a trivial one. Capitalised buyers do exist (Sanford, Talley's, Iceland majors), but they buy from a regulator-set number, not from Terranox's proof.
scored.step_up: Each quota share is a fixed fraction of the catch limit: 100m shares per stock, with ACE allocated pro rata to the TACC (source: MPI). Quota value is roughly ACE lease price / discount rate (source: Newell, Papps and Sanchirico, RFF). So the step-up is about the ratio of new TACC to old TACC, at best times a small liquidity re-rating. Real example: southern blue whiting 6B TACC rose 32% after an acoustic survey, from 2,377t to 3,145t (Deepwater Group), which is about 1.3x. Precautionary TACs on data-poor stocks (e.g. Quebec 4S herring held at 4,000t "preventive" TAC, DFO) rarely more than double. Estimated range is 1.2-3x, nowhere near 10^3. The asset is never near zero: it already trades at a positive price per kg of ACE.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I found no published base hit rate. My estimate is that most surveys of underexploited stocks do show biomass at or above the precautionary proxy. The failure mode is not nature hiding the asset. It is the regulator declining to raise the TAC, or raising it by only 10-30% under harvest-control-rule caution. Cost per proving attempt (my estimate): NZ$1-3M for a dedicated acoustic/trawl survey, plus 1-3 years of assessment process. ML can cut the cost of choosing which stock to target, but it cannot replace the survey or the assessment acceptance. Those are the capex, so a 10x capex cut is not available. The lever is at most about 2x.
scored.data: The data is public, and part of it is illegible: EK60 raw echograms on NCEI/AWS, scanned NIWA trawl reports, ICES DATRAS, and GFW effort. But the outcome-relevant variables are already legible public fields: TACC/TAC per stock, ACE and quota trade prices (FishServe/MPI tender results), and stock status in the annual MPI plenary and NOAA stock assessment reports. Incumbents such as Sanford, Talley's and Deepwater Group fund and sit on the science working groups, so they read this data better than anyone. NZ quota is bought, not free, but the sellers are sophisticated, not illiterate. Overseas persons need OIA consent to own NZ quota, and aggregation caps apply.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought. NZ QMS quota shares, Iceland ITQs and US catch shares trade on brokered markets and Crown tenders. But it is not cheap relative to the information. Quota for minor stocks trades thinly, and the counterparties are the same majors who run the industry science. There is no asymmetric discount like a $1/ha mineral claim, and foreign-ownership limits (NZ Fisheries Act/OIA) constrain a new entrant.
scored.buyer: Vertically integrated fishers (Sanford, Talley's, Moana, Iceland's Brim/Samherji) buy quota at prices tied to the TACC and ACE lease value. They are capitalised, but they are also the incumbents at the assessment table, and they would rather lobby for TAC increases themselves than pay a premium to an arbitrageur.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are fishing vessels, processing and seafood brands, a commodity chain with thin margins. In theory: quota, then harvesting, then processing, then distribution. That is a multi-billion-dollar but low-margin, regulator-capped industry (Sanford's market cap is roughly NZ$0.5-1B, my estimate), not a trillion-dollar path. Aggregation caps limit how much quota one firm can hold.
scored.fatal_flaw: Quota value scales linearly with a regulator-set catch limit, so a "hit" yields only about 1.2-3x (e.g. SBW6B +32% after a survey). The outcome is decided politically and published in a legible TACC field. The proving step (survey plus accepted assessment) is the expensive, slow part that ML cannot shrink.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails as a Terranox analogue. The step-up is about 1.3-3x and set by a regulator, not 10^4x revealed by nature. Proving costs NZ$1-3M and years of process that ML doesn't remove. The outcome is already a public TACC field, and the incumbents who would buy the quota are the ones who already read the science.

scored.name: ClearSky Avian (eagle-clear wind sites from radar bio-scatter)
scored.one_line: Wind developers walk away from high-wind land when eagle and bat risk is unknown, because a bad 2-year eagle survey kills the project under the USFWS eagle-take rules. ML on NEXRAD biological returns, eBird and roost data picks the high-wind parcels that are actually avian-clear. Option them, prove clearance with the survey, and sell the de-risked site to a wind developer, who pays the step-up.
scored.unproven_right: Wind options on high-wind but 'avian-uncertain' land developers have discounted (e.g. near raptor corridors in Wyoming, the Dakotas and Montana), at a few $/acre/yr.
scored.proving_step: USFWS-protocol eagle use and point-count surveys plus acoustic bat monitoring (~$150-300k). Weakness: the standard protocol takes about 2 years, so the proof is not immediate.
scored.proven_buyer: Wind developers and IPPs (NextEra, Invenergy, PacifiCorp/BHE, Pattern), who pay late-early-stage prices for permit-de-risked sites.
scored.public_data: NEXRAD Level II dual-pol biological scatter (as used by BirdCast and aeroecology research); eBird and Movebank telemetry; USFWS eagle nest surveys (scattered state PDFs); scanned environmental assessments of cancelled wind projects. Eagle use per site is not in a legible field.
scored.rough_step_up: About 20-100x on options (a permitting-de-risked early-stage project at $20-50k/MW). The base rate of failing an eagle survey in these areas is maybe 30-50%, so the lever is about 2-3x. C2 about 3, and C3 is weak.
scored.frame: The rung would be an avian-cleared wind site option. Inside that rung, avian discovery is not 80%+ of the work. Wind resource, interconnection position, landowner aggregation, county permits and offtake together are what make an early-stage wind site worth something. My estimate is that avian clearance is about 10-20% of de-risking. Developers buy whole development packages, not a bare avian-clear option, so the rung is not separately sellable. The proving step is 2 years of surveys plus bat acoustics, which is slow and not trivial.
scored.step_up: Unproven: wind options at about $2-10/acre/yr (my estimate, from typical option payments). Proven: early-stage onshore wind trades at about $20k/MW and ready-to-build at $100k+/MW (Enerdatics European M&A, 2026). At roughly 50-80 acres/MW of lease area, $20k/MW is about $250-400/acre, which is about 50-100x the option price. Almost all of that comes from wind, interconnection and land aggregation, not avian clearance. The step-up that comes from avian clearance alone is probably under 3x (my estimate). Projects in eagle areas mostly proceed anyway with a take permit and compensatory mitigation rather than dying.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt: about $150-300k for 2 years of surveys (candidate's figure; I found no published survey budgets). FWS permit fees are $11k for a general permit and $28-36k for a specific permit (FWS FAQ). Base hit rate: no published 'failed survey' rate exists, because a survey rarely kills a project. A bad survey moves it to a specific permit with mitigation, so I estimate the 'pass' rate at 50-70%+. The lever is therefore capped near 1.5-2x, nowhere near 10x.
scored.data: The outcome is already summarised in a legible public field. Since the April 2024 USFWS eagle rule, there is a public FWS Eagle Permit Eligibility Map for Wind. It is built from eBird relative abundance for bald and golden eagles (data year 2020) at 3 km² resolution across several seasons, and combined with nest-distance rules (2 mi from golden eagle nests, 660 ft from bald eagle nests). It is downloadable from ScienceBase. It tells any developer, for free, which parcels qualify for the low-risk general permit. NEXRAD bio-scatter and eBird are public, but they are already legible and used (BirdCast, the FWS map itself). The remaining illegible data, scattered nest PDFs and cancelled-project EAs, adds little. On the right: wind options can be bought from ranchers, but developers and landmen already price eagle risk using the same FWS map, so there is no information discount to capture.
scored.right_bought: Wind lease/option agreements from private ranch landowners in WY, the Dakotas and MT, at a few $/acre/yr (my estimate). These are bought, not first-come, but they are not mispriced on avian grounds relative to the public FWS map.
scored.buyer: Wind developers and IPPs (NextEra, Invenergy, BHE/PacifiCorp, Pattern) are capitalised and buy early-stage projects at about $20k/MW. They do not pay for avian clearance alone, without interconnection and resource proof, and their in-house environmental teams already screen with the FWS map plus consultants (WEST Inc., SWCA, Tetra Tech).
scored.ladder: If the company expanded into full greenfield wind development, there are rungs above: development, then interconnection, construction and IPP ownership. That is a large industry but crowded, and the avian wedge gives no durable edge for climbing it.
scored.fatal_flaw: The answer is already public and legible. The 2024 USFWS eagle rule publishes a wind permit-eligibility map built from eBird eagle abundance at 3 km² resolution, so 'avian-uncertain' land is already sorted for free. A failed survey also rarely kills a project, because it only moves it to a specific permit with mitigation, so there is no large mispricing and no 10x hit-rate lever.
scored.one_line_reason: Avian clearance is a small part of what makes a wind site valuable, and the 2024 FWS eagle eligibility map already shows the outcome in a public field. It costs 2 years to prove, the hit-rate lever is under 2x, and there is no illegible-data edge.

scored.name: SeeingSite (clear-sky, low-turbulence optical ground station sites)
scored.one_line: Laser satellite links (SDA's Transport Layer, Starlink and Kuiper optical backhaul, NASA LCRD successors) need ground sites with rare combinations of cloud-free hours and low atmospheric turbulence. ML on 25 years of geostationary cloud masks plus scanned observatory site-testing reports finds them. Option the land, prove it with a 6-month DIMM and all-sky-camera campaign, and sell or lease the certified site to constellation operators.
scored.unproven_right: Options on small (10-100 acre) private high-desert and ridge parcels, plus rooftop or easement rights, bought at rural land prices.
scored.proving_step: A 6-month seeing monitor (DIMM/MASS), all-sky cloud camera and scintillometer deployment (~$30-60k). Trivial hardware.
scored.proven_buyer: Optical-network operators and integrators (SpaceX, Amazon Kuiper/AWS Ground Station, SDA contractors, Mynaric, Aalyria, KSAT).
scored.public_data: GOES/Himawari/Meteosat cloud-mask archives (petabytes); IGRA radiosonde-derived Cn2 profiles; scanned 1960s-1990s NOAO, ESO and Air Force site-testing reports. The outcome is not written in any field.
scored.rough_step_up: Perhaps 10-50x on tiny parcels. The market is narrow (dozens of sites, with buyers paying perhaps $0.5-3M each), and most operators self-survey. C2 about 2-3; C5 is limited.
scored.frame: The rung would be "optioned parcel plus a certified 6-month seeing and cloud campaign" (around $30-60k per the candidate). Inside that rung, discovery is most of the work, roughly 70-80% by my estimate, and the hardware is trivial. The frame still fails because nothing scarce is being proven. Cloud-free line-of-sight (CFLOS) availability is a regional property: cloud fields stay correlated over tens to hundreds of km, which is why optical ground station networks are designed around spatial de-correlation between distant sites (SPIE feeder-link architecture paper). Once a region qualifies, any nearby parcel substitutes for the proven one. The buyer is paying for a location, not for the specific parcel's title.
scored.step_up: Unproven: rural high-desert land at about $500-5,000 per acre (my estimate from typical US Southwest rural land prices, not searched). Proven: there is no observed market price for a "certified OGS site". The candidate's own guess is $0.5-3M per site. I think that overstates it: the buyer could buy the next parcel over at rural prices and repeat a $50k campaign, so a realistic premium is about 2-5x on land value plus the cost of the campaign data. That is far from 10^3x. Cailabs' planned network is about 15 stations worldwide, at least 4 in the US (Cailabs OGSaaS announcement, Sept 2026), which shows demand is only dozens of sites globally.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt is about $30-60k (the candidate's figure; the ANAtOLIA-type mobile site-characterisation stations described at SPIE are similar kit). The base hit rate is high, probably 30-60% of shortlisted desert or ridge parcels meeting CFLOS and seeing requirements (my estimate), because the shortlist already comes from public cloud climatology. JPL's Lasercom Network Optimization Tool already runs discrete optimisation on cloud climatology and finds that 4-5 CONUS plus Hawaii sites reach 90% availability. Since the lever is capped at 1/base hit rate, the most ML can cut costs is about 2-3x, not 10x, and the campaign is cheap to begin with.
scored.data: GOES, Himawari and Meteosat cloud masks are huge but fully legible gridded products. They are exactly the input incumbents use: JPL's LNOT and published network-optimisation papers (SPIE 11852) compute CFLOS availability from them directly. In practice the outcome IS summarised in a legible, computable field. Turbulence (Cn2 and seeing) is the less legible part, and scanned old site-testing reports add some signal. But LEO and GEO laser downlinks tolerate moderate seeing with tip-tilt or adaptive optics, so turbulence is a second-order selection factor. The illegible-data edge is weak.
scored.right_bought: Yes in form: options on 10-100 acre private parcels can be bought cheaply. But the sellers do not have an information disadvantage that matters, because the relevant signal (regional clear-sky climate) is common knowledge (Arizona and Chile deserts are famous for it), and the right is not exclusive. Neighbouring parcels give the same climate, so the step-up cannot be captured.
scored.buyer: Possible buyers: optical ground station operators and GSaaS providers such as Cailabs OGSaaS (about 15 planned stations), SSC (commissioning optical stations in Australia and Chile), Archangel Lightworks with Omantel, KSAT, AWS Ground Station, SpaceX and Kuiper, and SDA contractors. They are well capitalised, but they mostly self-site using JPL-style cloud-climatology tools, often co-locate at existing teleports or observatories, and need only dozens of sites globally.
scored.ladder: The ladder above is limited: site, then ground station build, then optical GSaaS network. The company would be climbing into a capex-heavy, competitive ground-segment service business (Cailabs, SSC, KSAT, RBC Signals) whose value is in the terminals and the network, not the land. The total market is perhaps a few billion dollars. There is no trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: No scarcity or exclusivity in the proven right. CFLOS and seeing quality are regional climate properties, already computable from legible public cloud-mask archives (JPL LNOT does exactly this). A proven parcel is therefore interchangeable with adjacent cheap land, and the buyer can self-survey for about $50k. The 10^3-10^4 step-up never forms, and demand is only dozens of sites.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is cheap and the outcome is computable from legible public cloud masks that incumbents already optimise over. A clear-sky parcel is substitutable with its neighbours, so proving one yields roughly a 2-5x premium on tiny land values, not 10^3x, in a market of dozens of sites.

scored.name: Lunar/Martian stone sweeps on private desert playas
scored.one_line: Runs ML on sub-metre archival satellite and aerial imagery of deflation surfaces and playas to find dense collection areas of dark exotic stones, where the rare lunar and Martian meteorites sit among ordinary chondrites. It buys collection rights on private or state-leasable desert land and sells classified achondrites to collectors and institutions.
scored.unproven_right: Collection rights on private desert parcels and state trust land in the US Southwest, and licensed collection concessions where national law allows (for example Oman or Chile parcels). Landowners value the land at a few dollars per hectare.
scored.proving_step: A drone and walk sweep of ML-ranked surface patches, followed by classification at a university lab (about $500 per stone). Today hunters wander at random, and lunar or Martian finds are about 0.1-1% of finds.
scored.proven_buyer: Collectors, museums and planetary-science buyers who pay $1,000-$10,000/g for lunar and Martian material (single stones regularly sell for $100k-$1M+), plus sample-return-calibration programmes.
scored.public_data: USDA NAIP, USGS historical aerial photos, declassified KH-9, Landsat/Sentinel albedo time series, and the Meteoritical Bulletin dense-collection-area database. Where the stones sit is hidden by nature; no registry records it.
scored.rough_step_up: Land worth about $1-10/ha yields one lunar or Martian stone worth $100k-$1M, an implied 10^3-10^4x on the right. Volume is lumpy, and this is best treated as a second product line of Fallfinder.
scored.frame: The rung is surface meteorite recovery plus classification. Finding the stone is perhaps 80-90% of the work and the physical step (pick it up, send it for a roughly $500 classification) is trivial, so the shape matches Terranox. The buyer side does not. Buyers are a fragmented hobby collector market plus a few museums, with no capitalised developer behind them. A 2025 dealer report says lunar and Martian material is "recovered and classified at a pace that is outstripping demand." I left the exclusion flag unset, but this is borderline: it is surface prospecting for rocks, close to the "mineral prospecting" exclusion.
scored.step_up: The step-up lands on the stone, not on the right. Once a patch has been swept it is depleted, so the land does not rise in value the way drilled land does. Lunar prices fell about 90% from roughly $1,000/g around 2005 to about $100/g on average by 2022 (Galactic Stone), and one dealer blog puts 2025 wholesale for most lunars at about $8-12/g. Martian material holds better, around $100-200/g retail for small fragments. A typical hot-desert lunar find of 20-200 g is worth about $0.2k-20k (my estimate). The $100k-$1M+ cases are rare outliers, such as the 24.67 kg Martian stone that sold for $5.3M at Sotheby's in 2025. Against $1-10/ha land, the nominal multiple is large, but per hectare swept it is close to zero.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate is very low. Oman's central desert had 15 lunar or Martian stones (4 lunar, 11 Martian) out of 14,775 meteorites recovered, about 0.1% (LiveScience, 2014 figures). In theory the lever is up to 1000x, but ML cannot reach it. A stone of 2-20 cm is below the 0.3-1 m pixel size of NAIP, KH-9 and Sentinel imagery, so imagery can at best rank deflation surfaces, and those are already mapped as dense collection areas. Imagery cannot tell a lunar breccia from an ordinary chondrite, so the 0.1% share among finds would barely move. Cost per attempt (my estimates): a drone or walk sweep runs about $100-1,000 per km², plus $500 per stone classified. That attempt is already cheap, so there is little capex for ML to save.
scored.data: The imagery is public but cannot carry the signal, because the stones are sub-pixel. The Meteoritical Bulletin dense-collection-area database is legible and already published, so the locations of productive surfaces are effectively a lookup table, which removes the ML edge. Nature does hide where the exotic stones sit, but nothing in the data reveals it either.
scored.right_bought: This is weak. US Southwest playas are mostly BLM or state trust land. BLM allows casual collecting up to 10 lb a year for personal use and requires a FLPMA land-use permit for commercial collecting (BLM IM-2012-182), so the right is obtained by permit, not bought cheaply from owners who cannot read the data. Private playa parcels exist, but almost no lunar or Martian stones have been recorded from US hot deserts (my estimate; the search found no count). Supply comes from the Sahara (NWA) and Oman. Oman treats meteorites as national heritage controlled by its Ministry of Heritage and Culture and is concerned about smuggling, which makes a foreign commercial concession unlikely. The search did not confirm a formal export ban.
scored.buyer: Private collectors and dealers, a few museums and planetary-science institutions, and occasional high-end Sotheby's or Christie's auctions. The market is small, fragmented, has oversupply, and prices are falling. There is no capitalised buyer that needs the output to keep its business running.
scored.ladder: There is essentially no ladder. Climbing it means more meteorite dealing, auction, curation or classification services, which is a small hobby market (my estimate: well under $100M a year globally). Sample-return calibration programmes rely on their own returned samples and Antarctic collections. There is no path to a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: Both the signal and the market are missing. The stones are sub-pixel in archival imagery, and a lunar stone cannot be told from a chondrite from above, so ML cannot raise the 0.1% hit rate. Lunar and Martian finds come from Saharan nomad hunters and Oman, not from rights that can be bought in the US Southwest, and that cheap supply has driven lunar prices down about 90% to roughly $8-100/g. Most finds are worth thousands, not the $100k-$1M the pitch assumes, and buyers are hobbyists rather than a capitalised developer.
scored.one_line_reason: The shape is right (discovery-heavy, trivial pickup), but ML cannot see sub-pixel stones, the rights are permits or sit in jurisdictions that are closed or have produced no lunar or Martian finds, prices have collapsed, and there is no ladder or capitalised buyer.

scored.name: Salvor (insurer-owned dead GEO satellites)
scored.one_line: Insurers take title to satellites written off as total losses. ML runs over public light-curve photometry, radar cross-section and TLE histories to infer which of these 'dead' birds are still stable, power-positive and have intact payloads. The company buys salvage title from the underwriters for close to nothing and sells the proven-healthy asset to a GEO operator or life-extension servicer, which reactivates it (precedent: the AsiaSat 3 / HGS-1 lunar-flyby rescue in 1998).
scored.unproven_right: Salvage title to an insured total-loss satellite, sold by the underwriting syndicate (Lloyd's and others) at a nominal price because the insurers cannot interpret the orbital data.
scored.proving_step: An ML attitude and health inversion from light curves, then a short licensed ground-station contact (telemetry command or listen) to confirm the bus and transponders are alive. That costs about $50-500k, against write-offs worth $100M-$400M. Most write-offs are truly dead, so the base hit rate is low.
scored.proven_buyer: GEO operators (SES, Intelsat, Eutelsat, regional sovereign operators that need slot continuity) and servicers such as Northrop SpaceLogistics' MEV, which already docks with and moves old GEO birds.
scored.public_data: The Mini-MegaTORTORA public light-curve database, Space-Track TLE history, amateur SatObs photometry archives, published insurer loss records, and FCC/ITU filings, which contain no health field. Whether the satellite is physically alive is hidden by orbital physics, not written in a registry.
scored.rough_step_up: Title bought for $0.1-1M becomes a reactivated asset worth $10-100M, about 10^2-10^3x. The physical step (boost and servicing) is not trivial and loss cases are few (about 1-5 per year), so the frame is narrower than Terranox's.
scored.frame: The rung is "salvage title to an insured total-loss GEO satellite, proven reactivatable." Discovery is not 80%+ of the work inside it. My estimate is 10-30%. The rest is physical and regulatory: moving the satellite into an orbit and slot it can use (HGS-1 needed a lunar flyby planned by Hughes, the satellite's builder), getting a licensed TT&C ground segment, the encryption keys and command database (which only the manufacturer or operator holds), ITU and FCC slot rights, and often a MEV-class servicing mission. Most of the value is created at that physical step, which is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure mode.
scored.step_up: AsiaSat 3 was written off by 27 insurers. Hughes Global Services got title in April 1998 for no reported cash; instead it agreed to share profits with the insurers. It turned the satellite into HGS-1, and PanAmSat bought it in early 1999 as PAS-22. The PanAmSat price was not disclosed. So the unproven right effectively cost $0 plus a revenue share, and the proven asset was worth about $10-100M (my estimate). That jump only happened after an expensive orbit-recovery campaign by the satellite's own manufacturer, not at the moment of a hit. Also, policies routinely include title salvage and revenue salvage clauses (UNIDROIT 2010), so insurers keep part of the upside. The step-up captured purely from proving health is about 3-10x, not 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I found no real base hit rate. My estimate: well under 10% of total-loss GEO satellites can be reactivated. Inmarsat-6 F2 lost power and Intelsat 33e broke up (and was uninsured). But the proving step is not a mostly-failing, expensive search. The operator already streams telemetry from the satellite, which tells it whether the bus is alive. Constructive total losses are declared at a 70-90% capability-loss threshold (IISL 2018), and the operator often keeps flying the satellite (ViaSat-3 F1 runs at reduced capacity, with Viasat claiming about $420M). The ML lever on light curves has nothing to beat, because ground truth is already known for free. The pool is also tiny: 2023 insured losses were about $995M paid against $557M in premiums, concentrated in roughly 2-3 satellites (Breaking Defense 2024).
scored.data: The public data (Mini-MegaTORTORA light curves, Space-Track TLEs) is somewhat illegible. But it can only show spin state and orbit, not whether transponders, batteries or the payload work. The outcome sits in proprietary telemetry held by the seller side: the operator and the insurers' technical advisors, who adjust every claim with full telemetry and manufacturer anomaly reports. So the owners can read far better data than we can, which is the reverse of Terranox, where the owners are blind. Titles are not bought cheaply from naive owners. They are negotiated with revenue-share clawbacks, and in ORBCOMM-style settlements title often stays with the operator. Incumbents in recovery: the satellite's manufacturer (Hughes/Boeing did HGS-1), Northrop SpaceLogistics MEV, and operators themselves.
scored.right_bought: Salvage title, or the revenue-salvage interest held by the underwriting syndicate (insurers' rights under the title-salvage and revenue-salvage clauses). In practice it is negotiated together with the operator, who holds the command keys and the ITU filing.
scored.buyer: GEO operators (SES, Intelsat, Eutelsat, PanAmSat as the HGS-1 buyer) and sovereign operators that need slot continuity. Life-extension servicers such as Northrop MEV are suppliers to this trade, not buyers of salvaged satellites. Demand is thin and episodic.
scored.ladder: Possible rungs above: salvage, then servicing and refuelling, then a GEO capacity operator, then in-orbit manufacturing and assembly. This is a real but crowded ladder (Northrop, Astroscale, Starfish Space, Orbit Fab), and the bottom rung's deal flow of about 1-5 losses a year is too small to fund the climb.
scored.fatal_flaw: The information asymmetry runs the wrong way. The sellers (operator and insurers) already hold the satellite's private telemetry, a near-perfect health signal, while ML on public light curves and TLEs can only infer attitude and orbit. Nobody is unable to read the data, so there are no mispriced titles to buy. On top of that, the value is created by a hard physical step: orbit recovery or servicing, plus control over command keys and slots.
scored.one_line_reason: Owners already know health through telemetry, the deal flow is about 1-5 a year, and the value comes from an expensive physical recovery rather than discovery, so it fails C1, C3 and C4.

scored.name: DeepPeat: carbon rights on hidden deep peat from airborne gamma
scored.one_line: Buy carbon or rewetting easements from farmers on drained land sitting over deep peat. Peat depth is invisible at the surface but shows up as gamma attenuation in public airborne radiometrics. Prove depth with cheap probing and block the drains (a trivial physical step). Sell forward offtake to corporate removal and avoidance buyers.
scored.unproven_right: 30-100 year rewetting or carbon easements on agricultural parcels at a few hundred $/ha. Owners value the land only as pasture or crop.
scored.proving_step: An ML depth map from radiometric attenuation, soil maps and LiDAR, verified by gouge-auger probing (days and hundreds of dollars per site). Ditch blocking is a cheap civil works job.
scored.proven_buyer: Frontier and Symbiosis-type corporate buyers, plus Microsoft and Shell forward offtakes for peatland credits (Verra VM0036 / UK Peatland Code).
scored.public_data: BGS Tellus airborne radiometrics (UK/Ireland), GSI Tellus Ireland, Geoscience Australia radiometric grid, USGS NURE, national soil/peat maps, open LiDAR DTMs.
scored.rough_step_up: An easement at about $300/ha against 10-30 tCO2e/ha/yr × $20-50 × 30 years (about $6-45k/ha NPV) is about 20-100x. Buyers usually pay on issuance rather than at proof. Forward offtake partly fixes that.
scored.frame: The rung would be "own a rewetting easement on peat that has been shown to be deep and get it to validated or issued Peatland Code / VM0036 units". Inside that rung, finding the peat is maybe 10-20% of the work (my estimate). The rest is negotiating with landowners over decades-long land-use change, agreeing water levels across neighbouring parcels and drainage boards (lowland fen is pump-drained), validation, and 30+ years of monitoring before credits are issued. Blocking drains on lowland agricultural peat is not the trivial physical step that drilling is for Terranox. It ends farming on that land, and often on the neighbours' land too. Some capitalised buyers exist (UK corporates buying Peatland Code Pending Issuance Units, and REDD/peat buyers such as Shell in Katingan). But Frontier buys only durable removals and would not buy rewetting, which is mostly avoided emissions. And buyers pay at issuance or on forward contracts, not at the point of proof.
scored.step_up: All figures are my estimates; search was unavailable. The candidate assumes an easement at about $300/ha. That is not realistic for a long-term rewetting easement on farmland. Lowland pasture rents for about £150-250/ha/yr, and Grade 1 fen cropland sells for roughly £20-30k/ha. A permanent no-drainage easement costs close to the land's farming value, which is thousands to tens of thousands of $/ha, not hundreds. Proven value: 15-30 tCO2e/ha/yr avoided × 30 years × £15-30/t for Peatland Code PIUs, less a 15-20% buffer and validation and monitoring costs, gives about $5-15k/ha gross, received over decades. Against a realistic easement cost the step-up is about 1-3x, not 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving the peat is cheap and usually succeeds. A gouge-auger survey costs hundreds to low thousands of dollars per site, and inside areas already mapped as peat, most probes confirm deep peat (my estimate is over 70%). The real failure points are landowner refusal and hydrology, not finding the peat. With a base hit rate that high, the lever is capped at about 1.5x, nowhere near 10x. Physics adds a further limit: airborne gamma comes from roughly the top 30-50 cm, so attenuation saturates once peat is about 0.5-1 m thick. It shows that peat is present or wet, but it cannot resolve depth in the range that matters. These are my estimates from known Tellus/BGS work; search was unavailable.
scored.data: The data (Tellus radiometrics, LiDAR) is public and somewhat illegible. But the answer is already published in legible form. National peat maps cover where peat is and broadly how deep: the Natural England England Peat Map (2023-25), LandIS/NSRI soil series, Irish national peat and soil maps, the Scottish carbon and peatland map, and in Northern Ireland peat mapping that already uses Tellus radiometrics. Incumbent peat-restoration developers and NGOs already use these maps, for example Wildlife Trusts, Fens East / Great Fen, Forest Carbon, and Nattergal-type developers. Landowners know their fen land is peat, because black peat soil and wastage are obvious to them and visible in the price of fenland.
scored.right_bought: The right is bought, not free first-come, so that part fits. But the sellers are not unable to read the data. Fen farmers know they farm on peat, and their asking price reflects the land's high crop value. There is no information discount to capture. The purchase price is set by the farming income forgone, not by uncertainty about how deep the peat is.
scored.buyer: UK corporates buying Peatland Code PIUs at about £15-30/t (my estimate), and voluntary market buyers of VM0036 credits. Frontier and Symbiosis-type durable-removal buyers are mostly out, because rewetting is avoidance plus slow removal. Payment comes on issuance or as forward offtake at a discount.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are modest: paludiculture crops (sphagnum, reed), owning the land outright, biodiversity net gain and nutrient credits stacked on the same parcels, and landscape-scale fen restoration. There is real stacking of revenue streams, but no obvious path to a very large company. The total market is bounded by deep-peat farmland area and carbon prices.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value is not locked behind discovery. National peat maps already publish where deep agricultural peat is, and airborne gamma cannot resolve depth past about 0.5-1 m. What actually blocks the business is the cost of the right itself: rewetting ends farming on high-value fen land, so the easement costs about as much as the land, and the step-up collapses to roughly 1-3x.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is a small share of the work and the outcome is already in public peat maps. The costly step is buying the farmer out of farming, not finding peat, so the step-up is about 1-3x and ML has nothing to lever.
sources: Web search budget was exhausted (shared limit), so none of these figures was checked by search this turn; all numbers are estimates from prior knowledge
Natural England, England Peat Map (2023-2025 release) - prior knowledge
IUCN UK Peatland Code v2 (lowland agricultural peat category, Pending Issuance Units) - prior knowledge
BGS/GSNI Tellus airborne radiometrics and peat mapping studies (gamma attenuation depth limit ~0.5-1 m) - prior knowledge
Frontier offtake criteria (durable removals only) - prior knowledge

scored.name: Wild Mussel and Oyster Seed Bed Several Orders (UK/Ireland/Netherlands)
scored.one_line: Use ML over fisheries survey and sonar archives to find ephemeral wild mussel-seed and native-oyster beds. Apply for or buy several-fishery orders and seabed leases in those areas, prove the bed with a grab survey, then sell the seed rights to mussel growers, who depend on wild seed every year.
scored.unproven_right: Several-fishery orders and Crown Estate or state seabed shellfish leases, plus purchase of dormant existing orders from retiring holders who cannot see where seed has settled.
scored.proving_step: A dredge or grab sample survey (about $10-20k) confirming seed density. Spatfall is patchy and most blind surveys come up empty.
scored.proven_buyer: Vertically integrated rope and bottom mussel growers and native-oyster restoration programmes, who buy seed at once each season.
scored.public_data: Cefas and Marine Institute scanned shellfish survey reports, EMODnet seabed habitat maps, INFOMAR multibeam backscatter, Wadden Sea monitoring data, Sentinel-2 intertidal imagery.
scored.rough_step_up: Order or lease: about $5-20k. Proven seed bed: $0.5-3M per season. About 10^2x. The value recurs but is less discrete.
scored.frame: Rung = holding seabed rights over a wild seed-mussel or native-oyster settlement and selling the seed. Discovery (where spat settled this year) might be about 50% of the work if the right could be held, but it can't: wild subtidal seed beds in the Irish Sea, Wadden Sea and English/Welsh IFCA districts are regulated commons, opened to licensed vessels once the state survey is done. Dredging, relaying and Natura appropriate assessment are a large share of the work. The buyers (bottom growers) are mostly the same licensed vessels that fish the seed themselves, so there is no separate capitalised buyer for a 'proven bed'.
scored.step_up: Unproven: the candidate's own $5-20k for an order or lease, my estimate, and you cannot get a several order or lease over an ephemeral seed bed on speculation. Proven: a subtidal seed bed of a few thousand tonnes at about EUR100-300/t of seed (my estimate; the whole Irish bottom-mussel sector made only about EUR12M on 16,000 t in 2016, about EUR750/t for grown mussels, per BIM via thefishsite/fishfarmingexpert) is worth roughly EUR0.3-1M once, not each season, because beds are ephemeral and get washed out or eaten by starfish. That is about 10-50x on paper, and it isn't capturable because the right is not exclusive.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt: grab or dredge survey at about $10-20k (candidate figure, plausible; my estimate is $5-15k of vessel time a day). Base hit rate: not low. The state already runs side-scan sonar plus grab surveys every year, so the industry is not making blind shots: BIM (MV T'Burke II, east coast), DAERA (four NI sites, 2024), Wageningen Marine Research (autumn and spring inventories since 2005, with a fishing plan built from them) and the NW-IFCA cockle and mussel reports. Spatfall is patchy, but there are only a few known recurring settlement areas. At most ML gives about 2x, not 10x. The whole sector's discovery spend is under EUR1M a year.
scored.data: The data mostly is public: BIM seed mussel survey reports, Marine Institute and INFOMAR backscatter, EMODnet, Wadden Sea monitoring. But the outcome is already written down in legible form. The state surveys publish bed location, biomass and seed quality each season, and those results directly decide which beds open or close (BIM 2025 Shellfish Survey Programme). This is the same 'regulator writes the answer' failure seen in earlier hunts. ML on historical archives can't predict this year's spatfall better than this year's sonar survey, because spatfall depends on larval supply and weather in that season.
scored.right_bought: No. Irish Sea seed is fished under a DAFM Fisheries Natura Plan (2023-2027) by licensed vessels, as a commons. Dutch Wadden seed fishing is allocated to licence holders under a fishing plan (and is being replaced by seed-collector ropes). English and Welsh several orders take years, need consultation and a Habitats Regulations assessment, and cover fixed areas, so they can't follow ephemeral beds. Dormant orders exist, but the holders are growers who know their grounds, and most are not over recurring wild seed.
scored.buyer: Bottom mussel growers (Irish, Welsh Menai/Conwy and Dutch PO Mosselcultuur members) and native oyster restoration NGOs. It is a small, thinly capitalised sector (Irish bottom mussel about EUR12M a year in revenue). They catch the seed themselves with their own dredgers instead of buying proven beds, and the restoration programmes are grant-funded and small.
scored.ladder: Weak. Seed beds, then bottom-culture plots, then processing: the whole EU mussel industry is about EUR0.5B a year and in structural decline, and the Netherlands is moving to rope seed-collectors (MZI) that remove wild seed discovery altogether. Owning the seed doesn't lead toward a large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proven outcome is already public, and the right is not exclusive or buyable. Each season state agencies (BIM, DAERA, WMR, IFCAs) survey the seed beds with sonar and grabs, publish location and biomass, and open them to licensed vessels as a regulated commons, so there is nothing to 'discover' and no exclusive right to buy before the hit.
scored.one_line_reason: Regulators already survey and publish where the seed is every season and give it out as a licensed commons, so the ML edge and the step-up from buying the right both disappear in a small, declining market.

scored.name: TuskLease (permafrost mammoth ivory and Pleistocene skulls on private Alaskan and Yukon land)
scored.one_line: Leases fossil-recovery rights on Alaska Native corporation and private parcels where thawing riverbanks expose Pleistocene bone beds. ML on time-series imagery of bank erosion and permafrost slumping times recovery, and tusks and skulls sell into the legal fossil-ivory and natural-history market.
scored.unproven_right: Surface fossil-recovery leases from Native corporations and private owners. US mammoth ivory sale is legal federally but banned in some states, such as NY, NJ and CA, which limits the market.
scored.proving_step: An ML change-detection model finds bank retreat and thaw slumps, so collectors are on site the season a deposit is exposed. Proof is a riverbank walk or float trip that recovers tusks, at about $10-20k per season.
scored.proven_buyer: Ivory carvers and dealers, natural-history auction houses and decor collectors. Woolly rhino and saber-tooth skulls reach $50k-$250k, but the buyer pool is fragmented.
scored.public_data: Sentinel-2 and Landsat time series, ArcticDEM strip DEMs, USGS permafrost maps, scanned 1930s-50s AMNH and Frick placer-mine bone collection field notes, and Alaska DNR land status.
scored.rough_step_up: Leases at about $1-5/acre yield $50k-$1M per productive bank-mile, roughly 10^2-10^3x. Bans in some states, ethics and the optics of ivory hold it back.
scored.frame: The rung would be "lease a riverbank parcel and recover the tusks it gives up." There is no proven right to sell at the end of it. You harvest a one-off commodity, and recovery (float trips, crew, digging frozen bank, conservation, logistics) is about 50-60% of the work in my estimate, with discovery the rest. Discovery is also partly solved already: locals and Native shareholders know which eroding banks produce bone. Buyers are fragmented carvers, knife-handle makers and decor collectors, not a capitalised developer paying for a proven right. Not hard-excluded, since this is fossil collecting rather than mineral exploration, but it is placer-style surface recovery in spirit.
scored.step_up: No land or right step-up exists, because what you sell is the material and the parcel is not worth more afterwards. Unproven lease: the candidate's $1-5/acre, which I could not verify. Output: Anchorage wholesale mammoth ivory is about $25-125/lb (KTUU; Alaska's News Source), so a 50-100 lb tusk is worth roughly $1.5k-12k (my estimate). Siberian field prices are $300-460/kg, after a CITES-reported peak of $1,900/kg in 2014. Woolly rhino skulls sell for $5-20k at auction (Tennants £4,200; Bruneau about $20,480), and only one estimate reached £60-100k. Woolly rhino is also essentially absent from Alaska and Yukon, so the $50-250k skull figure in the pitch does not apply there. The claimed $50k-$1M per productive bank-mile is unsupported. A realistic return is a few to tens of x on a tiny base, from a resource that is used up once collected.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate puts the proving cost at $10-20k per season. On known eroding banks the base hit rate is fairly high (my estimate), since locals regularly find tusks on beaches and banks (Shaktoolik, Scripps reports). The lever is capped at about 1/base rate, maybe 2-5x, and it applies to a cheap step. Saving 10x on $15k is not a meaningful capex lever. Change detection from Sentinel-2 and ArcticDEM tells you when a bank is eroding, not whether bone is in it.
scored.data: The core signal (Sentinel-2, Landsat, ArcticDEM, USGS permafrost maps) is public and already legible. Anyone can run bank-retreat change detection, and permafrost researchers already do. Only the scanned 1930s-50s AMNH and Frick field notes are illegible, and they point to old placer-mine districts that are already known. No "outcome field" exists, but no hidden outcome exists either: where bone erodes is common local knowledge.
scored.right_bought: The rights could be bought on paper: collecting on private and Native corporation land is legal with permission, while public land needs a permit (BLM). But the owners are not blind to the value. Native corporation shareholders and village residents already collect and sell fossil ivory as a traditional income source, so there is no information asymmetry to buy into cheaply. Leasing ivory-producing land from Native corporations so an outsider can harvest it also carries serious political and ethical friction.
scored.buyer: Fragmented and uncapitalised: Anchorage and Fairbanks wholesalers, carvers, knife and cue makers, and Heritage-style natural-history auctions. The US market is shrinking under state bans that cover mammoth ivory (NY, NJ, CA, HI, NV, IL, possibly WA). The world market is flooded with Siberian supply: Yakutia produces about 70-100 t/yr, with an estimated 30-40 t moving through the shadow market. At about $300-500/kg the global wholesale market is roughly $30-50M/yr (my estimate).
scored.ladder: The ladder is very short: carving, finished goods and retail, all inside a niche luxury market of roughly $30-50M/yr wholesale that is being legislated down. There is no path to a large company and no chain above it that compounds.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no step-up to realise and no capitalised buyer. You are harvesting a finite, low-value commodity of about $25-125/lb into a market of roughly $30-50M/yr that Siberian supply floods and US state bans keep shrinking. The discovery signal (eroding banks) is public, legible and already known to the landowners, so ML adds little and the rights carry no information discount.
scored.one_line_reason: This is commodity fossil-ivory harvesting with cheap, already-high-hit-rate recovery, legible satellite data, owners who already know their banks produce ivory, and a tiny, shrinking, fragmented market with no 10^3 jump in what a proven right is worth.

scored.name: QuietValley (terrain-shielded radio-quiet land for large radio arrays and RF-sensitive facilities)
scored.one_line: Next-generation arrays (DSA-2000, ngVLA, SKA-scale private arrays) and RF-sensitive industry (quantum and spectrum-test ranges) need large tracts in rare natural terrain bowls shielded from satellite and terrestrial RF. ML on public spectrum and terrain data finds them. Option the land, prove the RF quietness with a portable spectrum survey, and sell or lease the certified tract.
scored.unproven_right: Options on large (1,000-10,000 acre) ranch tracts in terrain-shielded basins (Nevada, Utah, New Mexico), bought at grazing prices.
scored.proving_step: A 1-3 month calibrated RFI spectrum survey across bands (~$20-50k). Physically trivial.
scored.proven_buyer: Observatory consortia (Caltech DSA-2000, NRAO ngVLA, private SETI and astronomy funders) and spectrum-test-range operators.
scored.public_data: FCC ULS and antenna structure registration (legible for transmitters, but the shielding outcome is not); USGS 3DEP terrain; NTIA spectrum surveys; scanned historical NRAO site-selection reports. Satellite RFI is not summarised anywhere.
scored.rough_step_up: About 3-20x. Buyers are poorly capitalised, grant-funded institutions and few. Included as a non-obvious, low-scoring option: C2 about 2, C1 has a weak buyer, and C5 is weak.
scored.frame: The rung would be "option a ranch, certify that it is RF-quiet, sell or lease it". On paper, discovery and proving are about 90% of that rung, since a spectrum survey is physically trivial. But nobody buys that rung's output on its own. Observatories do their own site selection as part of the project. DSA-2000 built its own mobile RFI monitoring station and ran its own surveys across candidate valleys: Big Smoky, then Hot Creek, Monitor, and Spring Valley near Ely. So the rung is captive to the buyer, not a market. Radio-quietness is also only one of the buyer's constraints. DSA needs a flat 19 x 15 km plain, plus fiber, power, water, environmental clearance and BLM permitting, which narrows the frame further.
scored.step_up: There is no evidence of a real step-up. Unproven land is Nevada rangeland. One 2025 Humboldt County assessor record shows about $207/acre on 372 acres, and Acretrader's blended farmland figure is about $2,675/acre with an unclear date. Proven land: there is no public record of any observatory paying a premium for certified quiet land. Large arrays usually sit on federal BLM or NSF land, or on leases and easements at near-agricultural rates. The VLA and the planned ngVLA core on the Plains of San Agustin are an example. My estimate is at most 1.5-3x over grazing value, through a lease or a hold-up premium. A single holdout parcel might extract more, but that is hold-up value, not proving value. That gives C2 = 1.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving attempt is cheap and its base hit rate is high. My estimate is $20-50k per survey (the candidate's own figure, unverified). Remote Great Basin valleys with no cell towers are quiet by default: Monitor Valley has under 50 people and 0 cell towers, per the DSA site slides. Satellite RFI is roughly uniform across all sites, so terrain shielding barely changes it. My estimate is a base hit rate of 30-60% among candidate valleys picked from public FCC tower data. That caps ML leverage at about 2-3x, on a cost that is already trivial next to a $200M+ array. That gives C3 = 1.
scored.data: The signal is mostly legible already. FCC ULS and ASR transmitter locations plus USGS 3DEP terrain give standard propagation and shielding models (ITU-R P.452 style), and observatories run these routinely. Satellite RFI is not site-specific, so there is no hidden local signal for ML to extract. The data edge is low. On the right itself: about 80% of Nevada is federal land, so the best valleys are BLM land and cannot be optioned from a ranch owner at all. The private parcels inside them are often small inholdings. Ranch options can be bought, but the seller is not giving up hidden value. That gives C4 = 1.
scored.right_bought: Purchase options on private ranch tracts at grazing prices (about $200-2,700/acre; the two sources above). Many target valleys are mostly BLM land, which cannot be bought; there you would apply for a right-of-way, first come first served. That undercuts the "bought cheaply from owners who cannot read the data" thesis.
scored.buyer: Grant-funded observatory projects (Caltech DSA-2000, NRAO/NSF ngVLA, SKA-scale efforts) arrive about once a decade per region, and each already picks its own site in-house. Secondary buyers would be spectrum-test-range and quantum-facility operators, but they are few and their need for quiet is modest. There is no deep pool of capitalised buyers paying 10^3x.
scored.ladder: The ladder above is weak. The next rungs would be hosting or operating the array, or running a radio-quiet-zone landlord business, both small and grant-dependent markets. There is no path toward a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no step-up and no independent buyer. Radio-quiet land is common in the Great Basin and much of it is BLM land. The few buyers run their own cheap RFI surveys (DSA-2000 built its own mobile RFI station), and they pay close to agricultural land value. Proving the land does not move its price by 10^3-10^4x; it moves it by perhaps 1-3x.
scored.one_line_reason: A cheap, high-hit-rate survey on land that is mostly public and abundant, sold to a handful of grant-funded buyers who do their own siting: no 10^4 jump, no ML leverage, no ladder.

scored.name: Warbird Wrecks (aircraft buried in ice, sand and lakes)
scored.one_line: Uses declassified CORONA/KH-9, Landsat glacier-retreat time series and lake-shoreline change detection to locate WWII and early Cold War aircraft that have emerged from or settled into glaciers, deserts and lakes. It buys title from legal owners where title is transferable and sells unrestored 'projects' to warbird collectors.
scored.unproven_right: Title or salvage rights from governments and estates that sell them: ex-civil aircraft, some Soviet types sold through Russian regional authorities, Greenland and Canadian ice-locked civilian aircraft, and private-land lake wrecks. US Navy and RAF wrecks are excluded because those states retain title.
scored.proving_step: An ML-ranked site check by drone, magnetometer or side-scan sonar, about $10-50k. Proof means locating and identifying the airframe and its condition.
scored.proven_buyer: Warbird collectors and foundations (Flying Heritage, Collings, private billionaires), which pay $0.2-2M for rare unrestored projects. The full value ($5-15M) comes after restoration, and restoration is a bespoke build, which is a failure mode like the geothermal counter-example.
scored.public_data: USGS declassified satellite film, the Landsat glacier archive, scanned national accident and loss reports (Aviation Archaeology, MACR files) and digitised squadron diaries. Last known positions are recorded, but where the wreck lies now is hidden by ice and sediment.
scored.rough_step_up: $10-50k of rights becomes a $0.2-2M project, about 10-100x at the proof stage. Legal title is messy. This is a weaker candidate.
scored.frame: No clean rung where discovery is 80% or more of the work. A located but unrecovered wreck under ice, sand or a lake does not trade on its own: collectors buy airframes that have been recovered and shipped. Recovery is a heavy physical job. Glacier Girl's 1992 recovery from about 80 m of Greenland ice cost about $650-700k by forum accounts, and the full total including restoration has been put at about $10M. My estimate is that discovery is 10-30% of the work in the smallest sellable rung (a recovered, unrestored project), and under 5% of the restored value. This is the geothermal counter-example again: the physical step dominates.
scored.step_up: Unproven: rights are often nominal or ambiguous, roughly $0-50k (my estimate; recoverers like Jim Pearce typically got wrecks for the cost of permits and expedition). Proven and recovered: the P-39Q 44-2911, pulled from Lake Mart-Yavr after a fisherman spotted it in 2004, was listed unrestored at $445k in 2005 and sold to the Ira G. Ross museum for $400k in 2009 (HistoryNet). Restored: Glacier Girl was rumoured at $7-10M+ (WIX forum, unverified). The ratio of right price to project price is about 10-100x, but only after recovery spending of $100k-$700k, so the net multiple on capital at risk is about 1-5x. My estimate is 2-3x for a typical project.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base rate of finding a target given its last known position is moderate to high, not low. Accident reports, MACRs and Pacific Wrecks already give positions, and many famous finds were spotted by locals (the Mart-Yavr P-39 was found by a fisherman). Glacier Girl took about 10 years of expeditions, but that was a recovery problem, not a search problem. A site check costs about $10-50k (the candidate's own figure, plausible). Recovery is about $0.1-0.7M per airframe and ML does not touch it. My estimate is that a proving check succeeds 20-50% of the time, so the lever is at most 1/base rate, about 2-5x, applied to the smaller cost line.
scored.data: USGS declassified CORONA/KH-9, Landsat glacier time series and MACR/accident scans are public and partly illegible, so there is some ML edge in tracking glacier flow and shoreline change. However, the outcome is often already summarised in legible enthusiast databases: Pacific Wrecks, Aviation Archaeology, Goodall's warbird directories and WIX threads catalogue wreck locations and status. Last known position plus glacier-flow physics gets most of the way without ML.
scored.right_bought: Mostly cannot be bought cleanly. Military wrecks generally stay the property of the state: the US under the Sunken Military Craft Act, the UK under the Protection of Military Remains Act, and German and Japanese claims. Russian export depends on approval; one WIX forum account says a Brewster Buffalo needed Yeltsin's personal sign-off to leave Russia, and since 2022 sanctions have effectively closed the route. Greenland and Canada have heritage permit regimes. Ex-civil and private-land lake wrecks can be bought, but they are the low-value types. Owners do not 'fail to read the data': title is unclear and disputed rather than mispriced.
scored.buyer: Warbird collectors and museums such as Flying Heritage, Collings, Ira G. Ross and private billionaires. The buyer pool is tiny, about tens of serious buyers worldwide, and the volume of rare unrestored projects is probably tens per year at $0.2-2M (my estimate). The total addressable market is roughly $10-50M a year. Incumbents already exist: Jim Pearce, the Lost Squadron/Greenland Expedition Society, Pacific Wrecks, and Russian and Finnish recovery teams.
scored.ladder: Recovery leads to restoration (a bespoke build, $1-10M+ and 3-10 years per airframe), then to airshow operation or museum ownership. Each rung is a craft business with a fixed, shrinking supply of historic airframes. There is no path to a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: Finding the wreck is not the bottleneck. Clear title and the physical recovery and restoration are. A located wreck has no buyer until someone spends $0.1-0.7M digging it out, and the end market is a tiny, capped collector niche.
scored.one_line_reason: Weak candidate. The proving step does not create a sellable asset, because recovery and restoration dominate the cost and value. Title is mostly retained by states or blocked by sanctions, wreck positions are largely catalogued by enthusiasts, and the market is about tens of millions a year with no ladder.

scored.name: Heat-Tolerant Livestock Allele Scouting
scored.one_line: Find commodity-priced animals that carry rare high-value alleles (for example SLICK heat tolerance), buy them at market price, confirm with a genotype test, and sell the genetics rights to breeding companies.
scored.unproven_right: Ownership of individual animals bought at commodity prices
scored.proving_step: SNP genotype test, about $30-50, binary
scored.proven_buyer: Genus/ABS, Select Sires, tropical breeding programs
scored.public_data: 1000 Bull Genomes summaries, published allele-frequency studies. Coverage is thin, so this is weak on C4.
scored.frame: The rung is "buy an animal, genotype it, sell its genetics rights." Discovery takes almost none of the work inside it. The test is a commodity: SLICK1 can be typed with a public KASP assay (UF Hansen Lab), and a full genomic panel costs about $43 (Zoetis Clarifide Plus, Holstein, US list price). The real work is everything after the test: raising and housing a bull, collecting and freezing semen, progeny or genomic evaluation, and marketing. For an AI stud, an animal's value comes from its overall genomic merit index (NM$, BPI), not from one allele. Genetics Australia sells its SLICK bulls (HONDA P, ICEMAN PP) on BPI. Discovery is therefore about 5-10% of the work in this rung (my estimate), the reverse of the Terranox pattern. Breeding companies (Genus/ABS, Select Sires) do have capital, but they get SLICK by doing their own introgression from Senepol, not by buying lucky carriers.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a commodity Holstein bull calf is worth roughly $100-500, or a beef or crossbred cull animal is priced by the pound (my estimate; my search found no published AI-stud purchase prices). Proven: a SLICK carrier with ordinary genomic merit is perhaps worth $1k-10k as a niche tropical sire, my estimate. Semen from an average-merit sire sells for about $15-30 a straw, and SLICK Senepol and SLICK Holstein semen is already sold openly. That is about 3-30x at best, and only when merit is also high. The SLICK allele by itself does not make an animal a 10^3x asset, because it is not scarce: it is close to fixed in Senepol, Carora and Romosinuano cattle.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Testing is cheap: about $30-50 per animal (Clarifide Plus $43; a SLICK1 KASP assay is likely under $20, my estimate). So there is no expensive, mostly failing proving step for ML to cheapen. The base hit rate is bimodal, which removes the lever entirely. In commodity Holsteins outside known introgression pedigrees, SLICK frequency is effectively 0, so no model can find carriers that are not there. In tropical Criollo and Senepol-derived herds the allele is common, and the slick coat can be seen by eye. The study frequency of 0.247 comes from deliberate SLICK1 matings (Uludag/UF inheritance study), not from random herds. Even with a perfect model, total testing cost per hit stays at a few hundred dollars, so there is no meaningful capex to cut.
scored.data: The outcome is already legible. SLICK is a dominant, visible phenotype: a short, sleek hair coat that a farmer can see. It is also traceable in published pedigrees (Senepol ancestry, introgression lines from UF/ARS and Genetics Australia) and in the CDCB and breed-association genomic databases where elite animals are genotyped. The public sources the candidate names (1000 Bull Genomes summaries, allele-frequency papers) are small and aggregated. They are not a large illegible corpus that points to individual animals. The right cannot be captured either: the allele is a natural variant with no exclusivity, and anyone can buy Senepol semen and introgress it. Owners can read the signal (the coat) just as well as an ML model can, so they would not sell a carrier at commodity price.
scored.right_bought: Yes, individual animals can be bought at market price. But a single animal does not give you exclusive rights to the trait. The allele is freely available through existing SLICK semen lines, so owning a carrier gives no moat and no scarcity premium.
scored.buyer: In principle Genus/ABS, Select Sires, STgenetics, Genetics Australia, and tropical dairy programs in Brazil, India and the Caribbean. In practice they already run SLICK introgression in-house (Holstein x Senepol backcrossing since the 2000s with UF and USDA-ARS) and choose sires on genomic merit. They have little reason to pay a premium to an outside scout for a random carrier.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are a sire stud, a semen and embryo business, a proprietary heat-tolerant breed line, and possibly a gene-edited line. Acceligen/Recombinetics already pursued PRLR-edited SLICK cattle with FDA low-risk status in 2022, and editing makes scouting for natural carriers unnecessary. The global bovine genetics market is roughly $5-6B, and Genus plc's market cap is roughly $1.5-2B (my estimates). That market is real but bounded, and incumbents with editing and genomics already hold the higher rungs.
scored.fatal_flaw: The signal is neither hidden nor scarce. SLICK is a visible, dominant coat phenotype, and it is nearly fixed in the source breeds (Senepol, Criollo). In commodity Holsteins it is effectively absent outside documented introgression pedigrees. Breeders already introgress it at will through openly sold semen, and gene editing (Acceligen PRLR edit) can create it directly. There is no 10^3x step-up for a single allele carrier, and ML has nothing illegible to extract. The proving test also costs about $40, so there is no discovery capex to cut.
scored.one_line_reason: Fails. The allele is either absent or visible and freely available. Testing costs about $40, so ML has nothing to cheapen. A carrier is worth about 10x at most, and only when its overall genomic merit is also high. Incumbents and gene editing already supply the trait.

scored.name: QuietGround: seismic-quiet land banking for gravitational-wave and precision sites
scored.one_line: Option the land at the few sites that are truly seismically and anthropogenically quiet, found with ML over public broadband noise archives. Next-generation detectors (Cosmic Explorer needs a ~40 km L of flat, quiet land), deep-underground physics labs and precision fabs pick sites from exactly this kind of data. The plan is to own the options before the consortium does.
scored.unproven_right: Purchase options on rangeland at about $500-2,000/acre in candidate corridors.
scored.proving_step: ML on EarthScope Transportable Array and IRIS station PSDs, plus microseism modelling and a cheap temporary nodal-seismometer deployment.
scored.proven_buyer: NSF/DOE-funded detector consortia (Cosmic Explorer), national labs and hyperscale or fab developers that need vibration-quiet ground.
scored.public_data: EarthScope/IRIS Transportable Array continuous waveforms and PSD/PDF noise products (MUSTANG), USGS NSHM, Sentinel-1 InSAR ground stability (EGMS/OPERA).
scored.rough_step_up: Optioned land sold to a federal project at about 2-5x. Step-up is weak (<10x), there are very few buyers and they can take land by negotiation or condemnation. Included as an honest weak entry.
scored.frame: The rung is "option quiet rangeland and sell it to a detector, lab or fab developer". Discovery could be 80%+ of the work inside that rung, because the physical step (a nodal-seismometer survey, my estimate $20-100k per corridor) is cheap. The problem is that the rung is barely sellable. Seismic quiet is one of many site criteria. Cosmic Explorer site work also weighs flatness over about 40 km, federal or state land availability, water, power, workforce, tribal and environmental review, and political support. Fabs and hyperscalers choose on power, water, labour and subsidies, and they handle vibration with isolated foundations. So the "proven quiet" label does not decide a sale, and the buyer does not buy the output of this rung as a discrete product.
scored.step_up: Unproven: rangeland at about $500-2,000/acre. This is from my memory of USDA NASS Land Values (US pasture averages about $1,800/acre, with Mountain-region pasture lower); I could not verify it this session. Proven: there is no real "proven quiet land" market. A federal project buys under the Uniform Relocation Act at appraised fair market value, or by condemnation, so the realised step-up is about 1-2x. The candidate's own 2-5x is optimistic (my estimate). Option premiums (perhaps 5-10% of price) could give a few-x return on the option itself, but only if the consortium picks your exact parcels. Nowhere near 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive, mostly-failing proving step to improve. Quiet ground is cheap to check directly: MUSTANG PSDs are free and pre-computed, and a temporary nodal survey costs about $20-100k (my estimate, not sourced). Base "hit rate" is not low in the Terranox sense. Large areas of the Great Basin and Great Plains are quiet, and the binding constraint is buyer selection, not finding quiet. ML might cut a cheap survey cost marginally. The lever is roughly 1-2x at most.
scored.data: The data is public but already legible. IRIS/EarthScope MUSTANG publishes processed PSD/PDF noise metrics per station, which is effectively the answer in a ready-made field. The USGS NSHM hazard grids and the OPERA/EGMS InSAR displacement products are also processed and legible. The Cosmic Explorer project and LIGO site teams already run exactly this analysis in public, and incumbents (the consortium itself, national labs, fab site-selection consultants) do extract it. There is little illegible-data edge.
scored.right_bought: Rangeland options can be bought cheaply from ranchers, so this part works. But the buyer can avoid you. Federal projects can condemn land, choose federal or state land instead (LIGO Hanford sits on DOE land), or move the 40 km arms a few km to skip a held-out parcel. Holding land against a federal science project also brings political and reputational backlash. The right is buyable but gives no capture.
scored.buyer: There are almost no buyers. Cosmic Explorer plans one or two US sites over about 20 years and is not yet funded for construction. DUSEL-type underground labs need underground space (for example SURF), not rangeland. Fabs and hyperscalers are capitalised but do not pay a premium for seismic quiet. The buyer is a monopsony with condemnation power and appraisal-based pricing, and "raw dollars work for everyone" fails.
scored.ladder: Above the rung are only weak steps: build or lease facility infrastructure, or develop vibration-quiet industrial parks. None of these is a trillion-dollar chain. A quiet-site developer for precision manufacturing is a niche real-estate business, and the gravitational-wave market is one or two projects in total.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no step-up and no capturable buyer. The only buyer who truly needs quiet land is a single, slow, federally funded project. It pays appraised fair market value, can condemn land or reroute around a holdout, and picks sites mostly on criteria other than noise. Meanwhile the noise signal is already published in processed, legible form by MUSTANG.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a weak entry. The step-up is about 1-2x (2-5x at best), the noise data is already summarised in legible MUSTANG PSD products, the proving step is cheap and not failure-prone, and the one real buyer is a monopsony with condemnation power, so there is no 10^4 jump to capture.
sources: The web search budget was used up on the first query, so no live sources were retrieved this session. All figures are from memory or are marked as my estimates.
From memory: USDA NASS Land Values summary (US pasture about $1,800/acre in 2024; Mountain region lower)
From memory: IRIS/EarthScope MUSTANG noise PSD/PDF metrics (service.iris.edu/mustang)
From memory: Cosmic Explorer Horizon Study and site-evaluation work (cosmicexplorer.org), which weighs seismic, topographic, environmental and land-availability criteria
From memory: the Uniform Relocation Assistance and Real Property Acquisition Policies Act (federal acquisition at appraised fair market value; eminent domain)
From memory: LIGO Hanford sits on DOE Hanford Site land

scored.name: Satellite Biocovers: methanotroph consortia from landfills that under-emit methane
scored.one_line: Compares satellite and airborne methane plumes (TROPOMI, Carbon Mapper, MethaneSAT) with each landfill's reported generation model to find sites emitting far less methane than predicted. Buys the cover-soil culture rights, proves high-rate methanotrophs in serum-bottle assays, and sells them as biocover or gas-fermentation strains.
scored.unproven_right: Rights to cover-soil samples and derived strains from smaller municipal or private landfill owners, at $1-5k.
scored.proving_step: Serum-bottle methane oxidation rate assays at landfill-gas concentrations and temperatures, with isolation of top consortia. About $2-5k. True biological anomalies are rare compared with gas-collection and reporting artefacts.
scored.proven_buyer: WM and Republic (facing EPA landfill methane rules and seeking offsets), carbon-credit developers, and gas-fermentation firms (Calysta, Unibio, Mango Materials) that want robust methanotrophs.
scored.public_data: EPA GHGRP Subpart HH filings, the EPA LMOP database, Carbon Mapper and TROPOMI plume data (huge, illegible), and state Title V landfill reports (scanned).
scored.rough_step_up: $3k to $0.1-2M: about 10^2-10^3. Lower ceiling and weaker C2. Included as a stretch.
