verified.name: Captive Scent (natural odorant discovery from public GC-MS spectra)
verified.one_line: Mine public GC-MS and NMR spectra of plant, fungal and insect volatiles for unassigned peaks whose predicted structure is a high-impact odorant (musk, ambergris, sandalwood). Make a few mg and run an odour panel. File composition-of-use IP and sell the captive molecule to a fragrance house, which pays $5-50M for a patented captive.
verified.unproven_right: The right to the unassigned molecule is not bought but filed. Weak point: there is no cheap purchase from an owner. The only purchasable variant is buying lapsed odorant patent families from defunct fine-chemical firms.
verified.proving_step: Synthesis of 10-100 mg (~$10-30k CRO) plus a trained odour panel and threshold measurement; this takes weeks. Nature hides whether a molecule smells, and the odour-threshold outcome is in no database.
verified.proven_buyer: Givaudan, dsm-firmenich, IFF and Symrise, which pay heavily for captives (e.g., Ambrox-class and musk captives worth hundreds of millions a year in compound sales)
verified.public_data: MassBank, NIST/Wiley GC-MS literature spectra, the Pherobase, decades of scanned Flavour & Fragrance Journal and Perfumer & Flavorist chromatograms with unassigned peaks, and GNPS
verified.rough_step_up: ~$30k proof to $5-50M (~10^3x). The C4 'bought right' criterion fails, because the IP is filed rather than bought. Ladder: the molecule, then biocatalytic manufacture, then ingredient supply, then a fragrance-house-scale ingredients company.
verified.frame: The rung is "a novel odorant with a filed patent and panel data, licensed exclusively to a fragrance house". Inside that rung, discovery (which structure smells, and how strongly) is roughly 70-85% of the work; synthesising a few mg and running a panel is cheap (my estimate: $10-30k). The buyer is real and capitalised: Osmo launched an auction in June 2026 of exclusive perpetual licences to 10 captives, open to houses and chemical makers. But buyers know a lot of work remains after the rung. Scale-up process development is the first part (Givaudan tried 19 routes before Pomarose worked), followed by REACH/IFRA toxicology and stability/performance in base, before the molecule earns money. That discounts what the rung is worth, and discovery is not cleanly 80%+ of what the buyer pays for.
verified.step_up: Unproven: about $0 as an asset, plus about $20-50k for filing and synthesis (my estimate). Proven: no public price exists. I found no Osmo auction results or licence fees, and no disclosed royalty or sales numbers for Ambrox, Helvetolide or Javanol. The candidate's $5-50M per captive is unsourced. My estimate for an unscaled, untox'd odorant licence is $0.5-5M upfront plus royalties. That is about 10-100x on the cost of proving, or ~10^2-10^3 only if you assume the top of the range. The lift is also not "immediate on a hit": a binding bid needs a 12-week diligence and sampling period.
verified.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: 0.25% of molecules made and tested become commercially interesting. This is Osmo's own figure (Jan 2026 press release) and is not independently verified. Osmo claims its AI gives about 10x the hit rate and 5-10x better discovery cost efficiency. Cost per attempt: about $10-30k for CRO synthesis of 10-100 mg plus a panel (my estimate, matching the candidate). Traditional time to a captive is 7-10 years (Osmo blog). The lever is large; 1/base rate allows up to ~400x. But an AI incumbent with $130M raised has already taken the ~10x gain.
verified.data: Public and illegible, partly: MassBank, GNPS, Pherobase and scanned Flavour & Fragrance Journal / Perfumer & Flavorist chromatograms. Odour threshold and quality are in no structured field, so the outcome is not written down legibly, which is a point in its favour. But the signal is not uniquely unextracted. Fragrance houses have run headspace and natural-product odorant programmes for decades (Givaudan ScentTrek; GC-olfactometry is standard). Osmo trains odour-prediction models on structure and generates candidates de novo, so it does not need natural-product spectra at all. Also, an unassigned peak usually gives too little information to fix the structure (stereochemistry, which drives odour, is especially ambiguous), so the "predicted structure" step is weak.
verified.right_bought: This fails. Nothing is bought. The IP is filed first-come, and for this candidate's own category it is weak. Naturally occurring compounds cannot be patented as compositions in the US, and a molecule found in nature fails novelty (Chemistry in Australia, Patenting opportunities in the fragrance industry, 2020). So a natural odorant found from published spectra gets only use or process claims. Competitors could make the nature-identical molecule by another route, and the published spectrum itself may be prior art. The only purchasable version, lapsed odorant patent families, has no step-up: once lapsed, the molecule is in the public domain.
verified.buyer: Givaudan, dsm-firmenich, IFF and Symrise, plus chemical makers. Osmo's 2026 auction is the first open market for captive licences, so the buyer class exists. No clearing prices are public.
verified.ladder: The rungs are: molecule licence, then biocatalytic or chemical manufacture, then supply of the ingredient, then a full ingredients house, then finished fragrance. This is plausible, and Osmo is trying it now (a manufacturing site in Elizabeth, NJ). The whole flavour and fragrance market is about $30B a year: big, but not a trillion-dollar chain. A new entrant is also climbing behind a better-funded AI incumbent.
verified.fatal_flaw: There is no defensible owned asset. Natural odorants found in public spectra are generally unpatentable as compositions (natural products in the US) and may be anticipated by the publication itself. So the "captive" is a weak use patent, not a cheaply bought right. And Osmo ($130M raised) already owns ML odorant discovery using synthetic novel scaffolds, which avoids that patent problem.
verified.one_line_reason: The hit rate is low (0.25%) and there is a real buyer class, but the right is filed rather than bought and naturally occurring molecules are barely patentable. The proven price is unverified, and Osmo already occupies the ML-discovery rung with patentable synthetic molecules.

Search budget note: the shared WebSearch budget for this turn was used up before my first query, so this check rests on direct fetches of known URLs. Several of those fetches also failed (Rutland Herald 429, Chemistry Australia 503, Chemistry World 405, Osmo blog 404). The evidence is thin, so the finalist's key claim stays unsupported.

(1) Proven price is unsourced. No public clearing price exists for any licence to an odorant molecule. Cosmetics Business on the Osmo auction (June 2026): the terms are 'exclusive, perpetual licenses' sold by 'open, competitive auction', with samples for 'target buyers who have the infrastructure to deploy these ingredients broadly'. No reserve, bid, fee or royalty figure is disclosed. Premium Beauty News on Osmo's $70M round ($130M total): 'no revenue, licensing, pricing, hit-rate, or captive-value figures, and no named customer deals.' Avery Gilbert's Substack: Osmo had 5 patent applications published in 2025 and 0 granted, and its 10x success-rate claim 'remains undocumented'. Revenue still depends on passing tox and regulatory review, on cheap manufacture, and on outperforming existing materials. So the $5-50M per captive comes from no transaction.

(2) The buyer is not proven to pay at once. Historically, houses develop captives in-house. Osmo's auction is billed as 'first-of-its-kind', which means there was no prior open market for buying a captive licence. Its results are not public. A binding bid comes after sampling and diligence. Scale-up, REACH/IFRA toxicology and in-base stability all sit on the buyer's side after the rung. That pushes the price paid for an un-tox'd, unscaled molecule well below the value of a commercial captive. My estimate is $0.1-2M upfront plus contingent royalties.

(3) Step-up: proof costs about $20-50k. On a realistic $0.1-2M upfront, that is about 5-100x and not immediate. That is near or below the ~30x refutation threshold, far from 10^3-10^4. 10^3 requires assuming the $5-50M figure, which no evidence supports.

(4) Market size: houses launch only a handful of new captive molecules a year industry-wide (single digits to low tens; my recollection, not verified this session). Before Osmo's 2026 auction, external licence transactions were essentially zero per year, against Terranox's continuous land market.

(5) The right is not bought and is weak. Naturally occurring compounds generally fail novelty or patentable-subject-matter tests as compositions, and a published spectrum can be prior art. That leaves only use or process claims, which lowers any buyer's willingness to pay further. Osmo files 50-250 synthetic molecules per patent, which squeezes a natural-product entrant out of the patentable space.
verifiers.killer: No real transaction shows a buyer paying millions for an unscaled, un-tox'd odorant licence. Osmo's 2026 auction is the first open market of its kind and its clearing prices are undisclosed, so the $5-50M 'proven' value is invented. Realistic upfront value is about $0.1-2M on a $20-50k proof, roughly 5-100x, delayed by diligence, tox and scale-up. The 'right' is a weak use patent on a natural molecule, which may be anticipated by the very spectrum it was found in, rather than a bought asset. Historically almost no licence transactions per year.

Search note: the shared web-search budget for this turn was already used up (200 calls), so I could run no new searches. I fetched two sources directly. The cosmeticsbusiness.com article on the Osmo auction is paywalled. It confirms only three things: exclusive perpetual licences to 10 molecules, an auction open to "all industry players", and Osmo's own claim of a 10x higher success rate and 5-10x better cost efficiency. It gives no prices, and that claim is not independently checked. The chemaust.raci.org.au article on patenting returned HTTP 503. Everything below therefore comes from the finalist's own sources plus established domain knowledge. The unverified points are flagged.

Data lens, point by point:

(1) The outcome is already in legible form, which kills the "illegible" claim. For natural volatiles, the standard method for decades has been GC-olfactometry (GC-O) and AEDA dilution analysis. A human sniffs the GC effluent and records an odour descriptor and potency (the FD factor) against a retention index. That includes peaks that are still unidentified, typically reported as "unknown, musky, RI 1xxx". Published GC-O papers therefore already flag which peaks smell and how strongly. That is the exact outcome the finalist says no database holds. Odour thresholds and descriptors for known compounds are also compiled in legible references: the van Gemert odour-threshold compilations, the Leffingwell databases, Flavornet and TNO's Volatile Compounds in Food database. This matches the prior-hunt pattern in which the answer is already written into a field.

(2) The proving step is not mainly what nature hides. The binding constraint is structure elucidation of the unassigned peak. Library-free structure prediction from EI GC-MS spectra is weak, and stereochemistry, which largely determines musk, ambergris and sandalwood odour, is invisible to EI-MS. Each candidate therefore needs isolation or several stereoisomer syntheses, not one $10-30k synthesis. The real cost per attempt is a multiple of that, and many "hits" turn out to be known compounds.

(3) The space is occupied. Fragrance houses run natural-odorant mining in-house: Givaudan ScentTrek headspace, and standard GC-O programmes at Givaudan, dsm-firmenich, IFF and Symrise. Firmenich, for example, has a long history of trace-impact-compound work such as rotundone. On the AI side, Osmo has raised about $130M, files many novel-ingredient patents and is auctioning captives. Symrise has used IBM's Philyra, and the houses have their own AI tools (Givaudan Carto, for example). The ML hit-rate gain is being captured by players with synthetic, patentable scaffolds.

(4) Commercial captives are overwhelmingly synthetic or semi-synthetic. Helvetolide and Javanol are synthetic, and Ambrox is semi-synthetic from sclareol. Naturally occurring molecules fail novelty and, in the US, product-of-nature eligibility. The published spectrum may itself be prior art. What remains are use and process patents, so there is no owned, cheaply bought right. That is a fail on the rubric's "bought, not filed" test.

(5) The base hit rate of 0.25% is Osmo's own unverified figure, and it applies to de novo molecules, not to GC-O-pre-screened natural peaks. Pre-screened peaks already have a much higher prior of smelling, so the ML lever over existing GC-O practice is small.

(6) The step-up is unsourced. No licence prices are public, and the upfront value of an unscaled, untox'd odorant is likely $0.5-5M. That is about 10-100x, not 10^3.
verifiers.killer: The supposedly hidden outcome (does this peak smell, and how strongly?) is already measured and published. GC-olfactometry and AEDA papers record odour descriptors and potency even for unidentified peaks, and threshold compilations (van Gemert, Leffingwell, VCF) cover known compounds. On top of that, a natural molecule found in public spectra is unpatentable as a composition and probably anticipated by the publication itself, so there is no owned asset to sell. The ML-discovery rung is meanwhile occupied by Osmo ($130M raised, patentable synthetic scaffolds) and by the fragrance houses' own headspace, GC-O and AI programmes.

verifiers.evidence:
Limits on this check: the shared WebSearch budget was already used up when this agent started, so I ran no new searches. Of two WebFetch attempts, the Chemistry in Australia patent article returned HTTP 503 and Cosmetics Business returned only a paywalled extract. The verdict therefore rests on the finalist's own cited evidence, the readable Cosmetics Business extract and established patent law. The key claim (the unproven right can be bought) is not supported, and the finalist concedes this itself.

(1) RIGHT IS NOT BOUGHT, IT IS FILED. Nothing is bought from an owner who cannot read the data. The molecule's IP is a first-come filing, which is exactly the "free first-come" case that C4 excludes. The only buyable variant is lapsed odorant patent families, and a lapsed patent is public domain, so buying one secures no exclusivity and gives no step-up.

(2) THE FILED RIGHT IS WEAK FOR THIS CATEGORY. In the US, the product-of-nature exception (Funk Bros; AMP v. Myriad, 2013; USPTO 2014 subject-matter guidance) means a molecule identical to a natural one cannot be claimed as a composition unless it is 'markedly different'. The EPO is more lenient: a natural substance first isolated and characterised can be patentable. But essential oils and extracts that already contain the molecule, and that were already used in perfumery, threaten novelty for use-in-fragrance claims. The finalist's cited Chemistry in Australia piece (2020) makes the same point. A natural compound can also be made by another route and sold as 'nature-identical', so a process claim does not exclude competitors. The asset is therefore a narrow use or process claim, not a captive.

(3) THE PHYSICAL STEP IS NOT TRIVIAL TO THE BUYER. Making 10-100 mg and running a panel is cheap (about $10-30k), so it is trivial inside the rung as defined. But what makes a captive valuable to a fragrance house lies after the rung, and the buyer prices that in:
- process scale-up: the Chemistry World feature on Pomarose reports Givaudan tried 19 routes;
- a RIFM/IFRA safety dossier and REACH registration: years of work, and in my estimate (unsourced) costing $10^5-10^6+;
- stability and performance testing in product bases.
The readable Osmo extract shows the market treats safety as an AI prediction, not a tested property, and gives no prices. This is less extreme than geothermal plants, where building the plant is the whole problem. But discovery is closer to 50-70% than 80%+ of what the buyer pays for.

(4) STEP-UP IS UNVERIFIED. No public clearing price exists for an unscaled, untested odorant licence. The Osmo auction shows a buyer class exists, but I found no published results. The $5-50M per captive in the finalist is unsourced, and the realistic range (my estimate, unsourced) is $0.5-5M on about $30k, so 10-100x.

(5) HARD EXCLUSIONS: none triggered. This is not drilling or prospecting, and the company would own the IP rather than sell a service. It fails on the right, not on an exclusion.

(6) HIT-RATE LEVER: the 0.25% base rate comes only from Osmo's own press release. Osmo ($130M raised) already sells the ~10x ML gain using synthetic, patentable novel scaffolds, which avoids the natural-product patent problem altogether.

(7) LADDER: molecule, then manufacture, then ingredient supply, then an ingredients house. The flavour and fragrance market is about $30B a year, so this is a large company path but not a trillion-dollar chain.
verifiers.killer: There is no buyable right. The asset is filed first-come, and for a naturally occurring odorant found in published spectra it is mostly unpatentable as a composition (US product-of-nature doctrine), or anticipated or easy to design around (nature-identical molecule made by another route). That leaves a weak use claim with no exclusivity. The value the buyer pays for (scale-up, IFRA/REACH safety work, performance in product bases) sits outside the rung. Osmo already holds the ML-discovery rung with patentable synthetic novel molecules.

verified.name: Enzyme Claims from Metagenomes (owned biocatalysts for one hard API step)
verified.one_line: Mine public metagenomes for an enzyme that performs one costly, metal-catalysed or chiral step in a top-selling API's route (the sitagliptin-transaminase pattern). Express the top ~50 candidates and prove activity in a plate assay. Patent the enzyme-in-process and sell or license it to the API maker.
verified.unproven_right: None bought; the right is the filed enzyme-use IP. To score on C4 it needs a purchase variant, such as buying environmental sample banks or lapsed enzyme patent families from defunct industrial-biotech firms (Codexis-era spinouts).
verified.proving_step: Gene synthesis plus expression plus activity assay on the real substrate (~$20-50k). Nature hides which of 10^9 sequences does the reaction.
verified.proven_buyer: Pharma process groups and CDMOs (Merck, Pfizer, Lonza), which save $10M+ a year on large-volume APIs
verified.public_data: MGnify, JGI IMG/M, UniProt, the AlphaFold DB, BRENDA, and scanned process-chemistry papers in OPRD (Organic Process Research & Development) describing pain-point steps
verified.rough_step_up: $50k proof to $5-30M licence (~10^2-10^3x). This is the closest to the 'discovery is 95%' frame, but it is weak on the bought-cheap-right criterion. Ladder: enzyme, then engineered variants, then biocatalytic API manufacture.
verified.frame: The proposed rung is "a wild-type enzyme sequence that catalyses one named API step, proven in a plate assay." Inside that rung, finding the sequence genuinely is most of the intellectual work. But the rung is not discrete or sellable, and the physical step is NOT trivial — it is the hard part. A plate-assay hit on the real substrate is typically 10^2-10^4 fold short of industrial requirements (space-time yield, substrate loading, co-solvent and temperature tolerance, cofactor recycle, >99.5% ee, metal-free ICH-compliant product). The sitagliptin transaminase that this pitch invokes is the counter-example to its own thesis: the starting ATA-117 wild type had essentially no activity on the bulky prositagliptin ketone, and the asset was created by ~11 rounds of directed evolution with ~27 mutations and a multi-year Codexis/Merck joint campaign (my characterisation of the published OPRD/Science account). So discovery is more like 15-30% of the work to a sellable asset, and the "physical step" (engineering campaign, kg-scale process development, re-filing the API route with regulators, requalifying a commercial process) is 70%+. Buyers are real and capitalised (Merck, Pfizer, Lonza, Dr Reddy's, WuXi), but they buy a validated process at scale, not a hit; a wild-type hit plus a use claim is a conversation starter, not a purchase order. Estimate, not a sourced number.
verified.step_up: Unproven side: the sequence itself costs $0 (open MGnify/IMG-M/UniProt download); the proving spend is the candidate's own $20-50k panel (my check: 1 kb gene synthesis at roughly $0.07-0.15/bp is ~$100-300/gene, so 50 genes plus expression, purification and substrate assay is ~$15-40k — the candidate's figure is about right). Proven side: the candidate claims $5-30M per licence. That is the price of a *developed, scaled, engineered* biocatalytic process, not of a wild-type hit. For a hit-stage enzyme-use patent family with no engineering and no scale data, realistic consideration is an option/research licence in the $50k-$500k range plus back-loaded milestones — i.e. ~3-10x over the $50k proving cost, realised years later and contingent on someone else doing the 70% of work that remains. Also, unlike a drill hit, the step-up is not immediate: it does not exist until the evolution campaign and the regulatory route change land. All figures here are my estimates; WebSearch was blocked by a classifier on the licensing-terms query, so I have no sourced comparables and am scoring the step-up conservatively (2) rather than taking the pitch's own 10^2-10^3 claim at face value.
verified.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate is genuinely low and the lever is genuinely large: in metagenomic/homology panel screening for activity on a specific non-natural industrial substrate, roughly 1-10% of expressed candidates show any detectable activity and well under 1% show activity worth developing (my estimate from published enzyme-discovery campaigns; I could not verify with a search). Cost per proving attempt ~$20-50k per ~50-member panel, i.e. ~$400-1,000 per sequence tested. So 1/base-hit-rate is in the 10-100x range and a sequence-to-function model that reorders the panel could plausibly cut discovery capex ~5-10x. That earns a 3, not a 5, for two reasons: (a) the assay is cheap and parallel enough that brute force at 10^4-10^5 variants is already affordable to incumbents, so the lever is not gated on ML; (b) this exact lever is the business of a crowded, well-capitalised field — protein language models (ESM-family), function predictors (CLEAN/DeepEC-style), and companies including Codexis, Ginkgo, Arzeda, Cradle, Basecamp Research, Enzymit and the big-pharma internal biocatalysis groups. Raising the hit rate is not a proprietary edge here; it is the industry's current default workflow.
verified.data: Wrong kind of public data for this rubric. MGnify, JGI IMG/M, UniProt and AlphaFold DB are public and enormous but they are maximally LEGIBLE — FASTA and PDB, already clustered, already embedded, already mirrored into every competitor's pipeline, with standing public benchmarks. There is no scanning, no OCR, no 1970s typewritten assessment report that nobody has parsed. The one genuine plus is that the OUTCOME is not summarised in a legible field: EC numbers and GO annotations in these databases are mostly transferred by homology and are known to be wrong or absent for the specific non-natural substrate that matters, so "does this enzyme do the prositagliptin ketone" is not written down anywhere. That is real and is why C4 is 1 rather than 0. The OPRD pain-point literature is likewise only semi-illegible and is read closely by exactly the process chemists who would be the buyer. Net: illegibility of the data is near zero; illegibility of the outcome is high.
verified.right_bought: This is where the candidate collapses, and the candidate admits it. Nothing is bought. The sequence is free to everyone simultaneously, so the "right" is only a first-to-file patent position in a race against better-funded players reading the same databases — the opposite of the Terranox structure, where the right is bought cheaply from an owner who cannot read the data and who hands over exclusivity before the proving spend. The two offered purchase variants do not fix it: (i) environmental sample banks — buying soil or marine sample collections gives physical DNA, but the public metagenome is what the ML reads, so the purchase buys no exclusivity over the signal you are actually acting on, and sequencing a bank just adds capex; (ii) lapsed enzyme patent families from defunct industrial-biotech firms — a lapsed family is in the public domain, so you can buy the file but not the exclusion right; and anything still in force claims the *old* enzyme, not the new metagenomic one you would find. There is also freedom-to-operate risk running the other way: broad enzyme-class and process claims held by Codexis and others can block your use claim rather than your claim capturing value.
verified.buyer: Real and capitalised: pharma process chemistry/API groups (Merck, Pfizer, Novartis) and CDMOs (Lonza, WuXi, Siegfried, Dr Reddy's CPS). Savings on a large-volume API route are genuinely $5-50M/yr, so willingness to pay exists. But the buyer's purchase trigger is a demonstrated kg-scale process with the enzyme at commercial loading and a regulatory path for the route change — not a plate-assay hit. And they buy late: the API route is frozen at filing, so for an approved product a route change means a post-approval change filing, which pushes adoption to generics, new NCEs pre-filing, or process-improvement programmes with multi-year cycles. The buyer is capitalised but does not buy the output of the rung you are selling.
verified.ladder: Genuinely good, the strongest criterion here. Enzyme hit, then engineered variant families, then enzyme supply, then biocatalytic step-as-a-service, then owning the API manufacture itself. Codexis and Lonza are the existence proof that each rung is real and that the top rung is a multi-billion-dollar business; a vertically integrated biocatalytic API manufacturer is a plausible very large company. 4 not 5 because the rungs are not cleanly sellable to each other the way a mineral claim is — each step up requires a new capability (evolution platform, cGMP fermentation, GMP API plant, DMF filings) rather than just capital, so climbing is a series of company rebuilds, not a ladder you buy your way up.
verified.fatal_flaw: There is no unproven right to buy cheaply — the sequence is free and simultaneously available to every well-funded competitor, so there is no exclusivity to acquire before the proving spend and no owner who cannot read the data. Compounding it, the "physical step" is the hard part: a plate-assay hit is 10^2-10^4 fold short of an industrial biocatalyst, and the directed-evolution plus process-development plus regulatory-route-change work that creates the actual value is far harder than the discovery. That is precisely the geothermal-in-abandoned-coal-mines failure mode — finding the right candidate is easy relative to building the bespoke thing that makes it worth money.
verified.one_line_reason: Scores 12/25: real ladder and a real capitalised buyer, but the data is fully legible and free rather than illegible and purchasable, there is no unproven right to buy, and the engineering step after the hit is harder than the discovery — the counter-example pattern, not the Terranox pattern.

NO NEW EVIDENCE RETRIEVABLE THIS TURN: the shared WebSearch budget for the turn (200 calls across all agents) was exhausted before my first query returned, and a classifier stopped the attempt, so zero searches ran. Every figure below is explicitly flagged as either (a) the candidate's own unsourced claim or (b) my prior-knowledge estimate. Under the lens's instruction ("Default to refuted=true if the key claim cannot be supported with real evidence"), the key claim fails on evidence alone.

UNPROVEN-RIGHT PRICE: $0, and this is not an estimate — it is structural. MGnify / JGI IMG/M / UniProt sequences are free public downloads. There is no transaction, no seller, no price. A step-up multiple is defined as (proven price / acquisition price of the right); with acquisition price $0 there is no acquirable asset to re-price, which is the Terranox mechanic the rubric is actually measuring. The candidate's own text concedes this ("None bought"). The only thing it can divide by is its own proving spend ($20-50k), which is a cost of goods, not an asset basis — Terranox's $1/ha → $10,000/ha is a price-per-asset ratio, not a cost-of-work ratio. So C2 as written cannot be scored above the floor on real terms.

PROVEN-RIGHT PRICE: the candidate claims $5-30M per licence. I could retrieve no comparable. From memory and clearly unverified: the deal archetype it invokes (Codexis/Merck sitagliptin transaminase) was a multi-year joint development campaign ending in an enzyme-supply relationship, not a one-time purchase of a sequence; Codexis's pharma biocatalysis revenue historically arrived as R&D/development fees plus per-kg enzyme product sales and modest milestones, i.e. an operating revenue stream over years, not a lump-sum asset purchase. I have no sourced number for any one-time payment for an unproven, wild-type, plate-assay-stage enzyme-use patent family, and I am not aware that a public comparable exists. Absence of a comparable is itself the finding: there is no observable market price for the output of this rung.

STEP-UP, HONESTLY BOUNDED: at hit stage the realistic consideration is an option or research licence plus back-loaded milestones — my estimate, same order of magnitude as the $20-50k proving spend up to maybe a few hundred k, i.e. roughly 1-10x, and received years later contingent on someone else completing the directed-evolution, kg-scale process development and the regulatory route-change filing. That is below the lens's ~30x refutation threshold even on the candidate's own most favourable framing, and it is not "immediately on a hit" in any sense: nothing re-prices at the assay read-out, because the asset is not an asset until the engineering campaign lands. Contrast the drill hit, where the step-up is realised on the assay certificate because the buyer's own economics ($40k/ha in, $100k/ha out, per the gold rubric) make the payment rational that day.

MARKET SIZE / TRANSACTION COUNT: unverified estimate, but the direction is not in doubt. New commercial-scale biocatalytic steps entering top-selling API routes are a handful per year industry-wide, not a flow of transactions; approved products freeze the route at filing, so a route change means a post-approval change filing, pushing the addressable set to pre-filing NCEs and generics. There is no auction, no broker, no standing bid, and no recurring transaction stream for unproven enzyme-use IP. A rung with no observable transaction market has no price, and a buyer with no standing bid at that stage is not a buyer of this rung's output.

BUYER REALITY: Merck, Pfizer, Lonza, WuXi are real and capitalised and the underlying savings ($5-50M/yr on a large-volume route, candidate's unsourced figure, plausible to me) are real. But capitalisation is not the test — the test is whether the capitalised buyer buys THE OUTPUT OF THIS RUNG at once. Their purchase trigger is a demonstrated process at commercial loading with a regulatory path. They are also the same process-chemistry groups who read OPRD and run in-house biocatalysis, so they are the incumbent extractor of the signal, not an uninformed owner. The mine developer in the gold rubric pays on the drill hit because the hit is the whole informational gap; the pharma process group does not pay on the plate hit because the plate hit is the cheap part of its own workflow.
verifiers.killer: There is no transaction on either side of the step-up: the unproven right costs $0 because it is a free public sequence with no seller, so there is no asset basis to multiply, and no observable price exists for an unproven, wild-type, assay-stage enzyme-use patent family — I could find no comparable and am not aware that one exists. The claimed $5-30M is the price of a developed, engineered, scaled biocatalytic process (the Codexis/Merck archetype was a multi-year joint campaign ending in an enzyme-supply stream, not a lump-sum purchase of a sequence), so the candidate is pricing the far end of a 70%-remaining engineering and regulatory programme and booking it as the proceeds of the discovery step. At the actual hit stage the realistic consideration is an option fee in the same order of magnitude as the $20-50k proving spend — roughly 1-10x, below the lens's ~30x threshold — and it is never immediate, because nothing re-prices until the directed-evolution campaign and the route-change filing land. The capitalised buyer is real but buys a different product at a different stage, and there is no recurring transaction market: a handful of new commercial biocatalytic API steps per year, no standing bid, no broker, no price discovery.

verifiers.evidence:
SOURCED (this session; note: WebSearch budget for the whole workflow turn was exhausted before my first query returned, so all evidence below is from direct WebFetch of primary/official pages, and several other fetches failed — PubMed 20430975 cookie-walled, science.org 10.1126/science.1188934 HTTP 403, esmatlas.com/about and docs.mgnify.org empty/404).

1) The canonical example the pitch is built on refutes the "discovery is 95%" frame, and this is now sourced rather than my estimate. EPA's own write-up of the 2010 Presidential Green Chemistry Challenge award (Merck + Codexis, sitagliptin/Januvia): "Merck's tests of available transaminases found none with detectable activity on the sitagliptin ketone." Codexis started from an R-selective transaminase with "only slight activity on a smaller, truncated methyl ketone analog" and evolved it to a "compounded activity improvement of over 25,000-fold." Process benefits came from the engineered enzyme: eliminates 250 psi hydrogenation, removes rhodium and iron, +56% productivity, +10-13% yield, -19% waste. So in the one case the pitch names, the discovery rung produced ZERO sellable hits — the asset was manufactured by engineering (>10^4-fold), not found. A metagenomic search for a wild-type that performs a bulky non-natural ketone amination is searching for an object that, on the best-documented precedent, does not exist in nature. That caps C1 and C2 hard: there is no discrete sellable "wild-type hit" rung.

2) The data is not an edge, and the best-funded entrant's own behaviour proves it. Basecamp Research (basecamp-research.com): claims "Over 100 billion novel genes discovered from across all 7 continents," called "the largest biological AI training dataset created to date," a 28B-parameter model (EDEN), a $140M round at a reported ~$800M valuation, with Nvidia and Anthropic/Menlo among backers. The point for this lens: the player with the most capital in exactly this workflow spent it going to all 7 continents to SAMPLE PROPRIETARY sequence data — i.e. it treats the public metagenome (MGnify/IMG-M/UniProt) as a non-moat. If free public FASTA were the edge, nobody raises $140M to go collect their own. (Also notable: Basecamp has pivoted its stated focus to therapeutics, not industrial enzymes, so it is not even the direct competitor — the direct competitors are below.)

3) The proving step is commoditised off the shelf, and the ML lever is the incumbent's default, trained on data the candidate cannot get. Codexis (codexis.com/products, codexis.com/about): sells "Enzyme Screening Kits and Panels" and "Tailored Enzymes" as catalogue products for pharma biocatalysis — i.e. the candidate's $20-50k "panel on the real substrate" proving step is a purchasable service, not a proprietary capability. Its CodeEvolver platform is "powered by AI, machine learning, and deep enzymology expertise," designs-builds-tests variants "in as little as one week," and its ML is "trained on more than 20 years of Codexis experimental data." Named partners: Merck, GSK, Novartis — the exact buyers this pitch names. So (a) the space is occupied by the buyer's existing vendor, (b) the real moat is 20 years of private sequence-function assay data, which is the opposite of a public-data play, and (c) the candidate would be selling a worse version of a product the buyer already procures.

4) C3 specifically inverts. The lens question is whether ML raising the hit rate cuts discovery capex ~10x, capped at 1/base-hit-rate. EPA's "none with detectable activity" means the base hit rate on the hard, valuable substrates is effectively zero — and a lever capped at 1/0 is not a large lever, it is a dead end: reordering a panel cannot surface a hit that is not in the search space. ML reranking helps only on the easy substrates where many wild-types work, which are precisely the substrates with no $10M licence attached. My earlier 1-10% hit-rate figure stays unverified (search blocked), so I am scoring C3 on the sourced structural point, not on that number.

5) C5 downgraded on sourced numbers. The existence proof for the top of this ladder is Codexis: revenue US$68.5M (FY2019), ~165 employees (April 2020), per the Wikipedia company page (which itself carries a paid-editing/NPOV warning, so treat as indicative). A fully climbed ladder whose public exemplar is a sub-$100M-revenue company is weak evidence for a trillion-dollar path, even granting Lonza at the manufacturing rung. 3, not 4.

6) Unchanged from the prior scoring and still true: nothing is bought. The sequence is free and simultaneous to every competitor; a lapsed patent family is public domain (you buy the file, not the exclusion right); buying environmental sample banks buys physical DNA but no exclusivity over the public signal the ML actually reads. There is no owner who cannot read the data and who can hand over exclusivity before the proving spend. That alone keeps C4 at 1 — the single genuine plus is that the OUTCOME ("does this enzyme do this non-natural ketone") is not written into any legible EC/GO field, which EPA's account corroborates (Merck had to run the tests to find out).
verifiers.killer: For the one case this pitch invokes as its own proof, EPA's official award write-up states Merck "found none with detectable activity on the sitagliptin ketone" and the final biocatalyst required a >25,000-fold engineered improvement — so the "wild-type hit" rung produced nothing sellable and the value was created entirely by the step the pitch calls trivial. METHOD NOTE: the shared WebSearch budget for this workflow turn was exhausted before my first query ran, so I verified by direct WebFetch only. Numbers below are either fetched (marked F) or flagged as my own unsourced reasoning (marked E).

RIGHT LEG — the right is not buyable, and the part you would "own" is not ownable.
1. (F) US patent law blocks the composition claim on exactly this asset. Myriad: "a naturally occurring DNA segment is a product of nature and not patent eligible merely because it has been isolated"; cDNA is eligible, and the Court expressly did not reach method claims. So a wild-type metagenomic enzyme pulled from MGnify/IMG-M cannot be owned as a composition in the US. What remains is a method/use claim on one named API step — the narrowest and least enforceable species of claim, against a buyer who may run the step offshore, and trivially designed around by a competitor who finds a different homolog catalysing the same reaction from the same public FASTA. (E) Exclusivity over a signal that is simultaneously downloadable by every competitor is not an unproven right; it is a race.
2. (F) The two offered purchase variants do not create a cheap exclusive right, and one of them imports a liability. Buying environmental sample banks runs straight into ABS law: the CBD/Nagoya framework requires prior informed consent and mutually agreed terms, and defines covered "utilization" to include "research and development on the genetic or biochemical composition of genetic resources" plus later applications and commercialization. (F) For sequence data specifically, COP-15 (2022) agreed to establish a multilateral benefit-sharing mechanism for digital sequence information and COP-16 decision 16/2 adopted its modalities, including the "Cali Fund for the Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits from the Use of Digital Sequence Information on Genetic Resources." Net: commercial use of public metagenomes now attracts a diffuse, non-exclusive payment obligation and confers no exclusivity — the exact inverse of the Terranox structure (pay little, get exclusive).
3. (E) Lapsed enzyme patent families are in the public domain; buying the file buys documents, not an exclusion right. Families still in force claim the old enzyme, and broad enzyme-class/process claims cut against you (FTO risk), not for you.
4. (F) "Owners who cannot read the data" do not exist here — the one buyable version of this is already owned at scale by a funded competitor. Basecamp Research reports "over 100 billion novel genes discovered from across all 7 continents" as a 100T-token training set, $140M new (Series C) funding, a reported ~$800M valuation, and investors including Nvidia and Anthropic. Entering that trade means buying sample access at market against an incumbent with a four-year head start and no purchase discount available to you.

FRAME LEG — the physical step dominates, i.e. the geothermal-plant failure mode.
5. (E, could not re-verify in session: PubMed blocked by cookie wall, no search budget) The sitagliptin transaminase the pitch invokes was created by a multi-round directed-evolution campaign on a wild type with essentially no activity on the bulky substrate — the discovery was the cheap part. (F) Wikipedia's directed-evolution page corroborates only the structural shape of that work: "Rounds of these steps are typically repeated, using the best variant from one round as the template for the next," with success scaling in library size — an open-ended iterative engineering campaign, not a trivial or abstracted physical step.
6. (E) The sellable unit is therefore not a plate-assay hit. It is an engineered variant at commercial loading, kg-scale process data, >99.5% ee, cofactor recycle, and a regulatory route change (post-approval change filing for marketed products). The capitalised buyer is real (Merck, Pfizer, Lonza) but buys the output of a rung two or three above the one on offer, which is precisely the C1 failure.

EXCLUSION CHECK: not a formal hard exclusion, but adjacent to one. "Patent the enzyme-in-process and sell or license it to the API maker" leaves the incumbent owning the manufacture and realising the step-up while the company takes a cut — close to the barred "sell a service/software to incumbents" pattern. Scored as a C1 penalty rather than excluded=true.

SCORE DELTAS vs the finalist's 2/2/3/1/4: C1 2->1 (rung not discrete, buyer is two rungs up, engineering dominates); C2 2->1 (3-10x magnitude would be a 2, docked one band because the criterion requires the step-up to land immediately on the hit and here it does not exist until someone else completes the evolution and regulatory work); C3 3->2 (the premise "expensive and mostly failing" is weak — the assay is cheap and parallel, incumbents already brute-force 10^4-10^5 variants, and sequence-to-function reranking is the industry's default workflow, not an edge); C4 1->0 (conjunctive criterion: data is maximally legible FASTA/PDB AND no right is buyable AND the natural sequence is not even patent-eligible; outcome-illegibility alone does not carry it); C5 4 unchanged (ladder is genuinely good). Total 8/25.
verifiers.killer: There is no right to buy, and the thing you would own you cannot own: under Myriad an isolated naturally occurring DNA segment is not patent-eligible, leaving only a narrow method claim on a sequence every competitor can download simultaneously — while the one purchasable variant (proprietary sampled biodiversity under ABS agreements) is already held at scale by a $140M-funded competitor and now carries a non-exclusive Cali Fund benefit-sharing obligation instead of exclusivity. Compounding it, the physical step is the hard part: a plate-assay hit is not the sellable unit, the multi-round evolution plus kg-scale process plus regulatory route change is, and the capitalised buyer only buys at that later rung — the abandoned-coal-mine geothermal pattern, not the Terranox pattern.
sources: [Association for Molecular Pathology v. Myriad Genetics (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_Molecular_Pathology_v._Myriad_Genetics,_Inc.) — FETCHED: holding that "a naturally occurring DNA segment is a product of nature and not patent eligible merely because it has been isolated"; cDNA eligible; method claims not reached.

[CBD — About the Nagoya Protocol](https://www.cbd.int/abs/about) — FETCHED: prior informed consent and mutually agreed terms required; "utilization" defined to include R&D on the genetic or biochemical composition of genetic resources and subsequent commercialization.

[CBD — Digital sequence information on genetic resources](https://www.cbd.int/dsi-gr) — FETCHED: COP-15 (Dec 2022) decision to establish a multilateral DSI benefit-sharing mechanism; COP-16 decision 16/2 adopted modalities including the Cali Fund for the Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits from the Use of Digital Sequence Information on Genetic Resources.

[Basecamp Research](https://basecamp-research.com/) — FETCHED: "Over 100 billion novel genes discovered from across all 7 continents", >100T-token biological AI dataset, $140M new funding (Series C), reported ~$800M valuation, investors including Nvidia and Anthropic.

[Directed evolution (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_evolution) — FETCHED: iterative rounds templated on the prior best variant, success scaling with library size; no sitagliptin/Codexis detail on the page.

verified.name: FreeMag: rare-earth-free magnet compositions
verified.one_line: Uses DFT-trained ML on OQMD and Materials Project to find metastable Fe-, Mn- and Co-based phases with high magnetocrystalline anisotropy, then proves each with arc-melting and VSM measurement in a week. It licenses proven compositions to motor and magnet makers desperate for supply chains outside China.
verified.unproven_right: Self-filed provisional on the alloy composition and processing route, about $3k. Also optioning abandoned 1980s-2000s magnet patents and DOE lab inventions (Ames, ORNL) for $10-50k.
verified.proving_step: Arc-melt or melt-spin plus anneal plus XRD plus VSM for coercivity and remanence, about $2-5k and a week per composition. Historical base hit rate for a new hard-magnet phase is well under 1%, so the ML lever is high in principle (capped at 1/hit rate).
verified.proven_buyer: Automotive OEMs and magnet makers: GM, Toyota, Tesla, Niron, Proterial, VAC, MP Materials. Proven composition licences or acquisitions are $10-100M, given the strategic premium.
verified.public_data: OQMD, Materials Project magnetic orderings, AFLOW, the Novamag database, NIST/Ames scanned historical alloy reports, expired magnet patents.
verified.rough_step_up: $3k to $10M+: 10^3-10^4 if a hit is real. The risk is that a lab-scale coercivity hit is not yet bulk-processable, so the buyer may pay an option first and the full price later.
verified.frame: The candidate's rung is "lab-proven composition (arc-melt + VSM) sold as a licence". Inside that rung discovery is maybe 80% of the work. But buyers do not pay for that rung. They pay for a bulk-processable magnet with real (BH)max, coercivity and temperature stability. For the known candidates (MnBi, MnAl, L10 FeNi, Fe16N2), getting from a phase with high anisotropy to a bulk magnet with real coercivity has taken decades. The work is microstructure engineering and processing, at least 80% of the effort. My estimate is that discovery is about 10-20% of the rung that has a buyer. This is the geothermal counter-example: the physical step is the hard part. Ames was still at 1.2 kOe coercivity in Ni-rich L10 FeNi, well short of a usable magnet, with next steps of scaling to 1-10 g and filing IP (Ames CMI highlight).
verified.step_up: Unproven: a $3k self-filed provisional, or a $10-50k option on a DOE/old patent (the candidate's figures; I could not verify the Ames/ORNL licence fee terms). Lab-proven: I found no public deal paying $10-100M for a lab-scale composition. Niron, the closest proven case (iron nitride), had to become a manufacturer to capture value. It raised $21.3M (2021), $33M (2023) and $25M (2024, Samsung/Magna/Allison), received a $17.5M DOE grant, and got a conditional $150M Office of Strategic Capital loan (2026) for a plant. I found no disclosed licensing deal values. My estimate is that a lab-scale hit commands a $50k-$1M option or sponsored-research deal, roughly 10-300x on $3k. A 10^3-10^4 jump comes only after bulk processing and plant-scale work, which costs $10-100M+.
verified.hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate is plausibly well under 1% for a new phase that is stable, has high anisotropy and is hard. The literature reports no measured experimental success rate. In a 2026 APS abstract (Fe-Co-S), ML screening narrowed >300,000 structures to 1,418, and DFT then left 3 (about 0.001%), none yet synthesized. Single ML-guided syntheses such as Fe3CoB2 (Xia et al. 2024) are anecdotes. Each proving attempt costs about $2-5k and a week (the candidate's figure, which is reasonable for arc-melt + XRD + VSM). Because attempts are cheap, a 10x hit-rate gain saves little capex in dollars: 100 attempts cost only about $300-500k. The lever is real as a ratio but small in dollars, and lab hits mostly fail later at bulk coercivity, which ML on intrinsic properties does not predict.
verified.data: The signal is in LEGIBLE, structured databases: OQMD, Materials Project, AFLOW and Novamag are clean, API-accessible and already carry computed magnetic moments and anisotropy fields. Everyone screens them: Ames/CMI, the Novamag consortium, Fraunhofer's MagnetPredictor, NIST, and big-lab generative models (GNoME, MatterGen). The intrinsic outcome is effectively already in a legible field, which is the failure mode named in the rubric. The only illegible part is scanned historical NIST/Ames alloy reports, a thin layer. The right is not bought cheaply from owners who cannot read the data: a provisional is free first-to-file, and published DFT entries and old literature create prior art that weakens composition claims. Optioning DOE patents is possible, but the labs know exactly what they hold.
verified.right_bought: A self-filed provisional (about $3k, first-to-file, not bought from an uninformed owner) or an option on an Ames/ORNL/expired-era patent ($10-50k, the candidate's estimate). The licensors are sophisticated and actively licensing (ORNL has licensed two high-performance magnet technologies per CMI). Composition claims are vulnerable to prior art from public DFT databases.
verified.buyer: The buyers are capitalised and strategically motivated: GM, Stellantis, Samsung, Magna, Volvo and Allison all invested in Niron, and DoD/OSC lends for plants. They want supply chains outside China. But they buy proven bulk magnets or manufacturers, not arc-melted buttons, so no buyer exists for the rung that FreeMag actually wins.
verified.ladder: The rungs above are real: bulk processing, magnet manufacturing (Niron's Sartell plant), motor supply and an EV/defense magnet market worth tens of billions. But the next rung up, bulk processing, is the expensive part that took decades, so winning the bottom rung gives little advantage in climbing.
verified.fatal_flaw: The rung with a buyer is not a discovery rung. A lab-scale phase with high anisotropy is worth little until someone solves bulk coercivity and processing, which is capital- and time-heavy and has taken decades for MnBi, MnAl, L10 FeNi and Fe16N2. That is the geothermal counter-example. On top of that, the input data is already legible, structured and screened by many well-funded groups, so FreeMag has no informational edge.
verified.one_line_reason: This fails like geothermal. Buyers pay for bulk-processable magnets, and processing, not discovery, is the decades-long bottleneck. The DFT databases are already clean and widely screened, so the ML edge and the cheap-right edge are both weak.

(1) Proven-side buyer behaviour. Niron's own 2026 release describes Niron as a manufacturer with a "proprietary manufacturing platform", not a licensor. It lists no licensing revenue or terms. The money in its iron-nitride magnet came as plant debt and equity:
- a conditional OSC loan of up to $150M (20-year term, conditional on due diligence and a minimum equity raise)

- equity rounds of $21.3M (2021), $33M (2023) and $25M (2024, led by Samsung)
- partnerships (Bimotal, Moog, Aspina) with no disclosed values.
So the capitalised buyers (GM, Samsung, Magna, Honda, DoD) paid for manufacturing scale-up, not for a composition.

(2) Lab-proven side. Ames MnBi rare-earth-free magnets won a 2025 R&D 100 award. The page says the performance comes mainly from the "preparation and fabrication process". It mentions no licensee, spinout or deal value, even after decades of MnBi work. Ames CMI's critical-element-free highlight reports no coercivity value, no licensee and no terms. Its next steps are still research-stage: optimise the process and scale up to tens to hundreds of grams. Even the national labs' best lab hits have no disclosed buyer at any price.

(3) Recalled background, not re-verified this session. Historical value capture happened at process and manufacturing scale. Examples are the Sumitomo/Hitachi sintered NdFeB patent royalties and the Magnequench melt-spun business, which GM sold for about $70M in 1995. Neither was a lab-button composition sale.

Implied step-up for the rung FreeMag actually wins (an arc-melted, VSM-measured composition plus a provisional): about $3k going in. A plausible exit is a $0-$1M option or sponsored-research deal, and no public comparable exists. That is 0-300x with heavy uncertainty, and the realistic median is well under 30x, because most lab coercivity hits never reach bulk. The claimed $10-100M licence has no public precedent. Market size: zero disclosed lab-composition licence transactions per year found. The relevant deal flow is a handful of manufacturer financings per year.
verifiers.killer: No capitalised buyer pays for a lab-proven magnet composition. Niron, the strongest rare-earth-free case, is a manufacturer funded by about $79M of equity plus up to $300M of plant loans, with no disclosed licensing deal. Ames's award-winning MnBi magnets credit their performance to processing and still show no licensee. The 10^3-10^4 step-up only appears after the $10-100M+ bulk-processing and plant rung, so the rung FreeMag wins realises well under 30x, with no observable transactions.

MatNex (Materials Nexus) already runs FreeMag's exact model: AI-designed rare-earth-free magnet IP that it owns and licenses, with a magnet announced in 2024. It still shows no disclosed licence buyer. The input data (OQMD, Materials Project, AFLOW, Novamag) is clean, legible and screened by Fraunhofer, Ames, DeepMind/Microsoft-class models and MatNex, so there is no illegible-data edge. Value is unlocked by bulk processing, not discovery.

verifiers.evidence:
The web search budget for this turn was used up after the first attempt. Only 2 primary-source fetches were possible, and the rest rests on the finalist's cited sources.
(1) Niron/OSC release (Aug 7, 2026). The iron nitride technology "was developed at the University of Minnesota and scaled over the last 13 years." Right: a provisional is first-to-file, not bought from an owner who cannot read the data. Published OQMD/Materials Project entries are prior art that weakens composition claims, and the composition is the very data FreeMag screens. DOE lab IP (Ames, ORNL) is held by sophisticated tech-transfer offices that know what they have, so there is no information arbitrage. Fe16N2 took 13 years of scaling after its University of Minnesota discovery, and Niron still had to build its own $150M+ plant rather than license. Ames L10-FeNi is still at gram scale on microstructure work. An arc-melted button has no capitalised buyer at a 10^3-10^4 premium. The 'right' is also not bought cheaply from uninformed owners. verified.name: Suppressa: buying the microbiomes of fields that nature protects
verified.one_line: Use ML on public crop-loss and satellite data to find fields that stay healthy under severe regional disease pressure (natural disease-suppressive soils). Buy exclusive sampling and microbe-commercialisation rights from those farmers for a few hundred dollars, isolate the causal strain, and sell or license the proven biocontrol strain to ag-biologicals majors.
verified.unproven_right: Exclusive contractual right to isolate and commercialise microbes from a specific field. The farmer cannot see that his soil is suppressive: the outcome is hidden in a yield anomaly, not in any record. Cost about $200-2,000 per field.
verified.proving_step: Paired 16S/shotgun metagenomics of suppressive vs conducive neighbour fields, then culturomics, then a greenhouse pathogen-challenge assay (Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, take-all, SCN). Cheap ($10-30k per field). Drilling-equivalent physical work is a soil core.
verified.proven_buyer: Syngenta Biologicals (paid $50M upfront for Rizobacter tie-up), Bayer (Ginkgo/AgBiome lineage), Corteva (Stoller/Symborg acquisitions), Novonesis, Indigo-type buyers. They actively scout biocontrol strains with greenhouse data.
verified.public_data: USDA RMA cause-of-loss by county/crop (decades), Sentinel-2/Landsat NDVI time series at field scale, USDA plant disease survey reports, state extension disease bulletins (PDF), NRCS SSURGO soils, SRA soil metagenomes from published suppressive-soil studies.
verified.rough_step_up: $1k field right to a greenhouse-validated strain licensable at $1-5M (10^3-10^4x). Base rate of a suppressive anomaly yielding a single transferable strain is maybe 2-5%, so the lever is about 20-50x. Caveat: majors increasingly want one field season before paying full value.
verified.frame: The candidate rung runs from a field sampling right to a greenhouse-validated strain. Inside that rung, discovery is plausibly 60-80% of the work, and the physical step (soil core, sequencing, greenhouse assay at $10-30k) is cheap. The problem is that this rung's output is not what capitalised buyers pay for. Buyers pay for consistent field efficacy plus formulation, shelf life and registrability. Greenhouse-to-field translation is the documented bottleneck: reviews describe a "translation gap" and "poor reliability of efficacy in the field". Development and launch cost $3-6M (Marrone exec) to $10-15M per product. Once you redraw the rung to end where a buyer pays real money (a field-proven strain), discovery falls to maybe 10-25% of the work (my estimate), and multi-season field trials dominate.
verified.step_up: Unproven right: $200-2,000 per field (candidate's figure; plausible, since US farmers have no Nagoya-type leverage). Proven value: no public price exists for a greenhouse-validated strain on its own. The closest reference points both sit well below the $1-5M claim. (1) In April 2024 Ginkgo bought AgBiome's platform assets: 115,000+ sequenced strains plus a dozen product candidates with greenhouse or field validation. Terms were undisclosed and widely read as a distressed sale, so per-validated-candidate value was probably far below $1M (estimate). (2) MustGrow-Bayer, a registered-stage, field-proven technology, was worth about $35-40M over 5-7 years, mostly milestones and not upfront. My estimate: a greenhouse-only strain licenses for $0-250k upfront, with value backloaded into field milestones. Against the true cost basis (about $1k right + $10-30k proving), the multiple on a hit is roughly 3-20x, not 10^3-10^4x. The 10^3x figure only appears if you ignore proving cost and take an optimistic license value.
verified.hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt: $10-30k per field (candidate's estimate, reasonable for paired metagenomics + culturomics + greenhouse challenge). Base hit rate (suppressive anomaly yields a transferable strain): 2-5% (candidate's estimate; I found no source quantifying it). The expensive, mostly-failing step is the greenhouse-to-field transition, where costs run $1-10M of R&D per biological (Xite Bio CEO). ML on NDVI and RMA data does nothing to raise that hit rate. So the lever applies to a step that is already cheap. Spending $25k x 30 attempts (about $750k) to get one greenhouse hit is not a capex problem worth a 10x reduction.
verified.data: The data is public but weak, and legible where it matters. USDA RMA cause-of-loss is reported at county x crop level, not field level, so it can only flag regional disease pressure. Field-level 'healthy under pressure' from Sentinel-2/Landsat NDVI is heavily confounded by variety, planting date, fungicide use, drainage, rotation and tillage. A yield anomaly is not evidence of microbial suppression. Classic suppressive soils (take-all decline, Fusarium-wilt-suppressive soils, SCN-suppressive soils) are already well characterised and published, with SRA metagenomes, so the best-known cases are not hidden. Incumbents do not need hidden soils: Ginkgo/AgBiome alone holds 115k strains from 8,000+ environmental samples, and Bayer, Novonesis and Corteva have comparable libraries. Microbial diversity is not the scarce input.
verified.right_bought: Yes, an exclusive sampling and commercialisation contract can be bought cheaply ($200-2k) from farmers who cannot see suppressiveness. But the right is weakly excludable. The causal taxa (Pseudomonas with DAPG, Streptomyces, Bacillus and others) usually also live in neighbouring fields and other regions, so a competitor can isolate a near-identical strain elsewhere. Commercial protection comes from the patent and strain deposit on the isolate, not from the field contract. So the bought right does little to capture the step-up.
verified.buyer: Syngenta Biologicals, Bayer (Ginkgo partnership), Corteva (Stoller, Symborg), Novonesis, UPL NPP, FMC are capitalised and do in-license. They pay meaningful money mostly for field-validated, formulated or registered assets. MustGrow-Bayer was about $35-40M total, but over 5-7 years and milestone-heavy. Greenhouse-only strains are abundant, and in the AgBiome-Ginkgo deal a dozen validated candidates were folded into a platform asset sale. Competitors and incumbents in suppressive-soil discovery: Ginkgo Ag Bio (AgBiome library), Pivot Bio, Indigo, Loam, Biome Makers (soil metagenomics data across many fields), and academic labs (Raaijmakers/NIOO, Weller/USDA-ARS take-all decline).
verified.ladder: The ladder is: strain, then field-validated candidate, then registered biocontrol product (US EPA biopesticide about $300-400k in fees, about 13 months), then formulation, manufacturing and distribution, then a full biologicals company. The ladder exists, but its track record is poor for independents: AgBiome sold its platform, Marrone was sold to Bioceres, and Indigo restructured. The total biologicals market is real (about $15B) but fragmented. A path to a large company exists in principle, not a trillion-dollar one.
verified.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the scarce step. Majors already hold 100k+ strain libraries (Ginkgo/AgBiome: 115k strains, a dozen greenhouse-validated candidates sold as part of a platform deal). verifiers.evidence:
Limits on this check: the shared web-search budget was already used up when I started, so all three of my searches failed. Two direct fetches (the USDA RMA cause-of-loss page and Ginkgo's AgBiome press release) also returned nothing useful: one was a 404 and the other redirected to Ginkgo's homepage. This verdict therefore rests on the finalist's own cited sources plus well-documented domain knowledge. I could not re-confirm figures live, and every figure below should be read with that in mind.

(1) The data is not illegible where it matters.
- USDA RMA cause-of-loss files are structured, machine-readable tables. They report state x county x crop x cause-of-loss code x month, plus indemnity and acres. Field-level resolution does not exist in them.
- So the only public outcome field gives regional disease pressure only, and that is already legible. It is not hidden in scanned or unstructured documents.
- Sentinel-2 and Landsat NDVI is clean, analysis-ready raster data, and many ag-analytics vendors already process it at field scale. It is not illegible either.
- A field that stays healthy under regional pressure is confounded by cultivar resistance, fungicide programmes, seeding date, drainage, rotation and tillage. None of these are in public data.
- The ML signal therefore says little about microbial suppression specifically. I found no evidence that NDVI anomalies predict suppressive soils.

(2) The outcome is largely predictable from known agronomy, the same 'answer already written down' failure seen in prior hunts.
- Classic suppressive soils follow from management history, and this is well established:
  - Take-all decline develops after about 4-6+ years of wheat monoculture (Weller et al., USDA-ARS).
  - SCN-suppressive soils follow long-term soybean monoculture.
  - Fusarium-wilt-suppressive soils (Chateaurenard, Salinas) and the Dutch Rhizoctonia-suppressive soil (Mendes et al. 2011, Science) are well characterised.
- An agronomist can name candidate fields from rotation history alone. The causal taxa are already known: DAPG-producing Pseudomonas, Streptomyces, Bacillus.
- A model buys little over that domain-knowledge lookup. This is analogous to the interconnection-queue result (a lookup table matched ML).

(3) The space is occupied, and the thesis has been tried and found wanting.
- Indigo Ag's founding thesis was nearly identical: find plants and fields that thrive under stress and isolate their microbes. It raised over $1B, then wrote down its valuation and restructured.
- AgBiome sampled about 8,000+ environments into a 115k-strain library. That library was sold to Ginkgo in April 2024 on undisclosed, distressed-looking terms, along with a dozen validated candidates (per the finalist's own sources).
- Soil-metagenomics data vendors already sequence soils across large numbers of farm fields and sell disease-risk and biology data: Biome Makers (BeCrop), Pattern Ag, Trace Genomics. These names come from my knowledge; I could not check their current scale.
- Bayer, Syngenta, Corteva, Novonesis and UPL each hold large in-house strain libraries.
- Microbial diversity and candidate strains are abundant inputs, not scarce ones.

(4) The proving step is cheap, not the expensive failing step.
- Paired metagenomics plus a greenhouse assay costs about $10-30k per field (the finalist's figure).
- The expensive, mostly-failing step is greenhouse-to-field translation: $1-15M and multiple seasons per product (Marrone and Xite Bio figures in the finalist's sources; reviews of biocontrol field-efficacy failure).
- ML on NDVI does not move that hit rate, so the lever is roughly 1-2x on a step that is already cheap.

(5) The bought right is weakly excludable.
- The same causal taxa recur across fields and regions, so a rival can isolate a near-identical strain elsewhere.
- Protection comes from the strain patent and deposit, not from the field contract.
- So the purchased right captures little of any step-up, and C4 fails on both of its tests.

Revised scores:
- C1 = 1: the buyer pays for field-proven strains, not greenhouse-proven ones.
- C2 = 2: about 3-20x against the true cost basis.
- C3 = 1: the lever sits on an already-cheap step.
- C4 = 1: data is legible or confounded, the outcome is predictable from rotation history, and the right is non-exclusive.
- C5 = 2: the independents' track record is poor, as AgBiome, Marrone and Indigo show.
verifiers.killer: Suppressiveness is neither hidden nor scarce. The best-known suppressive soils follow from management history that agronomists can already read: take-all decline after 4-6 years of wheat monoculture, SCN suppression after soybean monoculture. The only public outcome data (RMA cause of loss) is a legible county-level table, and field NDVI anomalies are confounded by fungicide use, cultivar and drainage. Indigo Ag already ran the 'isolate microbes from plants and fields that thrive under stress' thesis with over $1B and had to restructure. AgBiome's 115k-strain library was sold off in what looked like a distressed deal, and soil-metagenomics vendors (Biome Makers, Pattern Ag, Trace Genomics) already sequence soils across large numbers of farm fields. So ML adds no real edge on a discovery step that is cheap and crowded. The expensive, mostly-failing step is greenhouse-to-field translation, and ML does not touch it.
sources: https://www.rma.usda.gov/ (cause-of-loss county-level files; live fetch returned 404)
Mendes et al. 2011 Science 332:1097 (Rhizoctonia-suppressive soil microbiome)
Weller et al. 2002 Annu Rev Phytopathol 40:309 (take-all decline after wheat monoculture)
