verifiers.evidence:
Caveat on method: the shared WebSearch budget was used up before this check ran, so both searches came back unexecuted. The evidence below comes from one source I fetched directly, Pam Marrone's 2026 No-Till lecture PDF (converted to text locally), plus legal background I know but could not re-verify by search this turn. Two more searches might add detail, but I do not expect them to overturn the verdict.

(1) The physical step dominates once you redraw the frame to where buyers pay. Marrone's slides show development of a biopesticide from discovery to launch takes "3-5 Years & <$10 Million". Her own pipeline follows this order: microbe isolation, 16S, miniaturised screening, greenhouse, field trials, formulation, toxicology and regulatory, manufacturing. Discovery and greenhouse sit at the front. Field trials, formulation, tox, EPA registration and scale-up make up most of the time and money. This has the same structure as the geothermal counterexample: finding the asset is easy, and turning it into something a buyer will pay for is bespoke multi-season work.

(2) Discovery is not scarce. Marrone's funnel ran thousands of isolates, then about 60, then about 20, then 14 advanced, then 2 selected. Ginkgo bought AgBiome's 115k+ strain library, as the finalist itself states; the Ginkgo page I fetched did not mention AgBiome, so I could not confirm that figure. Majors can produce greenhouse-active strains in bulk from ordinary environmental samples, so a hidden suppressive field is not the bottleneck.

(3) The right is buyable but captures almost nothing. A US farmer can legally sell an exclusive sampling and commercialisation contract for $200-2,000, since there is no Nagoya-type ABS (access-and-benefit-sharing) regime on US private land. But the contract only stops people sampling that one field. The causal taxa (DAPG Pseudomonas, Streptomyces, Bacillus) recur in neighbouring fields and other regions. Separately, US patent law under Funk Bros v. Kalo (1948), AMP v. Myriad (2013) and USPTO subject-matter eligibility guidance since 2014 treats a naturally occurring isolated strain as an ineligible product of nature, unless it has markedly different characteristics. That leaves formulation, method-of-use claims, strain deposit and trade secret, and none of these come from the field contract. So the bought right is not the asset that realises the step-up.

(4) The step-up on a greenhouse-only hit is small. No public price exists for a greenhouse-validated strain. Deals with disclosed value are field-proven and milestone-heavy (MustGrow-Bayer, about $35-40M over 5-7 years). Against about $1k for the right plus $10-30k of proving cost, a realistic upfront multiple is roughly 3-20x, not 10^3x.

(5) Hard exclusions: it is not mineral, oil, gas or other prospecting, and it aims to own and license the strain rather than sell a service, so it is technically not excluded. However, with weak IP and greenhouse-stage output, the realistic business drifts into contract discovery for majors, which is close to the "sell a service to incumbents" exclusion.
verifiers.killer: The rung that is cheap and discovery-heavy (field contract, then a greenhouse-validated strain) has no capitalised buyer paying a 10^3x premium. Buyers pay for field-proven, formulated, registrable strains, and getting there is the multi-year, up-to-$10M physical/development step, which makes this the geothermal pattern. The bought field right also does not exclude rivals: the causal microbes recur in other soils, and a naturally occurring isolate is a product of nature that is hard to patent in the US. So the right neither holds the value nor can be defended at scale.
sources: Funk Bros. Seed Co. v. Kalo Inoculant Co., 333 U.S. 127 (1948)
Association for Molecular Pathology v. Myriad Genetics, 569 U.S. 576 (2013)

verified.name: DropIn: electrolyte additives for existing Li-ion lines
verified.one_line: Searches computed molecular and electrolyte databases for electrolyte additives (SEI formers, HF scavengers, overcharge shuttles) that drop into existing cell production at under 2 wt%, so there is no bespoke build. It files on the hits, proves them with cheap cell cycling, and licenses to electrolyte makers, who pay at proof because adoption is a recipe change.
verified.unproven_right: Self-filed composition and use provisionals on additive molecules, about $3k each. New-use claims are also possible on old molecules found in scanned 1970s-90s non-English electrochemistry literature.
verified.proving_step: Coin and pouch cells cycled 300-500 cycles at elevated temperature, about $5-20k per candidate, in parallel. Base hit rate for a beneficial additive is roughly 2-5%. ML on redox windows, reduction potentials and SEI chemistry can plausibly lift it 5-10x.
verified.proven_buyer: Electrolyte formulators and cell makers: Capchem, Tinci, Soulbrain, Mitsubishi Chemical, Enchem, CATL. A proven additive that adds 20% cycle life is worth $5-50M as a licence or acquisition.
verified.public_data: Materials Project MPcules/electrolyte genome; PubChem/QM9-type quantum sets; NIST electrolyte data; full text of electrolyte patents; scanned historical journals (Elektrokhimiya, Denki Kagaku) via OCR.
verified.rough_step_up: $3-20k to $5-50M: about 10^3. The physical step really is trivial (blend into an existing line). The ladder: additive IP to own formulation supply to electrolyte manufacturing to cell components.
verified.frame: The candidate's rung is 'additive molecule with a provisional patent and 300-500-cycle coin/pouch data'. Buyers do not purchase that rung. Cell makers and OEMs requalify every additive in their own chemistry and format. Market reports put automotive qualification at 2-4 years and $200k-800k per candidate, covering extended cycling, gas evolution, abuse testing and OEM integration, and say the results do not transfer between cell makers (Mordor Intelligence, repeated by GII). A novel molecule also has to be synthesised at battery-grade purity at scale and supplied reliably. That is a real physical and supply-chain step, not a 'recipe change'. My estimate is that discovery is about 30-40% of the work needed to reach a rung someone actually pays for. The physical step is cheap for a known commodity additive such as VC or FEC. It is not cheap for a new molecule.
verified.step_up: Unproven: a provisional costs about $3k (the candidate's figure). The proving spend brings the cost basis to about $10-25k. Proven at coin-cell level: I found no published price for licensing or acquiring an electrolyte-additive patent. The ORNL-to-Safire licence (5 patents, 2022) and the Ascend-Samsung SDI cross-licence (2022) had confidential terms. My estimate is that an additive proven only in coin or pouch cells licenses for about $50k-500k upfront plus contingent royalties. The candidate's $5-50M figure only applies after customer qualification, 2-4 years later, and after the buyer has paid for that qualification. That makes the immediate step-up roughly 10x (score 2), not 10^3. 10^3 is reachable only after multi-year qualification, which belongs to a different rung.
verified.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate is about 2-5% (the candidate's estimate, consistent with how screening campaigns usually run, but unsourced). Cost per attempt is $5-20k at the coin/pouch stage (candidate figure). By reported market figures it is $200k-800k per candidate at qualification. So the theoretical lever is capped at 20-50x, and ML raising the hit rate 5-10x is plausible. However, the expensive, mostly failing step is customer qualification, not coin cells, and ML does little to cut that cost. At the coin-cell stage the absolute capex is already small (about $0.5-1M per hit at a 2-5% hit rate), so a 10x cut saves little.
verified.data: Most of the data is legible already. Materials Project, the electrolyte genome, QM9 and PubChem are structured, computed databases built specifically for ML screening. Patent full text is searchable. The only illegible slice is scanned Soviet and Japanese literature from the 1970s-90s, which is a niche source. Incumbents already extract this signal. SES AI (NYSE: SES) runs Molecular Universe, sells enterprise subscriptions and has a term sheet for a 90%-owned joint venture with Hisun to supply the materials it discovers. Aionics, a Stanford spinout, screens billions of formulations with ML plus quantum mechanics and now develops formulations itself. Microsoft/PNNL, Chemix and the in-house teams at Tinci, Capchem, LGES and CATL do similar work. No regulator status field records the outcome, so that part passes. Whether an additive works is not public until it is patented or published.
verified.right_bought: The right is not bought from owners who cannot read the data. It is a patent filed first-come, in an extremely crowded field: thousands of additive patents, many from Chinese formulators. New-use claims on old molecules face obviousness and prior-art problems precisely because the molecule is already published. The plan has no arbitrage between an owner who cannot read the data and a buyer who can, which is the core of the Terranox structure.
verified.buyer: The capitalised buyers exist: Tinci, Capchem, Soulbrain, Enchem, Mitsubishi Chemical, CATL and LGES. They buy qualified supply, not coin-cell IP. They usually run additive R&D in-house and take licences cheaply or work around patents with analogue molecules. The economics are not shown to work for both sides at the proof stage.
verified.ladder: The rungs are additive IP, then synthesis and supply of additives, then electrolyte formulation (Tinci and Capchem are multi-billion-dollar companies), then electrolyte manufacturing, then cell components and cells. It is a real ladder, but the rungs are low-margin, commoditised chemicals dominated by Chinese incumbents at scale. Moving up requires chemical plants, so it is not discovery-led. SES AI is already trying to climb this exact ladder.
verified.fatal_flaw: No capitalised buyer pays a step-up at the point of proof. Coin-cell cycling is not the proving step that matters. The value appears only after 2-4 years of customer-specific qualification that costs $200k-800k per candidate, and the buyer controls that step. On top of that, the right is a first-come patent in a crowded field, the data is already legible and mined by SES AI and Aionics, and there is no discounted-right arbitrage.
verified.one_line_reason: The physical step looks trivial, but the real proving step is a multi-year qualification run by the buyer. The right is a contested first-come patent rather than an undervalued asset bought cheaply, and the computed molecular data is already legible and being mined by SES AI, Aionics and the incumbents.

Search budget note: the shared WebSearch budget for this turn was already spent when I started, so every search I tried was refused. I used only WebFetch on known URLs. What follows is what those pages support, plus clearly labelled estimates.

1) Price of the unproven right. A self-filed provisional costs about $3k, plus $5-20k of cycling (candidate's own figures, no independent source). That puts the cost basis at about $10-25k.

2) Price of the proven right. I found no public transaction price for an electrolyte-additive patent or licence at any stage.
- ORNL to Safire (2022): an exclusive licence to 5 patents on an impact-solidifying electrolyte additive. No price or financial terms disclosed (executivegov).
- Ascend and Samsung SDI (Trinohex Ultra, HTCN): settled patent invalidation fights with a non-exclusive licence from Samsung SDI to Ascend. Terms confidential. This matters because the cell maker held the use patent, and a commercial additive supplier had to take a licence from it. Cell makers already own use claims, which blocks newcomers rather than paying them.
- Mitsubishi Chemical to CATL (May 2025): electrolyte patents licensed. No fee disclosed (Mordor).
So the candidate's $5-50M proven value is not backed by any observed price.

3) When value appears and who controls it. Mordor puts automotive additive qualification at 2-4 years and $200k-800k per candidate, run by the cell maker or OEM. Value is realised only after that qualification, which the buyer controls and pays for, not at coin-cell proof. An immediate payment at coin- or pouch-cell proof is plausibly $0-500k upfront (my estimate; no source). That is about 0-20x over the $10-25k cost basis, below the 30x refutation threshold and far from 10^3-10^4.

4) Market size. The whole battery electrolyte additives market is about $1.87B (2025), rising to $3.92B by 2031 (Mordor). Industrially adopted new additive molecules are few: VC, FEC, PS, DTD, LiPO2F2, LiDFOB, HTCN, TMSP and similar entered over roughly two decades (my recollection, not sourced here). That means perhaps 0-3 meaningful new-molecule adoptions a year industry-wide, almost all from incumbent in-house R&D (UBE, MU Ionic, Tinci, Capchem, Samsung SDI). So transactions at the claimed $5-50M per additive are rare to nonexistent, and none were found in public.

5) Is the buyer real? The capitalised buyers exist (Tinci, Capchem, Mitsubishi Chemical/MU Ionic, Soulbrain, Enchem, CATL), but they buy qualified supply and cross-license among themselves. There is no evidence that any of them buys coin-cell-stage IP from outsiders at a step-up.
verifiers.killer: No public price exists for a proven electrolyte-additive right. The only comparable deals (ORNL-Safire, Ascend-Samsung SDI, Mitsubishi-CATL) have confidential terms, and the Ascend case shows the cell maker holding the patent and the supplier paying for it. Value appears only after the buyer runs 2-4 years and $200k-800k of qualification per candidate. So the immediate step-up at coin-cell proof is roughly 0-20x, below the 30x threshold, and the market sees perhaps a handful of such adoptions a year inside a roughly $1.9B segment.

verified.name: Survivor Budwood Co. (citrus greening survivors)

verified.public_data: USDA NAIP 0.6-1m aerial imagery (2005-2024), Sentinel-2 and Landsat NDVI time series per tree crown, Florida DOACS/FDACS grove and citrus tree inventory surveys, UF/IFAS HLB survivor reports (Buckhill grove), NCBI SRA sweet-orange resequencing. Mosaic already had US Navy and NASA agreements, so the material was deployed, not unproven. Baker Hughes' plan was to add its own "modular design" capability to develop and scale the technology. The physical work sat with the buyer, and the value was paid for an operating company.

(2) Svante and BASF on CALF-20. The hydrocarbonengineering.com page now returns 404, so I could not re-check it. From prior knowledge: CALF-20 came out of the Shimizu lab at the University of Calgary and was published in Science in 2021 together with Svante. Svante had raised about $318M (Series E, 2022) before BASF scaled the material to tonnes. This is a case where the discovering party did not capture the step-up at the milligram rung. Svante's filter-and-plant engineering did.

(3) The "unproven right" is not bought. It is a self-filed provisional patent, which is free and first-come, on structures sitting in public databases (CoRE MOF, hMOF, Deem). That fails C4's requirement that the right be bought from owners who cannot read the data. US anticipation does require an enabling disclosure, and hypothetical structures with no synthesis route may not count as prior art. Even so, anyone screening the same public CIF files (CuspAI with about $130M per Fortune, Sept 2025; Meta's OpenDAC; Orbital Materials) can file on the same hits, so the right has no scarcity. University options cost $0-15k (UMich and UNL express licences), but tech-transfer offices are not information-blind about scale-up, and that is where the value sits.

(4) Physical step. The milligram synthesis and isotherm proving step is cheap ($5-15k). What buyers pay for comes after it: kg-to-tonne synthesis, pelletising or shaping into contactors, humid cycling and pilot data. That costs $1-10M+ and takes years, as Svante, BASF and Mosaic all show. This is the geothermal pattern: the bespoke physical and process work dominates the rung that has a paying buyer.

(5) Exclusions. It is not drilling or prospecting. The model is licensing IP to incumbent licensors (UOP, BASF, Linde). Under the "own the asset" rule that is borderline, because it is IP monetised through incumbents rather than an asset whose step-up the company realises itself.

(6) Step-up. I found no public deal showing $5-30M for an unpiloted, milligram-validated sorbent licence. The observed deals are acquisitions of whole companies (Mosaic) or co-development or supply agreements (Svante-BASF), with terms undisclosed. A realistic step-up at the proving rung is about 10-100x, not 10^3x.
verifiers.killer: The right is not bought from an information-blind owner. It is a free, first-come provisional on structures from public, already-mined databases, which better-funded AI players (CuspAI, Meta OpenDAC) can file on just as easily. And the rung a capitalised buyer actually pays for comes after kg-to-tonne scale-up, shaping and pilot cycling, costing $1-10M+ and taking years, as Svante/BASF CALF-20 and Baker Hughes/Mosaic show. That physical step dominates, which is the geothermal counter-example again.

deep.name: Captive Scent (natural odorant discovery from public GC-MS spectra)
deep.memo:
# Captive Scent: feasibility memo

*Method note: the shared WebSearch budget was used up before this run, so I ran no searches. The evidence below comes from direct fetches. These fetches failed: Chemistry World (405), Rutland Herald (429), Pherobase (403), Osmo blog posts (404). Unsourced figures are marked as estimates.*

## Frame of reference
The rung: a novel odorant with a filed patent and odour-panel data, licensed exclusively to a fragrance house. Making 10-100 mg and running a panel is cheap. But a captive earns money only after process scale-up, a RIFM/IFRA/REACH safety dossier and in-base stability testing, and all of that sits on the buyer's side. Osmo's auction only offers buyers "who have the infrastructure to deploy these ingredients broadly" ([Cosmetics Business](https://cosmeticsbusiness.com/osmo-to-auction-ten-ai-developed-fragrance-ingredients)). I estimate discovery is about 50-70% of the value the buyer pays for, not 80%+.

## Step-up ratio
- **Unproven:** about $0 for the asset, plus about $20-50k for filing, synthesis and panel (estimate).
- **Proven:** no public price. Osmo's June 2026 auction of exclusive, perpetual licences to 10 molecules discloses no reserves, bids or fees ([Cosmetics Business](https://cosmeticsbusiness.com/osmo-to-auction-ten-ai-developed-fragrance-ingredients)). Osmo has raised $130M and published no revenue, licensing or customer figures ([Premium Beauty News](https://www.premiumbeautynews.com/en/ai-fragrance-startup-osmo-raises,27048)). My estimate for an unscaled, untox'd licence is $0.1-5M upfront plus royalties.
- **Ratio:** about 5-100x (estimate). The value does not arrive at once, because diligence and sampling come before any bid.
- **Transactions per year:** before 2026 there was essentially no external market. Osmo calls its auction "first-of-its-kind". Houses launch only single digits to low tens of new captives a year (estimate).

## Hit rate and proving capex
- **Today:** about 0.25% of molecules made and tested become commercially interesting. This is Osmo's own January 2026 figure, cited by the scorer; I could not fetch the source to confirm it. Each attempt costs about $10-30k at a CRO (estimate). Time to a captive is about 7-10 years (Osmo blog, cited by the scorer; not refetched).
- **With ML:** Osmo claims a "10x higher success rate" and "5-10x greater cost efficiency" ([Cosmetics Business](https://cosmeticsbusiness.com/osmo-to-auction-ten-ai-developed-fragrance-ingredients)). Avery Gilbert calls that claim undocumented, and notes Osmo got 0 patent grants from 5 applications published in 2025 ([Substack](https://averygilbert.substack.com/p/the-great-and-powerful-osmo)).
- **For this candidate:** the cost per attempt is higher than $10-30k. Electron-impact GC-MS cannot resolve stereochemistry, and stereochemistry drives musk, amber and sandalwood odour. So each peak needs isolation or several stereoisomer syntheses (estimate: 3-5x the cost).

## Data source
- **Datasets:** MassBank, GNPS (an "open-access knowledge base" with 1000+ public datasets; analysis needs a login, [GNPS](https://gnps.ucsd.edu/ProteoSAFe/static/gnps-splash.jsp)), Pherobase, NIST/Wiley libraries (licensed, not public), and scanned Flavour & Fragrance Journal and Perfumer & Flavorist chromatograms.
- **Why illegible:** scanned figures, peaks that were never assigned, and spectra scattered across decades of journals.
- **Is the outcome summarised?** Yes, largely. GC-olfactometry (GC-O) and AEDA papers record an odour descriptor and potency for each retention index, including for unknown peaks. Flavornet publishes structured columns for "Odorant, Odor, Kovats RI" on four GC phases ([Flavornet](https://www.flavornet.org/h_kovats.html)). This is the same failure seen in earlier hunts: the answer is already written into a legible field.

## How the right is bought
It isn't bought. The IP is filed first-come, and nobody holds an unreadable asset that we could buy at a discount.

The filed right is also weak. Under USPTO guidance, a product of nature is ineligible unless it has "markedly different characteristics", and "if there is no change in any characteristic, the claimed product lacks markedly different characteristics" ([MPEP 2106.04(c)](https://www.uspto.gov/web/offices/pac/mpep/s2106.html)). The spectrum it was found in may also be prior art. That leaves use or process claims, and a competitor can make the nature-identical molecule by another route. The one purchasable variant, lapsed patent families, is public domain and carries no step-up.

## Capitalised buyer
Givaudan, dsm-firmenich, IFF and Symrise, plus chemical makers. The class is real and rich. Ambroxide alone is sold under three house brands: Ambrox (Firmenich), Ambrofix (Givaudan) and Ambroxan (Kao) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambroxide)).

But the houses build captives in-house, and the Ambrox example shows a nature-identical molecule ends up in several houses' hands. Exclusivity fails exactly where this candidate would operate.

## Integration ladder above
1. Molecule licence
2. Biocatalytic or chemical manufacture (e.g. the patented homofarnesol route to ambrox, [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambroxide))
3. Ingredient supply
4. Ingredients house
5. Finished fragrance

The flavour and fragrance market is about $30B a year (estimate, unsourced). That supports a large company but not a trillion-dollar chain.

## Who else does this
- **Osmo:** $130M raised. Files 50-250 synthetic molecules per patent ([Premium Beauty News](https://www.premiumbeautynews.com/en/ai-fragrance-startup-osmo-raises,27048)), and is auctioning captives.
- **Fragrance houses:** they run headspace and GC-O programmes, such as Givaudan ScentTrek, and their own AI tools, such as Givaudan Carto and Symrise with IBM's Philyra (from my own knowledge; not refetched).

ML for natural odorants is not an empty niche. And synthetic scaffolds avoid the product-of-nature problem completely.

## Smallest feasibility test (2 weeks)
Two tests. Either failing kills the idea.
1. **IP test (about $5k of patent-counsel time):** take 3 candidate unassigned natural peaks and get a written opinion on whether the US and EPO would grant composition or use claims on a molecule that occurs in nature and appears in a published spectrum. If the answer is "use/process only", stop.
2. **Price test (no cost):** ask 5 house or chemical-maker business-development leads, plus Osmo auction participants, what they would pay upfront for an exclusive licence to an untox'd, unscaled odorant with panel data and use-only claims. If the median is under $1M (under about 30x the proving cost), stop.

A side check: sample 50 "unknown" peaks from GC-O papers and see how many already carry an odour descriptor and potency. If more than 50% do, the data edge is gone.

## Verdict
**Not feasible. Score about 9-10 of 25 (C1 2, C2 2, C3 3, C4 0-1, C5 2).**
- The hit-rate lever is real (0.25% base rate, per Osmo), and a capitalised buyer class exists.
- The right fails twice. It is filed rather than bought, and natural molecules face product-of-nature and anticipation barriers ([MPEP 2106.04(c)](https://www.uspto.gov/web/offices/pac/mpep/s2106.html)).
- The step-up is unsourced and probably 10-100x. The outcome data is already legible in GC-O literature and Flavornet. Osmo already holds the ML-discovery rung with patentable synthetic scaffolds.

Do not use this for the YC memo.

deep.memo:
# Enzyme Claims from Metagenomes — feasibility memo

*Method note: WebSearch budget for this workflow turn was exhausted, so all evidence below comes from direct WebFetch of primary sources. Failed fetches noted at the end. Every figure is sourced or marked (est).*

## Frame of reference
Proposed rung: "a wild-type metagenomic sequence that catalyses one named API step, proven in a plate assay," sold or licensed as enzyme-in-process IP. The rung fails the discreteness test for a sourced reason. EPA's official write-up of the 2010 award for the sitagliptin route — the exact precedent the pitch invokes — states that "Merck's tests of available transaminases found none with detectable activity on the sitagliptin ketone," and that the usable catalyst was produced by evolving an enzyme with "only slight activity on a smaller methyl ketone analog" to a "compounded improvement in biocatalytic activity of over 25,000-fold" ([EPA](https://www.epa.gov/greenchemistry/presidential-green-chemistry-challenge-2010-greener-reaction-conditions-award)). On the best-documented case, the discovery rung yielded **zero** sellable hits; value was manufactured by the engineering step the pitch treats as trivial. Discovery is plausibly 15–30% of the work to a sellable asset (est).

## Step-up ratio
**Unproven price: $0, structurally.** MGnify, JGI IMG/M and UniProt sequences are free downloads with no seller, so there is no asset basis to re-price — only the candidate's own proving spend (~$20–50k, which checks out: ~$100–300 per 1 kb gene at $0.07–0.15/bp, 50 genes plus expression and assay ≈ $15–40k) (est).

**Proven price — now sourced, and it prices the wrong thing.** Codexis's FY2019 10-K gives the only public comparables for enzyme-value transactions with the named buyers ([10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1200375/000120037520000008/cdxs-20191231.htm)):
- GSK (2014): contingent payments of **$5.75M–$38.5M per project** plus royalties on a limited product set; a **$2.0M** milestone recognised in Sept 2019.
- Merck (2015): up to **$15.0M per API** Merck manufactures using a CodeEvolver-developed enzyme, over a 10-year window.
- Novartis (2019): up to **$14.0M** through ~March 2021 ($5.0M near signing, $4.0M and $5.0M on two technology-transfer milestones), plus **$8.0M** of annual payments over the Improvements Term, plus termination fees of $9.0M/$5.0M.

These are the figures the pitch's "$5–30M licence" is reaching for, and they are real — but every one is payment for **transfer of a protein-engineering platform and its improvements**, not for a discovered sequence. Note the structure: money is staged against technology transfer and per-API manufacture, i.e. against the engineering and scale-up work. No public comparable exists for a one-time purchase of an unproven, assay-stage enzyme-use family; absence of such a comparable, after targeted SEC full-text search, is the finding. Realistic hit-stage consideration is an option/research licence of the same order as the proving spend — **roughly 1–10x, received years later and contingent on someone else finishing the work** (est). Transactions/yr at the rung on offer: effectively zero; at the platform rung, a handful ever (three named pharma licences in ~5 years, per the 10-K).

## Hit rate and proving capex, today and with ML
Base hit rate on the *valuable* substrates is sourced at approximately zero: "none with detectable activity" (EPA, above). A reranking model cannot surface a hit that is absent from the search space, so the C3 lever inverts — ML helps only on easy substrates, which carry no $10M+ licence. Proving capex is also already a catalogue product: Codexis sells Codex biocatalyst panels and kits and "Tailored Enzymes," with in-house manufacturing "dedicated to producing both Codex biocatalyst panels and kits" (10-K), and its CodeEvolver ML is trained on 20+ years of its own private assay data. The moat in this field is proprietary sequence-function data, the opposite of a public-data play.

## Data source
MGnify (ebi.ac.uk/metagenomics), JGI IMG/M, UniProt, AlphaFold DB — free, open, maximally legible FASTA/PDB, already clustered and embedded in every competitor's pipeline. No OCR, no scanned archive. The one genuine plus: the **outcome** is not written into any legible field — EC/GO annotations are homology-transferred and silent on non-natural substrates, corroborated by Merck having had to run the tests to find out (EPA). Outcome-illegibility is high; data-illegibility is zero.

## How the right is bought
It isn't. Under *Myriad*, an isolated naturally occurring DNA segment is not patent-eligible, leaving only a narrow method/use claim on a sequence every competitor can download the same day ([Myriad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_Molecular_Pathology_v._Myriad_Genetics,_Inc.)). The purchasable variant — proprietary sampled biodiversity — now carries ABS obligations (prior informed consent, mutually agreed terms, "utilization" covering R&D and commercialisation, [CBD](https://www.cbd.int/abs/about)) and, for sequence data, the Cali Fund benefit-sharing mechanism adopted at COP-16 ([CBD DSI](https://www.cbd.int/dsi-gr)) — a diffuse non-exclusive payment obligation instead of exclusivity. Lapsed patent families are public domain: you buy the file, not the exclusion right.

## Capitalised buyer
Real and concentrated: Merck was 28% and Novartis 23% of Codexis's FY2019 revenue (10-K). But they buy at the platform/per-API rung (above), are the incumbent readers of the same literature, and for marketed products the route is frozen at filing, pushing adoption to pre-filing NCEs and generics.

## Integration ladder above
Hit → engineered variants → enzyme supply → step-as-a-service → owning API manufacture. Genuinely real, but the public exemplar of a fully climbed ladder is Codexis at **$68.5M revenue (FY2019)** and ~165 employees ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codexis), carries a paid-editing/NPOV warning), with net losses of $11.9M (2019) and $10.9M (2018) (10-K). Weak evidence for a trillion-dollar path; each rung also needs a new capability (evolution platform, cGMP fermentation, DMFs), not just capital.

## Who else does this
Codexis (incumbent vendor to the exact named buyers, ML on 20 years of private data). Basecamp Research: "over 100 billion novel genes… across all seven continents," >100T-token dataset, **$140M Series C** at a reported **~$800M** valuation with Nvidia and Anthropic backing ([basecamp-research.com](https://www.basecamp-research.com/)) — the best-capitalised entrant spent the money collecting *proprietary* samples, which is direct evidence that public metagenomes are not a moat (its stated focus is now therapeutics, not industrial enzymes). Plus Ginkgo, Arzeda, Cradle, Enzymit and in-house pharma biocatalysis groups (unverified this session).

## Smallest feasibility test
Two weeks, no lab: pick 3 named high-value non-natural API steps; for each, search the public databases for any wild-type with *published* measured activity on that substrate class, then try to obtain a written indication of consideration from one CDMO or pharma process group for an exclusive use licence on an assay-stage wild-type hit, with no engineering and no scale data. If no buyer will name a number above ~$250k, C2 is settled at 1 and the thesis is dead. This also costs nothing and tests the only load-bearing unknown.

## Verdict
**Fail — consistent with the three refuting verifiers (≈8–9/25).** The sourced comparables price platform transfer and per-API manufacture, not discovery; the sourced precedent says the wild-type hit does not exist in nature for the substrates worth money; the data is free and legible; and there is no unproven right to buy from an owner who cannot read it. This is the counter-example pattern — finding the candidate is the cheap part, building the bespoke thing is the business.

*Failed fetches: businesswire Merck/CodeEvolver release (403), ir.codexis.com news pages (404), ebi.ac.uk/metagenomics (title only). WebSearch unavailable (turn budget exhausted), so no broker/landscape survey was possible.*

# FreeMag: feasibility deep-dive (rare-earth-free magnet compositions)

*Method note: the shared WebSearch budget for this turn ran out before any search ran. The evidence below comes from direct WebFetch of primary pages plus the finalist's cited sources. Any figure without a URL is marked as an estimate.*

## Frame of reference
FreeMag's rung would be a lab-proven composition (arc-melt, XRD, VSM) plus a provisional patent, sold as a licence. Inside that rung, discovery is maybe 80% of the work. No buyer pays for that rung, though. Buyers pay for a bulk-processable magnet with usable coercivity, (BH)max and temperature stability.
- **Niron:** its iron nitride came out of the University of Minnesota and was "scaled over the last 13 years" before it reached a plant ([Niron](https://nironmagnetics.com/niron-magnetics-receives-conditional-150-million-department-of-war-commitment/)).
- **Ames L10-FeNi:** it reports no measured coercivity. Its next steps are still "optimize… chemistry, microstructure, compaction" and scale to 10–100 g ([Ames CMI](https://www.ameslab.gov/cmi/research-highlights/high-performance-critical-element-free-permanent-magnets)).
- **Ames MnBi:** its R&D 100 award credits the result to the preparation and fabrication process ([Ames](https://www.ameslab.gov/news/ames-lab-technology-wins-r-d-100-award)).

In the rung that has a buyer, discovery is about 10–20% of the work (estimate). This is the geothermal counter-example: the physical step is the hard part.

## Step-up ratio
- **Unproven:** a self-filed provisional at about $3k, or a $10–50k option on DOE lab IP. Both are the candidate's estimates and are unverified.
- **Lab-proven:** I found no public deal for a lab-scale magnet composition. MatNex has announced an AI-designed rare-earth-free magnet since June 2024 and still lists no licence, customer or manufacturing partner ([MatNex news](https://matnex.ai/news)). My estimate is a $0–1M option or sponsored-research deal, which is 0–300x and probably under 30x at the median.
- **Proven at scale:** the large money goes to manufacturers.
  - Niron raised $21.3M in equity in 2021 ([BusinessWire](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20210729005344/en/Niron-Magnetics-Raises-21.3M-to-Commercialize-Rare-Earth-Free-Magnets-for-a-More-Sustainable-Electric-Economy)), $33M in 2023 (reported by earlier scorers, no URL) and $25M in 2024 ([Fastmarkets](https://fastmarkets.com/insights/niron-magnetics-gets-25-million-to-develop-rare-earth-free-magnet)).
  - It also has a conditional OSC loan of up to $150M for a 1,500 t/yr plant opening in 2027 ([Niron](https://nironmagnetics.com/niron-magnetics-receives-conditional-150-million-department-of-war-commitment/)).
- **Transactions per year:** zero lab-composition licences were observed. Manufacturer financings run at a handful per year (estimate).
- **Score: C2 = 1–2.**

## Hit rate and proving capex, today and with ML
- **Base hit rate:** there is no measured experimental rate. ML/DFT funnels are extremely selective. One 2026 APS abstract on Fe-Co-S went from more than 300,000 structures to 1,418, then to 3 (about 0.001%), with none synthesized ([APS](https://meetings-archive.aps.org/smt/2026/mar-m46/8/), which returned 403 on re-fetch; the figures come from the earlier scorer).
- **Proving cost:** about $2–5k and one week per composition (candidate's estimate, plausible).
- **Capex today vs with ML:** 100 attempts cost about $300–500k (estimate). A 10x lift in hit rate therefore saves only a few hundred thousand dollars.
- **The real failure point** is extrinsic coercivity at bulk scale. ML trained on intrinsic DFT properties does not predict it.
- **Score: C3 = 2.**

## Data source
- **Named datasets:** OQMD, Materials Project, AFLOW, Novamag, scanned NIST/Ames alloy reports, and expired patents.
- **Access:** structured and API-accessible (estimate). Materials Project exposes computed magnetic ordering and collinear moments. Its methodology page does not list anisotropy as a field ([MP docs](https://docs.materialsproject.org/methodology/materials-methodology/magnetic-properties)). That leaves a small gap where computed anisotropy is not yet a legible field.
- **Already screened by:** Fraunhofer MagnetPredictor ([IWM](https://iwm.fraunhofer.de/en/press/press-releases/03_09_18_magnetpredictorpredictingthemagneticpropertiesofmateria.html)), Ames CMI, MatNex's magnetic MACE potentials ([MatNex](https://matnex.ai/news)), and GNoME- and MatterGen-class generative models.
- **Is it illegible?** Mostly no. The only illegible part is scanned historical reports, a thin layer.
- **Is the outcome summarised anywhere?** Coercivity is not summarised anywhere, but it is a processing outcome, not a data-extraction outcome.
- **Score: C4 = 1.**

## How the right is bought
- **Provisional:** first-to-file at about $3k (estimate). Published DFT entries create prior art that weakens composition claims.
- **DOE lab IP (Ames, ORNL):** licensed by sophisticated tech-transfer offices, so there is no information arbitrage.
- **Expired patents:** these are in the public domain and cannot be optioned.
- **Conclusion:** no owner exists who cannot read the data and would sell cheaply.

## Capitalised buyer
The buyers are real and well capitalised: Samsung, Magna, Allison ([BusinessWire](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20240220199737/en/Niron-Magnetics-Secures-Funding-from-Samsung-Ventures-Allison-Transmission-and-Magna-to-Accelerate-Production-of-Rare-Earth-Free-Magnets)), GM, Honda and DoD/OSC. They fund manufacturing scale-up. None was observed buying arc-melted buttons.

## Integration ladder above
1. Bulk processing (powder, alignment, sintering or bonding)
2. Magnet manufacturing (Niron's Sartell plant, then a planned 10,000 t/yr plant breaking ground in 2028 ([Niron](https://nironmagnetics.com/niron-magnetics-receives-conditional-150-million-department-of-war-commitment/)))
3. Motor and actuator supply
4. The EV and defence magnet market, worth tens of billions of dollars (estimate)

The ladder is real. But rung 1, the expensive and decades-long one, is exactly where the bottom rung gives no head start. **Score: C5 = 3.**

## Who else does this
- **MatNex (Cambridge, UK):** the same model of designing and owning magnet IP, then licensing it. It raised a £2M seed in 2023 and announced an AI magnet in 2024 ([MatNex](https://matnex.ai/news)).
- **Niron:** iron nitride, as a manufacturer.
- **Ames CMI:** MnBi and L10-FeNi.
- **Fraunhofer IWM**, plus big-lab generative models.

## Smallest feasibility test (2 weeks)
The question is whether anyone pays for the bottom rung at all.
1. Email 10 licensing or business-development leads, at Niron, Proterial, VAC, MP Materials, GM, Toyota, Magna, Bosch, Ames TTO and MatNex (as a comparable).
2. Pose one concrete hypothetical: "a new Fe/Mn-based phase with Ku ≥ 1 MJ/m³ and Tc ≥ 600 K (both estimates), arc-melt verified at gram scale, with Hc and (BH)max measured on a button. What would you pay for an exclusive option?"
3. **Decision rule:** two or more term-sheet-level answers at $1M or more, without bulk data, keep the idea alive. Answers that amount to "come back with bulk (BH)max at kg scale" kill it.

Separately, ask MatNex or ex-MatNex staff whether their 2024 magnet ever drew a paid option. This needs no lab spend.

## Verdict
**Fails the rubric.** Scores: C1 = 1, C2 = 1–2, C3 = 2, C4 = 1, C5 = 3, for a total of about 8–9 out of 25.

The rung where discovery dominates has no buyer. The rung with a buyer is dominated by processing and plant capital: 13 years plus about $150M of debt for Niron, and Ames still at gram scale. The input data is already structured and heavily screened, and the right is first-to-file, not bought from owners who cannot read the data. MatNex has run this exact model since 2023 and shows no disclosed licence.

I would not use this as the Terranox-analog in the YC memo, except as a second counter-example alongside geothermal.
